title: [RFC][SpecDecode] Move MTP completeness validation to the weight-update transaction boundary
body:
## Summary

Several vLLM MTP implementations perform checkpoint completeness validation inside
`model.load_weights()`. This assumes that one invocation receives a complete MTP
checkpoint. RL weight transfer does not have that property: IPC/NCCL may split one
logical update into multiple transport buckets and invoke `load_weights()` once per
bucket.

The result is a false missing-layer or missing-parameter error on the first partial
bucket, even when the complete update contains every required weight.

This RFC separates two concerns:

1. immediate validation of each received item (name, shape, shard mapping,
   divisibility, dtype/quantization metadata), which should remain in
   `load_weights()`;
2. completeness validation of a logical checkpoint/update, which must run once at
   the transaction boundary after all buckets have been accounted for.

## Affected MTP loaders

The current checks use three different notions of completeness:

- **MTP layer coverage:** DeepSeek, DeepSeek V3.2/GLM-5.2, DeepSeek V4,
  MiniMax M3, and Bailing infer loaded MTP layer IDs from successfully loaded
  parameters and require every configured MTP layer to appear.
- **Exact parameter coverage:** Step3.5 compares the required parameter set (minus
  explicitly optional scales) with the set returned by the loader.
- **Required parameter subset:** Inkling checks a model-specific required subset.

These differences reflect checkpoint mappings, not a need for three validation
lifecycle implementations. The validation boundary and set-difference algorithm can
be unified once each model provides canonical expected weight IDs.

## Current behavior

### Initial model loading

The default loader calls `model.load_weights(...)` for the startup checkpoint and,
when supported, compares the returned loaded parameter set with the model parameters
expected on the local rank.

This generic startup check is intentionally relaxed for quantized and online-
quantized models because checkpoint keys do not always have a one-to-one relationship
with runtime parameters. Examples include fused parameters, TP/PP/EP shards,
shared/tied parameters, optional scales, and parameters created or replaced by
quantization.

MTP loaders additionally run their model-specific completeness checks during startup.
Because startup normally supplies the complete checkpoint stream to one logical load,
those checks are valid at that boundary.

### RL IPC/NCCL updates

The checkpoint-format RL update flow is:

```text
start_weight_update()
  -> update_weights(bucket 0)
  -> update_weights(bucket 1)
  -> ...
  -> finish_weight_update()
```

Each bucket is passed to `model.load_weights()` independently. The transfer engines
currently discard the returned loaded set and do not aggregate it into an
expected-vs-loaded check for the complete update. Main-model parameters therefore
retain their immediate per-item loader checks, but do not currently receive a generic
aggregate completeness check at the end of an RL update.

The MTP checks are different only because they currently try to enforce complete
checkpoint coverage inside every individual `load_weights()` call. That causes the
false failures described by this issue.

## Short-term fix

The minimal fix is tracked in
[#49175](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49175) (development PR:
[aoshen02/vllm#4](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/4)).

IPC and NCCL wrap only their incremental `model.load_weights()` calls in a scoped MTP
completeness-suppression context. The scope is automatically restored on success or
exception. It does not mutate every model submodule, and `start_weight_update()` /
`finish_weight_update()` do not manage a persistent flag.

This preserves:

- normal startup MTP completeness validation;
- parameter name, shape, shard mapping, divisibility, dtype, and quantization checks;
- layerwise reload initialization/finalization.

It intentionally does **not** claim that RL updates now have aggregate completeness
validation. It only removes the incorrect per-bucket assertion until the transaction-
level solution lands.

## Target architecture

After the `WeightLoadSession` lifecycle refactor in
[#48908](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48908) lands, both startup loading
and checkpoint-format RL reloads should use the same logical transaction:

```text
session.prepare()
  -> load one complete startup stream, or load multiple RL buckets
  -> record canonical IDs for successfully mapped local weights
session.finish()
  -> finalize model-specific loading
  -> validate expected_ids - loaded_ids
```

The session should provide generic accounting and validation APIs conceptually like:

```python
session.record_loaded_items(owner=self, loaded_items=canonical_ids)
session.register_validator(owner=self, validator=self.validate_completeness)
```

For an RL update, `record_loaded_items()` unions IDs across all IPC/NCCL buckets.
For startup, the same mechanism usually records one complete stream. In both cases,
the validator runs exactly once from `finish()`.

### Canonical weight manifest

The unified check should operate at canonical weight/parameter-ID granularity, not
only at MTP-layer granularity and not directly on raw checkpoint names. A manifest
must account for:

- fused parameters and individual fused shards;
- TP/PP/EP local ownership;
- shared/tied parameters;
- optional and format-specific scales;
- quantization mappings and generated/replaced parameters;
- checkpoint aliases such as shared MTP head/embedding weights;
- model/platform-specific post-load finalization.

Therefore `set(model.named_parameters())` is not a sufficient universal expected
manifest. Models/loaders define the manifest and canonicalization rules; the session
owns the lifecycle, aggregation, and common `expected_ids - loaded_ids` algorithm.

Example canonical IDs may distinguish whole parameters and fused shards:

```text
("parameter", "model.layers.61.mtp_block.fc.weight")
("parameter_shard", "model.layers.61.qkv_proj", "q")
("shared_parameter", "embed_tokens.weight")
```

## Follow-up PR plan

1. **Stop per-bucket MTP completeness failures.** Keep the short-term scoped
   suppression small and restricted to incremental IPC/NCCL `load_weights()` calls.
2. **Land the shared load lifecycle.** Complete #48908 so startup and RL reloads have
   a common `prepare() -> load -> finish()` transaction boundary. This PR should not
   attempt to define every model's required-weight manifest.
3. **Add generic session accounting.** Record canonical loaded IDs across one or many
   load calls, register validators, define cleanup/error semantics, and validate once
   at `finish()`.
4. **Migrate MTP loaders.** Replace layer-level, exact-parameter, and required-subset
   lifecycle code with model manifests plus the generic validator. Remove the
   temporary suppression context after all affected MTP loaders are migrated.
5. **Extend aggregate validation to main-model RL updates.** Reuse the same session
   accounting and model manifests so startup and RL have equivalent transaction-level
   completeness guarantees where the checkpoint format supports them. Preserve
   explicit relaxations for quantized/online-quantized and non-one-to-one formats.
6. **Harden checkpoint canonicalization.** Treat silently skipped or mis-normalized
   keys as a separate loader correctness class. For example, #43456 is not fixed by
   moving the validation boundary: missing DeepSeek V4 top-level head/embed aliases
   require key normalization and parameter-level accounting.

## Required tests

- complete single-stream startup loading succeeds and validates once;
- incomplete startup loading fails at `finish()`;
- complete multi-bucket RL loading succeeds after aggregation;
- a genuinely missing aggregate MTP or main-model weight fails at `finish()`;
- per-item name/shape/mapping errors still fail immediately;
- duplicate canonical IDs and fused-shard accounting behave deterministically;
- optional/shared/quantized parameters follow the model manifest;
- failed or cancelled updates clean up the session and cannot leak suppression state;
- IPC packed/non-packed and NCCL packed/non-packed paths use identical semantics.

## Non-goals of the short-term fix

- It does not solve silently ignored or incorrectly normalized checkpoint keys.
- It does not make layer-level coverage equivalent to parameter-level completeness.
- It does not add aggregate main-model validation to current RL updates.
- It does not make #48908 itself a completeness checker; accounting and manifests are
  explicit follow-up work.

AI assistance was used to investigate the loader behavior and prepare this RFC.

title: [Bugfix] Recover DSML tool calls when the start wrapper token is missing
body:
## What this fixes

1. At long context, DeepSeek V4 and V3.2 sometimes skip the opening `<｜DSML｜tool_calls>` wrapper but still write a valid `<｜DSML｜invoke ...>` block.
2. The parser only enters tool mode on the wrapper, so the whole tool call leaks to the user as raw text and no tool call is made.

FIX #48931

## The fix

1. New state table entry: a complete invoke marker seen in plain content now starts a tool call. Purely additive; when the wrapper is present nothing changes.
2. New FOREIGN_BLOCK state: each parser passes the other DeepSeek dialect's wrapper through as plain text, so V4 never parses V3.2 blocks and vice versa. A real tool call that starts inside an unclosed foreign wrapper is still parsed.
3. Guard against false matches: a recovered call is held until its name completes, then accepted only if the request declared that exact tool. If it fails, the text is released unchanged as content.
4. The hold gives up as soon as the text can no longer become a declared tool name, so streaming is never stalled and a genuine tool call that follows quoted prose is still parsed.
5. Recovery is skipped entirely when the request declares no tools, or when `tool_choice` is `none`. The declared names are refreshed on every request, so nothing carries over on a reused engine.
6. Text written after a recovered call is returned as content rather than dropped. Padding straight after a call is held back first, so spacing before a following call is still ignored, matching what the normal wrapped path already does.

## Limitations

1. Prose containing the exact marker with a real declared tool name, correctly formed, is still read as a tool call. The marker is ordinary text with no dedicated token, so nothing text based can distinguish it from a real call whose wrapper was dropped. Limiting recovery to declared names narrows this but cannot close it.
2. Recovery only applies in content, not inside reasoning text. A model that drops both the end of reasoning marker and the wrapper is not covered.
3. A response cut off mid name flushes back to text; cut off mid arguments closes with partial arguments, same as today.
4. The other dialect's wrapper markers now appear in content. Where a tokenizer treats them as special tokens they used to be removed. Suppressing them would change content the parser otherwise returns untouched.
5. Verified at parser level only. No serving run against a real DeepSeek V4 model, since that needs a GPU.
6. Brought up to date with main using a merge commit rather than a rebase, because the commits were already published. Say the word if you want it rebased before it lands.

## Testing

1. 137 tests across the two DeepSeek engine test files, 99 for V4 and 38 for V3.2, covering both streaming and non streaming: the recovery itself, name validation, quoted marker cases, `tool_choice` set to `none`, a declared tool name that is not ASCII, an unclosed foreign wrapper, text kept after a recovered call, and state not carrying between requests.
2. Fail then pass shown for every commit, and every behavior change was checked by removing it and confirming a test fails.
3. Full run of the parser engine and DeepSeek tool parser suites: 3855 passed, 0 failed. Lint clean on all changed files.
4. AI assistance was used for this change (Claude Code).

title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] DSpark: build draft under its own model/quant config (NVFP4 target corrupts MXFP4 draft experts)
body:
## Purpose

Fix silent numerical corruption of the DSpark drafter when the target model is quantized differently from the draft checkpoint — most visibly, a modelopt-NVFP4 DeepSeek-V4 target (`nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-{Flash,Pro}-NVFP4`) paired with the official DSpark drafter (`deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-{Flash,Pro}-DSpark`, natively MXFP4 experts).

**Symptom**: with an NVFP4 target, acceptance length collapses — DeepSeek-V4-Pro drops to exactly **AL = 1.0** (the drafter proposes token id 0 at every position; zero drafts accepted over 80k+ steps), DeepSeek-V4-Flash drops to **2.57** vs 3.55 with the FP8 target. No error or warning is emitted anywhere.

## Root cause (two layers)

1. **Draft `quantization` resolves to plain `fp8` instead of `deepseek_v4_fp8`.** `SpeculativeConfig.hf_config_override` rewrites the draft `hf_config.model_type` from `deepseek_v4` to `deepseek_mtp` (for MTP arch resolution) *before* `ModelConfig._verify_quantization` runs, so `DeepseekV4FP8Config.override_quantization_method` (which requires `model_type == "deepseek_v4"`) never matches. The DSpark branch later restores `model_type = "deepseek_v4"`, but `quantization` is already frozen at `"fp8"`.

2. **The draft is built under the target's config context.** `load_dspark_model` constructs the draft with the target's `vllm_config`, so the draft modules reuse the **target's `quant_config` instance**, and `DeepseekV4FP8Config.expert_dtype` / `moe_quant_algo` resolve lazily from `get_current_vllm_config().model_config.hf_config` (the *target's*) and are memoized. With an NVFP4-experts target (`moe_quant_algo: "NVFP4"`), the draft's MXFP4 experts are constructed with `ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE`. The ue8m0 scales load into e4m3 scale buffers with matching shapes, so **weight loading succeeds silently** and the draft MoE computes garbage.

Diagnostic tell in the logs: with an FP8 target the draft build prints `Using 'FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8' Mxfp4 MoE backend`; with an NVFP4 target that line never appears, and instrumentation shows the draft's `routed_experts` quant method is `ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE` and its greedy draft output degenerates to constant token id 0 (Pro).

## Fix (2 files, +20 lines)

- `vllm/config/speculative.py`: after the DSpark branch restores `model_type = "deepseek_v4"`, restore the draft quantization to `deepseek_v4_fp8` so expert-dtype-aware MoE dispatch applies to the draft.
- `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/utils.py`: build the draft under its own `model_config` and a freshly derived `quant_config` (`VllmConfig.get_quantization_config(draft_model_config, load_config)`) instead of inheriting the target's.

Both parts are required: (2) alone regresses FP8 targets (draft would resolve plain `Fp8Config` → `KeyError: ...w13_weight_scale` at load), which is exactly what (1) prevents. Non-DeepSeek DSpark drafters (Qwen3/Gemma4 `*DSparkModel` architectures) are unaffected by (1); (2) is strictly more correct for them (an unquantized drafter no longer inherits a quantized target's quant config).

## Test Plan

Hardware: 1× node, 8× B300 (TP8/EP8), fp8 KV cache, greedy (temp 0), `num_speculative_tokens=5` (`dspark_block_size=5`).

```
--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}'
```

Ran MT-Bench (80 prompts × 2 turns, 1024 output tokens) through an `AsyncLLM` acceptance-length harness, plus smoke runs with this exact patch verifying (a) the draft experts get `Mxfp4MoEMethod` / `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8`, (b) FP8-target no-regression, (c) healthy acceptance histograms.

## Model evaluation results

MT-Bench average acceptance length (higher is better):

| Target | Draft | AL before | AL after |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash (FP8) | Flash-DSpark | 3.554 | 3.554 (unchanged) |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4 | Flash-DSpark | 2.572 | **3.577** |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro-DSpark (FP8, self) | Pro-DSpark | 3.525 | 3.525 (unchanged) |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro-NVFP4 | Pro-DSpark | **1.000** | **3.492** |

Per-position conditional acceptance rates for the NVFP4 targets recover to parity with FP8 (≈0.70–0.79 at positions 2–6). Generated text quality is unaffected (target-side verification is unchanged; this only fixes the drafter).

## Duplicate-work check

Searched open PRs/issues for `dspark`, `dspark quantization`, `dspark nvfp4`: no open PR addresses draft quant-config resolution. Closest issue (#47934, DSpark + FP4 target launch failure on GLM 5.2) had its content removed and is likely a different path (GLM DSpark drafters don't take the deepseek_v4 branch), though (2) may also help such cases.

## AI assistance disclosure

This bug was root-caused, fixed, and validated with AI assistance (Claude Code). The submitter reproduced the issue, reviewed every changed line, and ran all validation jobs end-to-end on 8×B300 hardware.

title: [Bugfix][Kernel] Fix persistent top-k histogram reuse after short rows
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Purpose

Fix a correctness bug in `persistent_topk` when one persistent CTA group
processes a radix row (`seq_len > 32768`), followed by a short or medium row
(`seq_len <= 32768`), and then another radix row.

The kernel previously used the outer row iteration counter to rotate its
triple-buffered radix histograms. Short rows advanced that counter without
executing `radix_topk`, causing the next radix row to reuse a histogram that
could still contain counts from an earlier row.

This PR introduces a separate `radix_iter` counter that advances only when
`radix_topk` executes. It also adds a CUDA regression test that constructs the
long-short-long scheduling pattern in one persistent CTA group.

Related to #41748, which addresses workspace initialization between kernel
launches. This PR fixes histogram-ring misalignment within a single launch.

## Test Plan

- Compare the long-short-long case against `torch.topk`.
- Run a consecutive-radix case as a control.
- Repeat both cases ten times on an RTX 3080.
- Exercise the adaptive CTA-group layout used by the regression test.
- Run the checked-in regression test in CI:

```bash
python -m pytest \
  tests/kernels/test_top_k_per_row.py::test_persistent_topk_reused_group_after_short_row \
  -v
```

- Run static checks:

```bash
python -m py_compile tests/kernels/test_top_k_per_row.py
ruff check tests/kernels/test_top_k_per_row.py
git diff --check origin/main...HEAD
git clang-format --diff origin/main -- \
  csrc/libtorch_stable/persistent_topk.cuh
```

## Test Result

RTX 3080 results before the fix:

```text
middle_len=32768: match=False, set_diff=8
middle_len=32769: match=True,  set_diff=0
```

Results after rebuilding the production `topk.cu` with the fix:

```text
middle_len=32768: failures=0/10
middle_len=32769: failures=0/10
```

Adaptive regression layout:

```text
ctas_per_group=7, num_groups=9, rows=(0, 9, 18)
set_diff=0
```

Python compilation, Ruff, `git diff --check`, and clang-format checks passed.

The complete `_C_stable_libtorch` extension and checked-in pytest were not run
locally; they are left for CI. Local GPU validation compiled the production
`topk.cu` and modified `persistent_topk.cuh` for SM86.

No documentation update is required because this is an internal kernel
correctness fix with no public API or configuration changes.

AI assistance disclosure: OpenAI Codex was used for source analysis,
implementation, regression-test construction, and validation. I reviewed and
understand all submitted changes.

title: [KV-offload][FS] : Batch store/load_block in C
body: ## Purpose We have pools of python threads to read and write KV files from/to disk. These python threads compete for the GIL and submit bursty read/write commands to the disk. This prevents the disk from reaching 100% utilization. ### Changes: 1. Add C implementations for store_block and load_block that does the heavy-lifting inside a GIL-free region. Note that we still use the python thread pool, the optimization is just that the work done by the threads is now GIL-free. 2. Batching : This PR introduces a semantics change to thread work assignment. - On `main` : 1 request == 1 job == many keys == many reads/writes == each thread consumes a single read/write at a time. - This `PR` : 1 request == 1 job == many keys == many reads/writes == 1 thread does all the reads/writes. This 1 request to 1 thread mapping is likely detrimental at low concurrency. We can batch at the "keys" level and this I believe would be better to introduce in a followup PR and have this PR focus on the C implementation. ### Performance MODEL="openai/gpt-oss-120b" TP_SIZE=2 CPU_BYTES=25769803776 # 25GB ``` KV_TRANSFER_CONFIG=$(cat < #### PR n_read_threads=4, n_write_threads=4 ``` ℹ Server Throughput Statistics (All Requests) |============|=======|======|=========|==============|===============|==============| | Benchmark | Requests ||| Input Tokens | Output Tokens | Total Tokens | | Strategy | Concurrency || Per Sec | Per Sec | Per Sec | Per Sec | | | Mdn | Mean | Mean |||| |------------|-------|------|---------|--------------|---------------|--------------| | concurrent | 64.0 | 63.7 | 2.3 | 54333.4 | 1209.0 | 55542.3 | |============|=======|======|=========|==============|===============|==============| ``` n_read_threads=16, n_write_threads=16 ``` ℹ Server Throughput Statistics (All Requests) |============|=======|======|=========|==============|===============|==============| | Benchmark | Requests ||| Input Tokens | Output Tokens | Total Tokens | | Strategy | Concurrency || Per Sec | Per Sec | Per Sec | Per Sec | | | Mdn | Mean | Mean |||| |------------|-------|------|---------|--------------|---------------|--------------| | concurrent | 64.0 | 63.7 | 2.3 | 53658.9 | 1181.1 | 54840.0 | |============|=======|======|=========|==============|===============|==============| ``` #### Things to note - 1. increased throughput - 2. title: [Spec Decode] Make DFlash draft compute honor dynamic K
body:
## Purpose

Make DFlash's physical draft workload honor the batch-uniform speculative K
selected by the existing dynamic speculative-decoding scheduler.

Today the scheduler can request fewer than the configured maximum draft
tokens, but DFlash still builds and executes its maximum query shape before
the worker discards unused proposals. This change:

- carries the scheduled K in `ExecuteModelState`, binding it to the matching
  execute/sample iteration under async scheduling;
- skips proposal generation for K=0;
- advertises dynamic physical shapes as a speculator capability, enabled only
  for DFlash;
- sizes DFlash query inputs, attention metadata, sampling buffers, and CUDA
  graph dispatch from the scheduled K; and
- publishes exactly K proposals while retaining the configured global maximum
  for allocation and graph coverage.

Unsupported speculators keep their existing maximum physical shape. DSpark
explicitly opts out because its sequential head needs separate model-specific
validation. The common K=0 skip applies to all speculators.

### Related work

This does not duplicate #48692. That PR implements per-request adaptive
verification and explicitly initializes DFlash with
`allow_dynamic_decode_shapes=False`; this PR shortens the batch-uniform
DFlash drafter computation selected by the existing scheduler. It is also
separate from the per-request proposal API in #48202/#48204.

PR #47737 handles DSpark K=0 graph capture, #46399 disables dynamic schedules
for fixed-K proposers, and #48329 addresses autoregressive graph selection.
This PR does not replace those changes.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest -q \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2_spec_decode.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2_eplb.py

mypy tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2_spec_decode.py
```

Relevant Ruff, Ruff format, and typos pre-commit hooks were run on every
changed file.

GPU validation uses one NVIDIA H100 80GB, Qwen3.5-4B with
Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash, Model Runner V2, async scheduling, compiled CUDA graphs,
and K=0/1/3/7. The serving matrix covers concurrency 1/64/128/256 with three
repeats per point.

## Test Result

- Worker tests: 7 passed.
- Mypy: no issues.
- Relevant pre-commit hooks: passed.
- Serving smoke: 48/48 runs completed, zero failed requests, and DFlash full
  CUDA graph capture/replay succeeded for K=1/3/7; K=0 skipped the drafter.

A five-repeat natural mixed-prompt A/B isolates the physical-shape change:

| Batch | K=0 TPS delta | K=1 TPS delta | K=3 TPS delta | K=7 control |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | +37.3% | +15.3% | +2.3% | -3.7% |
| 128 | +40.0% | +5.1% | +4.4% | -2.6% |
| 256 | +36.9% | +6.2% | +4.6% | +0.4% |

K=7 retains the original maximum physical shape and is the no-op control; its
small positive/negative deltas indicate run/system variance. The lower-K gains
come from removing unused drafter work. Acceptance length for each fixed K is
stable across batch sizes (K=1: 1.879-1.882, K=3: 3.158-3.160, K=7:
4.415-4.429).

An independent standard Sonnet serving sweep covers K=0/1/3/7 and concurrency
1/64/128/256 with three repeats per point (48 runs, zero failures). At
concurrency 1, robust TPS rises from 204.33 at K=0 to 317.27 at K=7 (+55.3%).
At concurrency 64, K=0 reaches 3511.24 while the best positive candidate,
K=3, reaches 3042.50. TPS, `tpot:50` goodput, and mean TPOT therefore all
select the genuinely dynamic schedule `[[1, 63, 7], [64, 256, 0]]`.

The global maximum K still controls worker allocation, scheduler lookahead,
and KV-cache reservation. This patch reduces draft compute, not reserved KV
memory, and does not add an online K-selection policy.

## AI assistance

This patch was developed with OpenAI Codex assistance and the commit includes
the required attribution trailer. This is a Draft PR; the human submitter must
review every changed line and confirm the test/benchmark evidence before
marking it ready for review.

title: [Bug] Deepseek-V4-Pro corruption: H100 multi-rank startup can select a FlashInfer block-FP8 path with a cold JIT cache race
body:
## Environment

- vLLM: `v0.25.1` (`752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34`)
- Container: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.25.1`
- FlashInfer: `flashinfer-python==0.6.13`, `flashinfer-cubin==0.6.13`
- GPU: NVIDIA H100 80 GB HBM3, driver 580.105.08
- CUDA: 13.0 (`torch==2.11.0+cu130`)
- Model: `nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-NVFP4`
- Serving topology: flat TP16 on two eight-GPU nodes
- FlashInfer issue: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4062

## Summary

vLLM 0.25.1 selects `FlashInferFp8DeepGEMMDynamicBlockScaledKernel` before its pure DeepGEMM
candidate for a compatible dense block-FP8 linear. At runtime, the hybrid sends `M < 32` to
FlashInfer's `fp8_blockscale_gemm_sm90`.

DeepSeek-V4-Pro's mandatory mixed warmup reaches that branch at `M=16` on every TP rank. Eight
workers on each node then cold-build the same embedded TensorRT-LLM DeepGEMM kernel against one
shared cache. FlashInfer 0.6.13 has no inter-process cache-key build lock and can fail in its CUDA
driver-library load sequence. In the captured failing launch, startup terminated with eight
copies of:

```text
CUDA error: invalid argument
```

The server starts, captures CUDA graphs, and serves coherent output when the existing vLLM
candidate gate is disabled:

```bash
export VLLM_BLOCKSCALE_FP8_GEMM_FLASHINFER=0
```

A direct eight-H100 operator A/B established that this is a cold-cache race, not an unsupported
`M=16` shape: the exact operator passes on all eight GPUs with per-worker JIT caches. A separate
cold stock/default-selector full-server launch also succeeded and served coherent output, which
confirms that failure is timing-dependent rather than inevitable. The final source-level patch
passed both a genuinely rebuilt-wrapper shared-cache test and a complete two-node/16-H100 TP16
server with the FlashInfer selector enabled.

## End-to-end reproduction

Start one process launcher on each eight-GPU node, with `NODE_RANK=0` on the API node,
`NODE_RANK=1` on the second node, and `HEAD_NODE` set to the API node's routable hostname. Leave
`VLLM_BLOCKSCALE_FP8_GEMM_FLASHINFER` at its default value of `1`:

```bash
ENDPOINT=--headless
if [ "$NODE_RANK" -eq 0 ]; then
  ENDPOINT="--api-server-count 1 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000"
fi

vllm serve /model \
  --served-model-name deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro \
  --tensor-parallel-size 16 \
  --nnodes 2 --node-rank "$NODE_RANK" \
  --master-addr "$HEAD_NODE" --master-port 29500 \
  --max-model-len 2200 \
  --max-num-seqs 256 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --block-size 256 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  $ENDPOINT
```

The selected backends and captured failure were:

```text
Selected FlashInferFp8DeepGEMMDynamicBlockScaledKernel for Fp8LinearMethod
Using 'MARLIN' NvFp4 MoE backend
Warming up DeepSeek V4 sparse MLA attention for mixed tokens=16.
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
CUDA error: invalid argument
```

A separate localization launch used `--enforce-eager` and failed before CUDA graph capture, so the
error is not a graph replay failure. Operator-boundary synchronization places it in the dense
replicated `fused_wqa_wkv` projection before routed-expert MoE in that forward pass. The
reproduction command above does not require eager mode.

Repeat with:

```bash
export VLLM_BLOCKSCALE_FP8_GEMM_FLASHINFER=0
```

The same image, checkpoint, and launch select `DeepGemmFp8BlockScaledMMKernel`, retain the Marlin
NVFP4 MoE backend, complete mixed warmup and normal CUDA graph capture, and start the API. An
additional check completed eight simultaneous requests with exactly 1,024 input and 1,024 output
tokens each: 8/8 responses, zero errors, followed by a clean CUDA/illegal-memory-access scan.

## Direct operator evidence

The model projection has these exact arguments:

```text
activation:   [16, 7168], torch.bfloat16
weight:       [2048, 7168], torch.float8_e4m3fn
weight scale: [16, 56], torch.float32, stride=(56, 1), contiguous
blocks:       128x128
```

With a new shared `TRTLLM_DG_CACHE_DIR`, eight concurrent workers reproduced `CUDA error: invalid
argument`. With the cache path made unique per local rank, every worker passed:

```text
PASS cosine=0.99966240 relative_l1=0.02618705
EXIT=0
```

The complete reproducer, lower-level source analysis, cache-hardening results, and patched
full-server validation are in the linked FlashInfer issue.

## Why vLLM reaches the race

`FlashInferFp8DeepGEMMDynamicBlockScaledKernel` is an eligible CUDA block-FP8 candidate and its
`apply_block_scaled_mm` invokes `dynamic_flashinfer_deepgemm_blockscale_gemm`. That operation uses
`torch.cond` to dispatch:

```text
M < 32  -> flashinfer.gemm.fp8_blockscale_gemm_sm90
M >= 32 -> vLLM DeepGEMM
```

This is why the mandatory `M=16` warmup is sufficient to trigger the problem before the API is
ready. The FlashInfer operator internally JIT-compiles a shape-specific SM90 cubin. All local TP
workers inherit the same default TensorRT-LLM cache root and reach the cold cache together.

The direct A/B also rules out a suspected scale handoff bug. On H100, vLLM's DeepGEMM
post-processing leaves this checkpoint's 128x128 FP32 scale tensor contiguous at `[16, 56]` with
stride `(56, 1)`. Both BF16-weight and FP8-weight forms pass when the JIT build is not raced.

## Expected behavior

A stock, supported multi-GPU vLLM configuration should not fail mandatory startup because all
local ranks cold-compile the same selected backend kernel.

## Actual behavior

The candidate passes vLLM's support checks, but FlashInfer 0.6.13 can fail during its first
multi-process JIT build. In the captured failing launch, the engine exited before serving any
request. Another stock cold launch passed, as expected for a timing-dependent race.

## Suggested resolution

The primary fix belongs in FlashInfer's embedded TensorRT-LLM compiler: serialize each cache-key
build, recheck after acquiring the lock, reject failed or empty NVCC output, require a regular
nonempty cached cubin, and propagate publication failures. The lower-level patch has completed its
exact eight-H100 rebuilt-wrapper before/after and three two-node cache-hardening tests. It also
passed a complete two-node/16-H100 TP16 server: every rank selected the FlashInfer candidate,
mixed warmup and CUDA graph capture completed, and both functional requests returned HTTP 200 with
coherent answers.

For vLLM, please consider gating this candidate for the affected FlashInfer release in
multi-worker serving, or changing its default to the pure DeepGEMM candidate until a fixed
FlashInfer version is packaged. Once the lower-level fix is available, the small-`M` optimization
can be enabled again without forcing users to know about the cache race.

## Workaround and tradeoff

```bash
export VLLM_BLOCKSCALE_FP8_GEMM_FLASHINFER=0
```

This removes only the hybrid FlashInfer block-FP8 candidate. It does not cap request concurrency,
dequantize the checkpoint, change KV-cache precision, or alter the separate NVFP4/Marlin MoE
operators. The tradeoff is that small-`M` dense block-FP8 operations use pure DeepGEMM instead of
FlashInfer's swap-AB path, so some decode shapes may lose an optimization.

## FlashInfer tracking

https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4062

title: [ROCm] Added warmup for AITER unified attention
body:
## Purpose

Adds a dedicated warmup pass that precompiles the AITER unified-attention Triton
kernels (`ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` backend) during vLLM startup, so their JIT
compilation cost is paid once at warmup time instead of on the critical path of
the first user requests.
This mirrors the existing warmup modules (e.g. `sparse_mla_triton_warmup`,
`flashinfer_sparse_mla_decode_autotune_warmup`) and hooks into the shared
`kernel_warmup(worker)` entry point.

### What changed

- **New module `vllm/model_executor/warmup/rocm_aiter_unified_attn_warmup.py`:**
  - Discovers every attention layer using the `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` backend
    and deduplicates them by a compile-relevant `_AttnSignature`
    (heads, KV heads, head size, block size, num blocks, sliding window, KV-cache
    dtype, sinks, query dtype), so each unique configuration is warmed exactly
    once.
  - Derives an input-space sweep from the live vLLM config (`max_model_len`,
    `max_num_seqs`, `max_num_batched_tokens`, and speculative-decoding token
    count).
  - Builds a set of representative launch specs that exercise the different
    kernel code paths:
    - **Prefill** launches (2D kernel) across power-of-two query lengths.
    - **Decode** launches (small-q) that hit both the 2D kernel (small context)
      and the 3D + reduce path (large context) across power-of-two context
      lengths and batch sizes.
    - **Non-decode small-q** launches (e.g. speculative decoding, `ALL_DECODE=False`).
    - A **mixed varlen** prefill+decode batch that hits both kernels together and
      reaches AITER's large-prefill (`>= 256`) config where the budget allows.
  - Launches `unified_attention` against the real KV cache with zero-filled
    query/output tensors and valid block tables (warmup only reads the cache),
    handling both uniform and varlen (`cu_seqlens_q`) batches, and quantized
    (fp8) KV caches.
  - Runs under `torch.inference_mode()`, synchronizes the accelerator afterward,
    and is fully best-effort: any failure is logged as a warning and skipped
    rather than aborting startup.
- **`vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py`:**
  - Imports and calls `rocm_aiter_unified_attn_warmup_if_needed(worker)` as part
    of the standard kernel warmup sequence.

## Test Plan

Server:
```
VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \
HIP_FORCE_DEV_KERNARG=1 \
SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1 \
TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT=1 \
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 \
vllm serve --model mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN \
    --max-model-len 16384
```

Client:
```
python3 -c "
import urllib.request, json
long_prompt = 'word ' * 9000
payload = json.dumps({
    'model': 'mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3',
    'prompt': long_prompt,
    'max_tokens': 50
}).encode()
req = urllib.request.Request(
    'http://localhost:8000/v1/completions',
    data=payload,
    headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
)
with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
    print(r.read().decode())
"
```

title: [Bug][KV Offload]: failed secondary-tier load livelocks the request — async lookup cache is never invalidated on load failure
body:
## Your current environment

vLLM **v0.25.1** (pip install, Python 3.12); the trace below was also
re-verified against **current `main`** (2026-07-19). The defect is in
scheduler-side tiering code (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/`) and is
platform-independent — the reproduction script below runs with **no GPU**
on a stock install. We hit it while developing the Apple Silicon port of
the offloading connector (vllm-project/vllm-metal#530), but the affected
code is exactly what the CUDA path runs.

## Describe the bug

**Impact:** if a secondary-tier (e.g. `fs`) block load fails once —
torn/truncated file, bit rot, `EIO`, or a file deleted out from under the
store — the requesting request can never complete. The scheduler
re-initiates the same doomed promotion every scheduling step, forever,
until the request is aborted. Worse, the failure handling actively destroys
the evidence: `fs/io.py::load_block` deletes the block file on any failure,
yet the lookup layer keeps reporting the block as present, so every retry
is guaranteed to fail. One bad block file converts a request into an
infinite promotion loop and a busy-loop of wasted I/O and scheduler work.

### Background: how the pieces fit (for readers new to this subsystem)

The tiering offload path has four cooperating layers, all scheduler-side:

1. **Connector scheduler** (`kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py`) —
   on each scheduling step, asks the manager per block-hash key: "do you
   have this block?" A deferred answer means "ask again next step".
2. **`TieringOffloadingManager`** (`tiering/manager.py`) — checks the
   primary (CPU) tier first; on MISS it consults each secondary tier. A
   secondary HIT triggers a *promotion*: an async load of the block from
   the secondary tier into the CPU pool.
3. **Secondary tier**, e.g. the filesystem tier (`tiering/fs/manager.py`)
   — owns the block files and the load/store thread pool.
4. **`AsyncLookupManager`** (`tiering/async_lookup.py`) — because a
   filesystem stat per key per step would be slow, lookups are answered
   from a per-request cache: the first query enqueues a background
   existence check; once it resolves, the verdict (`True`/`False`) is
   **cached for the lifetime of the requesting request** and served to
   every subsequent query.

The cache write happens only in `drain_results()`
(`async_lookup.py:160-173`); entries are removed only in `cleanup(req_id)`
when the request finishes (`:175-185`). **No code path anywhere writes a
failure back into this cache.** That is the bug: a load failure has no way
to correct the cached `True`, and everything downstream trusts the cache.

### The livelock loop, step by step (file:line against v0.25.1)

1. Connector re-queries per key each step: `scheduler.py:688` `_lookup` →
   `_maximal_prefix_lookup` (`:390-410`); a deferred verdict returns `None`
   from `get_num_new_matched_tokens` (`:684-693`), so the scheduler retries
   next step. There is no connector-level memory of failures.
2. `TieringOffloadingManager.lookup` (`manager.py:238-280`): primary MISS →
   secondary `tier.lookup(key, req_context)` at `:270` → fs tier delegates
   to the async lookup cache (`fs/manager.py:152-156`) → cached HIT.
3. HIT → `_initiate_promotion` (`manager.py:272, 282-329`) → batched
   `tier.submit_load` in `_flush_pending_promotions` (`:331-353`).
4. The load fails. `fs/io.py::load_block` (`:75-98`) **deletes the file on
   any failure** (`:91-97`).
5. `_process_finished_jobs` (`manager.py:202-235`) sees
   `is_promotion=True, success=False` →
   `primary_tier.complete_write(keys, ctx, False)` →
   `cpu/manager.py::complete_store` failure branch (`:256-261`) frees the
   primary blocks. Primary is MISS again.
6. Next step: primary MISS → secondary lookup → **the cached `True` from
   step 2 is still there** → HIT → re-promotion of a now-deleted file →
   fail → goto 5. The loop exits only when the request is aborted
   (`cleanup(req_id)` finally drops the cache entry).

### Reproduction (runnable, no GPU, ~1 second)

Verified on a stock v0.25.1 install. The script drives the real
`FileSystemTierManager` (which owns the real `AsyncLookupManager` and the
real `io.load_block`): store a block, let a request's lookup cache a HIT,
corrupt the file, let the promotion fail — then watch the lookup keep
answering HIT for a file that no longer exists.

```python
# repro_livelock.py — vLLM v0.25.1, no GPU. `python repro_livelock.py`
import hashlib, os, tempfile, time
from types import SimpleNamespace
import numpy as np
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.base import LookupResult, ReqContext, ScheduleEndContext
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.tiering.base import JobMetadata
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.tiering.fs.manager import FileSystemTierManager

BLOCK_BYTES = 4096
spec = SimpleNamespace(  # minimal stand-in for an OffloadingSpec
    block_size_factor=1,
    kv_bytes_per_offloaded_block=BLOCK_BYTES,
    vllm_config=SimpleNamespace(
        model_config=SimpleNamespace(model="repro-model", dtype="float16"),
        cache_config=SimpleNamespace(block_size=16, cache_dtype="auto"),
        parallel_config=SimpleNamespace(
            tensor_parallel_size=1, pipeline_parallel_size=1,
            prefill_context_parallel_size=1, decode_context_parallel_size=1,
            rank=0,
        ),
        additional_config={},
        use_v2_model_runner=False,
    ),
    kv_cache_config=SimpleNamespace(
        kv_cache_groups=[SimpleNamespace(
            kv_cache_spec=SimpleNamespace(block_size=16), layer_names=["l0"]
        )]
    ),
)
pool = np.zeros((4, BLOCK_BYTES), dtype=np.uint8)
tier = FileSystemTierManager(
    offloading_spec=spec, primary_kv_view=memoryview(pool), tier_type="fs",
    root_dir=tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="kv-livelock-"),
    n_read_threads=1, n_write_threads=1,
)

def await_verdict(key, ctx, timeout=10.0):
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        r = tier.lookup(key, ctx)
        if r is not LookupResult.RETRY:
            return r
        tier.on_schedule_end(ScheduleEndContext(set(), set()))
        time.sleep(0.02)
    raise TimeoutError

try:
    key = hashlib.sha256(b"block-A").digest() + (0).to_bytes(4, "big")
    path = tier.file_mapper.get_file_name(key)

    # 1. Store a block through the tier (as a CPU->fs cascade would).
    pool[0] = 7
    tier.submit_store(JobMetadata(job_id=1, keys=[key],
        block_ids=np.array([0]), is_promotion=False,
        req_context=ReqContext(req_id="storer")))
    tier.drain_jobs()
    assert [(r.job_id, r.success) for r in tier.get_finished_jobs()] == [(1, True)]

    # 2. Request R looks the block up; the async lookup cache records True.
    ctx = ReqContext(req_id="R")
    assert await_verdict(key, ctx) is LookupResult.HIT

    # 3. The file goes bad AFTER the cached verdict (truncation stands in
    #    for a torn write, bit rot, EIO, or external deletion).
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(b"x" * 10)

    # 4. The promotion the HIT triggered now fails; io.load_block deletes
    #    the file on failure.
    tier.submit_load(JobMetadata(job_id=2, keys=[key],
        block_ids=np.array([1]), is_promotion=True, req_context=ctx))
    tier.drain_jobs()
    time.sleep(0.1)
    print(f"promotion: {[(r.job_id, r.success) for r in tier.get_finished_jobs()]}"
          f"  file_exists={os.path.exists(path)}")

    # 5. THE BUG: the same request's lookups still answer HIT for a block
    #    whose backing file no longer exists -> the scheduler re-promotes
    #    it every step, forever (until the request is aborted).
    for step in range(1, 4):
        verdict = tier.lookup(key, ctx)
        print(f"step {step}: lookup={verdict.name}  "
              f"file_exists={os.path.exists(path)}")
        assert verdict is LookupResult.HIT, "fixed? lookup no longer stale"
finally:
    tier.shutdown()
```

Observed output on v0.25.1:

```
ERROR ... [thread_pool.py:169] Job 2 block I/O failed: Short read: expected 4096 bytes, read 10
promotion: [(2, False)]  file_exists=False
step 1: lookup=HIT  file_exists=False
step 2: lookup=HIT  file_exists=False
step 3: lookup=HIT  file_exists=False
```

Each of those HITs is the manager's cue to schedule another promotion of a
file that is gone. In a live server this is the per-step loop of section
"The livelock loop" above; the request never finishes.

To see it end-to-end instead: serve any model with
`--kv-offloading-size N` plus an `fs` secondary tier, warm the store with a
long prompt, truncate one of the `.bin` block files under `root_dir`, then
resend the prompt after the block has been evicted from GPU and CPU tiers —
the request hangs while the log repeats the failed-load error.

### Aggravating detail

`batch_lookup` in the fs tier (`fs/manager.py:64-72`) is a bare existence
check (`os.path.exists` / the `faccessat` C fast path), so a truncated or
foreign-layout file also produces a confident HIT that then fails fatally
at load time and enters the same loop — the failure does not need to race
anything to occur.

## Suggested fix directions

Any one of these breaks the loop; (1) is the minimal correct fix, (2) and
(3) harden the entry points. We implemented (2)+(3) in the Metal port's fs
tier subclass (vllm-metal#530, `vllm_metal/v1/kv_offload/fs_tier.py`) and
are happy to upstream any of it:

1. **Invalidate on failure**: when a promotion job completes with
   `success=False`, write `False` into the async lookup cache for the job's
   keys (or drop the entries) so the next lookup is an honest MISS.
2. **Negative-cache failed loads at the tier**: remember keys whose load
   failed and answer MISS until a fresh store for those keys lands (a
   re-store legitimately recreates the file).
3. **Validate at lookup time**: `batch_lookup` should stat for the expected
   file size rather than bare existence, turning truncated/foreign files
   into clean misses before a promotion is ever scheduled.

Related but distinct: #46027 (closed) fixed `on_request_finished` contract
inconsistencies in the same subsystem; RFC #38260's KV-event discussion
explicitly scopes secondary-tier invalidation out — this issue is the
in-process correctness case, not the cross-instance routing case.

---

Found while building and adversarially testing the Apple Silicon port of
the offloading connector (vllm-project/vllm-metal#530); the trace was
verified against both v0.25.1 and `main` as of 2026-07-19, and the
reproduction script above was run against a stock v0.25.1 install.

title: [Bugfix] Disable DeepGEMM on GH200 to workaround illegal memory access
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->
PLEASE FILL IN THE PR DESCRIPTION HERE ENSURING ALL CHECKLIST ITEMS (AT THE BOTTOM) HAVE BEEN CONSIDERED.

> **Note:** I haven't verified this in a real GH200 environment yet. I'll first
> rely on GitHub CI for regression testing. Once I get access to a GH200 machine,
> I'll run the end-to-end check below and update this note.

## Purpose

Fix #49158.

Running `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7` with TP2 and FP8 KV cache on NVIDIA GH200NVL2
(SM 9.0 integrated GPU / UMA) crashes during vLLM 0.25.1 startup:

```
RuntimeError: CUDA driver error (.../deepgemm-src/.../runtime_utils.hpp:144): 700
(CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS, an illegal memory access was encountered)
```

The stack trace ends in `vllm.utils.deep_gemm.fp8_gemm_nt` → `_fp8_gemm_nt_impl`,
i.e. **DeepGEMM's JIT kernel triggers an illegal memory access on GH200**. This
is a compatibility issue in the third-party DeepGEMM library with GH200's UMA
architecture, not a bug in vLLM model code.

### Duplicate-Work Check

Searched open PRs on `vllm-project/vllm` before submitting:

```bash
# by issue reference
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "49158 in:body"      # 0 results
# by area keywords
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "GH200 DeepGEMM"     # 0 results
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "support_deep_gemm"  # 2 results
```

No open PR addresses this GH200 crash. The two open PRs touching
`support_deep_gemm()` are unrelated in intent:

- #41062 — extends DeepGEMM device gates to SM 12.x consumer Blackwell (enables
  more GPUs; does not touch GH200 / SM 9.0 integrated).
- #45470 — DeepSeek V4 hardware-agnostic model definition (unrelated).

This PR is therefore not a duplicate.

### Fix

Add a GH200 check in `CudaPlatformBase.support_deep_gemm()`: when the GPU is
both SM 9.0 and integrated (`is_integrated_gpu()`), return `False` and emit a
one-time warning so that vLLM falls back to alternative FP8 GEMM kernels
(e.g. Cutlass / Triton).

```python
if cls.is_device_capability(90) and cls.is_integrated_gpu():
    logger.warning_once(
        "DeepGEMM is disabled on GH200 (SM 9.0 UMA). "
        "Falling back to alternative FP8 GEMM kernels."
    )
    return False
```

**This is a temporary workaround.** A `FIXME` comment has been added in the code:

```python
# FIXME: This is a temporary workaround for a DeepGEMM bug: its JIT
# kernels trigger illegal memory accesses on GH200 (SM 9.0 integrated
# GPU / UMA). Remove this check once DeepGEMM upstream fixes GH200
# support. See vllm-project/vllm#49158.
```

This check should be removed once DeepGEMM upstream fixes GH200 support.

### Impact

- **GH200 users**: Fixes #49158; models using FP8 block-scaled linear layers such
  as MiniMax-M2.7 can now start successfully.
- **Other platforms**: No impact.
  - Discrete Hopper (H100/H200, SM 9.0 non-integrated) continues to support
    DeepGEMM.
  - Blackwell (B100/B200/DGX Spark, SM 100/120 family) continues to support
    DeepGEMM.
- **Kernel selection**: `FlashInferFp8DeepGEMMDynamicBlockScaledKernel` uses
  `DeepGemmFp8BlockScaledMMKernel` as its fallback. When DeepGEMM is unsupported,
  the dynamic kernel is also marked unsupported and vLLM falls back to
  `CutlassFp8BlockScaledMMKernel`, etc.

## Test Plan

Added `tests/cuda/test_platform_capabilities.py` covering three scenarios:

- GH200 (SM90 + integrated) → `support_deep_gemm()` returns `False`
- Discrete Hopper (SM90 non-integrated) → `support_deep_gemm()` returns `True`
- DGX Spark Blackwell UMA (SM100 integrated) → `support_deep_gemm()` returns `True`

Run the new unit test:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/cuda/test_platform_capabilities.py -v
```

End-to-end verification on GH200 (to be done once a machine is available):

```bash
VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M2.7 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8
```

## Test Result

**Unit test — all 3 tests pass:**

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/cuda/test_platform_capabilities.py -v
# test_gh200_excluded_from_deep_gemm            PASSED
# test_hopper_discrete_supports_deep_gemm       PASSED
# test_dgx_spark_blackwell_uma_supports_deep_gemm PASSED
# ========================= 3 passed in 1.56s =========================
```

Note: `tests/cuda/test_platform_capabilities.py` imports `vllm.platforms.cuda`,
which loads the native custom-ops extension `vllm._C_stable_libtorch` at module
import time. The test therefore requires a built/installed vLLM (or the native
extension stubbed in `sys.modules`); the function under test itself is pure
Python and does not call into the extension.

**End-to-end / model evaluation:** Not yet verified on real GH200 hardware. CI
will be used for regression testing. Once a GH200 machine is available, the
end-to-end serve command above will be run and the results pasted here.

title: [ROCm][MLA] Enable AITER sparse MLA decode + MQA-only prefill for GLM DSA
body:
## Purpose

Enables the ROCm AITER sparse MLA backend (`ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE`) used by
GLM DSA (Deepseek Sparse Attention) models to run end-to-end.

Two issues were blocking it:

1. **Missing decode/prefill metadata.** The generic `MLAAttention` /
   `unified_mla_kv_cache_update` path expects the attention metadata to expose
   the decode/prefill split counters and prefill metadata (`num_decodes`,
   `num_prefills`, `num_decode_tokens`, `prefill_max_seq_len`, `prefill`). The
   ROCm aiter sparse metadata class did not define these, raising
   `AttributeError` at runtime. Other sparse MLA metadata classes (e.g.
   `FlashMLASparseMetadata`) already expose them.

2. **No dense-MHA prefill.** The ROCm aiter sparse impl only implements the
   top-k MQA path (`forward_mqa`), which handles **both** prefill and decode; it
   has no dense-MHA prefill (`forward_mha`). The generic path still tried to
   build a dense prefill backend and eventually hit `NotImplementedError`.

> Note: this change is code-independent from the Quark MTP-unquantized fix
> (#49187), but that fix is required at runtime to *load* the
> `GLM-5.x-NVFP4` checkpoints used to validate this PR.

## Changes

- `rocm_aiter_mla_sparse.py`
  - Add `num_decodes`, `num_prefills`, `num_decode_tokens`,
    `prefill_max_seq_len`, and `prefill` to `ROCMAiterMLASparseMetadata`.
  - Compute them in the metadata builder via `split_decodes_and_prefills`.
  - Add `supports_mha_prefill = False` to `ROCMAiterMLASparseImpl` to advertise
    that it has no dense-MHA prefill path.
- `mla_attention.py`
  - In `MLAAttention.__init__`, when the impl is sparse and does not support
    dense-MHA prefill (`supports_mha_prefill == False`), set
    `prefill_backend = None` so prefill flows through the top-k MQA path instead
    of an unimplemented `forward_mha`.

## Test Plan

- Serve `amd/GLM-5.1-NVFP4` and `amd/GLM-5.2-NVFP4` (GLM DSA) on AMD Instinct
  MI350 (gfx950), TP=8, with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`.
- Run gsm8k (5-shot, lm_eval) against the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with and
  without MTP speculative decoding.

## Test Result

Model serves without `AttributeError` / `NotImplementedError`. gsm8k (5-shot,
lm_eval via `/v1/completions`), MI350 (gfx950), TP=8. Both filters
(flexible-extract / strict-match) reported identical values:

| Model         | Mode    | exact_match     |
|---------------|---------|-----------------|
| GLM-5.1-NVFP4 | non-MTP | 0.9507 ± 0.0060 |
| GLM-5.1-NVFP4 | MTP     | 0.9492 ± 0.0060 |
| GLM-5.2-NVFP4 | non-MTP | 0.9462 ± 0.0062 |
| GLM-5.2-NVFP4 | MTP     | 0.9507 ± 0.0060 |

title: [Bugfix][Test] Quantize q to fp8 in test_flashmla_dense_fp8_decode_unified_slot_view
body:
## Summary
`tests/kernels/attention/test_mla_cross_layer_kernel_equivalence.py::test_flashmla_dense_fp8_decode_unified_slot_view` raises `RuntimeError: Expected q.dtype() == torch::kFloat8_e4m3fn` when run on hardware with FlashMLA dense-fp8 support (SM90).

## Root cause
The test builds the query `q` in **bfloat16** and passes it to `flash_mla_with_kvcache_fp8`, whose kernel `fwd_kvcache_mla_fp8` asserts `q.dtype()==float8_e4m3fn`; the wrapper does not cast `q`. The case is guarded by `is_flashmla_dense_supported()`, so it is latent on CI runners lacking SM90 dense-fp8 and surfaces on SM90/H20.

## Fix
Quantize `q` to `float8_e4m3fn` before the call (the fp8 decode kernel expects a pre-quantized fp8 query with `descale_q`).

## Test
Reproduced the `RuntimeError` and verified the fix passes on stock `vllm==0.25.1` on an SM90 (H20) GPU.

Searched existing issues/PRs — no duplicate (#39787 touches a different file, `test_flashmla.py`).

AI assistance (Claude) was used; reviewed and defended by the submitter.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Summary Server runs healthy for hours under sustained concurrent load, then enters a livelock state: `Running: N reqs`, `Avg generation throughput: 0.0 tokens/s`, indefinitely. No crash, no traceback, no `EngineDeadError`. GPU (`nvidia-smi`) shows `utilization.gpu ~96%`, `utilization.memory 0%`, power draw far below TDP (~17W observed) — consistent with a spin-wait, not active compute. No Xid errors in `dmesg`/`journalctl` at the time of the incident. Only a container/process restart recovers service. Reproduced 6 times independently across different mitigation attempts and configs (see below), including once after a simple `docker restart` with no config change (livelock recurred after only ~3.5 minutes under organic production load) and once after reverting to a config close to defaults (`--attention-backend auto`, prefix caching enabled, no forced kernel backends). In the first 3 occurrences, onset coincided with `Running` reaching the configured `--max-num-seqs` ceiling. In later occurrences `Running` stalled below the ceiling with a `Waiting` backlog — the livelock is not tied to reaching the configured concurrency ceiling itself. Across all occurrences, the metrics immediately preceding the stall show an `Avg prompt throughput` spike (a prefill burst) in the 1-2 scheduler ticks (10s each) before generation throughput collapses to 0. This points to concurrent prefill+decode mixing as the trigger, independent of absolute concurrency count and, per the 6th occurrence, independent of which kernel backends are in use. ## Startup config (final attempt, most restrictive) ``` --quantization modelopt --attention-backend flash_attn --moe-backend marlin --linear-backend torch --ir-op-priority '{"rms_norm": ["native"], "fused_add_rms_norm": ["native"]}' --max-num-seqs 12 --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching --enforce-eager ``` Env: `VLLM_MARLIN_USE_ATOMIC_ADD=1` ## Diagnostic timeline / ruled-out causes 1. **Initial hard crash** (different bug, now fixed): `FlashInferFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel.is_supported()` in `vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/flashinfer.py` only checks `compute_capability < 100`, which incorrectly passes SM121 (121 >= 100) into a cuDNN GEMM path (`fp8_gemm_sm100`) hard-coded for SM100 tensor core layout → `CUDNN_STATUS_EXECUTION_FAILED_CUDA_DRIVER`. Worked around with `--linear-backend torch` (forces `PerTensorTorchFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel`). This is a separate, reproducible, deterministic bug — happy to file separately if useful, but flagging here since it may be architecturally related (SM121 not being treated as its own family in enough places). 2. **After the above fix, the livelock described in this issue appeared instead** (soft hang, no crash) under sustained load at full `--max-num-seqs` concurrency. 3. Captured `py-spy dump --pid --locals` on **four independent occurrences**. Three (before/after forcing `--ir-op-priority native`, and after a plain `docker restart`) show the byte-for-byte identical frame: MainThread active inside `fused_add_rms_norm` → `GemmaRMSNorm.forward_native/forward_cuda` → `Qwen3_5DecoderLayer.forward` (`layer_idx: 19` in all three captures) → ... → `step_with_batch_queue`. The fourth (different config, see 6th occurrence below) instead shows `torch.cuda.Event.synchronize()` inside the async-scheduling output path (`AsyncGPUModelRunnerOutput.get_output`) — a different frame entirely. 4. Forcing `rms_norm`/`fused_add_rms_norm` to `native` (pure PyTorch, no custom CUDA kernel) did **not** change the observed hang location or prevent recurrence. This strongly suggests RMSNorm is not the actual culprit — see next point. 5. Cross-referencing a separate, unrelated report on the NVIDIA DGX Spark forum (**FlashInfer sparse-MLA mbarrier livelock on GB10**, forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/377334, filed 2026-07-18 against a different model/kernel — GLM-5.2, `sparse_mla_sm120`, multi-node TP=4) describes the same class of failure with near-identical telemetry signature: `utilization.gpu 96%, power ~18W, utilization.memory 0%`, confirmed via `cuda-gdb` attach to be a resident kernel spin-looping on an mbarrier phase check (`SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT`) that never resolves — a TMA/`cp.async.bulk` expect-tx accounting race. Critically, that report explicitly notes: *"the Python-level frame is arbitrary (marlin_gemm, MoE workspace, triton launcher — bystanders)"* — i.e. once one kernel is wedged, every subsequent kernel launch queues behind it, and whatever Python code happens to be issuing the next launch is what `py-spy` shows, regardless of where the actual bug lives. 6. Given (4) and (5), we suspect our two RMSNorm frames are likewise **bystanders**, not the root cause. The model uses the GDN (Gated DeltaNet) hybrid linear-attention architecture (`vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/gdn/qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py`), and our startup log shows: ``` Using Triton/FLA GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128). ``` Inspecting `_resolve_gdn_prefill_backend()`: on SM121, `is_device_capability_family(100)` correctly excludes both the FlashInfer and CuteDSL GDN prefill paths (family check is 100–109, SM121 falls outside), leaving Triton/FLA as the *only* available backend — there is no config flag to select an alternative. This Triton kernel is comparatively new/untested code on SM121 specifically (per Qwen3.5 HF model card, upstream `fla`/`causal_conv1d` packages ship no SM121 build at all; vLLM's in-tree Triton port is the only path). We were not able to find a flag equivalent to `--max-num-partial-prefills` in this build (checked `--help`) to isolate prefill from concurrent decode for a cleaner repro. ## What we're asking - Has anyone observed similar Triton/FLA GDN prefill livelocks on SM121 specifically (vs. SM90/SM100 where this path is presumably better exercised)? - Is there a way to force the pure-PyTorch GDN fallback path (bypassing Triton entirely) to test this hypothesis, similar to `--linear-backend torch` for the FP8 GEMM kernel? We could not find one via `--help`. - Given the FlashInfer sparse-MLA precedent, could this be the same underlying class of mbarrier/synchronization bug appearing in a different in-tree Triton kernel rather than FlashInfer specifically? ## Log excerpt, 4th occurrence (2026-07-20, `--max-num-seqs 12`, `Running` stalled at 8/12) ``` 11:45:52 Running: 7 prompt: 118.6 tok/s gen: 61.9 tok/s 11:46:02 Running: 8 prompt: 2837.0 tok/s gen: 66.9 tok/s <- prefill burst 11:46:12 Running: 8 prompt: 3929.2 tok/s gen: 101.0 tok/s <- larger prefill burst 11:46:22 Running: 8 prompt: 0.0 tok/s gen: 53.6 tok/s <- decode already degrading 11:46:32 Running: 8 prompt: 0.0 tok/s gen: 0.0 tok/s <- fully wedged, indefinitely ``` ## Log excerpt, 5th occurrence (2026-07-20, fresh `docker restart`, no config change, organic production traffic, `--max-num-seqs 12`) Server ready at 12:41:44. Livelock at 12:45:11 — **~3.5 minutes uptime**, the fastest reproduction so far, under real (non-synthetic) traffic with a persistent `Waiting` backlog of 3-6 requests (scheduler continuously pulling new requests from queue, i.e. near-continuous prefill activity): ``` 12:44:51 Running:12 Waiting:4 prompt: 2901.9 tok/s gen: 117.3 tok/s <- large prefill burst 12:45:01 Running:12 Waiting:3 prompt: 82.4 tok/s gen: 23.9 tok/s <- sharp collapse 12:45:11 Running:12 Waiting:3 prompt: 0.0 tok/s gen: 0.0 tok/s <- fully wedged ``` `py-spy dump --pid ` immediately after: identical frame to the two prior captures (`fused_add_rms_norm`, `layer_idx: 19`, `GDNAttentionMetadata`), `num_scheduled_tokens: 12`, `max_num_scheduled_tokens: 1` — confirming the hang was caught mid-decode-step (1 token/request), consistent with the "bystander" theory: an earlier prefill-triggered kernel wedged the stream, and the next decode step's kernel launch queued behind it. ## Log excerpt + py-spy, 6th occurrence — different config, different bystander frame (2026-07-21) This occurrence used a **substantially different, closer-to-default config** (reverted several of our earlier workarounds to test whether they mattered): ``` --attention-backend auto (was: flash_attn) --enable-prefix-caching (was: --no-enable-prefix-caching) --max-num-seqs 8 # no --linear-backend override, no --ir-op-priority override ``` Same prefill-precedes-collapse pattern: ``` 06:58:05 Running:7 prompt:102.6 tok/s gen:175.4 tok/s 06:58:15 Running:7 prompt:340.1 tok/s gen:215.6 tok/s <- prefill burst 06:58:25 Running:6 prompt:0.0 tok/s gen:203.4 tok/s <- decode degrading 06:58:35 Running:5 prompt:0.0 tok/s gen:174.9 tok/s 06:58:45 Running:4 prompt:0.0 tok/s gen:73.4 tok/s 06:58:55 Running:4 prompt:0.0 tok/s gen:0.0 tok/s <- fully wedged ``` **Critically, this time `py-spy dump --locals` shows a completely different frame** — not `fused_add_rms_norm` at all: ``` Thread 249 (active): "MainThread" synchronize (torch/cuda/streams.py:254) Arguments: self: get_output (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:306) Arguments: self: result (vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:38) Arguments: self: step_with_batch_queue (vllm/v1/engine/core.py:604) ``` This is `torch.cuda.Event.synchronize()` blocking forever inside vLLM's async-scheduling overlap output path (`AsyncGPUModelRunnerOutput.get_output`), waiting on a CUDA event that never fires. **We consider this the strongest evidence yet for the "arbitrary bystander frame" theory** (per the NVIDIA forum precedent cited above): two different configs, using different kernel backends (native RMSNorm + flash_attn in occurrences 1-5 vs. auto attention-backend + prefix caching + default RMSNorm here), produce the *same* prefill-preceded collapse signature but *different* Python-visible frames. This strongly suggests the actual wedge is a CUDA stream/kernel-level event (most likely inside the GDN Triton kernel or the attention kernel actually resolved by `auto`, neither of which appear directly in either captured stack) that manifests wherever the next synchronization point in the code happens to be — RMSNorm's op call in one config, the async output event wait in another. This is consistent with, though not proof of, an mbarrier-class synchronization bug similar to the one documented for FlashInfer's sparse-MLA kernel on the same hardware family. This also means our earlier mitigations (`--linear-backend torch`, `--ir-op-priority native`) likely never addressed the actual root cause — they may have only changed which bystander frame gets caught, not whether the underlying wedge occurs. ## Attachments available on request - Full `py-spy dump --locals` output x2 (pre/post `--ir-op-priority native` change) - `nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,PERFORMANCE,CLOCK,POWER,TEMPERATURE` snapshot during live hang - `dmesg`/`journalctl` excerpts (no Xid present) - Full startup config dumps (`KernelConfig`, `IrOpPriorityConfig` resolved values) for both attempts ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [KV-offload][FS]: Batching for read/write threads
body:
PR #49152  introduced batched C versions of load_block / store_block. The batching was request-level, i.e. each thread in the thread_pool receives all the keys for a request and loads/stores them one after another. 

If there are 16 requests, each with say 100 keys to load, and we have 16 threads. Each thread will work on a separate request. This is less desirable as read jobs for different requests are interleaved on the disk, increasing any single request's total read time. 

This PR: 
device-saturation driven batching : We batch based on 2 factors,
 1. File size: Batch for small files. When file size is large, we already saturate the device bandwidth without batching. 
 2. inflight_jobs: When we see inflight_jobs piling up, we don't batch as aggressively. 
 Note that the decision to batch is not discrete. Based on the factors mentioned above, the degree of batching varies.

title: [Bugfix] Validate NIXL speculative config compatibility
body:
#### Overview:

Fail the NIXL prefill/decode handshake early when speculative decoding is set up incompatibly on the two workers, instead of crashing later during inference.

#### Details:

##### Problem

In disaggregated serving, prefill builds the KV cache and NIXL transfers it to decode. If decode enables a model-based speculative method such as EAGLE3, but prefill does not (or uses a different draft setup), the handshake can still succeed. Short prompts may work; long prompts can then hit CUDA / illegal-memory-access failures on decode.

##### Background

A **KV cache group** is a set of model layers that share one block table — think of it as one memory folder of KV blocks.

Speculative decoding methods fall into two buckets:

1. **Model-based methods** (`eagle`, `eagle3`, `mtp`, `dflash`, `dspark`):
   These load extra draft / MTP layers and can add another KV cache group (or change how blocks are counted). Prefill and decode must agree on that setup when NIXL transfers KV.
2. **Pattern-based methods** (`ngram`, `ngram_gpu`, `suffix`):
   These guess tokens from prompt / history locally. They do not add a draft-model KV group to transfer, so they are outside this handshake check.

##### What this PR changes

- Include transfer-relevant speculative settings in the NIXL compatibility hash for the model-based methods above.
- Reject cases where a model-based method is enabled on only one of prefill or decode.
- Bump the NIXL connector compatibility version from 5 to 6.
- Document that P/D speculative configs must be **compatible**. See `docs/features/nixl_connector_compatibility.md` **Configuration Notes** for what must match and what may differ (including that `num_speculative_tokens` may differ between prefill and decode).

##### Out of scope

- `ngram` / `suffix` are not hashed by this check.
- Generic `draft_model` is also outside `use_eagle()` today and is not hashed here. That can be a follow-up if needed.

##### Tests run

- `python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py -k "speculative_config_compatibility_hash or missing_speculative_config_changes_compatibility_hash" -q` — 10 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files docs/features/nixl_connector_compatibility.md vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/metadata.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py` — all applicable hooks passed.
- The existing GPU-oriented handshake regression test could not initialize on macOS because of its DeviceConfig/MPS fixture.
- AI assistance was used to investigate, implement, and test this change. Every changed line was reviewed by the human submitter before submission.

#### Where should the reviewer start?

Start with `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/metadata.py` (`_get_speculative_compatibility_factors()` and `compute_nixl_compatibility_hash()`), then the unit cases in `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py`, then the wording in `docs/features/nixl_connector_compatibility.md` (footnote 1 + Configuration Notes).

title: [Core][PCP] Support data parallelism with MRV2 PCP
body:
## Summary

- allow MRV2 prefill context parallelism (PCP) with data parallelism (DP)
- allocate each local DP engine's TP/PP/PCP device range correctly
- rebuild DP token metadata after PCP partitions the scheduled batch
- compose AgRs MoE dispatch across DP then PCP, reversing the order for combine
- replicate sequence-parallel token sizes across PCP ranks in flattened EP order
- mask empty MLA context chunks with `-inf` LSE before merging

Related to #46358.

## Why this is not a duplicate

I checked issue #46358 and searched open PRs by issue number and DP/PCP/MLA
keywords. No open PR enables generic MRV2 DP+PCP composition. #49109 is scoped to
Mooncake KV-connector PCP replica selection, while #43809 is model-specific
DeepSeek-V4 hybrid-KV/MegaMoE PCP work. Neither changes the generic DP supervisor,
post-PCP DP metadata, or hierarchical AgRs path implemented here.

## Validation

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/test_config.py \
  tests/entrypoints/openai/test_dp_supervisor.py -q
```

Result: `178 passed`.

Commit-time pre-commit hooks passed, including Ruff, formatting, mypy, SPDX,
configuration validation, and forbidden-import checks.

Runtime configuration (4 GPUs):

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 \
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 \
.venv/bin/vllm serve nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4 \
  --enforce-eager \
  --max-model-len 4096 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 \
  --safetensors-load-strategy prefetch \
  --moe-backend flashinfer_cutlass \
  --data-parallel-size 2 \

  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --trust-remote-code
```

Both DP ranks returned the expected answer (`18`) when addressed with
`X-data-parallel-rank`.

100-sample GSM8K smoke evaluation:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py \
  --num-questions 100 \
  --num-shots 5 \
  --max-tokens 256 \
  --max-concurrency 100 \
  --port 8000
```

| DP2+PCP2+EP4 | 94/100 | 0/100 |

The same rank-pinned runtime probe passed with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`, with
no synchronization detected during model execution.

title: [Feature]: Opt-in DeepGEMM BF16 grouped-GEMM MoE backend (unquantized bf16)
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

vLLM already integrates DeepGEMM's **FP8** grouped-GEMM kernels for fused MoE
(`DeepGemmExperts`, `BatchedDeepGemmExperts`). DeepGEMM also ships **BF16**
grouped-GEMM kernels (`m_grouped_bf16_gemm_nt_contiguous`,
`m_grouped_bf16_gemm_nt_masked`), but there is **no** vLLM path that uses them —
unquantized bf16 MoE currently runs only on Triton / FlashInfer.

This proposes adding an **opt-in** DeepGEMM bf16 MoE backend for unquantized bf16
weights, mirroring the existing FP8 integration and matching what **SGLang**
already does for bf16 MoE (SGLang uses the same `m_grouped_bf16_gemm_nt_*`
grouped-GEMM primitives + a separate silu-and-mul).

**Why it's useful**

- **Ecosystem parity.** DeepGEMM is DeepSeek's kernel library; bf16 grouped GEMM
  is the unquantized sibling of the FP8 path vLLM already ships, and is the same
  approach SGLang uses for bf16 MoE.
- **Enables the DeepEP low-latency (batched / comm-overlap) EP path for
  unquantized bf16.** FlashInfer's fused MoE (`cutlass_fused_moe`) is
  `Standard`-format only and cannot run in the `BatchedExperts` format used by
  `deepep_low_latency`; Triton's batched path can, but is slow. A DeepGEMM
  batched experts fills this gap.
- **Fast raw kernel.** DeepGEMM's grouped-GEMM primitive measures faster than
  FlashInfer's grouped-GEMM primitive on MoE shapes (see data below).
- **Zero impact on defaults.** Selected only via `--moe-backend deep_gemm`;
  never added to the auto-priority list.

**Honest trade-off.** On a single node (non-batched EP), FlashInfer's fused
CUTLASS MoE is faster end-to-end than the unfused DeepGEMM grouped-GEMM +
permute + separate activation path. This backend is not proposed as a
single-node speed win; its value is ecosystem parity + covering the
DeepEP-LL/batched EP path where FlashInfer is unavailable, plus DeepGEMM's raw
kernel headroom. Large-scale multi-node EP (DeepGEMM's target regime) is not
benchmarked here.

### Alternatives

- Keep unquantized bf16 MoE on Triton / FlashInfer only (status quo).
- DeepGEMM **MegaMoE** (fused, comm-overlapped) would be the fused competitor,
  but it is **SM100/Blackwell-only** (`csrc/apis/mega.hpp` dispatches only
  `arch_major == 10`), so it is not an option on Hopper and is out of scope here.

### Additional context

Prototype implemented and validated on 8×H200 (Hopper, CUDA 13) against a recent
`main`. Details, benchmarks and tests are in the accompanying PR.

title: [ROCm][Quark] Treat MTP/nextn draft layers as unquantized for NVFP4 checkpoints (e.g. GLM-5.1-NVFP4)
body:
## Purpose
Some NVFP4 Quark checkpoints (e.g. amd/GLM-5.1-NVFP4, amd/GLM-5.2-NVFP4)
ship their MTP/nextn speculative-decoding draft layers unquantized (bf16) but,
unlike the MXFP4 checkpoints handled by #46757, do NOT list those layers under
`exclude`. vLLM then allocates quantized experts/linears for the draft block and
crashes while loading the bf16 weights.

This PR detects the MTP/nextn draft-layer indices from the HF config
(`num_hidden_layers .. num_hidden_layers + num_nextn_predict_layers`) and routes
their MoE experts and linear projections through the unquantized methods,
without editing the checkpoint.

Note: this is orthogonal to #48886 (indexer `wk` per-channel FP8 dequant +
sparse-MLA metadata). The MTP-exclude logic in `quark.py` is not platform- or
scheme-specific, but so far it has only been validated on ROCm (AMD MI350,
gfx950 / MI35x family) with NVFP4 + MTP.

## Test Plan / Result
Served GLM-5.1-NVFP4 with MTP and ran GSM8K 5-shot via lm_eval
(local-completions endpoint). Tested on AMD MI350, TP=8; the fix targets the
gfx950 / MI35x family.

| Filter | exact_match |
| --- | --- |
| flexible-extract | 0.9507 |
| strict-match | 0.9515 |

No accuracy regression.

title: [DSv4 triton] Add a pure-Triton fp4 pack fallback so the mxfp4 indexer kernel
body:
This pull request refactors and extends the fp32-to-fp4 quantization logic in `fused_indexer_q.py` to support both CUDA and non-CUDA backends. The main change is to provide a pure-Triton implementation as a fallback for platforms without PTX support, improving portability and maintainability.

**Quantization logic improvements:**

* Renamed the original `fp32x2_to_fp4x2` function to `fp32x2_to_fp4x2_ptx` and introduced a new pure-Triton fallback implementation, `fp32x2_to_fp4x2_triton`, for non-CUDA platforms. The correct function is selected at runtime based on the platform.
* Added the `_encode_fp4_abs` helper function to encode the absolute value of `fp32` inputs into the 3-bit E2M1 magnitude code, matching the CUDA implementation's rounding behavior.

## Purpose
This pull request refactors the RMSNorm implementation in `fused_qk_rmsnorm.py` to improve code clarity and flexibility by extracting the normalization logic into a reusable helper function and allowing separate block sizes for Q and KV rows. The main logic for RMSNorm is now encapsulated in `_rmsnorm_row`, and the kernel and its caller have been updated to use this helper and to pass distinct block sizes for Q and KV.
