title: [Bug]: GLM-5.3-Flash: fp8 KV cache rejected by SM90 sparse MLA plan(), and the indexer prefill workspace is sized in tokens
body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

vLLM `main` at `98ed0856f` (right after #53906 landed), 2x H200 NVL (SM90), TP2,
CUDA 13.0, FlashInfer 0.6.18. Model: GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4
(`LibertAIDAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`), `--max-model-len 1048576`, MTP k=3, CUDA graphs on,
CPU offload connector with a 256 GiB region.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Two independent bugs hit on the same deployment. Both are in code that came in with
#53906; both are still on `main`.

**1. `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` cannot start on `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM90`.**

The fp8 KV cache is allocated as `uint8` storage and `run()` views it as
`float8_e4m3fn`, but `FlashInferMLASparseSM90Builder` hands `plan()` the storage dtype
(`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashinfer_mla_sparse_sm90.py`, the `_SM90State(...)`
construction). The wrapper rejects it:

```
ValueError: MLA kv_data_type torch.uint8 is not supported
```

Startup dies there. Dropping `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` avoids it at the cost of 1.78x less
KV capacity (2,532,577 tokens instead of 4,503,445 on this hardware).

**2. The indexer prefill workspace is sized in tokens, but its KV is pool-granular.**

`vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py:303` takes
`get_max_prefill_buffer_size(vllm_config)` as-is. That helper returns a token count
(`max_model_len * 40` entries of 132 bytes), while this indexer's spec carries
`compress_ratio == index_kpool` and `split_indexer_prefill_chunks()` is fed compressed
sequence lengths. `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/attention.py` already divides by
`compress_ratio` at the same call site.

At `--max-model-len 1048576` with `index_kpool = 4` this reserves ~5.16 GiB per GPU
during the memory profile and locks it for the process lifetime, straight out of the KV
budget. Right-sizing it here moves available KV memory from 29.44 GiB to 32.06 GiB and
the KV pool from 4,503,445 to 4,904,494 tokens, with needle retrieval on 1M-token
prompts unchanged at 4/4. Originally reported by @nood-co1 in the #53906 thread; #51252
fixes the neighbouring builder-side budget for DeepSeek and composes with this.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched open issues and PRs; #51252 covers the DeepSeek builder-side budget and
  #54743 covers offload group scoping, neither of these two call sites.

title: [Perf] Eliminate full-history reasoning scans for structured outputs
body:
## Purpose Structured-output constraints stay disabled until reasoning ends. Engine-based parsers currently find that boundary by reverse-scanning the full token history on every decode step—and at every draft position under speculative decoding. This makes the gate O(history) per check and O(n²) over a long reasoning generation. This PR derives safe, single-token reasoning-end IDs once per parser engine and scans only the new decode window. The existing monotonic `reasoning_ended` flag records the result, so no tracker or request lifecycle is added. Parsers without safely derivable IDs keep the legacy behavior. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Decode or draft window"] --> B{"Safe engine end-token IDs?"} B -->|yes| C["Scan new tokens
O(delta)"] B -->|no| D["Legacy full-history scan
O(history)"] C --> E{"Reasoning end found?"} D --> E E -->|yes| F["Open structured-output gate"] E -->|no| G["Keep gate disabled"] ``` ## Test plan ### 1. Microbenchmark `StructuredOutputManager.should_advance` timed exactly as the scheduler calls it — once per request per engine step, with reasoning still in progress. Same script on both branches. | Parser | Reasoning tokens | `main` | this PR | |---|---|---|---| | qwen3 | 2,000 | 197.46 µs | **0.52 µs** | | qwen3 | 16,000 | 1486.89 µs | **0.52 µs** | | qwen3 | 64,000 | 6006.92 µs | **0.52 µs** | | deepseek_v4 (real tokenizer) | 2,000 | 94.79 µs | **0.55 µs** | | deepseek_v4 (real tokenizer) | 16,000 | 743.79 µs | **0.55 µs** | | deepseek_v4 (real tokenizer) | 64,000 | 2999.24 µs | **0.55 µs** | | deepseek_v32 (**fallback control**) | 2,000 | 18.07 µs | 16.30 µs | | deepseek_v32 (**fallback control**) | 16,000 | 125.93 µs | 125.82 µs | | deepseek_v32 (**fallback control**) | 64,000 | 507.33 µs | 499.87 µs | Cost is flat across a 32× range of history length, not merely lower. The `deepseek_v32` fallback control is unchanged within noise at every length, which is the evidence that the legacy branch is untouched rather than merely believed to be. ### 2. Live serving performance (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 8×H100) Streaming requests at concurrency 32, `chat_template_kwargs: {"thinking": true}`, so all four conditions for the gate to run are satisfied. Identical workload and server config within each pair; only the branch differs. Configurations are **not** comparable to each other (MTP raises per-step latency by design, since each step drafts and verifies) — each row is its own A/B. | Config | metric | `main` | this PR | change | |---|---|---|---|---| | json_schema, no spec decode | TPOT p50 | 14.022 ms | **12.312 ms** | −12.2% | | | TPOT p99 | 19.818 ms | **16.297 ms** | −17.8% | | | throughput | 1541.7 chunk/s | **1934.4 chunk/s** | +25.5% | | | wall | 146.59 s | **115.63 s** | −21.1% | | json_schema + MTP | TPOT p50 | 43.105 ms | **17.966 ms** | **−58.3%** | | | TPOT p99 | 51.544 ms | **18.729 ms** | **−63.7%** | | | throughput | 549.4 chunk/s | **1483.1 chunk/s** | **+169.9%** | | | wall | 153.45 s | **56.88 s** | −62.9% | | structural_tag + MTP | TPOT p50 | 45.772 ms | **18.175 ms** | **−60.3%** | | | TPOT p99 | 46.430 ms | **18.321 ms** | −60.5% | | | throughput | 613.8 chunk/s | **1174.2 chunk/s** | +91.3% | | | wall | 143.41 s | **77.02 s** | −46.3% |

title: [Bugfix][EPLB] Reject unsafe dynamic weight updates
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Reject reloads and weight-update sessions for EPLB-managed models before they can change weights or session state.

## Claims

- Prevent checkpoint reloads from using stale expert placement after a rebalance.
- Prevent pending rebalance transfers from overwriting updated weights.
- Allow updates to a dense main or draft model when only the other model uses EPLB.

## Validation

The worker weight-transfer suite and scoped pre-commit hooks passed on this branch. Disabling the guard reproduces unsafe reload and update-session starts; dense-target controls still pass.

To run the related suites in a configured development environment:

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker
```

Earlier CPU loader/lifecycle reproductions showed incorrectly routed weights after a completed rebalance and old weights restored by a pending transfer. Those reproductions were not repeated after the rebase. Multi-GPU model validation is still needed; local tests used the pinned Humming dependency.

Upstream checks are stopped at contributor authorization; these local results do not establish a CI pass.

## Details

Checkpoint loading builds expert mappings from initial placement, while inference can use a newer EPLB map. Draining pending transfers leaves the completed-rebalance mismatch unresolved. The guard rejects updates before reload delegation or update-session mutation; callers needing updates must disable EPLB.

#59063 proposes synchronization and live expert mapping for DeepSeek V4.1 on NVIDIA. Generic loaders still need a safe live-layout reload, so it does not replace this guard. This conservative restriction also blocks that model-specific update path.

AI assistance was used for this change.

title: [Feature][Spec Decode] Add PARD-2 parallel draft model support with dual mode
body:
## Purpose

Add PARD-2 ([arXiv 2605.08632](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08632)) target-aligned parallel draft models as a speculative-decoding method, and fix a draft-input alignment bug that costs most of the acceptance on one of the three released checkpoints.

This builds directly on @ganeshr10's work in #49406 — the first seven commits here are his, unmodified. That PR has been open since July and its benchmarks were run on CPU; I'm one of the PARD-2 authors, and in validating it on GPU I found that the draft is fed a left-shifted sequence, which drops the row PARD-2 was trained to start from. The last two commits fix that and add regression tests. I'm opening this as a separate PR because the fix is not meaningful on its own (it only touches the code path #49406 introduces) and #49406 has had no maintainer review in six weeks; I'd be equally happy for this to land as #49406 plus my two commits, whichever maintainers prefer. Closes/supersedes #49406.

### What PARD-2 is, and why add it

PARD converts an autoregressive draft model into a parallel one at low training cost; PARD-2 adds target alignment, optimizing acceptance length rather than next-token accuracy, plus confidence-adaptive token weighting. Two properties are relevant for vLLM:

- **The draft is a small standalone LM, not a head grafted onto the target.** One draft serves a whole model family.
- **Dual mode.** The same checkpoint runs target-dependent (fusing target hidden states) or target-independent (plain parallel drafting). This PR already handles the fallback when the target's hidden size doesn't match what the draft was trained on.

Measured in vLLM on an RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell (greedy, 256 max tokens, 80 prompts per dataset, concurrency 1, PARD-2's own eval prompts), acceptance length / output tok/s. Baseline without speculation is 74 tok/s for both 8B targets:

| target | method | K | GSM8K | MATH-500 | HumanEval | MT-Bench |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | **PARD-2** `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B` | 15 | **7.72 / 398** | **8.09 / 417** | **8.72 / 443** | **4.02 / 214** |
| | DFlash `z-lab/Qwen3-8B-DFlash-b16` | 15 | 5.87 / 315 | 7.07 / 374 | 7.77 / 406 | 3.29 / 180 |
| | **PARD-2** | 5 | 4.86 / 255 | 5.00 / 262 | 5.09 / 266 | 3.44 / 183 |
| | EAGLE-3 `AngelSlim/Qwen3-8B_eagle3` | 5 | 2.69 / 150 | 2.53 / 141 | 2.85 / 158 | 2.24 / 125 |
| Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | **PARD-2** `amd/PARD2-Llama-3.1-8B` | 15 | **6.83 / 345** | **7.66 / 388** | **8.88 / 439** | **4.25 / 220** |
| | **PARD-2** | 9 | 6.06 / 310 | 6.37 / 326 | 7.12 / 358 | 4.05 / 210 |
| | DFlash `z-lab/LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct-DFlash-UltraChat` | 9 | 4.19 / 230 | 3.62 / 200 | 5.65 / 306 | 3.61 / 200 |
| | EAGLE-3 `yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B` | 5 | 3.64 / 197 | 3.13 / 171 | 4.16 / 224 | 3.34 / 181 |

EAGLE-3 here is vLLM's chain drafting (no tree) in non-thinking mode, and the AngelSlim Qwen3 draft may be tuned for thinking traces — read those rows as "what the released weights give you in vLLM today", not as the method's ceiling.

### The bug this fixes

PARD-2's draft input for position *t* is `embed(token[t]) + scale · target_proj(feat[t-1])` with `feat[-1] = 0`: the draft sees the whole sequence, starting at token 0 paired with a zero target feature.

The draft goes through the EAGLE input path, which left-shifts the token stream (`shift_input_ids=True`, `vllm/v1/spec_decode/utils.py`) while mapping hidden states unshifted. Row *i* of the draft input then holds `token[i+1] + feat[i]` — the correct pairing for *t ≥ 1*, but the *t = 0* row is gone. That is right for EAGLE, whose draft starts at token 1, and wrong for PARD-2.

That first row acts as an attention sink for the draft. How much its absence costs is checkpoint-dependent (HF reference, K=1 first-position acceptance, with vs. without token 0): Qwen3-8B 0.933 → 0.512, Llama-3.1-8B 0.937 → 0.917, Qwen3-14B 0.939 → 0.923.

**The fix**: an `ANCHOR` mode in `copy_and_expand_eagle_inputs_kernel`, used for PARD-2 only. A request whose first target position is 0 (its prefill) gets one extra leading row — its first token, position 0, zero hidden state — and its real rows shift by one so they keep true positions. Any other request instead gets one trailing junk row marked rejected, keeping the per-request row count uniform, and its draft `seq_len` grows by one for the anchor entry already in the draft KV cache. The CPU backend swaps this kernel for a C++ op that doesn't know about the anchor, so `cpu_triton_utils` gains a torch implementation of the same layout.

## Test Plan

```bash
# unit: anchored layout, and Triton ANCHOR path vs the CPU backend's torch path
pytest -v -s tests/v1/spec_decode/test_pard2_anchor_kernel.py

# e2e acceptance length (Llama case pre-existing, Qwen3-8B case added here)
pytest -v -s tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/acceptance_rates/pard2/

# serving
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B --max-model-len 4096 --no-enable-prefix-caching --port 8010 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 32 \
  --speculative-config '{"model": "amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B", "num_speculative_tokens": 15}'
```

Acceptance length is read from the `vllm:spec_decode_*` metrics; clients were greedy with `enable_thinking=false`.

## Test Result

Acceptance length before → after the fix, K=15, all three released checkpoints:

| target / draft | GSM8K | MATH-500 | HumanEval | MT-Bench |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B / `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B` | 1.99 → **7.72** | 2.23 → **8.09** | 2.06 → **8.72** | 1.59 → **4.02** |
| Qwen3-14B / `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-14B` | 7.42 → **7.63** | 7.99 → **8.12** | 8.51 → **8.71** | 3.95 → **4.02** |
| Llama-3.1-8B / `amd/PARD2-Llama-3.1-8B` | 6.08 → **6.83** | 6.77 → **7.66** | 7.79 → **8.88** | 3.82 → **4.25** |

All twelve improve; none regress.

Cross-checked against the PARD-2 reference implementation on the same prompts, and against the paper (Table 1, K=16, GSM8K):

| checkpoint | paper | reference impl | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 7.68 | 7.62 | 1.99 | **7.72** |
| Qwen3-14B | 7.65 | 7.61 | 7.42 | **7.63** |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 6.98 | 6.89 | 6.08 | **6.83** |

Across all twelve (model × dataset) settings the fixed path is within 0.25 of the reference implementation, except on the 20-problem MATH-500 subset (±0.5).

Mixed prefill/decode batches, Qwen3-8B GSM8K at concurrency 1 / 8 / 32: acceptance 7.72 / 7.70 / 7.52, throughput 398 / 2351 / 3231 tok/s.

### Target-independent mode

PARD-2's draft is a standalone small LM, so the same checkpoint can drive a target it was never trained for; this PR falls back to plain parallel drafting when the target's hidden size doesn't match what `target_proj` was trained on. To put a number on that, `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B` is used **unchanged** as a draft for **Qwen3-4B**, alongside drafts trained specifically for Qwen3-4B.

DFlash2 is not in this branch's base, so those rows ran on a current upstream-main nightly (`0.28.1rc1.dev19`). The `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` row was run on both builds and they agree within 0.12 (0.45 on the 20-problem MATH-500 subset), so the two groups are comparable. Same harness and settings as above; `acceptance / tok/s`.

**K = 15**

| build | draft | trained for Qwen3-4B? | GSM8K | MATH-500 | HumanEval | MT-Bench |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| this PR | **PARD-2 `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B`, TI** | no | **6.10 / 473** | 6.66 / 516 | 6.37 / 494 | **3.32 / 269** |
| this PR | PARD-1 `amd/PARD-Qwen3-0.6B` (parallel) | no | 6.06 / 466 | 6.01 / 464 | 6.10 / 465 | 3.37 / 267 |
| this PR | DFlash `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` | yes | 5.71 / 484 | **6.87 / 582** | **6.70 / 565** | 3.22 / 285 |
| main | DFlash `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` (build calibration) | yes | 5.83 / 504 | 6.42 / 557 | 6.70 / 575 | 3.21 / 290 |
| this PR | no speculation | — | — / 127 | | | |

**K = 8 / 7**, each DFlash2 checkpoint at its own trained block size, with PARD-2 at the same K:

| build | draft | trained for Qwen3-4B? | K | GSM8K | MATH-500 | HumanEval | MT-Bench |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| this PR | **PARD-2 `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B`, TI** | no | 8 | 5.27 / 412 | **5.43 / 424** | **5.29 / 409** | **3.19 / 255** |
| main | DFlash2 `RedHatAI/Qwen3-4B-speculator.dflash2` (b9) | yes | 8 | **5.36 / 455** | 5.29 / 460 | 4.73 / 412 | 3.08 / 275 |
| this PR | **PARD-2 `amd/PARD2-Qwen3-8B`, TI** | no | 7 | **5.02 / 394** | **5.23 / 407** | **5.04 / 387** | **3.16 / 251** |
| main | DFlash2 `shanjiaz/dflash2_qwen3_4b` (b8) | yes | 7 | 4.68 / 402 | 4.47 / 390 | 4.42 / 382 | 2.91 / 259 |

A draft that was never trained for this target holds its own against drafts that were: even on GSM8K and MATH-500 with DFlash2 at K=8, ahead of it on HumanEval and MT-Bench, and ahead of the other DFlash2 checkpoint on all four at K=7. DFlash2 is ~10% faster per token, its draft being 5 layers. Note both DFlash2 checkpoints are community-trained with `speculators` (z-lab has not released a 4B DFlash2) and were converted to the `dflash_config` layout to load, so read them as "DFlash2 as trained by the community", not as the method's ceiling.

## Notes for reviewers

- The two anchor commits touch `utils.py`, `llm_base_proposer.py` and `cpu_triton_utils.py` only; the ANCHOR path is a `tl.constexpr` branch, so EAGLE/DFlash/DSpark codegen is unchanged.
- `AutoWeightsLoader` lost its `skip_prefixes`/`skip_substrs` kwargs in #53106, so the PARD-2 draft would not load on current main; the last commit ports that call site the same way #53106 migrated the others.
- The per-dataset tables were measured before rebasing onto current main. After the rebase I re-ran GSM8K on the submitted tree end to end and reproduced it: acceptance 1.976 -> 7.618, throughput 109 -> 398 tok/s (previously 1.986 -> 7.715, 110 -> 398). Unit tests, the Triton-vs-CPU kernel comparison, and lint all pass on the submitted tree.
- Parts of this were written with Claude Code, per the AI-assistance policy in the contributing guide. The analysis, experiments and validation are mine.

title: [Bugfix][SM120] Scope sparse MLA warmup autotuning to attention
body:
## Purpose

The SM120 sparse-MLA warmup runs full-model dummy steps inside a FlashInfer tuning context. This PR changes three things:

- Tune only the sparse-MLA attention calls in those steps, not the GEMM/MoE kernels the steps also run.
- Refine the sparse-MLA cpb choice for each executable CUDA-graph capture bucket up to 64 tokens.
- On the legacy autotune path, run that tuning on every rank, not only the leader.

This builds on #55671, which landed the managed `autotune_v2` path and the legacy per-rank cache handling. The PR keeps both of #55671's paths and adds the three changes to them.

## Changes

Three commits on current main:

1. **Per-bucket cpb refinement.**
   - After the mixed-batch warmup triggers FlashInfer's SM120 sparse-MLA calibration, run one uniform-decode step per capture bucket so `refine_cpb` measures exactly the warmed shapes.
   - Bucket selection: sorted, unique capture sizes with `0 < tokens <= 64`, bounded by `max_num_reqs` × the decode query length and by the token budget. V2 runners need whole query-length multiples.
   - Microbatching: V1 microbatching is disabled for these steps; the warmup is skipped on V2 runners that use microbatching.
2. **Scope tuning to sparse MLA.**
   - Inside `autotune_sparse_mla_only(tune_context)`, FlashInfer's two sparse-MLA decode entry points run in a context built by `tune_context`; the rest of the model runs untuned.
   - The managed path builds `autotune_v2` contexts. The legacy leader builds plain `autotune()` contexts and loads/saves its cache file around the whole warmup, instead of in each call's context.
   - `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS` is honored on both paths.
3. **Every rank tunes on the legacy path.**
   - Until FlashInfer coordinates cache hits, the legacy path is what every multi-rank deployment uses (also multi-node, PP and elastic EP). On it, only the leader tuned and then shared its cache file.
   - FlashInfer's SM120 sparse-MLA calibration and `refine_cpb` don't live in that file. They measure the local device and persist under its device key, so non-leaders served heuristic cpb picks.
   - Every rank now tunes its own sparse calls; the leader still shares the cache file. No autotune process group is set, so ranks never block on each other's measurements.

## Update: rebased onto #55671 as merged

- Dropped this PR's earlier rewrite of the sparse warmup ("tune every rank, FlashInfer owns persistence", which removed the leader cache broadcast) in favor of #55671's two paths.
- The scoping, the bucket refinement and the every-rank fix are now applied to those paths: commit 3 above covers the legacy path; the managed path already tuned on every rank.
- `autotune_sparse_mla_only` now takes a context factory instead of `skip_ops`, so each path enters its own tuning context.
- #55671's sparse cache-selection test is adapted:
  - its stand-in scope enters the factory once per sparse call;
  - on the legacy path, every rank now enters the tuning context;
  - the leader now preloads its cache file.

## Tests

219 passed, CPU only (`tests/model_executor/test_*warmup*.py`, `tests/utils_/test_import_utils.py`):

```bash
python -m pytest tests/model_executor/test_*warmup*.py tests/utils_/test_import_utils.py
```

Coverage:
- bucket selection;
- the gates;
- sparse-only scoping on both paths, with the context each builds and the skip-ops;
- every-rank tuning on both paths;
- nested-scope restore after exceptions;
- rejection inside full-model tuning.

`pre-commit` passes on all changed files.

Earlier serving smoke tests (DeepSeek-V4 TP2; GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4 TP4 on RTX PRO 6000) predate this rebase and are not re-run here.

## Limitations

- Eager bucket warmup does not cover every speculative or CUDA-graph descriptor.
- No performance claim.

Developed with AI assistance; every changed line was reviewed and the tests above were run by the submitter.

title: [Bugfix][MoE] Warm up the Triton fused MoE GEMMs
body:
## Purpose

`fused_moe_kernel` is the expert GEMM whenever DeepGEMM declines the shape. The
dominant case is the `N <= 512` early-out in `_valid_deep_gemm`
(`experts/deep_gemm_moe.py`): a model with a small `moe_intermediate_size`
crosses that threshold as soon as TP is high enough, and from then on never uses
DeepGEMM. GLM-5.2-FP8 at TP=8 gives `w2 = (256, 6144, 256)`, i.e. `N=256`, so its
whole MoE stack runs on Triton for every request.

Nothing in the startup path compiles that kernel for the variants real batches
select. Two things vary with the token count `M`:

1. the tile config, chosen by `try_get_optimal_moe_config` from a tuned config
   file or `get_default_config`;
2. the 16-divisibility of `EM` and `num_valid_tokens`, which Triton attaches as
   a `tt.divisibility` attribute and keys separately.

Profiling and CUDA graph capture only reach a few of these combinations, so the
first request landing on an uncompiled one JIT-compiles mid-serving. Measured on
GLM-5.2-FP8 at TP=8, main compiles 4 distinct variants per rank during
inference (32 events across 8 ranks). With `--jit-monitor-mode=error` that is a
hard failure; with the default `warn` it is a latency spike.

## Changes

- New `vllm/model_executor/warmup/triton_moe_warmup.py`: walks the `M` values
  that can select a distinct tile config, pairs each with a neighbour that flips
  the 16-divisibility of `num_valid_tokens` so both variants compile, and runs
  the expert GEMMs through `TritonExperts.apply` once per value.
- Called from `kernel_warmup` inside the existing `enable_jit_warmup` block.

Design notes:

- Warmup drives `TritonExperts.apply` rather than reconstructing the ~30 kernel
  arguments. `invoke_fused_moe_triton_kernel` derives the strides, `EM`,
  `SWAP_AB` and the effective `BLOCK_SIZE_K` from the tensors it is handed, so
  going through the real path is the only way to guarantee the compiled key
  matches the serving key. A compile-only draft built on `TritonWarmupTensor`
  was discarded for that reason.
- Activations are quantized with `moe_kernel_quantize_input` using the layer's
  own `FusedMoEQuantConfig`, matching what the prepare step produces. When the
  MoE is unquantized this returns the input unchanged with a `None` scale.
- The companion `M` is chosen from the kernel's own predicate, not from `M`
  parity. `num_valid_tokens` is `M * top_k`, so `M + 1` does not always cross
  the 16-divisibility boundary: at `top_k=1` neither 24 nor 25 is divisible and
  one specialization would stay uncompiled. The search scans the neighbourhood
  for an `M` that flips the predicate, preferring larger `M` but falling back to
  smaller ones at the token budget, and yields no companion when `top_k` is a
  multiple of 16 (there the non-divisible class cannot exist).
- Routed expert ids are sampled from the global ids this rank owns
  (`expert_map >= 0`). `topk_ids` carries global ids, so sampling the local id
  range would leave every rank whose slice does not start at 0 with no valid
  ids at all -- `moe_align_block_size` maps them to `-1` and the GEMMs are
  skipped.
- MoE layers of one model share weight shapes, so one representative per
  `(w13, w2)` shape pair covers all of them (78 layers collapse to 1 on
  GLM-5.2).
- `M` is capped at the largest grid entry (4096); above it the tile config no
  longer changes, so warming the full token budget would only cost workspace
  memory.
- OOM while building warmup activations is caught and skips the remainder
  instead of failing startup.

## Why this is not a duplicate

- #42193 (`[Bugfix][V1][MoE] Warm up WNA16 MoE Triton kernels`, closed) targeted
  `fused_moe_kernel_gptq_awq` on the WNA16 path, proposing `do_not_specialize`
  plus a compile-only key contract. Different kernel, different quantization
  path, closed without merging.
- #47599 (closed) warmed the FlashInfer b12x NVFP4 MoE, a different backend.
- #53567 (`[7/N][warmup][DSv4] Migrate MoE execution and distributed kernels`,
  open) migrates the DSv4 top-k / fused router / MegaMoE prepare / fused batched
  / NVFP4 emulation / TRT-LLM LoRA kernels to the shared warmup contract. It does
  not touch `fused_moe_kernel` and adds nothing under `warmup/`, so the two do
  not overlap. See the note below on why this PR does not use that contract.
- On current main, `grep -rn "fused_moe_kernel" vllm/model_executor/warmup/`
  returns nothing; none of the modules under `warmup/` touch the Triton fused
  MoE path.
- Searches run: `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --search "moe warmup"`,
  `"triton moe warmup"`, `"fused_moe_kernel JIT"`, `"glm_moe_dsa"`.

On the shared warmup contract: `VllmJitKernel` / `JitWarmupRegistry` requires the
dispatch to be expressed as an AST-restricted pure expression (local assignments
plus `return self.CompileKey(...)`), while this kernel's key depends on 30+
tensor-derived arguments (strides, `EM`, `SWAP_AB`, and `BLOCK_SIZE_K` after the
`min(cfg_bsk, min(block_shape))` clamp). Rebuilding those by hand is easy to get
subtly wrong — a first draft did exactly that and produced keys that did not
match serving. Driving the real `apply()` mirrors the already-merged
`deep_gemm_warmup` and `b12x_warmup`.

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/test_triton_moe_warmup.py -v
SKIP=actionlint,shellcheck,clang-format,markdownlint,pip-compile,dockerfilelint \
  pre-commit run --files \
    vllm/model_executor/warmup/triton_moe_warmup.py \
    vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py \
    tests/model_executor/test_triton_moe_warmup.py
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files <same three files>
```

End-to-end on 8x H20-3e (SM90), GLM-5.2-FP8, TP=8, `--max-model-len 32768`,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 8192`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--block-size 64`,
`--jit-monitor-verbose` so every compilation is logged. Same three workloads
per build, run strictly one at a time:

1. prefill, 4.5k-token prompts, concurrency 32, 64 requests
2. decode, concurrency 32, 12 s warmup then a 40 s steady-state window
3. prefill, 31.5k-token prompts, concurrency 10, 10 requests (chunked)

## Test Result

Unit tests: 8 passed.

Lint: `ruff-check`, `ruff-format`, `typos`, `mypy-3.10` and `mypy-3.12` all pass.
(`actionlint` and the other non-Python hooks were skipped locally because
installing the `actionlint` Go binary needs network access this machine does not
have; the change is Python-only.)

Runtime JIT events reported by the JIT monitor across all three workloads
(8 ranks):

| build | `fused_moe_kernel` events | distinct variants per rank |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main | 32 | 4 (`BSM=16` and `BSM=64`, each for the w13 and w2 GEMM) |
| this PR | **0** | 0 |

Throughput on the same workloads:

| workload | main | this PR | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| prefill 4.5k x 32 | 3650.4 tok/s | 3650.0 tok/s | -0.01% |
| decode, 32 streams | 882.8 tok/s (27.59/stream) | 884.5 tok/s (27.64/stream) | +0.2% |
| prefill 31.5k x 10 | 3510.7 tok/s (p50 51.31 s, p90 89.55 s) | 3513.1 tok/s (p50 51.27 s, p90 89.49 s) | +0.07% |

Steady-state throughput is unchanged: this removes compile stalls, it is not a
throughput optimization.

Startup cost of the warmup: about 3 s for one weight shape (36 `M` values, all
ranks in parallel). For comparison, `deep_gemm_warmup` on the same machine runs
2139 steps.

How the divisibility half of the problem was identified, since it is not visible
in the Triton signature (which only carries `i32`/`i64`) but in the attrs
descriptor: with the tile config pinned, launching `M=2048` compiles and `M=2050`
hits the cache, but `M=2049` compiles again and `M=2051` then hits the cache. The
second compilation's attrs lack `tt.divisibility=16` on argument indices 12 and
13, which are `EM` and `num_valid_tokens`. A grid built from the tuned
config-file keys alone leaves one variant uncompiled, which is why each grid
entry is paired with a neighbour that crosses the boundary.

The predicate is `num_valid_tokens = M * top_k`, not `M` itself (raised in
review). Re-probing at `top_k=1` shows it directly: `M=24` (24, not divisible)
compiles, `M=25` (25) is a cache hit, and only `M=32` (32) compiles the variant
whose attrs carry index 13. At `top_k=8` the pairing is unaffected, so the
numbers above stand.

## Not covered by this PR

- The residual `BuildPrefillChunkMetadataKernel.kernel` events on the 31.5k
  workload (16 with this PR, 24 on main). Those come from a separate gap in that
  kernel's own `get_warmup_keys`, where `query_slice_start=WarmupIntRange(0, 2)`
  only supplies `0` and `1` and so misses the same non-divisible specialization
  class.
- Unquantized bf16 MoE was verified by code-path analysis only, not measured:
  `moe_kernel_quantize_input` returns the input unchanged with a `None` scale when
  `quant_dtype is None`, and the config falls into the `get_default_config` else
  branch (`block_m=128` for `M>512`, still covered by the 4096 grid cap). Happy
  to measure it on a real bf16 MoE model if a reviewer wants that before merging.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for this change (investigation, patch, tests, and this
description). All measurements above come from real runs on the machine
described, and I have reviewed every changed line.

title: [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next] Remove torch.compile for NVIDIA implementation
body:
## Purpose

Fixes #54688
- Remove `@support_torch_compile` as model decorator
- Remove all custom op registrations, which were meant to bypass torch.compile inspection: `qwen4_exp_compute_ple_ngram_ids`, `qwen4_exp_ple_short_conv`, `qwen4_exp_qsa_with_output`
- Eager break insertion points (**IMPORTANT**): 


Another benefit of removing torch.compile is that now we can load FP8 ckpt on a single GB300. Previously, torch.compile attempts to autotune the embedding op, causing an extra ngram table tensor that consumes ~50GB -> OOM. Removing torch.compile naturally removes this activation peak.

## Test Plan

Model | MTP tokens | GSM8K | MMMU-Pro
-- | -- | -- | --
BF16 | 0 | 96.85% | 77.23%
BF16 | 3 | 96.66% | 77.57%
FP8 | 0 | 96.74% | 76.99%
FP8 | 3 | 96.82% | 75.61%

## E2E perf result

Model | Concurrency | Output tok/s | Throughput delta | TTFT ms | TPOT ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 | 1 | 303.6 → 288.9 | -4.83% | 160.62 → 162.63 | 3.309 → 3.288 |
| BF16 | 4 | 759.8 → 742.6 | -2.26% | 195.19 → 188.14 | 5.020 → 5.259 |
| BF16 | 16 | 1582.2 → 1663.9 | +5.16% | 206.47 → 202.19 | 9.469 → 9.252 |
| BF16 | 64 | 3052.7 → 3123.3 | +2.31% | 231.19 → 222.05 | 20.354 → 20.173 |
| FP8 | 1 | 240.5 → 232.9 | -3.14% | 219.70 → 217.63 | 4.093 → 4.149 |
| FP8 | 4 | 642.8 → 631.8 | -1.72% | 238.66 → 238.27 | 5.858 → 6.150 |
| FP8 | 16 | 1345.7 → 1390.0 | +3.30% | 252.93 → 252.33 | 11.280 → 10.990 |
| FP8 | 64 | 2076.9 → 2066.3 | -0.51% | 308.32 → 309.84 | 30.071 → 30.199 |

Generally the results look noisy, so I don't think removing torch.compile right now is significantly worse. Future manual fusion will further improve perf.

## Test Result

title: [Model] Add DeepGEMM MegaMoE support to GLM with compressed-tensors MXFP4
body:
## Purpose

Extend the `deep_gemm_mega_moe` backend to DeepSeek-derived GLM model
implementations without changing compressed-tensors NVFP4 weights into a
different FP4 encoding.

This change:

- adds MegaMoE adapters for DeepSeek V2/V3.2 and GLM-5-next, including their
  MTP paths;
- supports unquantized BF16 and checkpoint-native MXFP4 expert weights;
- rejects compressed-tensors NVFP4 expert checkpoints instead of performing a
  lossy NVFP4-to-E2M1/UE8M0 conversion;
- preserves grouped routing, deferred-reduction, and sequence-parallel
  semantics;
- puts the reusable expert implementation in a shared module; DSv4 and Kimi K3
  model files and the existing DSv4 tests are unchanged;
- covers the adapters, checkpoint-format selection, and explicit NVFP4
  rejection with focused tests.

## Duplicate-work check

This does not duplicate the open related work:

- #40833 introduces the general DeepGEMM MegaMoE kernel integration; it does
  not provide these GLM/DeepSeek model adapters.
- #42844 experiments with FP4 activation dispatch for DeepSeek V4 using an
  external DeepGEMM package; this PR uses the existing FP8-activation/FP4-weight
  MegaMoE path.
- #53527 targets FP8 DeepSeek V4 on SM90; this PR adds model integration for
  MegaMoE on SM100.

## Test plan and results

Local checks after splitting the shared implementation from DSv4:

```text
pre-commit run
# all hooks passed on the staged split

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/test_deep_gemm_mega_moe.py tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_mega_moe.py -q
# 11 passed, 29 skipped (CUDA/SM100 unavailable locally)
```

The CPU tests cover checkpoint-format selection, NVFP4 rejection, mocked
BF16/MXFP4 loading and finalization, expert mapping, and deferred-reduction
scaling. Non-compressed-tensors quantization configurations are not rejected
by the MXFP4 format predicate.

DSv4 migration is kept separately on
[feature/dsv4-shared-megamoe](https://github.com/tlrmchlsmth/vllm/tree/feature/dsv4-shared-megamoe),
stacked on this PR. No follow-up PR has been opened. Kimi K3 file changes are
omitted from both branches.

The following results predate this extraction; no new GPU or model-accuracy
evaluation was run for the split.

GB200 kernel validation performed earlier on the PR:

- Random FP8 x FP4 MegaMoE, four ranks: relative L2 0.0252-0.0276 and cosine
  similarity greater than 0.9996.
- Exact GLM topology (EP8 across two GB200 nodes, hidden size 6144,
  intermediate size 2048, 256 experts, top-k 8): all ranks produced finite
  outputs.

MXFP4 performance validation used `RedHatAI/GLM-5.2-MXFP4xMXFP8` on two GB200
nodes with TP8/EP8. At concurrency 64, DeepGEMM MegaMoE reached 927.8 output
tokens/s, compared with 562.2 for TP8, 540.2 for EP8 with AGRS and CUTLASS
MXFP4, and 237.8 for EP8 with DeepEP-v2 and CUTLASS MXFP4. All 2,269 recorded
requests across the four runs completed successfully. These are single-run
client-side measurements, not repeated trials; Prometheus/DCGM series were not
exported.

No NVFP4 model evaluation is claimed: compressed-tensors NVFP4 is deliberately
unsupported by this PR because conversion into DeepGEMM's different FP4
representation showed unacceptable source-level error.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used to implement, debug, test, and draft this change.
Human review of the latest split and relevant GPU/model validation are pending.

title: [Bug][ROCm] GLM-5.3-Flash kpool 32-page split (hybrid block_size=1152) GPU Memory access fault on MTP decode
body:
ROCm gfx942, GLM-5.3-Flash, hybrid KDA + MLA + kpool indexer: after the hybrid aligner lands on `cache_config.block_size = 1152`, the kpool indexer virtually splits 288-entry storage into **32-entry** paged-MQA pages. MTP decode then dies with `Memory access fault by GPU node-N` (one `VllmWorker` abort → engine down). Not OOM.

Line numbers below are **vLLM `main` @ `156050598eea0bb1124b9c106b22ba4a8c56f82a`** (2026-09-04). Runtime numbers are from a gfx942 serving image derived from #53906 plus later local patches; they are labelled as such.

## Environment (runtime)

- 8× MI325X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.3
- GLM-5.3-Flash, TP=4, MTP `num_speculative_tokens=2`
- Hybrid KDA + MLA + kpool indexer (`index_kpool = 4`)
- Serving image: #53906-era tree. Crash B already included the V2 slot-mapping `in_range` guard from #54296.

## Symptom

Two serving aborts on 2026-09-03, same family:

- Crash A (03:41Z): ~41054 computed tokens, first MTP decode after that prefill. Image did **not** yet have the #54296 V2 guard.
- Crash B (09:18Z): 5-way mixed batch (4 MTP decode + one 2304-token chunked prefill). `new_block_ids` around **3809–3813**. Prefix-cache hit ~93%, KV usage ~4.25%. Image **already had** the #54296 V2 guard.

Banner is `Memory access fault by GPU node-N` → that rank’s `VllmWorker` exits → engine down. Not OOM. An aiter GEMM-shape miss in the same logs is not sufficient (same shape had been served earlier without abort). `scheduled_spec_decode_tokens=[-1,-1]` is the async placeholder, not the address.

## Why 1152 becomes a 32-page split

`PAGED_MQA_PAGE_SIZES = (32, 64)` (`vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py:35`).

`Glm5NextIndexerCache.get_kv_cache_spec` (`vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/attention.py:145-152`; there is no `amd/attention.py` sibling) picks the virtual page as:

- native if `storage_block_size <= 64`
- 64 if `storage_block_size % 64 == 0`
- **else 32**

On this host the hybrid mamba aligner set `block_size = 1152`. With `index_kpool = 4`:

`1152 / 4 = 288`, `288 > 64` and `288 % 64 != 0` → **page_size = 32**.

That is allowed by the assert at `attention.py:136-137` (only requires a multiple of 32). It is exactly the fallback the comment at `attention.py:132-134` describes as “virtually split”.

## CUDA already avoids this on sm120; ROCm does not align at all

Hybrid padding is applied in `Platform._align_hybrid_block_size` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py:927-929`):

```python
indexer_align = cls._get_indexer_block_alignment(vllm_config)
if indexer_align:
    attn_block_size = indexer_align * cdiv(attn_block_size, indexer_align)
```

`CudaPlatform._get_indexer_block_alignment` (`vllm/platforms/cuda.py:414-431`) returns `index_kpool * min(PAGED_MQA_PAGE_SIZES)` (= 128 for kpool=4), except **sm120**, where it already uses `max` (= 256) so the split lands on 64 not 32. The comment at `cuda.py:427-429` is the same 32-vs-64 issue.

`RocmPlatform` (`vllm/platforms/rocm.py:498`) does **not** override `_get_indexer_block_alignment`. It inherits `Platform`’s default (`interface.py:767-775`), which returns `None` and documents that “Other platforms impose no extra constraint.” So on ROCm the `if indexer_align:` branch never runs, and hybrid GLM stays on 1152 → 32-page.

Even CUDA’s non-sm120 `min` path is a no-op for 1152 (`1152 % 128 == 0`), so 1152 would still 32-page-split there. We did not measure a CUDA abort; the hard GPU fault we hit is ROCm.

## Suggested fix

Give `RocmPlatform` the same alignment CUDA already uses on sm120:

```python
@classmethod
def _get_indexer_block_alignment(cls, vllm_config: "VllmConfig") -> int | None:
    index_kpool = getattr(
        vllm_config.model_config.hf_text_config, "index_kpool", None
    )
    if not index_kpool or index_kpool <= 1:
        return None
    from vllm.utils.deep_gemm import PAGED_MQA_PAGE_SIZES
    return int(index_kpool) * max(PAGED_MQA_PAGE_SIZES)
```

On this model that turns 1152 → 1280. Then `1280 / 4 = 320` and `320 % 64 == 0` → native **64-entry** pages.

Local boot after that override (same host, MTP still on):

```
Setting attention block size to 1280 tokens
kpool-write: kv_cache shape=(42810, 64, 132) stride=(8448, 132, 1)
             contiguous=True page_size=64
paged-mqa:   KVBlockSize=64 n_blocks=42810 stride0=8448
             i32_limit_block=254200 overflow_layout=False
```

Indexer cache is contiguous (not the DeepSeek-V4 packed stride-1e6 layout). int32 `buffer_load` overflow is not this GLM layout (`overflow_layout=False`). Mamba page padding rose 6.27% → 18.08%; KV pool still ~10.77M tokens at `max_model_len=1000000`.

## Verified

- Hybrid `block_size=1152` → storage 288 → 32-page split, measured on the serving image (2026-09-04).
- Crash B already had the #54296 V2 `in_range` guard and still aborted, so that PR is not this fault.
- After aligning to `index_kpool * max(PAGED_MQA_PAGE_SIZES)`, boot log shows 1280 / `page_size=64` / contiguous. Replay: unique ~134k-token MTP request, plus mixed concurrency=5; **0** `Memory access fault`.
- On current `main` @ `156050598eea`: CUDA helper is `cuda.py:414-431` (sm120 already `max`); `RocmPlatform` still has no override (grep of `rocm.py` at that sha: 0 hits for `_get_indexer_block_alignment` / `PAGED_MQA` / `index_kpool`); `attention.py:145-152` still falls back to 32 when `storage % 64 != 0`.

The local serving image that stopped aborting also carried defensive store-masks / block-id clamps in the kpool write and paged-MQA helpers. Those were **not** A/B-isolated from the alignment change, so this report only claims the layout gap and that the 64-page image no longer faulted on replay.

## Not verified / not claimed

- HIP kernel name of the aborting launch. We did **not** recapture Crash A/B with `HIP_LAUNCH_BLOCKING` on the old tag; MTP decode is the scheduler step, not a named kernel.
- Repro on vanilla `main` (no #53906-era local image). The missing `RocmPlatform` override **is** on `main`; the 1152 hybrid number is from our serving image.
- CUDA abort for the same 1152 → 32-page geometry.
- Whether #54359’s “backend advertises `MultipleOf(16)`, no kernel-granular block table” is required for this abort. Different symptom (that issue is silent overwrite / fluent text; this is a GPU fault).

## Not a duplicate of

- **#54359** (open): ROCm indexer **silently overwrites** its own KV because the backend advertises a kernel block size the kernels do not use. Nothing crashes. This report is a hard `Memory access fault` from the 32-page split of a 1152 hybrid block.
- **#54296** (open): V2 slot-mapping `in_range`. Necessary, and Crash B already had it.
- **#53906** (merged 2026-09-03): GLM-5.3-Flash support, including the CUDA helper above. The ROCm platform still returns `None` for indexer alignment.
- **#52109** and [ROCm/aiter#4774](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/4774) (closed): DeepSeek-V4 packed indexer / gluon int32 offsets past 2 GiB. Different model and symptom (silent zero logits vs a GPU fault). This GLM indexer is contiguous (`overflow_layout=False`).

Happy to re-run on gfx942 against a PR that adds the `RocmPlatform` override.

title: [ROCm][Spec Decode] Let metadata builders declare multi-step support
body:
## Purpose

Fixes #53983.

ROCm multi-step speculative decoding currently checks generated attention metadata against a centralized tuple in `SpecDecodeBaseProposer`. That tuple requires proposer-side imports for every supported backend and has repeatedly missed valid metadata types.

This change:

- adds a fail-closed `supports_multi_step_drafting` capability to `AttentionMetadataBuilder`;
- moves existing ROCm allowlist entries to declarations on their corresponding builders;
- opts in FlashAttention and the QSA side-cache builder used by Qwen3.8-Flash-Next;
- derives MLA support from query-length support and rejects AITER FlashAttention when shuffle KV cache lacks a general multi-token fallback;
- shares one backend-level validation path between the base proposer and Step3.5; and
- removes the proposer-side metadata imports and optional-backend discovery.

The runtime gate remains ROCm-only, preserving behavior on other platforms while replacing the hand-maintained type registry.

Before submission, I searched open PR titles and bodies for `#53983`, `allowed_attn_types`, `attention metadata allowlist`, and `multi-step drafting`. I found no PR implementing this capability refactor.

AI assistance was used to inspect the codebase, implement the change, and run validation. I reviewed every changed line and understand the implementation and tests.

## Test Plan

```bash
git diff --check
pre-commit run ruff-check --files <changed files>
pre-commit run ruff-format --files <changed files>
pre-commit run mypy-3.10 --files <changed Python files>
PYTHONPATH=$PWD python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_llm_base_proposer.py -q
```

The unit tests cover the fail-closed default, rejection and acceptance on ROCm, unchanged behavior on non-ROCm platforms, MLA query-length capability derivation, and the AITER shuffle KV cache guard.

## Test Result

- `git diff --check`: passed
- `ruff-check`: passed
- `ruff-format`: passed
- `mypy-3.10`: passed
- `tests/v1/spec_decode/test_llm_base_proposer.py`: 8 passed

ROCm hardware end-to-end testing was not available locally. No model evaluation was run because this change does not alter model outputs, accuracy, or serving behavior for already-supported backends; it refactors the support gate and adds the two metadata builders identified in #53983.

---
<details>
<summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary>

- [x] The purpose of the PR, including the issue it resolves.
- [x] The test plan and commands are provided.
- [x] Test results and hardware limitations are provided.
- [x] No documentation update is needed for this internal capability refactor.
</details>

## September 23 Maintenance

Rebased onto upstream `157bcb7c4896`. The conflict resolution preserves both new DeepSeek V4 ROCm `get_cudagraph_support` methods and the original builder capability flags; it does not change the capability design.

Validation in an existing uv-managed Python 3.12 environment:

```bash
<venv>/bin/python -m pytest --noconftest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_llm_base_proposer.py -q
<venv>/bin/pre-commit run --from-ref HEAD^ --to-ref HEAD
git diff --check HEAD^ HEAD
```

Results: 8 tests passed, all applicable pre-commit hooks passed (including Ruff, Mypy, and test tethering), and the whitespace check passed. `--noconftest` bypasses repository-wide fixtures. These are focused CPU-side capability tests; no ROCm end-to-end or model evaluation was performed in this maintenance run.

title: [Bug]: Qwen3.8 + DSpark + streaming json_schema can desync XGrammar and emit 250k trailing spaces with HTTP 200
body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Output collected with the bundled vLLM collect_env.py</summary>

~~~text

Linux kernel: 6.8.0-137-generic

vLLM: 0.27.1
vLLM build commit: 6e448d0ea9bf3d88d898b65449ca6dc2aec170ac
Base image tag reported by the image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1-ubuntu2404
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 13.0
CUDA runtime: 13.0.88
CUDA image version: 13.0.2
Transformers: 5.15.0
Triton: 3.7.1
flashinfer-python: 0.6.16.post3
NumPy: 2.2.6

nvidia-nccl-cu13: 2.30.7

GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
NVIDIA driver: 580.173.02
CUDA architecture reported by collect_env.py includes 12.0
CPU: AMD EPYC 7302 16-Core Processor, 2 sockets, 64 logical CPUs
~~~

The output above is from the container that served the failing request. Very long CPU flag/vulnerability lines were omitted because they are unrelated; full non-secret collect_env.py output can be provided if needed.
</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary

With Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 served by vLLM 0.27.1 using the Qwen3 reasoning parser, streaming OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, strict response_format.type=json_schema with a top-level array schema, and DSpark speculative decoding K=7, XGrammar repeatedly logged Failed to advance FSM.

Most calls completed normally, but one call returned HTTP 200 with an incomplete JSON array followed by 249,698 whitespace characters. The vLLM container remained healthy and did not restart.

This looks related to #52852, #53181, #53777 and the accepted-block validation discussed in #52452, but this report adds a separately observed environment and a preserved client-visible failure mode: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, DSpark K=7, Qwen3 reasoning, explicit JSON Schema array, concurrent streaming, and a roughly 250k-character whitespace tail.

## Related issues / PRs already checked

- #43338 appears to be the same broad structured-output/speculative-decoding family, but focuses on multi-token GPT-OSS reasoning boundaries and reports Qwen3 as its working control.
- #52852 is the closest prior report: Qwen3.8 NVFP4 + streaming + XGrammar with token 271 FSM failures.
- #53181 reports recurrence after the fix referenced when #52852 was closed.
- #53777 reports a similar failure with DFlash2 and json_object.
- #52805 stops XGrammar token batches at grammar termination.
- #52452 validates speculative accepted blocks before commit, explicitly covers reasoning-boundary/grammar-termination invariants, and mentions DSpark K5 qualification.

Please close this as a duplicate if one of those fully covers this path. I am filing it because this is a new DSpark K7 + json_schema top-level array reproduction with a saved malformed response and detailed runtime statistics.

## Effective server launch

The private registry hostname is omitted. The container reports the upstream base tag shown in the environment section. The effective vLLM command was:

~~~bash
vllm serve /model/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-unsloth --served-model-name /model/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 --language-model-only --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-prefix-caching --gpu-memory-utilization 0.55 --port 80 --max-model-len 262144 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-num-seqs 12 --max-num-batched-tokens 24576 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"/model/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark-RadixArk","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
~~~

The startup wrapper maps the draft model architecture name DSparkDraftModel to Qwen3DSparkModel before exec'ing vllm serve. No vLLM Python source files are patched.

## Request shape

The real extraction text is private, so it is redacted below. This is the exact API/options/schema shape, but not yet a deterministic public minimal prompt:

~~~python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://<vllm-endpoint>/v1", api_key="<redacted>")

response_format = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "json_schema": {
        "name": "business_database_extraction",
        "strict": True,
        "schema": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "field_key": {"type": "string"},
                    "value": {"type": "string"},
                    "chunk_id": {"type": "string"},
                    "confidence": {
                        "type": "number",
                        "minimum": 0,
                        "maximum": 1,
                    },
                },
                "required": [
                    "field_key",
                    "value",
                    "chunk_id",
                    "confidence",
                ],
                "additionalProperties": False,
            },
        },
    },
}

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="/model/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Return only JSON matching the supplied schema."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "<redacted private extraction text>"},
    ],
    max_tokens=25000,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_p=0.95,
    presence_penalty=0.5,
    stream=True,
    stop=[],
    reasoning_effort="medium",
    response_format=response_format,
    extra_body={
        "top_k": 20,
        "repetition_penalty": 1.0,
        "chat_template_kwargs": {
            "enable_thinking": True,
            "preserve_thinking": False,
        },
    },
)
~~~

No tools were requested in these calls. The top-level array schema was accepted by vLLM and normally produced valid arrays in the other calls.

## Reproduction workload

- 10 application-level runs
- concurrency: 2
- each run split the same request into 3 model calls (12, 12 and 5 expected items)
- one downstream repair call after the malformed result
- 31 total model calls in the test
- 30 primary calls used the same private source text and field definitions

The failure was intermittent: 29 primary calls were parseable; one primary call was malformed.

## Client-visible failure

The anomalous application run took 646.055 seconds. The other nine runs took 60.406 to 69.917 seconds.

For the failing second batch:

- reasoning_content length: 3,201 characters
- no literal <thinking> or </thinking> tags
- no Markdown code fences
- response_content length: 250,070 characters
- response_content.rstrip() length: 372 characters
- trailing whitespace: 249,698 characters
- the first 3 array items were complete
- the fourth item stopped immediately after the beginning of its value string
- no chunk_id, confidence, closing object/array, or remaining 8 expected items followed

Sanitized shape of the response:

~~~json
[
  {"field_key":"f13","value":"<redacted>","chunk_id":"<redacted>","confidence":0.98},
  {"field_key":"f14","value":"<redacted>","chunk_id":"<redacted>","confidence":0.95},
  {"field_key":"f15","value":"<redacted>","chunk_id":"<redacted>","confidence":0.99},
  {"field_key":"f16","value":"<redacted prefix>"
<249698 trailing whitespace characters>
~~~

Strict JSON parsing therefore failed. A later application-level repair call returned only 3 of the 12 requested items; that partial-repair acceptance is a separate downstream completeness bug, not the cause of the original malformed vLLM response.

## Server logs from the same test window

During the test window, 20 distinct request IDs emitted backend_xgrammar.py:162 Failed to advance FSM. A representative sequence was:

~~~text
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 271. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 271. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 71093. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 271. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 71093. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 271. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 4566. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 220. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 16. Please file an issue.
ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-ac42b275cf469617-8f354a4e for tokens 60. Please file an issue.
[grammar_matcher.cc:612] Warning: The matcher has terminated after accepting the stop token, but is trying to accept new token with id 198.
~~~

That representative request later completed with HTTP 200. Speculative-decoding metrics were active (K=7; average draft acceptance was approximately 51.8% to 59.7%). There was no OOM and the container restart count remained zero.

Important correlation limitation: our client logs did not retain vLLM request IDs. The FSM errors and malformed response are confirmed in the same isolated test window, but I cannot prove that the representative request ID above is the exact malformed client call.

## Expected behavior

A strict json_schema request should either:

1. return JSON that validates against the schema, or
2. terminate with an explicit request/stream error.

It should not return HTTP 200 with a truncated JSON array and hundreds of thousands of whitespace characters. Once the grammar matcher accepts its stop token, later speculative tokens should not advance or corrupt the FSM.

## Controls and current status

- I have not yet run this exact workload with speculative decoding disabled.
- I have not yet tested a build containing #52452.
- I have not reproduced this through Transformers because the observed failure is in vLLM's streaming structured-output/speculative-decoding integration rather than model semantic quality.
- The prompt-level public minimal reproduction is still pending because the source text is confidential and the failure is intermittent.

Even if top-level array schemas are considered unsupported for this combination, the server currently accepts them and succeeds on most calls; an unsupported combination should fail validation explicitly rather than emit malformed output with HTTP 200.

## Questions

1. Is vLLM 0.27.1 expected to contain all fixes from #52805 for this execution path?
2. Does #52452 address this exact DSpark K7 + Qwen3 reasoning + XGrammar failure mode?
3. Is DSpark speculative decoding with streaming reasoning and strict json_schema currently supported, or should vLLM reject this combination?
4. Would maintainers prefer the full redacted malformed response and complete collect_env.py output in a follow-up attachment?

All private endpoints, credentials, database/table/file names, and business text have been removed from this report.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Bugfix][Kernel] Fix top-k selection when the radix threshold bin overflows the smem stash
body:
# Summary

## Purpose

The radix-select top-k paths used by the DSA sparse-attention indexers (`persistent_topk` / `cooperative_topk` / `top_k_per_row`) stash the stage-1 coarse threshold bin in shared memory before refinement. When that bin holds
more candidates than the stash can take, candidates beyond capacity were silently dropped in atomic arrival order — they never reached refinement, so the selected set could differ from `torch.topk` on rows with tied or tightly clustered scores. Related latent issues on the same paths: selection scalars were only initialized inside the threshold-finder branch (stale shared-memory consumption across rows of the persistent loop), and stash/selection stores were unguarded.

Fixed in all four selection paths:

| path | stash |
|---|---|
| `histogram_2048_topk` (decode, seq_len <= 8192) | 3708 |
| `histogram_256_topk` (medium, seq_len <= 32768) | 4096 |
| `FilteredTopKUnifiedKernel` (batch > 32) | 16384 |
| `histogram_4096_topk` (short path, tie buffer) | TopK |

* An oversized threshold bin now descends the remaining FP32 key bytes (24 -> 16 -> 8 -> 0) until the participant set fits the stash; a capacity clip only happens after full-key equality, where the remaining candidates are exact ties and any subset is a valid selection.
* Selection-state scalars are reset unconditionally, before the finder; a no-finder round degenerates to a bounded path instead of consuming stale state.
* Every stash and selection store is guarded by its capacity; an underfilled selection slot emits `-1` instead of a stale index.
* `histogram_2048_topk` published the threshold-bin population by reading `histo[threshold]` — which aliases `bufs[0]` (`histo = decode_smem`, `bufs[0] = decode_smem + 768`) in the same barrier interval as the collection loop's writes. The finder thread now publishes the count from its register into the unused scalar slot `sPOP`.

Trigger condition (before the fix): coarse-bin population > stash, i.e. strongly tied scores (e.g. relu-weighted fp8 dot products, quantized/pooled logits). Not reached by every deployment — measured on GLM-5.3-Flash indexer
logits — but any DSV3.2/V4 sparse-MLA, Qwen4-exp QSA, or GLM kpool workload with heavy ties can hit it.

Concept originates from the SGLang fix for the same class of bug [sglang#37625](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37625); this is an independent port to vLLM's kernels (the Xid 31 shared-memory overrun reported there does not reproduce in vLLM — vLLM's stash stores were already capacity-guarded; the selection divergence was).

## Test Plan

```bash
# Regression suite incl. new oversized-bin cases (tight clusters,
# clusters separating at each key byte, all-equal rows, state reuse across
# rows, per-kernel-path coverage), exact value comparison vs torch.topk:
pytest tests/kernels/test_top_k_per_row.py -q

# Differential harness: rows 6/36 x lengths 700..80000 x 6 score
# distributions (gaussian, relu-dot, pooled-relu, quantized, tight cluster,
# all-equal), value-multiset comparison vs torch.topk at tolerance 0:
python <path to harness>/diff_topk.py 512   # 2048  and 4096
```

## Test Result

* `pytest tests/kernels/test_top_k_per_row.py -q`: **189 passed, 19 skipped** (H100, B200 CUDA 13.0).
* Differential harness: **78/78 shapes match `torch.topk` exactly** (tolerance 0) on post-fix builds — the fix changes selection only on rows whose threshold bin overflows, which were wrong before; realistic distributions are bit-identical.
* No model-eval delta expected on GLM-5.3-Flash serving; GPQA/AIME scores outputs are unchanged by this patch.

title: [ROCm] gfx950 top-k policy is gated on topK==1024, leaving index_topk=2048 models (GLM-5.x) on the generic 10-way split
body:
## Summary

The measured gfx950 policy for the sparse-attention indexer's top-k, added in #52882, is gated on `topK == 1024`. Models with `index_topk: 2048` — GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3 — never reach it and fall back to the generic `multipleBlocksPerRowConfig = 10` with 512 threads per split block.

On MI355X that is the wrong choice for **every shape we measured**. A policy calibrated for `topK == 2048` gives a median 25 % and up to 64 % reduction in kernel time, with no shape getting slower and identical results.

## Where

`csrc/libtorch_stable/sampler.cu`, `top_k_per_row_decode`:

```cpp
const bool useGfx950DeviceLengthAwareTopK1024 =
    topK == 1024 && numRows > 64 && numRows <= 256 && gfx950;   // ~line 754
const bool useGfx950TopK1024 =
    topK == 1024 && numRows <= 64 && gfx950;                    // ~line 793
int multipleBlocksPerRowConfig = 10;                            // everything else
```

## Why the gap is larger, not smaller, at topK=2048

The merge kernel walks `B * topK` candidates in a **single** block per row:

```cpp
vllm::topKPerRowDecode<1024, true, false, true>
    <<<numRows, 1024, ...>>>( ..., multipleBlocksPerRowConfig * topK, ... );
```

At topK=1024 with B=10 that is 10 240 candidates; at topK=2048 it is **20 480**. The cost #52882 set out to remove is twice as large for the models that do not get the fix.

rocprofv3, 4 rows / 2 000 active columns, MI355X, GLM-5.3 (`index_topk: 2048`):

| kernel | grid | median |
|---|---|---|
| `topKPerRowDecode<1024,true,false,true>` (merge) | 4 × **1** | **95.4 µs** |
| `topKPerRowDecode<512,true,true,false>` (split) | 4 × 10 | 5.0 µs |

The split is irrelevant; the merge is the entire cost. In a full decode profile this kernel held 12 % of GPU time.

## Short contexts are the worst case, not long ones

`numColumns` is `logits.size(1)`, and the indexer's logits are allocated at `max_model_len` (`fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits(..., max_model_len=max_model_len)`). With a 1M model length the two-stage path is therefore taken **always**, including for a 2 000-token request — where the merge sorts 20 480 candidates to find the best 2 000 that exist.

Measured, same 4 rows: **2 000 tokens cost 112 µs, 116 000 tokens cost 63 µs.** The short context is nearly twice as expensive as the long one.

## Measurements

Micro-benchmark calling `torch.ops._C.top_k_per_row_decode` directly, checked against `torch.topk` on every point. 35 shapes (4–256 rows × 2k–600k active columns) × 9 split counts × 3 runs, plus a run with 1024 threads. MI355X, ROCm 7.2, AITER 0.1.21.

Best split count per shape (512 threads):

| rows | 2 000 | 8 000 | 32 000 | 64 000 | 116 000 | 256 000 | 600 000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 2 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 6 | 10 | 16 |
| 32 | 2 | 4 | 16 | 6 | 8 | 8 | 12 |
| 64 | 2 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 8 | 8 |
| 128 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 6 |
| 256 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 |

Two effects, both already exploited by #52882 for topK=1024:

1. **Split count.** Short rows want few blocks (the merge dominates); long rows with few of them want many (the split dominates); many rows want few (the device is already saturated).
2. **Threads per split block.** 1024 instead of 512 is worth a further **+8 %** on average — and it shifts the optimum toward *smaller* split counts, so the two must be tuned together. Our first attempt reused the split counts measured at 512 threads and was consequently *slower* than baseline at long contexts.

**Separate finding: `B = 1` is not merely slow, it is incorrect** — 137 of 2048 indices match `torch.topk`. Every other value we measured (2…16) is exact. This is reachable today by anyone editing `multipleBlocksPerRowConfig`, and may deserve a guard regardless of this issue.

## Policy we are running

Same structure as `topKPerRowDecodeDeviceLengthAware`: grid and workspace sized from `numRows` only (capture-stable), active block count decided **on device** from the real row length.

```
rowEnd <  4 096                     -> 2 blocks
rowEnd < 16 384                     -> 4 blocks
otherwise: numRows <= 32 -> 6, <= 64 -> 4, else 2
split launched with 1024 threads
```

Against the current generic path, same 35 shapes:

* mean **+26.2 %**, median **+24.6 %**, range **+0.4 % … +63.7 %**
* **no shape slower**
* identical results everywhere (2048/2048 matching indices, max |Δvalue| = 0)
* within 1.7 % of the per-shape optimum on average

End-to-end on GLM-5.3 (TP4, MI355X, same build, only the policy toggled): single user +4.8 % tok/s, 64 concurrent +3.2 % and +3.9 % (two seeds, paired), GSM8K 96.8 % → 97.0 % over 1319 problems, needle-in-haystack unchanged.

## Questions

1. Was the `topK == 1024` gate deliberate — is there a correctness reason we are missing — or simply the scope of what was measured for DeepSeek-V4?
2. Would you prefer a second calibrated branch for 2048, or a table indexed by `(topK, numRows, rowEnd)` covering both?
3. Should `B = 1` be rejected outright given it returns wrong results?

Happy to open a PR with the policy above plus the micro-benchmark, if that is useful.

---

Related, separate observation: `sparse_attn_indexer.py` gates `use_persistent_topk` / `use_cooperative_topk` on `current_platform.is_cuda()`, so on ROCm every `index_topk` in (512, 1024, 2048) falls through to `top_k_per_row_decode`. That is expected — the CUDA kernels do not port — but it means the generic path carries all ROCm DSA traffic.

title: [Bug]: Model Runner V2 never locks the workspace, so post-capture growth silently invalidates captured CUDA graphs
body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

- vLLM: reproduced against `main` at `9cd956c7e6`; the line numbers below are from that commit.
- Hardware: 8x GB200 (also reproduced on a single GB200).
- Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (43 layers, and a 4-layer proxy of the same architecture).
- Runner: Model Runner V2 (DeepSeek-V4 is a default-V2 architecture).

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`WorkspaceManager` hands out slices of one shared arena. When a request exceeds
the current arena, `_ensure_workspace_size` **replaces** the arena tensor:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/workspace.py

```python
self._current_workspaces[workspace_id] = None
del current_workspace
torch.accelerator.empty_cache()
self._current_workspaces[workspace_id] = torch.empty((required_bytes,), ...)
```

The old buffer is freed. Any CUDA graph captured earlier baked that buffer's
address into its kernels, so the next replay writes into memory the allocator
has handed to someone else.

The V1 runner guards this. After capture it locks the workspace, and a later
growth raises a precise error instead of corrupting memory:

`vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:6998`

```python
        # Lock workspace to prevent resizing during execution.
        # Max workspace sizes should have been captured during warmup/profiling.
        lock_workspace()
```

**The V2 runner never locks.** `grep -c lock_workspace vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py`
returns `0`; the only workspace API V2 uses is `use_workspace_lane`.

#### Why the guard matters even though V2 warms up per capture size

V2 does warm up before each capture (`gpu/cudagraph_utils.py`, `forward_fn(CUDAGraphMode.NONE)`
then the capture call), so every *captured* shape sizes the arena first. The gap
is what runs **after** capture: `gpu_worker.py` calls

- `capture_model()` at line 795
- `warmup_kernels(...)` at line 873

`warmup_kernels` builds a scheduler-realistic prefill plus a decode step at
`max_num_seqs`. If that shape needs a larger workspace than any captured shape
did, the arena grows *after* the graphs exist.

#### Observed failure

Serving DeepSeek-V4-Flash with `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, `--max-num-seqs 256`
and `cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE` or `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, the server dies during
startup with:

```
RuntimeError: Triton Error [CUDA]: an illegal memory access was encountered
```

The CUDA error is sticky, so it surfaces at whatever call happens next; across
runs it was attributed to three different kernels and to
`torch.accelerator.empty_cache()` inside `_ensure_workspace_size` itself. With
`CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` it consistently lands in `torch/cuda/graphs.py:186 replay`,
i.e. inside a captured graph.

Instrumenting the attention workspace requests shows the mechanism directly.
All three DeepSeek-V4 layer types share one arena base while asking for very
different widths, and the decode path executes *during* capture:

```
[DS4_DEC] cap=1 cr=1   width=128  kv=(1,128,512)  kv_ptr=0xd5e6e00000
[DS4_DEC] cap=1 cr=4   width=2688 kv=(1,2688,512) kv_ptr=0xd5e6e00000
[DS4_DEC] cap=1 cr=128 width=208  kv=(1,208,512)  kv_ptr=0xd5e6e00000
```

The first dimension is the decode batch, so the post-capture `warmup_kernels`
step at 256 requests needs `256 x 2688 x 512 x 2 B` = 704 MB against an arena
sized for the largest captured shape.

Two controls confirm it is the arena growth and not the batch size or the graph
sizes on their own (1-GPU 4-layer repro, ~4 min per run):

| `max_num_seqs` | `cudagraph_capture_sizes` | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 256 | up to 128 | illegal memory access |
| 128 | up to 512 | starts normally |

Reserving the worst-case decode workspace before the first capture makes the
256/PIECEWISE and 256/FULL_AND_PIECEWISE configurations start and serve.

#### What this issue asks for

1. **Lock the workspace in the V2 runner** the way V1 does, after
   `capture_model()`. This does not by itself fix a model that under-reserves —
   it converts a silent out-of-bounds write into the existing, precise message:

   ```
   AssertionError: Workspace is locked but allocation from
   '<file>:<line>:<fn>' requires 704.00 MB, current size is 2.75 MB.
   Workspace growth is not allowed after locking.
   ```

   #42544 is that same failure mode caught on V1, where the reporter could name
   the offending call site immediately. On V2 the same class of bug took hours
   to localise because the only symptom is an illegal memory access with a stack
   that points at an unrelated kernel.

2. **Make the shapes `warmup_kernels` uses reach the workspace before capture**
   (either by running that warmup ahead of `capture_model()`, or by sizing the
   arena for `max_num_seqs` during profiling). TensorRT-LLM does the equivalent
   explicitly — `tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/cuda_graph_runner.py` warms up
   before each capture with the comment *"This also lets us initialize states in
   the attn_metadata and resize the shared attention workspace before any graph
   is captured"* — and SGLang runs two warmup iterations per shape before
   capturing for the same reason.

Workspace sizing is already a recurring source of bugs (#42544, #41858, #50781,
#55132), so the missing V2 guard costs real debugging time each time.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] I searched for existing issues and PRs. #42544 reports the V1-side
  assertion for a different backend; I found nothing covering the missing
  `lock_workspace()` on the V2 runner or the `warmup_kernels` ordering.

---

AI assistance was used to investigate and write this report.

title: [RFC]: Unify ModelOpt MoE methods (mirror of #49381)
body:
The implementation is in #55997. Please review the changes there.

### Motivation.

PR #49381 cleaned up ModelOpt linear layers. Six nearly identical classes became one generic `ModelOptLinearMethod` driven by `resolve()` and `QuantSpec`.

MoE was left as-is on purpose. The PR says MoE keeps its own per-format methods.

Today we still have three big copy-paste MoE classes in `modelopt.py`:

- `ModelOptFp8MoEMethod` for `FP8`
- `ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE` for `NVFP4` and `W4A16_NVFP4`
- `ModelOptMxFp8FusedMoE` for `MXFP8`

Linears already go through `build_linear_method()`. MoE does not.

MoE dispatch is also duplicated in two places:

1. Homogeneous checkpoints (`modelopt`, `modelopt_fp4`, `modelopt_mxfp8`)
2. Mixed checkpoints (`modelopt_mixed`) in `ModelOptMixedPrecisionConfig.get_quant_method`

There is also a direct import in `deepseek_v4/quant_config.py`.

I'd like to fix this the same way #49381 fixed linears.

### Proposed Change.

**1. `build_moe_method(config, algo, prefix, moe_config)`**

Same idea as `build_linear_method()`. One entry point for homogeneous, mixed, and Deepseek V4 NVFP4 experts.

**2. One generic `ModelOptMoEMethod`**

`resolve()` still produces the QuantSpec. The method looks up one weight-key scheme in `MOE_SCHEME_FOR` (not linear `SCHEME_FOR`).

The scheme owns create, process, fused quant config, and backend setup. Apply stays on the method.

**3. Reuse existing pieces**

- Same `resolve()` rows as linear for FP8, NVFP4, W4A16_NVFP4, MXFP8
- Same oracle convert functions
- No kernel changes
- Config classes stay split

**4. Mixed block-FP8 MoE stays on `Fp8MoEMethod`**

`FP8_PB_WO` / `FP8_BLOCK_SCALES` experts are vLLM block-FP8 (`#55513`), not `ModelOptMoEMethod`.

**5. Delete the three old MoE classes**

`ModelOptFp8MoEMethod`, `ModelOptNvFp4FusedMoE`, `ModelOptMxFp8FusedMoE`.

### Decisions (was: questions)

1. Separate `MoEQuantKeyScheme` + `MOE_SCHEME_FOR`, not an extension of linear `QuantKeyScheme`. Layouts are different (w13/w2, expert dim). Same QuantKey, two tables.
2. One PR, same as #49381. Commits inside the branch are stacked (factory, then FP8, NVFP4, MXFP8, schemes).

### Feedback Period.

Implementation is up in #55997. Happy to adjust the scheme split or the mixed block-FP8 boundary from review.

### CC List.

@mgoin @pavanimajety @yewentao256

@juhi10071998 - you landed #49381 and mixed MoE dispatch in #42566. Would love your take on the MoE scheme split.

### Any Other Things.

W4A16 still registers NVFP4 expert input scales. Marlin drops them in convert. `use_a16` comes from `quant_config.quant_method == "W4A16_NVFP4"`. Linear `_DROP_INPUT_SCALE` is not applied to experts.

### Testing

Same class of evidence as #49381, on ModelOpt MoE checkpoints:

- Unit: `pytest tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py -k "not checkpoint_setup"`
- Per format (FP8, NVFP4 W4A4, W4A16_NVFP4, MXFP8): `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, `--enforce-eager`, old vs new weight/kernel hash and prefill logit delta, plus GSM8K (1319 Q, 5-shot, T=0, 512 tok)
- Mixed-precision (linear + MoE, including block-FP8 experts)
- Deepseek V4 with `moe_quant_algo=NVFP4`

### Related

- #55997 - implementation PR
- #49381 (merged) - linear template
- #42566 (merged) - mixed MoE dispatch
- #55513 (merged) - mixed block-FP8 MoE via `Fp8MoEMethod`
