title: [Perf] SM8x sparse-MLA prefill fallback re-reads the shared MLA latent once per head (~64x redundant KV traffic)
body:
## Summary

On Ampere (`sm_80`), the portable Triton sparse-MLA fallback used for DSA-style models
(`_sparse_mla_fwd_with_sink_kernel`) dominates long-prompt prefill — 58.8% of CUDA time on a
single 16K-token request in my measurements. When I went looking for why, the kernel turns out
to re-read the MLA latent KV once **per query head** even though that latent is shared across
heads, and on top of that it only reaches about 6% of HBM bandwidth. I think there are two
separate fixable problems here, and I wanted to write them up with numbers rather than just
say "the fallback is slow".

I'm filing this as a performance issue, not a correctness one — the kernel produces correct
results as far as I can tell, and I understand the SM8x path exists so Ampere can run at all
(the comment in `glm5next/common/attention.py` says as much). This is about the cost of that
choice being much larger than it needs to be.

## Environment

- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (DSA / `is_v32` sparse-MLA path, `index_topk=2048`,
  `num_attention_heads=64`, `kv_lora_rank=512`, `qk_rope_head_dim=0` — the NoPE layout)
- Hardware: 2x A100-PCIE-40GB (compute capability 8.0), tensor parallel = 2
- vLLM: recent mainline checkout (the commit I'm on maps to the tree that contains
  `vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_mla_kernels.py`)
- KV cache: bf16 (the SM8x path requires it)
- Workload: single request, 16384-token random prompt, concurrency 1

## What I measured

`torch.profiler` over one prefill request, CUDA time sorted:

```
_sparse_mla_fwd_with_sink_kernel     22.325 s   58.80%   (9 calls)
vllm::moe_forward_shared             11.628 s   30.28%
  Memcpy HtoD (Pageable -> Device)    6.157 s   16.22%
  down_kernel_fp8                     2.879 s    7.58%
  gate_up_kernel_fp8                  2.549 s    6.71%
  vllm::all_reduce                    2.084 s    5.49%
```

TTFT for that request was ~56 s. The attention kernel is the single biggest cost, and it is
the only thing on that list that is *not* doing useful work at a sane rate.

Scaling, measured at three prompt lengths (each with `MBT = L`, so one chunk per layer, and
the same profiler window throughout — so the comparison is apples to apples):

| prompt len | attention kernel | TTFT |
|---|---|---|
| 4,096 | 3.129 s | 28.7 s |
| 8,192 | 9.538 s | 38.5 s |
| 16,384 | 22.323 s | 56.0 s |

4x the prompt length costs 7.1x the kernel time, i.e. roughly `O(L^1.42)`. That's between
linear and quadratic, which is what I'd expect: the inner loop is capped by `topk`, so the
work per token is `min(position, topk)` and the total is `sum_t min(pos_t, topk)`. That sum
predicts 5.0x for the 4x increase, so the sparsity is doing its job — this is not a
complexity blowup. The per-unit cost is the problem: 22.3 s over 31.5M key-attends works out
to about 0.71 ns per key-attend.

## Problem 1: the KV tile is loaded once per head, but MLA shares it across heads

The kernel's grid is `(num_tokens, active_heads)`:

```python
# vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_mla_kernels.py
_sparse_mla_fwd_with_sink_kernel[(num_tokens, active_heads)](
    ...
    BLOCK_K=16,
    BLOCK_D=block_d,
    num_warps=8,
)
```

and inside the kernel:

```python
token_idx = tl.program_id(0)
head_idx  = tl.program_id(1)

q = tl.load(q_ptr + token_idx*stride_q_t + head_idx*stride_q_h + dim_offsets*stride_q_d, ...)

# note: no head_idx anywhere in this address computation
kv = tl.load(kv_ptr + row_safe[:, None]*stride_kv_r + dim_offsets[None, :]*stride_kv_d, ...)
```

`head_idx` appears in the `q` and `output` addressing but **not** in the KV addressing. That's
correct in the sense that the latent really is shared — but it means every one of the
`num_heads` programs covering the same token loads the same KV rows again.

For GLM-5.3 at L=16384 that is 64x the necessary traffic:

```
sum_t min(pos_t, topk)                    = 31.5M key-attends
KV bytes per head                         = 31.5M * 512 dims * 2 B  = 32.2 GB
x 64 heads (same rows, re-read each time) = 2062 GB
what the algorithm actually needs         =   32.2 GB
```

The 64x factor doesn't depend on my assumption about the row width — it's just `num_heads`.
(If the row is narrower than the 512 I assumed, the absolute GB numbers shrink, but the
redundancy ratio and the effective-bandwidth conclusion don't change.)

## Problem 2: even the redundant traffic runs at ~6% of HBM bandwidth

Reading 2062 GB at A100's 1555 GB/s would take ~1.33 s. The kernel takes 22.3 s, so it's
another ~17x off even the *redundant* bound. Effective bandwidth is about 92 GB/s against a
1555 GB/s peak.

I suspect `BLOCK_K=16` is a big part of this. With `topk=2048` each program runs
`2048/16 = 128` loop iterations, and every iteration issues a masked 2-D gather
(`k_mask[:, None] & dim_mask[None, :]`) of a `16 x BLOCK_D` tile. That's a lot of small
masked loads, and the `dim_mask` suggests `BLOCK_D` is padded above the real row width too.
I haven't profiled the individual loads so this part is a hypothesis — the 64x from Problem 1
is the part I'm confident in.

## Suggested direction

Problem 1 looks mechanical to fix without touching the sparsity semantics at all: keep the
same per-token topk indices, but stop giving each head its own program. Either put a head
block (`BLOCK_H`) in the same program so the KV tile is loaded once and reused for all heads
in the block, or make the second grid dimension index KV blocks and loop over heads
internally. Since the latent is genuinely shared, this is purely a matter of loop
restructuring.

Problem 2 is more of a tuning question — larger `BLOCK_K`, and/or checking whether the
`dim_mask` is forcing an over-wide `BLOCK_D` and how that interacts with Triton's
pipelining (`num_stages` isn't set here, so the default applies).

I'd be happy to try the restructuring and post numbers if that's useful — I just wanted to
check first whether there's a reason the grid is shaped this way that I'm not seeing,
e.g. a constraint from the `topk_lens`/sink handling or from how the SM8x backend has to
match the SM90 `flash_mla_sparse_fwd` contract.

## What I might be getting wrong

- I did not benchmark the SM90 sparse path, so I can't say how much of this is specific to
  the SM8x fallback versus inherent to the sparse formulation. On SM90 this goes through
  `flash_mla_sparse_fwd` (CUDA) rather than this Triton kernel, so I'd expect it to be much
  better, but that's an expectation, not a measurement.
- The 512-dim row width is inferred from the model config (`kv_lora_rank=512`, rope 0). If
  the kernel is actually called with a different `head_dim`, the absolute bandwidth figure
  changes; the redundancy ratio does not.
- The `9 calls` in the profile table is an artifact of my profiler window (`CALLS=40` on the
  MoE kernel), not a real per-request call count, so please disregard the call count. The
  timings are all from the same window, so the comparisons hold.
- I'm running this through a plugin that keeps expert weights in host RAM, which is why
  `moe_forward_shared` and the HtoD copies show up so large in my profile. Those are my
  plugin's costs and not relevant to this report — the attention kernel numbers are the
  vLLM-side ones.

title: [CI][ROCm] Match the AMD steps to the mirror declarations they carry
body:
Fixes [#57956](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57956).

`mirror.amd` blocks in `.buildkite/test_areas/*.yaml` declare, per suite, the label it carries in the AMD pipeline and the device class it runs on. `test-amd.yaml` is the file those declarations point at: its header describes `mirror_hardwares` as the selector tags for the AMD pipelines that should include the test. For 24 suites the two files disagreed, so the selectors and the agent pool pulled those suites somewhere other than the labels declared.

## What changed

- 23 steps re-tiered in `.buildkite/test-amd.yaml` to the tier and the device their mirror declares: label tier, the `mirror_hardwares` lane tags and `agent_pool`. Several of them are suites whose mirror came with [#57876](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57876); the others are mirrors from the earlier MI355 reallocation ([#57080](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57080)) whose step stayed on MI300. Each edit moves the label tier, `amdgfx942nightly` to `amdgfx950nightly`, `amdmi300` to `amdmi355`, and `agent_pool` to the device the mirror declares.
- two MI355 entrypoints steps, `Entrypoints Integration (Speech to Text)` and `Entrypoints Integration (Multimodal)`, carried `amdgfx942nightly` next to `amdmi355`. Their label, their device and their `amdmi355` tag all say MI355, so the gfx942 tag is dropped.
- three drifted names aligned: `Qwen3-8-Flash-Next-FP8` to `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` (the checkpoint reference and the eval configs spell the model `Qwen3.8`), `Rust Frontend Serve-Admin Coverage` to `Rust Frontend Serve/Admin Coverage` (the H200 group it mirrors spells it `Serve/Admin`, `.buildkite/test_areas/rust_frontend.yaml:70`), and the `Entrypoints Integration (Pooling)` mirror label gained the ` Shard %N` suffix its step has had since the sharding.
- new `.buildkite/scripts/check-amd-mirror-parity.py`: reports every AMD mirror that disagrees with its step and exits non-zero on a violation of the MI355 invariant. It is deliberately not wired into a pipeline step: that kind of change wants a container run to validate, and I could not run one here.

## What is left, and why

The checker reports 39 of 141 mirrors. All of them are either a mirror declaring a lower tier than the step it names (33 rows: `attention.yaml` declares `(MI300) V1 Attention Shard %N` against an MI355 step, `cuda.yaml` and `engine.yaml` declare MI250 against MI355 and MI300 steps, `Mamba Kernels`, `Plugin Integration`, `Samplers`, `Language Models (MTEB)` declare MI250 against MI300 steps), or a mirror naming a step `test-amd.yaml` does not have (6 rows: `LM Eval Spec Decode`, `Qwen4 Exp`, `Multimodal Models (PPL)`, `Spec Decode DeepSeek MTP Parallel Load`, `Spec Decode AL DFlash Nightly`, `Spec Decode AL DSpark Nightly`). Both need a placement call on the AMD side rather than a typo fix, so the checker reports them instead of failing on them.

## Verification

```
# the new checker, on the tree this pull request changes
python3 .buildkite/scripts/check-amd-mirror-parity.py
mirrors=141  violations=0  reported=39        # exit 0

# the same check before the change (throwaway audit script, not commited)
mirrors declared=141  tier_drift=28  cpu_lane=6  absent=9
```

The `test-amd.yaml` diff touches label, `mirror_hardwares` and `agent_pool` lines only: no `commands`, `timeout_in_minutes`, `source_file_dependencies` or `working_dir` value changed. No model-facing code, prompt or serving path is touched, so no eval run applies here.

## Duplication

No open pull request touches the AMD mirror/step agreement: `gh pr list --search "mirror parity"`, `--search "test-amd"` and `--search "57956"` come back with nothing on it. The closest earlier work is [#50519](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50519) (`[ROCm][CI] Add missing test coverage for upstream parity`), which adds coverage but does not reconcile the two files, and [#53840](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53840), which is about a `num_devices`/`num_gpus` mismatch, a different invariant.

AI assistance was used: the audit of the two files, the re-tier edit and the checker were produced with an AI coding agent under line-by-line review; the checker was run before and after the change.

Signed-off-by: Binbin Zhang <binbin36520@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: Hermes Agent <noreply@hermes.nousresearch.com>

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Keep activations MXFP8 between DeepGEMM kernels
body:
## Purpose

DeepGEMM's DeepSeek-V4.1 kernels can hand FP8 activations to each other, but vLLM re-quantized their BF16 outputs before every dense projection: 127 standalone MXFP8 quantize launches per decode step at C1 (TP4), plus the quantize half of the Mega-MoE input staging. This PR wires the FP8 outputs DeepGEMM already provides to the consumers, and runs those consumers on DeepGEMM.

One decoder layer, decode step. `[q]` = standalone MXFP8 quantize launch, `sf` = the UE8M0 group scales.

**Before** — every DeepGEMM kernel returns BF16, and a FlashInfer quantize kernel re-creates MXFP8 before each consumer:

```
attention sublayer
  mega_mhc (post+pre+RMSNorm) ──bf16──┬──▶ compressor score / indexer weights GEMMs (bf16, unchanged)
                                      └──▶ [q] ──mxfp8+sf──▶ FlashInfer GEMM  fused_wqa_wkv
  attention ──▶ fp8_einsum wo_a ──bf16──▶ [q] ──mxfp8+sf──▶ FlashInfer GEMM  wo_b ──▶ reduce-scatter

FFN sublayer
  mega_mhc (post+pre+RMSNorm) ──bf16──┬──▶ router gate + top-k (bf16, unchanged)
                                      └──▶ prepare_megamoe = [q] into symm buffer + pack top-k ──▶ fp8_fp4_mega_moe
```

**After** — the producers emit MXFP8 with packed scales directly, the consumers run on DeepGEMM `fp8_gemm_nt`:

```
attention sublayer
  mega_mhc ──bf16──────────────────────▶ compressor score / indexer weights GEMMs (unchanged)
           ──mxfp8+sf (y_fp8, y_gemm_sf)─▶ DeepGEMM GEMM  fused_wqa_wkv        (not under SP: input is all-gathered in bf16)
  attention ──▶ fp8_einsum wo_a ──mxfp8+sf ((z, sf) output)──▶ DeepGEMM GEMM  wo_b ──▶ reduce-scatter

FFN sublayer
  mega_mhc ──bf16─────────────────────────────────────▶ router gate + top-k (unchanged)
           ──mxfp8+sf written straight into the symm buffer (y_fp8, y_routed_sf, y_shared_sf)
                                                       ──▶ prepare_megamoe = pack top-k only ──▶ fp8_fp4_mega_moe
```

| per layer | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| standalone quantize launches | 3 (+ the quantize half of `prepare_megamoe`) | 1 under SP (`fused_wqa_wkv`), 0 otherwise |
| dense GEMM kernel | FlashInfer CuTe-DSL ×2 | DeepGEMM `fp8_gemm_nt` (1,1,32) ×2 |
| bytes between mHC / einsum and their consumers | bf16 out + fp8 in | fp8 out only |

Pieces:
- `DeepGemmMxfp8LinearKernel` (2D `fp8_gemm_nt`, recipe (1,1,32)); its activations carry a new `QuantKey` `kMxfp8DynamicDeepGemm` (int32 packed UE8M0 scales) so a FlashInfer-layout producer can never be routed to a DeepGEMM consumer or vice versa. The model marks `wo_b` / `fused_wqa_wkv` with `deep_gemm_activations`, and ModelOpt's post-load selects the kernel for them the same way it does for `is_bmm` layers.
- `mega_mhc` wrapper: optional `y_fp8`/`y_gemm_sf` and `y_fp8`/`y_routed_sf`/`y_shared_sf` outputs (DeepGEMM already implements them), reported as a typed `MegaMhcFp8Outputs`; the MoE leg is passed explicitly (`DeepseekV4MoE.forward(staged=...)` → `experts.forward_staged`) and `stage_megamoe_routing` repacks only the top-k.
- `deep_gemm_fp8_o_proj(fp8_z=True)`: `fp8_einsum` emits `(z, sf)`; also in the mega-attention backend's `_o_proj`.
- Under sequence parallel the attention input is all-gathered in BF16 after the norm, so `fused_wqa_wkv` stays on FlashInfer there (FP8 all-gather is follow-up work).
- The new `fp8_gemm_nt` variants are pre-compiled by the existing DeepGEMM startup warmup (layers found through the `deep_gemm_warmup_provider` protocol).
- Binds wherever SM100 + DeepGEMM are available (checked at construction; other platforms keep their kernels with a logged reason). No new flag.

Duplicate check: searched open PRs for `mega_mhc y_fp8`, `y_gemm_sf`, `fp8_einsum`, `DeepGemmMxfp8LinearKernel`, `prepare_megamoe_inputs`, `wo_b quantize`, and by touched file. #57679 (restores the `wq_b` query-quant fusion) is complementary and untouched here; #56751 (skinny GEMM, M ≤ 4) quantizes in-kernel for the same projections at tiny M, a separate mechanism; #55505 (input-scale contract) does not conflict.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest -v -s tests/kernels/test_dsv41_deepgemm_fp8_chain.py   # SM100
```
```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --kernel-config '{"moe_backend":"deep_gemm_mega_moe"}' --attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 64
```
Baseline: the same command on main. `vllm bench serve` random 4096/256, ignore-eos, one server at a time; GSM8K via lm-eval 0.4.12 (5-shot chat, thinking off, greedy, 1319 questions).

## Test Result

4×B200, TP4 + EP4, MegaMoE + SP, FlashInfer sparse MLA, fp8 KV.

- Unit tests: 21 passed (DeepGEMM kernel vs FlashInfer CuTe-DSL at M ∈ {1,4,7,64,300}; pre-quantized input bit-identical to in-kernel quant; `mega_mhc` FP8 outputs bit-exact MXFP8 of its BF16 output, MoE layout bit-identical to `prepare_megamoe_inputs`; einsum FP8 output vs quantized BF16 output; routing-only staging).
- Greedy outputs identical on 8/8 prompts × 64 tokens.
- C1 decode step (torch profiler, 61 steps): GPU busy 7.64 → 6.85 ms (−10 %), quantize launches 130 → 90.

| lane | baseline | PR | change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C1 ×3 TPOT | 6.58 / 6.58 / 6.58 ms | 6.50 / 6.50 / 6.50 ms | −1.2 % |
| C4 ×2 tok/s (TPOT) | 517 / 520 (6.97 / 6.94 ms) | 531 / 530 (6.83 / 6.86 ms) | +2.4 % (−1.6 %) |
| C4 ×2 TTFT | 201 / 199 ms | 184 / 183 ms | −8 % |
| C16 ×3 tok/s (TPOT) | 1347 / 1346 / 1340 (9.92 / 9.88 / 10.03 ms) | 1365 / 1357 / 1368 (9.85 / 9.86 / 9.73 ms) | +1.5 % (−1.3 %) |
| C64 ×1 tok/s (TTFT) | 1848 (2360 ms) | 1880 (2124 ms) | +1.7 % (−10 %) |
| GSM8K flexible / strict | 0.9621–0.9659 / 0.7817–0.7832 (3 baselines) | 0.9644 / 0.7877 | unchanged |

After the plumbing refactor (kernel selection through ModelOpt post-load, typed mHC outputs, explicit staged MoE input): 21 unit tests pass, C1 TPOT 6.50 / 6.50 / 6.50 ms, GSM8K 0.9636 / 0.7915, greedy outputs coherent on 12 prompts.

At C1 the host loop (~6.5 ms/step) bounds TPOT, so most of the GPU saving shows from C4 up. The FP8-output `mega_mhc` variants JIT-compile on first use per prefill shape, like the BF16 variants today (cache persists under `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR`).

Developed with AI assistance (Claude Code); the human submitter reviewed every changed line and ran the measurements.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Parallelise AITER MLA page-index expansion over token chunks
body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Scope: this is a kernel-level microbenchmark, not an end-to-end throughput claim.**
> The numbers below are measured from torch-profiler traces on the same build, same shapes. Against a multi-millisecond decode step a
> change of this size sits inside run-to-run variation (~1% on a conc=1 arm), so
> **no measurable serving throughput improvement is claimed, and none should be
> inferred.** The value is removing a serial per-request loop on a path that is
> on the critical path at low concurrency. Details under "End-to-end context".

## Purpose

`_expand_page_indices_kernel` in the AITER MLA backend is launched with a grid
of one program per request, and each program walks that request's tokens in a
serial loop:

```python
_expand_page_indices_kernel[(num_reqs,)](...)

    req_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    for i in tl.range(0, num_tokens, BLOCK_SIZE):
```

The parallelism is therefore entirely over the batch. That is fine at high
concurrency and degenerates at low concurrency: with `num_reqs == 1` a **single
workgroup** expands the whole sequence while the rest of the GPU idles. The
bug is invisible in the regime it was presumably tuned for.

On a long-context decode workload (MI355X, TP8, ~97k-token context, conc=1)
this measured **61.6 µs per call and 7 calls per model step — 0.431 ms, or
1.23% of a 34.9 ms step**. For scale, 97k int32 stores is ~388 KB, well under
a microsecond of HBM bandwidth. The kernel is not bandwidth-bound; it is
serialised.

This affects **any MLA model on ROCm at low concurrency**, not one model in
particular.

## The change

Add a second grid dimension over token chunks and drop the loop, so each
program handles exactly one `BLOCK_SIZE` chunk:

```python
num_chunks = max(1, cdiv(block_table.shape[1] * kernel_block_size, 1024))
_expand_page_indices_kernel[(num_reqs, num_chunks)](...)
```

The arithmetic, the masks and the stores are unchanged — only the iteration
space is mapped onto the GPU instead of onto one workgroup. The chunk count is
derived host-side from the block table width, an upper bound on tokens per
request, so **no device synchronisation is introduced**; over-launched
programs mask out entirely and cost nothing.

## Not a duplicate

Checked before opening:

```
repo:vllm-project/vllm is:pr is:open expand_page_indices      -> 0 results
```

No open PR touches this kernel or its launch. The nearby open ROCm MLA PRs
address unrelated concerns:

| PR | subject | overlap |
|---|---|---|
| #57085 | ROCM_AITER_MLA non-causal DSpark draft under DCP | none — DCP draft path |
| #53492 | sparse MLA Gluon kernel from Aiter | none — sparse kernel |
| #57923 | startup OOM in AITER MLA FP8 prefill workspace sizing | none — allocation sizing |
| #46172 | optimize rocm aiter sparse mla indexer | none — sparse indexer |
| #54899 | pad the AITER MLA decode head count to a native tile | none — head padding |

The kernel was introduced in #39616 (AITER MLA + Eagle3 on ROCm) and has not
been modified since.

## Test plan

**Bit-exactness against the existing serial kernel.** Both versions built from
source and compared on device — this is an index computation, so a wrong value
does not crash, it silently reads the wrong KV:

```
conc=1 long context, kbs=1    97000 indices identical
conc=1 long context, kbs=16   97000 indices identical
exact multiple of 1024         4096 indices identical
1024+1                         1025 indices identical
1024-1                         1023 indices identical
ragged 4 reqs                 38011 indices identical
kbs=16 ragged tail             4212 indices identical
single token                      1 indices identical
```

Cases cover chunk boundaries, ragged multi-request batches, and
`kernel_block_size > 1`.

### Kernel time — the direct measurement

This is what the change does, measured on the kernel itself rather than
inferred from an end-to-end delta. Torch-profiler traces, same build, same
workload, same serve config, six captured iterations each:

| | calls | total | **µs/call** | per step |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 18 | 0.402 ms | **22.4** | 0.067 ms |
| this PR | 18 | 0.059 ms | **3.3** | 0.010 ms |
| | | | **−85.4%** | |

**6.8× faster.** Identical call counts on both sides, so this is the same work
at the same frequency, no longer serialised onto a single workgroup. That is
the claim this PR rests on, and it is reproducible on any machine with a
profiler — it does not depend on our hardware, our workload mix, or run-to-run
variance.

Measured with `vllm serve --profiler-config.profiler=torch`, ISL 131072,
conc=1, TP8, MTP depth 6.

### Concurrency sweep — does the extra grid dimension cost anything?

Requested during review: the win above is at conc=1, where one workgroup walked
the whole context. At higher concurrency `num_reqs` already supplies
parallelism, so the question is whether the second grid dimension costs
anything there.

The kernel grid-strides rather than partitioning, so a grid width of 1
reproduces the pre-PR launch exactly. "Before" below is therefore the same
kernel launched the old way, not a reimplementation. Width is this PR's
launch-site formula, `num_chunks = max(1, cdiv(block_table.shape[1] * kernel_block_size, 1024))`
(an upper bound on tokens per request read from the block-table width, so
it needs no device sync; at `kernel_block_size=1` this gives 375 / 64 / 8 / 1
for the contexts below). MI355X, 256
CUs, `kernel_block_size=1`, `BLOCK_SIZE=1024`, median of 7 reps x 100
iterations on an idle node. Output compared byte-for-byte at every width and
shape; all agree.

| ctx | reqs | width | before µs | after µs | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 024 | 1 | 1 | 10.99 | 10.95 | 1.00x |
| 1 024 | 256 | 1 | 10.59 | 10.76 | 0.98x |
| 8 192 | 64 | 8 | 10.73 | 10.74 | 1.00x |
| 8 192 | 256 | 8 | 10.78 | 10.74 | 1.00x |
| 65 536 | 1 | 64 | 16.59 | 10.75 | 1.54x |
| 65 536 | 64 | 64 | 25.94 | 10.83 | 2.40x |
| 65 536 | 256 | 64 | 39.69 | 39.54 | 1.00x |
| 384 000 | 1 | 375 | 114.14 | 10.78 | 10.59x |
| 384 000 | 32 | 375 | 137.30 | 28.28 | 4.85x |
| 384 000 | 64 | 375 | 251.07 | 68.34 | 3.67x |
| 384 000 | 128 | 375 | 300.51 | 153.84 | 1.95x |

**No shape regresses.** The lowest ratio anywhere is 0.98x, on shapes sitting
at a ~10.7 µs floor where run-to-run spread is around ±2%. At 1k context the
width is 1, so the launch is bit-identical to before and those rows measure
noise rather than a change.

Ragged batches are the case worth checking explicitly, since
`num_token_blocks` comes from `max_seq_len` over the whole batch — one long
request widens the grid for every short request too, launching programs that
find nothing to do:

| batch | width | before µs | after µs | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1x384k + 7x1k | 375 | 115.60 | 10.86 | 10.64x |
| 1x384k + 63x1k | 375 | 115.67 | 13.80 | 8.38x |
| 1x65k + 127x512 | 64 | 16.62 | 10.74 | 1.55x |
| 8x65k + 56x1k | 64 | 17.01 | 10.80 | 1.58x |

The widened grid costs nothing measurable: 63 short requests at width 375 still
come out 8.4x ahead, because the programs with no work exit immediately.

Ratios converging to 1.00x at the high end (65k/256) are the expected
behaviour rather than a cost — the "before" side has enough requests to fill
the machine on its own. These remain kernel microbenchmarks; at high
concurrency this kernel is a small share of the step, so the table is here to
show the change does not cost anything there, not to claim a win.

### End-to-end context

The kernel runs 3 times per step on current main, so the 0.057 ms it saves is
about **0.24%** of a 23.40 ms step. That is below what a 1200 s conc=1 arm can
resolve, and it is the honest ceiling for this change on this configuration.

Earlier end-to-end arms are included for completeness, but should **not** be
read as the effect size:

| build | | interactivity p90 | tpot p90 | step time |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | baseline | 110.28 | 0.00907 | 34.01 ms |
| A | this PR | 112.06 (+1.61%) | 0.00892 | 33.45 ms |
| B | baseline | 140.97 | 0.00709 | 26.59 ms |
| B | this PR | 142.75 (+1.27%) | 0.00701 | 26.29 ms |

Both figures exceed what the kernel can physically save, so they are
noise-dominated at this effect size — a 1200 s conc=1 arm carries roughly 1%
run-to-run spread, against a ceiling here well under that. A third arm on
current main measured −0.35%, which is the same noise in the other direction.
The kernel measurement above is the reliable signal; these rows are not.

Worth noting why the end-to-end impact shrank across builds: the per-call cost
is essentially unchanged (23.3 µs then, 22.4 µs now), but upstream reduced the
call count from 6 per step to 3. The serialisation this PR removes is the same;
there is simply less of it to remove than there was.

**Accuracy** is unaffected by construction — the page indices are bit-
identical, so the model reads exactly the same KV. Confirmed anyway with
GSM8k over the full 1319 questions: 0.9659, unchanged.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for this PR (Claude). The measurements above are from
runs on real hardware, not estimates. The submitter has reviewed every changed
line.

title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Preserve config during GPU memory profiling
body:
## Purpose

Make the vLLM config available during both GPU `profile_run()` paths. Without it, the ROCm sparse-MLA indexer can fall back to `max_num_batched_tokens` when sizing its decode-logits workspace. The regression test checks that a configuration with `max_num_seqs=16` and five speculative tokens uses 96 rows instead of 32768.

Related to #55132; complementary to the pre-capture warmup fix in #55341, which does not provide the config context during memory profiling. The current main still calls both memory-profiling paths without this context, and the V2 runner does not establish it internally. Searches for existing profiling-context fixes found no replacement for this change.

## Validation

Rebased on main `ab5266769e702434a0968d47319d0731d8ccac35` on October 1, 2026. The conflict resolution preserves the new upstream `randomize_inputs` argument; the regression test also checks that it reaches both profiling paths.

- `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker.py`: 13 passed, 9 skipped, 14 PyTorch deprecation warnings on macOS Apple Silicon. Both regression-test cases passed.
- `.venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run --files vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker.py`: passed.
- `git diff origin/main --check`: passed.
- On our MI300X DeepSeek deployment with a 1M context, startup previously failed while attempting a 128 GiB decode-logits workspace allocation. With the equivalent local V2 config-context patch, startup succeeded and direct requests completed on all three replicas. These are historical results for the equivalent local patch, not an AMD run of the rebased PR.

AMD CI, including the MI300 V1 Executor + Worker step, remains desirable when permitted by the project workflow. This update does not claim a new GPU or model-evaluation run.

AI-assisted contribution: OpenAI Codex assisted with the implementation, regression test, and rebase. The human submitter owns the contribution.

title: [Perf][Model Loader] Skip checkpoint tensors a model does not load before reading them
body:
## Purpose

Drafters that ship inside their target's checkpoint are built from the target
path (`SpeculativeConfig`: `self.model = self.target_model_config.model` for
`dspark`, and likewise for MTP). The default loader then iterates every shard
of the target a second time, only for the drafter's `load_weights` to drop
everything that is not `mtp.*`.

When the checkpoint is larger than the host's page cache, that second pass is
a second full read from disk. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash with DSpark (165 GB, 46
shards, pipeline parallel over five GPUs) it runs on the last stage after all
stages have loaded their own weights, and took 255 s of a 10:25 min boot.

The EP weight filter already skips tensors by name before `get_tensor`. This
generalises the same idea to the model: a model can offer
`skip_checkpoint_weight(name) -> bool`, `DefaultModelLoader` reads it the way
it already reads `allow_patterns_overrides` and passes it through a new
`Source.skip_weight` field to `safetensors_weights_iterator`, which drops
accepted names before reading them. EP filter and model rule go through one
helper, `_keep_weight`, instead of being repeated per load strategy. Models
that do not offer the method are unaffected.

The DeepSeek-V4 DSpark drafter implements the rule with the mapping it already
uses in `load_weights`: `_remap_dspark_name(name) is None`. Other drafters that
load from their target's checkpoint (MTP variants, the other DSpark models)
can opt in the same way; this PR keeps to the one that was measured.

The multithreaded iterator is left as is: it reads whole files with
`load_file` before any filter can apply, so a name rule there would not save
I/O (#48891 addresses the same gap for the EP filter).

AI assistance was used for this change. Every line was reviewed and the tests
below were run by the submitter.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_ep_weight_filter.py
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files <changed files>
```

`tests/models/test_dspark_mla.py::test_deepseek_v4_dspark_skips_every_checkpoint_weight_it_does_not_load`
is added as a `cpu_test`; it could not be run locally (see Test Result).

End-to-end measurement on 3x V100 + 2x RTX 8000 with the same loader change on
a V100/Turing fork of vLLM (1Cat-vLLM), DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4 with DSpark,
PP5, cold boot.

## Test Result

39 passed, including the two new tests in the existing EP filter suite
(`test_model_skip_rule_drops_tensors_before_reading`: skipped names never reach
`get_tensor`; `test_loader_applies_the_model_skip_rule`). Both fail on `main`
without the change. mypy-3.12 passes. The new DSpark test did not run locally:
this machine's environment pins an older `humming-kernels` than main requires,
so the DeepSeek-V4 DSpark module does not import there; CI covers it.

| Boot phase (V100/Turing fork, same loader change) | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| target weights, all stages | 276 s | 286 s |
| drafter on the last stage | 255 s | 17 s |
| boot to `Application startup complete` | 10:25 min | 6:03 min |

Disk read during the boot after the change: 177 GiB (checkpoint once plus the
drafter's file). DSpark mean acceptance length afterwards 2.6–3.5.

## Not a duplicate

Open PRs searched for "skip checkpoint weight", "drafter load weights",
"dspark load", "safetensors skip before reading" and "load only mtp weights".
Related but different: #48023 (drafter inherits `model_weights` for object
storage), #40068 (staggers file order per rank in the same two functions),
#48891 (EP filter in the multithreaded loader).

title: [Frontend] Support strict MiMo-V2.6 tool calling
body:
## Purpose

MiMo-V2.6 Pro/Flash emit compact XML tool calls, but `--tool-call-parser mimo` currently selects Qwen3-Coder structural tags with mandatory newlines. Strict required/named calls therefore use the wrong wire format. The Qwen argument converter also removes a leading/trailing newline that MiMo emits as part of the string value.

Introduce a MiMo variant of the existing parser engine that preserves parameter whitespace, with a thin tool adapter selecting `mimo` structural tags. Prefer the new XGrammar builtin (https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/pull/916); keep a schema-constrained compatibility builder for the currently pinned 0.2.7 wheel. Honor `parallel_tool_calls=False`, retain server/per-tool strictness controls, and leave reasoning to the serving gate. No dependency change is required.

The shared registry change only declares the supported key. MiMo parsing and compatibility behavior live in the model's own modules. Document the existing `--tool-call-parser mimo --reasoning-parser mimo --enable-auto-tool-choice` flags and strictness options.

Duplicate-work check: open #54393 and #57933 add Rust frontend MiMo support. This PR changes the Python parser/structural-tag path; neither existing PR covers it. Also searched open MiMo/XGrammar/strict-tool PRs before submission.

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/tool_parsers/test_structural_tag_registry.py \
  tests/parser/engine/test_qwen3.py \
  tests/parser/engine/test_qwen3_reasoning.py \
  tests/parser/engine/test_deepseek_v41.py --tb=short
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files <changed files>
```

The local environment used the current checkout plus an isolated XGrammar build. Repeated MiMo cases with the actual 0.2.7 wheel first on `PYTHONPATH`. Supplemental replay loads revision-pinned official tokenizers, renders chat-template completions, checks each native token mask and EOS boundary, and parses the resulting calls in both non-streaming and token-streaming modes.

## Test Result

- Development XGrammar: **340 passed**. Pre-commit passed.
- Actual XGrammar **0.2.7 wheel**, MiMo subset (`-k mimo` across the registry/Qwen parser suites): **34 passed**, no skipped native tests.
- Official-template protocol replay with both development XGrammar and 0.2.7: **36 cases and 2,776 next-token masks per run**, all passed. Covers both checkpoints, reasoning on/off, auto/required/named choice, multiple calls, nullable values, nested JSON, verbatim strings, and non-strict parameters.

Official revisions:

- `XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL@54b10491b1811c76aa9681a9d0ff872396a4064c`

title: [Bugfix] Exclude SM107 (Rubin) from support_deep_gemm()
body:
## Summary

`support_deep_gemm()` uses `is_device_capability_family(100)`, which matches
*any* 10.x compute capability. That silently admits SM107 into the
DeepGEMM/CuTe-gated code paths alongside SM100/SM103 -- but the vendored
DeepGEMM/CuTe kernels aren't built for native `sm_107`, so any call behind
`is_deep_gemm_supported()` (e.g. the MHC TileLang prenorm-GEMM path) hits a
`cuModuleLoadData -> CUDA_ERROR_ASSERT` at kernel load time on that hardware.

This replaces the family-wide check with explicit `is_device_capability(100)`
/ `is_device_capability(103)` entries, matching how Hopper (`90`) and the
120 family are already enumerated individually in this same function. When
DeepGEMM ships kernels built for native `sm_107`, it can be added back the
same way -- this isn't a permanent hardware exclusion, just a "not built
yet" gap.

## Why this isn't a duplicate

Searched open PRs referencing `support_deep_gemm`/DeepGEMM SM gating. The
closest is #53055 ("Guard DeepGEMM in mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang with a
torch fallback"), which is a different bug: it adds a missing
`is_deep_gemm_supported()` check at one call site for platforms where
DeepGEMM isn't installed at all (SM121/GB10). This PR instead fixes the
shared platform-level gate itself, which currently *wrongly reports support*
on hardware where DeepGEMM is installed but not built for the native arch.

## Test plan

Validated live on real SM107 hardware, using the public
`vllm/vllm-openai:cu134-nightly` image (no NVIDIA-internal patches):

```
>>> from vllm.platforms import current_platform
>>> current_platform.get_device_capability()
DeviceCapability(major=10, minor=7)
>>> current_platform.support_deep_gemm()
True      # before this change
```

After applying this diff to the installed `vllm/platforms/cuda.py` in the
same container:

```
>>> current_platform.support_deep_gemm()
False     # after this change
```

Confirms the gate now correctly excludes SM107 while leaving SM100/SM103/
Hopper/120-family behavior unchanged (traced statically; no regression
hardware available to re-verify those paths, but the change is additive/
narrowing only for SM107 and doesn't touch their branches).

AI assistance disclosure: this change was drafted with Claude Code
assistance; I reviewed the diff and reasoning end-to-end, and validated the
behavior change live on SM107 hardware myself before submitting.

title: FlashInfer autotune for trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe wedges forever on SM103 (GB300): trtllm_gemm cubin is sm_100a-only, no PTX, and the autotuner has no timeout
body:
> **EDIT (2026-09-23):** The root-cause attribution below is **withdrawn**. `nm -D` shows the `fp4_block_scale_moe` symbols live in `fused_moe_trtllm_sm100.so` (which carries `sm_103a` cubins), not `trtllm_gemm.so` (the dense GEMM module — the sm_100a-only observation is real but irrelevant to this op). The "candidate can never execute on SM103" mechanism does not hold. The symptom stands (unbounded autotune at boot, 40+ min, zero progress lines, no cache write before termination); it is now considered a probable extreme-slow-crawl rather than a proven hang, since the autotuner logs nothing between start and end and only writes the cache on completion. See [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58031#issuecomment-5788562400) for the corrected analysis and proposed scoping (exclude SM103 from `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8` auto-selection; add per-bucket progress logging). The workaround below remains valid.

## Describe the bug

On a DGX Station GB300 (SM103, compute capability 10.3), the FlashInfer autotune for `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe` runs indefinitely at 100% GPU with zero progress and zero autotune cache writes, wedging engine startup forever. There is no error, no traceback, no timeout — the boot simply never completes.

The root cause appears to be an arch-coverage gap in FlashInfer's prebuilt `trtllm_gemm` cubin, combined with an autotuner that has no timeout for a candidate kernel that never terminates.

## Environment

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` pulled 2026-09-21 (vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev452+g3df4ae153`, FlashInfer `0.6.18.post1`), arm64
- GPU: NVIDIA GB300 (SM103), driver 610.43.02
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4 experts / MXFP8 rest), TP1, `--cpu-offload-gb 75`, DSpark speculative k=5
- Flags relevant: `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384`, moe backend auto-selects `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8`

## Reproduction

Serve DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (or any model that routes MoE through `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe`) on SM103 **without** skipping the op's autotune. Boot proceeds normally through weight load, CUDA graph capture, and JIT warmup, then reaches:

```
[flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup.py:267] Warming up DeepSeek V4 sparse MLA attention for mixed tokens=16.
[kernel_warmup.py:436] Using FlashInfer autotune cache file: .../autotune_configs.json
autotuner.py:972 - flashinfer.jit: [Autotuner]: Autotuning process starts ...
[kernel_warmup.py:358] Running FlashInfer autotune with 16384 tokens and token buckets (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280, 1536, 1792, 2048, 2560, 3072, 3584, 4096, 8192, 16384).
```

… and stays there. Observed: 40+ minutes at 100% GPU utilization, 0 new log lines in any 10-minute window, and the cache directory for the config hash created but left **empty**:

```
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Sep 21 15:35 .   # created when autotune started
# (no autotune_configs.json ever written)
```

By contrast, the JIT kernel warmup immediately before it completes with per-batch progress lines (10/10 batches in 47s), so the wedge is specific to this op's autotune, not to warmup in general.

The same behavior existed on the launch-day `deepseekv41-flash-0909` image, which is why this deployment has carried `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS="trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe,flashinfer::trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe"` since September 9. Reproducing it on current nightly shows the gap is not fixed.

## Root cause evidence

Inspecting FlashInfer's prebuilt cubins in the nightly image (`flashinfer_jit_cache`):

```console
# 907 .so files in flashinfer_jit_cache overall — sm_103a coverage exists:
$ for so in $(find . -name "*.so"); do cuobjdump -lelf $so 2>/dev/null | grep -oE "sm_103[a-z]?"; done | sort | uniq -c
   3380 sm_103a

# …but the cubin the fp4 block-scale MoE autotuner benchmarks:
$ cuobjdump -lelf .../jit_cache/trtllm_gemm/trtllm_gemm.so | grep -oE "sm_[0-9]+[a-z]?" | sort | uniq -c
      1 sm_100a

$ cuobjdump -ptx .../jit_cache/trtllm_gemm/trtllm_gemm.so | grep -oE "target sm_[0-9]+" | sort | uniq -c
      (empty — no PTX section at all)
```

`trtllm_gemm.so` ships **only an `sm_100a` cubin and no PTX**. An arch-specific (`a`-suffixed) cubin runs on exactly its target arch and never on a later one (this is the same mechanism as the `cooperative_topk` SM103 gap documented in the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash SM103 patch work — `sm_100a` cubins are unusable on SM103, and without PTX there is nothing to JIT forward).

So on SM103 the autotuner launches a candidate that either fails its launch silently or spins in a grid-stride loop sized for a different arch, and the `cudaEventSynchronize` in the timing loop blocks forever. The autotuner has no per-candidate timeout, so one non-terminating candidate wedges the whole boot.

## Suggested fixes (either would do; both would be robust)

1. **Ship an `sm_103a` (and ideally `sm_103`-JITable PTX) build of `trtllm_gemm`** — the rest of the JIT cache clearly builds for 103a (3,380 cubins), so this specific module looks like an omission rather than a fundamental limitation.
2. **Add a timeout to the FlashInfer autotuner per candidate/bucket** — a wedged candidate should be skipped and logged, not hang the engine forever. Right now one bad kernel costs an unbounded boot.

## Workaround

```
VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS="trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe,flashinfer::trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe"
```

With the skip, the same configuration boots to serving in ~8 minutes; the op then runs on its default (untuned) kernel selection. Measured decode on this deployment is ~91 tok/s single-stream with the skip in place.

## Additional context

- Full deployment config and the SM103 patch history: https://github.com/ebfio/deepseek-v4.1-flash-gb300
- The engine does not log *which* candidate config it was benchmarking when it wedged — if maintainers want a `py-spy dump` from a wedged process or a CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING run, I can reproduce the wedge on demand and capture it.

title: [Bugfix][NIXL] Don't fail a completed KV transfer when telemetry is unavailable
body:
## Purpose

`get_xfer_telemetry()` is called inside the `xfer_state == "DONE"` branch of
`_pop_done_transfers` — i.e. *after* NIXL has already reported the transfer complete. The enclosing
`except Exception` then routes any telemetry error into `_handle_failed_transfer()`, discarding a
transfer that succeeded.

Telemetry is optional. NIXL builds shipped with it compiled out log:

```
W nixl_agent.cpp:215] NIXL telemetry is disabled; ignoring telemetry requested through agent config
```

and then raise `nixlNoTelemetryError` from `get_xfer_telemetry()`, even though the agent was
created with `capture_telemetry=True`. vLLM enables telemetry unconditionally — the comment above
the agent config says *"Enable telemetry by default for NIXL 0.7.1 and above"*, but the code only
checks that `nixl_agent_config` imports; there is no version or capability check, and
`nixlNoTelemetryError` is not handled anywhere in the tree.

## Impact

On DeepSeek-V4.1 P/D disaggregation over the default UCX backend with a stock `nixl-cu13==1.4.1`
wheel, this failed **100% of requests**:

```
vllm:nixl_num_failed_transfers_total  17960
"Num successful transfers=0"
"Skipping KV post-processing for failed request ..."
"backend emitted finish_reason=error without a message"
→ HTTP 500 to every client
```

Guarding the call restored serving with no other change — which also confirms the KV transfers
themselves were fine throughout. Measured before/after on the same image and config:

| | unpatched | patched |
|---|---|---|
| 60k-token prompt | `{"error":{"code":500}}` | streams content |
| `nixl_num_failed_transfers_total` | 17,960 | 0 |
| benchmark | every request failed | 3526 valid / 15 errors |

## Relationship to existing work — please read before reviewing

This overlaps with work already in flight, and I want to be explicit rather than quietly duplicate it:

- **#57734** — *[Bugfix][NIXL] Guard `record_transfer` against None telemetry* (open). It supersedes
  **#57403**, which is now closed.
- **ai-dynamo/nixl#2271** — *return `None` from `get_xfer_telemetry` when telemetry is disabled* (open),
  and its issue **ai-dynamo/nixl#2266**

Those two are a **matched pair**: nixl#2271 changes the raise into a `None`, and vllm#57734 then
handles that `None`. Together they fix it properly, and I'd consider that the better long-term
shape.

**The gap this addresses:** vllm#57734 adds `if res is None: return` inside `record_transfer`
(`nixl/stats.py`). That handles the `None` return **but not a raised exception**. Against NIXL as
shipped today — which raises rather than returning `None` — the guard is never reached, because
`get_xfer_telemetry()` raises before `record_transfer()` is called. vllm#57734 alone therefore does
not fix the failure above. It takes effect once nixl#2271 lands *and* users upgrade their NIXL wheel.

So this PR is complementary rather than competing:

- it guards the **exception** path, which is what current released NIXL actually does
- it is **version-independent** — no NIXL upgrade required
- it keeps working as defense-in-depth after nixl#2271 ships

**I am happy to close this** if maintainers would rather land nixl#2271 + vllm#57734 and require a
NIXL upgrade, or to reduce it to just the `base_worker.py` hunk if the OBJ-tier change is
unwelcome. Equally happy to fold the exception guard into #57734 instead, if its author prefers.

## Changes

- `nixl/base_worker.py`: extract `_try_get_xfer_telemetry()`, which returns `None` and
  `warning_once`s instead of raising; skip the stats sample when telemetry is unavailable. The
  transfer is released and counted as DONE either way.
- `v1/kv_offload/tiering/obj/manager.py`: same guard. There the call sits **outside** any `try`, so
  it would propagate rather than be misclassified.

No behaviour change for backends that do provide telemetry.

## Test Plan

- Reproduced on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 2P1D disaggregated, UCX backend, `nixl-cu13==1.4.1`.
- Before: 100% request failure, 17,960 failed transfers.
- After: 0 failed transfers; full benchmark 3526 valid / 15 errors; a 60k-token prompt streams
  content.

### Unit tests

`tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py`:

- `test_telemetry_exception_does_not_fail_completed_transfer` — `get_xfer_telemetry` raises on a
  `DONE` handle. Asserts the request lands in `done_req_ids` and not `failed_req_ids`, that the
  handle is still released, that `_log_failure` is not called, and that no `num_failed_transfers`
  sample is recorded. Fails on `main` without this patch.
- `test_telemetry_still_recorded_when_available` — pins the no-change case: when telemetry works,
  all four stats fields are recorded exactly as before.

`tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_obj_tier.py`:

- `test_telemetry_failure_does_not_lose_successful_transfer` — a raising `get_xfer_telemetry` must
  still yield `JobResult(success=True)` with `transfer_time is None`. Only the timing is lost.

These sit beside the existing `test_post_transfer_cleanup_failure_does_not_lose_result` and
`test_release_xfer_failure_retries_without_losing_result`, which cover the same shape for the other
post-transfer cleanup calls.

title: [Bug]: keep-mode pause stops pending KV receive polling with HiSparse/NIXL
body:
`pause_generation(mode="keep")` can stop decode-side KV completion polling before asynchronous receives finish. With HiSparse mixed DRAM/VRAM NIXL reads, this also prevents the decode worker from sending completion notifications to prefill, leaving prefill waiting for remote cleanup during its own pause.

The deployment that exposed this uses GLM-5.3, B300, DP/EP=8 per replica, NIXL P/D, HiSparse on decode, and MooncakeStore through MultiConnector. This was investigated on a patched v0.28.1 development runtime; the scheduler condition below is also present on main at `0bce411a`. A live patched restart is in progress; we do not yet have an end-to-end pause-time result.

### Confirmed mechanism

1. D has a request in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`, in `waiting` or `skipped_waiting`.
2. `pause(mode="keep")` sets `PAUSED_ALL`. `get_num_unfinished_requests()` returns zero; the waiting receive does not count as a finished request retained for cleanup either. With no other work, `Scheduler.has_requests()` returns false.
3. The engine stops issuing zero-token connector steps.
4. Mixed-memory NIXL reads create multiple transfer handles without `notif_msg`, then record `_pending_recv_notifs`. `get_transfer_results()` sends those notifications only after polling all handles complete.
5. Even completed transport handles therefore do not notify P if D stops polling. P can remain active solely to wait for delayed connector frees.

This differs from the ordinary NIXL READ path in v0.27, where `make_prepped_xfer(..., notif_msg=...)` attaches the notification to the transport. Mixed-memory software notification bookkeeping was introduced by #53780 and is exercised by the HiSparse path. The scheduler's delayed-free gate itself predates v0.27; it is not a newly introduced change.

### Reproduction evidence

A CPU reproducer used the existing `recv_worker` unit-test fixture with two completed transport handles and the real `_read_blocks_mixed`, `get_finished`, and scheduler methods:

```
all_transport_handles_done: true
mixed_handles_have_transport_notification: [false, false]
producer_notifications_before_poll: 0
decode_scheduler_has_work_while_paused: false
producer_notifications_after_one_explicit_poll: 1
finished_recving_after_one_explicit_poll: [request]
```

The scheduler state can be reproduced in the existing scheduler suite by admitting an asynchronous KV load, setting `PAUSED_ALL`, and checking `has_requests()` before passing back `KVConnectorOutput(finished_recving={request_id})`.

### Proposed fix and scope

Keep `has_requests()` true during `PAUSED_ALL` while a queued `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` request has not been reported in `finished_recving_kv_req_ids`. This permits connector-only polling; the paused scheduler still schedules zero model tokens. Once receive completion is delivered, the engine can become idle without promoting the request until resume.

Live symptoms included multi-minute P pause waits while D had already acknowledged pause. The reproducer establishes this polling gap, but does not establish that it explains every second of those waits. Requests not yet admitted on D and producer lease behavior are distinct cases. Pause retry handling is outside this proposed fix.

Related PR #51371 prioritizes KV admission/polling while the scheduler is **unpaused**; it does not address this pause progress gap. #57810 controls cache retention across pause/sleep, which is separate.

Investigation and draft patch prepared with AI assistance (OpenAI Codex).

title: [Bugfix][HiSparse][NIXL] Keep a paused decoder stepping while split reads are in flight
body:
> [!NOTE]
> Rescoped by @MatthewBonanni (1fab475): this PR now carries only the HiSparse split-read fix, done in the NIXL connector with no core change. @S1ro1's general P/D change (cache-preserving keep pauses no longer waiting on retained KV exports) moved to #59670. The original description and live RL validation are preserved there.

## Purpose

Fix a P/D pause stall with HiSparse decoders. Since #53780, a NIXL read into a decoder with mixed DRAM/VRAM KV (HiSparse) is split into one transfer per memory type, and the producer is notified only once a worker polls both done. A `pause(mode="keep")` on the decoder hides its `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` requests, so the engine stops stepping, nothing polls, and the notification is never sent. The producer keeps those blocks until its lease expires, and a keep pause on the producer waits for them.

## Changes

`NixlBaseConnectorScheduler` tracks reads it has handed to the workers (`awaiting_kvs`) until they come back in `finished_recving`, and reports them through the existing `has_pending_push_work()` hook, which `Scheduler.has_requests()` already honors. A paused decoder keeps running zero-token connector steps until its in-flight reads complete and their notifications go out.

- Failed reads and aborted waiting requests also arrive in `finished_recving`, so the set always drains.
- Unpaused behavior is unchanged: waiting requests already keep the engine stepping.
- Push mode overrides the hook and never marks a read as awaiting.

## Test Plan

title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Use model-wide block drop for Mamba tail
body:
## Summary

Use the model-wide EAGLE block-drop decision when selecting the Mamba prompt-tail checkpoint boundary.

## Why

In a hybrid model, the group containing draft attention is marked as the EAGLE group, while a sibling Mamba group can have `manager.use_eagle == false`. The scheduler still applies EAGLE trailing-block drop model-wide. If the Mamba manager keys its tail checkpoint from the group-local flag, it can publish a state at a boundary where the attention group cannot resume.

`drop_eagle_checkpoint_block` is the model-wide decision already propagated by the coordinator, so the Mamba tail now reads the same bit as the scheduler.

## Scope

One production-line change plus a regression test that exercises a Mamba group outside the annotated EAGLE group. No KV connector or wire-protocol changes.

## Validation

Current-main branch `18ab9dc1fe`:

- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on both changed files.
- Focused scheduler suite on two AMD MI355X nodes: 12 passed per node.
- Kimi-K3 single-node TP8/DCP8, DSpark K4 block rejection, fine-grained prefix caching. Graph capture was disabled to shorten correctness validation.
- GSM8K full, concurrency 64: 1267/1319 = 0.9606, 0 request errors.
- No traceback, EngineCore failure, or HSA error in the server log.

The final amend changes only the explanatory comment; executable code and tests are identical to the E2E-validated revision.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for review and test orchestration. The human submitter is responsible for the final change.

title: [Bugfix][XPU] Guard DeepSeek V4 CuTe DSL dispatch with CUDA platform
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4-Flash on Intel XPU can select NVIDIA CuTe DSL kernels when CuTe DSL is installed. Three dispatch sites check `has_cutedsl()` without first checking the active platform.

This caused two successive startup failures on Stampede3 Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550:
- Indexer Q RoPE/quantization imported the NVIDIA implementation and failed because CUDA FlashAttention extensions were unavailable.
- After guarding that path, mixed prefill/decode warmup reached the CuTe DSL K-cache gather kernel and failed with `expected device_type=cuda`.

Require `current_platform.is_cuda()` before `has_cutedsl()` at the FP8 and MXFP4 indexer-Q dispatches and the K-cache dequantize/gather dispatch. Existing XPU kernels and the Triton fallback remain in use on non-CUDA platforms. CUDA selection is unchanged.

## Duplicate-work check

Searched open PRs for `cutedsl xpu`, `"has_cutedsl" XPU`, and `"dequantize_and_gather_k_cache" "XPU"`.
Inspected #54460's patch: it skips XPU warmup and initializes indexer metadata; it does not fix these dispatch sites. This change fixes the runtime dispatch instead of skipping warmup. #41834 is broader NVIDIA SM12x enablement, not this targeted XPU fix.

## Test plan and results

- Human-reported hardware validation: after applying these three guards locally, DeepSeek-V4-Flash startup succeeded on Intel XPU, TP=8. The previously reported exceptions occurred before startup.
- Reproduction environment: vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev422+gd05da62e9.xpu`, `vllm-xpu-kernels==0.1.14.1`, PyTorch `2.13.0+xpu`, Triton `3.7.2+xpu`, Python 3.12.
- That environment also needed a separate local workaround for the MoE `topk_softplus_sqrt` 10/12-argument mismatch. That compatibility fix is proposed separately in #58049 and is **not** in this PR; startup success must not be attributed to these guards alone.
- Agent-side command: `.venv/bin/python review-vllm/check_dispatch.py`. An isolated temporary harness executed the changed functions extracted from source with mocked tensor allocation and kernel entrypoints: **18/18 dispatch cases passed** (CUDA/XPU/ROCm, CuTe DSL available/unavailable, FP8/MXFP4 indexer and cache gather). The same harness reproduced the three XPU dispatch failures against the original conditions. This is control-flow validation, not numerical or hardware testing; the temporary harness is not a repository test.
- Full repository pytest/pre-commit, CUDA numerical regression tests, generated-output correctness, and model evaluation have **not** been run. The exact rebased PR commit has not been run on XPU; hardware evidence is from the equivalent local edits on the version above.

## Draft status / AI assistance

Prepared with OpenAI Codex assistance. The submitter applied the proposed local fixes and reported successful startup. Keep as draft pending review of the final diff and the outstanding repository/hardware tests; no inference accuracy or 1M-context validation is claimed.

title: [Bugfix][XPU] Support legacy topk_softplus_sqrt operator schema
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4-Flash startup on Intel XPU failed because `topk_hash_softplus_sqrt` passed 12 arguments to a loaded `_moe_C::topk_softplus_sqrt` operator exposing the older 10-argument schema.

Reported environment: Stampede3 Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550; Python 3.12; vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev422+gd05da62e9.xpu`; `vllm-xpu-kernels==0.1.14.1`; PyTorch `2.13.0+xpu`; Triton `3.7.2+xpu`.

## Changes

- Inspect the loaded default operator's schema and forward the original 10 arguments for the legacy interface.
- Reject non-default `bias_vl` or `image_sentinel_lo` on the legacy interface instead of silently dropping requested routing features.
- Forward all 12 arguments for the newer interface.
- Fail explicitly for unknown argument counts.
- Add nine parametrized wrapper regression cases to the existing MoE test module, covering argument/output-buffer forwarding and rejection before kernel invocation.

Related: #58048 addresses separate CuTeDSL dispatch failures encountered during the same XPU startup. These PRs are independent changes; this PR contains the MoE compatibility patch that is not part of #58048.

## Validation

- **9/9 isolated wrapper tests passed.** The added test functions and production wrapper were extracted with Python AST and run under pytest using mocked operator/schema objects, without importing the full vLLM/PyTorch stack.
- The same harness against the unchanged base wrapper produced **5 failures and 4 passes**, identifying the missing compatibility/guard behavior.
- Ruff **0.14.0** lint and format checks passed for both changed files. Lint explicitly classified `vllm` as first-party because this was a partial source checkout.
- The reporter confirmed successful local model startup after applying the equivalent schema compatibility patch together with the separate dispatch fixes.

The full test module, accelerator numerical tests, generation correctness, and torch.compile behavior were **not run** in this environment. Startup success is not a claim of successful end-to-end generation. Runtime schema-inspection overhead has not been measured.

Suggested follow-up in a complete vLLM environment:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py -k topk_hash_softplus_sqrt_schema
```

## Draft / AI disclosure

Implementation, regression tests, and this PR description were prepared with OpenAI Codex at the contributor's request. Keeping this as a draft pending human diff review and accelerator/model validation. Maintainer feedback is welcome on whether compatibility belongs in this wrapper or should instead require a coordinated XPU kernel update.

title: [Bugfix][GLM-5.3-Flash] Run the dense MLP layers on the sequence-parallel shard
body:
## Purpose

GLM-5.3-Flash served with DP > 1, TP > 1 and `--enable-expert-parallel` (the configuration that turns on `use_sequence_parallel_moe`) sporadically emits a wrong first token, stray `</think>` tokens followed by a repeated reasoning block, and occasionally byte garbage such as `ԥԥԥԥ� Canadian French, ԥԥ�1ԥ…`. DP with TP=1 and TP-only serving are clean.

`Glm5NextModel` follows the DeepSeek-V4 sequence-parallel layout: the token dimension is sharded across the TP group once at the model entry (`sp_shard`) and every layer runs its mHC and MLP on that shard, gathering only for attention. Every non-MoE module on the shard therefore has to be sequence-parallel aware. The dense MLP of the first `first_k_dense_replace` (3) layers was still constructed as a standard TP MLP, so its `down_proj` all-reduce summed the partial outputs of *different* tokens held by the two TP ranks:

- multi-token batches (prefill, concurrent decode): rows of the first three layers are mixed pairwise, hence the wrong first token / garbage under load;
- single-token decode: the peer rank holds a zero padding row, so the real token only loses half of the intermediate dimension, which is why the model still looked mostly coherent and the bug went unnoticed.

The shared experts already pass `is_sequence_parallel` (replicated weights, `disable_tp`, no collective). This PR passes the same flag to the dense `Glm5NextMLP` and adds a unit test for the layout. TP-only and DP-with-TP1 deployments do not enter this branch and are unchanged.

Related but different: #50154 describes a sequence-parallel bug in the `deepseek_v2` path (GLM-5.2), where the SP boundary sits inside the MoE block; glm5next shards the whole model, so the fix lives in the dense layer construction instead.

## Test Plan

Unit test (single process, fakes a TP=2 world in the parallel linear layers and forbids the all-reduce):

```bash
pytest tests/models/glm5next/test_sequence_parallel.py -v
```

The layer-level case fails on `main` (the dense `gate_up_proj` weight is sharded to half the intermediate size) and passes with this PR.

End to end on 4x GB300, `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (FP8), FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE attention, FLASHINFER_TRTLLM FP8 MoE, `allgather_reducescatter` all2all, default CUDA graphs, prefix caching disabled, `--max-num-seqs 64`:

```bash
vllm serve zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash --data-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 64 --no-enable-prefix-caching
```

Each chat completion is scored as anomalous if the parsed reasoning/content contains U+FFFD, non-printable characters, a run of 8+ identical non-whitespace characters, a 4-gram repetition ratio above 0.5, or more than one `</think>`. `lm_eval` gsm8k 5-shot on 200 problems via `local-completions`.

## Test Result

| config | 16 prompts sequential (temp 0) | 64 prompts, concurrency 64, 1024 tok | 8 x ~15k-token prompts + 8 short, concurrent | gsm8k |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DP4 TP1 EP | 0 / 16 | 0 / 64 | 0 / 16 | 0.935 |
| DP4 TP1 EP + MTP(3) + kv fp8 | 0 / 16 | 0 / 64 | 0 / 16 | 0.94 |
| TP4 EP | 0 / 48 (3 runs) | - | - | - |
| DP2 TP2 EP, **before** | 4 / 16 | **31 / 64** | 3 / 16 | 0.95 |
| DP2 TP2 EP, **after** | 0 / 48 (3 runs) | 0 / 64 | 0 / 16 | 0.935 |

Before the fix the three temperature-0 runs of the same prompt typically diverged at the first or second character (the prefill result itself was wrong). After the fix they diverge only late (character 84 to 724), the same as the TP4 EP baseline (47 to 1228), which is the usual batch-dependent nondeterminism. gsm8k is insensitive to this bug because the answers are short.

Ruled out on the way: the MNNVL Lamport custom all-gather / reduce-scatter kernels used by `sp_all_gather` / `sp_reduce_scatter` on this platform pass a 2-GPU stress test against NCCL (3000 iterations, 1 to 1024 rows x 4096 bf16, all-gather and reduce-scatter back to back, 0 mismatches).

`pre-commit` hooks `ruff-check` / `ruff-format` pass on the changed files.

This change was made with AI assistance (Claude Code); the analysis and results above were reviewed by the submitter.

title: [Bugfix][Attention] Fixed-width sparse indexer prefill logits so long prefills reuse allocator blocks (#55569)
body:
## Purpose

Fixes #55569. Related: #56457 reports the same allocation pattern in the Qwen4Exp QSA indexer, with fixes proposed for that path in #56500 and #57105 (both open); #55572 (closed) lowered the default logits budget on integrated GPUs instead.

The dense sparse-MLA indexer (`sparse_attn_indexer.py`, and the GLM-5.3-Flash kpool variant under `models/glm5next`) scores each prefill chunk with DeepGEMM's `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits`, which allocates its `[M, N]` fp32 logits inside the C++ API. `N` is the request's compressed context so far, so every chunk of a long prefill asks for a tensor of a new, larger size: one launch per chunk of growing size while `M * N * 4` fits the `VLLM_SPARSE_INDEXER_MAX_LOGITS_MB` budget (512 MiB), and, once a chunk exceeds it (about 116k tokens at a 4,608-token chunk with kpool 4), several launches per chunk that are all close to the budget but never the same size twice. PyTorch's caching allocator serves a request from a cached block only if it fits, and returns segments to the driver only on `empty_cache` or an OOM-time release, so once the free space that happens to be around is used up, each chunk step adds a new segment for the rest of the prefill. On a discrete GPU this is reserved-but-idle memory; on unified-memory devices (DGX Spark / GB10) it comes out of the host's share, and the driver-level failure (`NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY`) arrives before the allocator's OOM retry can help, ending in the swap storms reported in #55569.

**Change.** Allocate the logits at a fixed width instead of the chunk's kv length, using the `max_seqlen_k` argument DeepGEMM already provides: the kernel still computes only `[cu_seqlen_ks, cu_seqlen_ke)` per row, `max_seqlen_k` is only the allocation stride, and DeepGEMM asserts `clean_logits=False` with it (verified at vLLM's pinned commit). The width is `ceil(max_model_len / compress_ratio)` (the page-table width), computed once in the metadata builder, and the planner sizes its query sub-chunks against it, so every sub-chunk of a prefill requests an identically sized tensor from the first chunk to the last and the allocator recycles the same blocks. At the call sites the returned view is narrowed back to `[M, N]`, so every consumer sees exactly the shape it sees today; only the storage behind it is constant-size. This is safe for all of them because they take strides explicitly: `top_k_per_row_prefill` receives `logits.stride(0)` and `stride(1)`, and both candidate-block Triton kernels unpack `*logits.stride()`. The DeepSeek V4.1 sparse-logits backend already keeps a fixed `max_logits_bytes` workspace; this brings the dense DeepGEMM path in line with it.

- `vllm/envs.py`: `VLLM_SPARSE_INDEXER_FIXED_LOGITS_WIDTH`. Unset (default): on for integrated (unified-memory) GPUs only; `1` / `0` force  it on / off on any GPU.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py`: `DeepseekV32IndexerPrefillChunkMetadata.logits_width`; `_split_indexer_prefill_chunks`  budgets and sub-chunks against `max(N, logits_width)`; the builder computes the width once (`self.fixed_logits_width`) for the standard  path (`dcp_world_size == 1`). The PCP/DCP planner path is left at the per-chunk width because the DCP merge consumes the logits directly.
- `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py`: `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits(..., max_seqlen_k: int = 0)` forwards the kwarg (0 = current behaviour).
- `vllm/model_executor/layers/sparse_attn_indexer.py`, `vllm/models/glm5next/nvidia/sparse_indexer.py`: pass the width, narrow the view.
- `tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_prefill_chunk_logits_width.py`: planner test (constant launch shapes at every step; `logits_width=0`  is identical to the current plan; width never below the kv length; packed requests are budgeted at the fixed width).

**Costs and non-goals.** Total kernel work is unchanged (same rows, same `[ks, ke)` bounds), but the launch count is not: with a 512 MiB budget and a 102,400-column width (`max_model_len` 409,600, kpool 4) a 4,608-token chunk is 4 launches from the first chunk on, where today it is 1 launch until ~116k tokens; and packed short requests stop sharing a launch once `rows * width * 4` exceeds the budget (the test shows two 1,000-row requests at kv length 100 becoming two launches), so a batch of many short prefills becomes more launches. Neither
was measured for latency at short prompts, which is why the default is integrated-only, where the allocator growth is what fails. The decode path (paged kernel) is untouched. This change does not address the separate first-use growth of the activation working set on unified memory (see the note under Test Result), which is not the indexer.

This PR was prepared with AI assistance; the measurements were run on my hardware under my direction, and I reviewed every changed line.

## Update (2026-10-08): rebased onto `main`

Rebased onto `main` @ `f4dde3132`. One conflict: #59211 (DCP for the kpool indexer) added an empty-local-chunk guard around the `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` call in `models/glm5next/nvidia/sparse_indexer.py`. The width and the narrowed view now sit inside its kernel branch, so a rank with no local kv still skips the kernel exactly as on `main`. The fixed width stays off whenever `dcp_world_size > 1`, as before. Everything else applied unchanged.

Checked against what moved on `main` since this was opened:

- #55222 now counts the indexer prefill workspace in compressed rows. The planner's `logits_width` is in the same units, and #55222's `test_indexer_prefill_budget_matches_compressed_workspace` passes on this branch.
- The DeepGEMM pin moved from `e1f418c2` to `1e1842a8`. `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` has an identical function body at both (`csrc/apis/attention.hpp`, including the `max_seqlen_k` allocation path), `max_seqlen_k` is still a keyword of the Python binding vLLM calls (default 0), and the new torch op schema carries it too.

Re-run on the rebased head (CPU-side tests; Python 3.12, torch 2.13.0):

- `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_prefill_chunk_logits_width.py`: 5 passed. Against `main`'s planner, all 5 fail (no `logits_width` parameter).
- `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_deepseek_v4_slot_mapping.py`: 32 passed, 1 failed. The failure is DeepGEMM's architecture assert on the local GPU, which DeepGEMM does not support, and it fails identically on `main`. The test helper's default model was swapped for an ungated mirror of Llama-3-8B for this run, because the gated repo is not available here.

The rebased head has not been served. The end-to-end numbers below are still from the build described under Limitations.

## Test Plan

- Unit: `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_prefill_chunk_logits_width.py`
- End to end, A/B (two DGX Spark / GB10, 121 GiB unified memory each, vLLM TP=2 over the pair, `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`, expert  parallel, MTP 3, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_ds_mla`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 8192` (scheduler chunk 4,608 = the prefix-cache block), one  client at a time): a fresh serve, then cold prefills of ~100k tokens, another ~100k (different content, same length), then ~200k,  sampling host `MemAvailable` on both nodes after each request. Profile `--max-model-len 204800 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.87` (memory  profiling on), chosen for host headroom; fixed width 51,200 columns. The stock width was run on the same serve configuration with the  fixed width disabled, so the allocation width is the only difference.
- Issue scenario: one cold ~230k-token prefill on the production profile (`--max-model-len 409600 --kv-cache-memory 4.62e9`; fixed width  102,400 columns) with the change applied.
- Per-call telemetry: a debug build logged `torch.cuda.memory_reserved()`, `num_device_alloc` and host `MemAvailable` after every  indexer call (one per indexer layer per chunk step) on both ranks, to attribute growth to the caching allocator.
- Allocator behaviour in isolation: a standalone loop replaying the planner + `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` + `top_k_per_row_prefill` for a  98k-token prefill (12 × 8,192-token chunks × 45 layers) with and without the fixed width, no model. Available on request.

## Test Result

Per-rank caching-allocator growth over the whole A/B ladder (fresh serve → 100k → 100k → 200k), identical on both ranks:

| width | reserved growth | cudaMallocs | where |
|---|---|---|---|
| per-chunk (stock) | +4,782 MB | 14 | +900 MB on the first chunk; **from ~156k tokens, one new segment every 4,608-token step, sized to that step's tail launch (+180, +198, +220, +240, +260, +280, +300, +320, +342 MB)**; +1,542 MB at the final chunk (a larger chunk shape, see the note) |
| fixed (this PR) | +2,134 MB | 3 | +594 MB on the first chunk (the second live logits block); zero growth for every later step of all three prefills; +1,540 MB at the final chunk (same shape effect) |

Host `MemAvailable` deltas per request (rank 0 / rank 1, MB):

| request | stock | fixed |
|---|---|---|
| first 100k (cold) | −2,399 / −2,222 | −2,720 / −2,824 |
| second 100k (cold, same length) | −33 / −19 | −60 / −8 |
| 200k (cold) | **−3,316 / −3,796** (+409 MB swap on rank 0; 2 new `NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY` kernel lines) | −1,583 / −1,444 |

Time to first token: 100k 53.9 / 52.6 s stock vs 54.1 / 52.9 s fixed; 200k 116.5 s stock vs 109.6 s fixed (single samples; we read the 100k numbers as parity and do not claim the 200k difference).

Issue scenario with the change, production profile: a 231,751-token cold prefill completed (TTFT 127 s, correct answer) with no `NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY` lines, leaving 1.7 GB / 3.1 GB of host `MemAvailable` on the two nodes from an idle 5.5 / 6.9 GB; the difference is the first-use working-set growth described below plus the two logits blocks, not per-chunk growth. The stock width was not re-run at 230k on that profile; its per-step growth is the A/B row above.

In isolation (reserved bytes after 98k tokens): stock +2,810 MB, one new segment per chunk until the sub-chunk sizes stabilise; fixed +1,190 MB, flat from the second chunk (two live logits blocks — the loop keeps chunk *k*'s `logits` referenced while chunk *k+1* allocates — plus a tail block). With a fixed pattern of interleaved transient allocations: stock +3,650 MB, fixed +1,960 MB (transients alone +1,410). For completeness, `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:256` and a private `torch.cuda.MemPool` for the logits made the fixed case worse (+2,312 / +2,470 MB) because they stop the freed logits blocks from serving other allocations. #55569 lists `expandable_segments:True` as a mitigation; in our run on the stock width it did not hold (five `NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY` lines during a 100k prefill, −1.5 GB retained), consistent with the NemotronH data point later in that thread.

Note for anyone measuring this on unified memory: the first deep prefill after a fresh start also grows the process by the activation working set of each new chunk shape (about 5 GiB per device here up to the 8,192-token chunk, as `gpu_memory_utilization` profiling reports). That growth is independent of the indexer and of this change; it dominates the first-100k row in both columns above, and only the second-100k and 200k rows isolate the indexer. Our own first measurement of this patch was confounded by exactly that.

Limitations of the evidence: the end-to-end numbers were measured on vLLM 0.28.1rc1.dev580 (the NVIDIA arm64 CUDA 13 build for this model) with an equivalent patch; the port to `main` applies and its planner test passes, but `main` itself was not served. One model family (GLM-5.3-Flash, kpool path) and one hardware class, TP=2. The standard `sparse_attn_indexer.py` path shares the planner and the DeepGEMM call, and the planner test covers its arithmetic, but the DeepSeek V3.2 / V4 variants were not run end to end. DCP is intentionally left at the current width. Short-prompt latency and many-short-request batches with the higher launch count were not measured.

title: [Model] Use circular buffer for DeepSeek V4 C128 state
body:
## Summary

DeepSeek-V4 C128 compressor state is request-local bounded history rather than reusable attention KV cache. On CUDA, representing it with SlidingWindowMLASpec allocates more blocks than the state requires.

This PR stores CUDA C128 state in one CircularBufferSpec block per request, reducing its KV-cache footprint. C4 and CPU/ROCm/XPU remain on their existing paged layouts. These can be in the follow-up PRs and tests.

## Implementation

- Size each ring for 128 history rows plus speculative lookahead.
- Address rows as block_id * capacity + position % capacity.
- Use Triton to build ring/tail metadata and skip padding or null blocks.
- Let CuTeDSL read current-chunk rows from raw inputs and older rows from the ring before saving the new tail, preventing wraparound overwrite.
- Keep C4 and non-CUDA backends unchanged.

## Results

- TP4+EP and DP2×TP2+EP serving passed
- NIXL PD GSM8K accuracy: 0.9469
- Mooncake PD (TP2 prefill + TP2 decode + EP) GSM8K accuracy: 0.9515
- SimpleCPUOffload GSM8K accuracy: 0.955
- KV capacity: `335,514 → 478,421` tokens (`+42.6%`)

This change was developed with AI assistance and manually reviewed and validated by the submitter.
