title: [Rust Frontend] Share `SchemaRoot` between argument coercion and grammars
body:
## Purpose

Rust tool parsers coerce raw parameter text by the tool's JSON schema (`tool/parameters.rs`), and argument grammars (#59395) constrain the same parameters by it, but each interpreted the schema on its own. Coercion ignored `$ref`: a parameter whose schema is `{"$ref": "#/$defs/Place"}` came back as the JSON text string `"{\"city\": \"Paris\"}"` instead of an object. Pydantic v2 `model_json_schema()`, which most SDKs use to build tool schemas, emits exactly this for nested models, enums, and `Optional[Model]`:

```json
{"$defs": {"Place": {...}, "Unit": {"enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"], "type": "string"}},
 "properties": {"place": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Place"},
                "unit": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Unit", "default": "celsius"},
                "backup": {"anyOf": [{"$ref": "#/$defs/Place"}, {"type": "null"}], "default": null}}}
```

This affects every schema-coercing parser: Qwen Coder and MiMo, GLM, MiniMax M2/M3, Hy. DeepSeek DSML and Kimi K3 decode by their `string=`/`type=` labels instead. Coercion and grammars also disagreed on `nullable`, `const`, single-schema `allOf`, and type-name aliases such as `"int"`, so a grammar could admit a value that the parser then decodes as another type.

The open-PR search found #50933, which resolves `$ref`/`$defs` for the Python Qwen3-Coder path; there is no Rust counterpart. Python parity is not a goal here. #59190 (the Kimi K3 full-output grammar) is stacked on this PR.

- New `schema::SchemaRoot`, the tool's parameters schema that references resolve against, owns how a parameter's schema is read:
  - `resolved` returns the root after following local `$ref` chains and single-schema `allOf`; unresolvable, cyclic, and remote references accept any value and are never fetched;
  - `options` expands each reference target at most once per value, as the argument grammar walker from #59395 already did, so shared definitions cannot blow up exponentially;
  - `options` splits a value schema into typed options: `const`/`enum` literals, one option per `anyOf`/`oneOf`/type-array alternative, `object`/`array` inferred from `properties`/`items`, `nullable: true` adding `null`, and aliases such as `int` or `dict` parsed to the canonical type;
  - `JsonType` gains `Integer`, since coercion distinguishes integers.
- Argument grammars read value options from `SchemaRoot` instead of their own walker.
- Coercion reads the schema one level at a time. `ToolSchema` keeps the parameters schema, and object and array types resolve their fields and items only when a structured value reaches them. A recursive schema therefore costs only as deep as the value; expanding it ahead of time is exponential in its branching, and a tree with two recursive children took over 60 s to build that way.
- Kimi K3 labels values through its own `xtml_type` mapping, which follows `_xtml_type` in the checkpoint's `encoding_k3.py`; integers and floats are both `number`. Its grammar is unchanged.

Behavior changes in coercion:

- `$ref` resolves at the parameter level, in nested fields and items, and inside `anyOf`.
- `const` and single-schema `allOf` are understood, and `enum` values coerce by their own type, so `"2"` under `{"enum": [1, 2, 3]}` becomes `2`.
- Text that spells a non-string `const` or `enum` value as JSON decodes to that value before any type is tried, so `1` under `{"enum": ["fast", 1]}` becomes the number `1`, as the argument grammar already constrains it, instead of the string `"1"`. Text matching no literal converts as before.
- `anyOf`/`oneOf` whose alternatives all have unknown types now falls back to the raw string, like an unknown `type`, instead of being treated as an object.

Behavior changes in argument grammars (Kimi K3): `nullable: true` admits `type="null"`, an aliased type such as `"int"` constrains its value instead of dropping the parameter, and a schema with `properties` or `items` but no `type` admits only objects or arrays.

## Test Plan

```bash
cd rust
cargo nextest run -p vllm-parser -p vllm-chat
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
```

- `schema` unit tests: the Pydantic schema above, unresolvable, cyclic, and remote references, aliases in type arrays, `nullable`, mixed enums, single `allOf`, and `items` without `type`.
- Coercion tests: Pydantic-style references (including `Optional` taking `null`), recursive and branching recursive schemas converted from structured values, and integer enums.
- Qwen Coder `parse_complete` with referenced parameters returns an object and an integer.

## Test Result

- `vllm-parser` + `vllm-chat`: 940 tests passed, including all 36 XGrammar replay cases; the roundtrip grammar files are unchanged.
- Workspace Clippy and pre-commit passed.

AI assistance: implementation and validation assisted by Claude Code.

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Small-head sparse decode on SM90
body: ## Purpose On SM90, FlashMLA's sparse decode tiles query heads by 64 (the WGMMA M dimension). A DeepSeek V4.1 TP8 rank owns only 8 heads (16 at TP4), so it pads them to 64 and spends most of the tensor-core work on padding. This adds a Triton sparse decode kernel that tiles heads by 16 with `tl.dot` (mma.sync), reads the existing packed FP8 MLA cache directly, and recovers parallelism by splitting the key set across programs, merging the partial results with log-sum-exp. **Why it is faster at small batches.** At a few decode tokens per step, FlashMLA launches roughly one CTA per token and each CTA does 64-head work for 8 real heads. This kernel launches `tokens × splits` programs, each doing 16-head work over its share of keys. The best split count depends on both token count and key width: 32 splits at ≤3 tokens fills the GPU, but by 8 tokens 8 splits wins because the merge cost and per-program gather overhead dominate. `_pick_config` encodes this measured table. At larger batches the step becomes gather/dequant-bound rather than MMA-bound, so removing the padding no longer helps and FlashMLA is kept. **Dispatch** (automatic, no flag): SM90, 8 or 16 local heads, decode only, and | Layer key width (SWA + compressed top-k) | Uses this kernel at | Otherwise | | --- | --- | --- | | ≤256 (SWA-only layers) | ≤16 decode tokens per step | FlashMLA | | >256 (compressed layers, `index_topk=512`) | ≤12 decode tokens per step | FlashMLA | The gate is decode tokens per rank per step (≈ batch × (1 + spec tokens)), so the gain is limited to **low-concurrency decode**. It does not depend on context length, since sparse attention reads a fixed number of keys per token. Prefill always uses FlashMLA. **JIT warmup:** both launches register every split config, `HAS_EXTRA` variant and DSpark SWA width with the startup JIT warmup, so no Triton compile happens on the serving path. Related to #48168. **Not a duplicate:** I checked the issue discussion and open PRs for #48168 and for small-head sparse decode; none implements this SM90 decode path. #57673 has since been reworked into an opt-in backend that reuses this PR's decoder (with attribution) but does not add the automatic FlashMLA dispatch. #55866 targets FA4 sparse MQA on *Blackwell*, #51403 targets *ROCm*. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla_sparse.py -k small_head -q python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_dsv41_small_head_decode.py --heads 8 16 --topk 0 64 512 --rounds 3 pre-commit run --all-files ``` End-to-end on 8× H20 (one node), TP8, DSpark K=2, same flags as our production deployment except `--max-model-len 32768`. Both arms ran on the same node and the same image, back-to-back: ```bash vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --ignore-eos --seed 42 \ --max-concurrency {1,2,4,8,16,32} lm_eval --model local-chat-completions --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 \ --apply_chat_template --fewshot_as_multiturn --gen_kwargs temperature=0 ``` ## Test Result ### End-to-end (8× H20, TP8) Median ITL is per decode step; concurrency 1–4 falls inside the gate (≤12 tokens/step with K=2). | Concurrency | Stock median ITL | This PR | Δ ITL | Stock tok/s | This PR tok/s | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 8.99 ms | 8.37 ms | **−6.8%** | 239.6 | 264.4 | | 2 | 10.96 ms | 9.87 ms | **−9.9%** | 365.5 | 400.8 | | 4 | 13.91 ms | 13.11 ms | **−5.7%** | 574.2 | 621.9 | | 8 | 19.52 ms | 19.39 ms | −0.7% | 825.7 | 824.7 | | 16 | 27.48 ms | 27.13 ms | −1.3% | 1135.1 | 1178.9 | | 32 | 41.05 ms | 41.29 ms | +0.6% | 1510.6 | 1522.3 | Throughput also reflects DSpark acceptance length, which varied by run (2.06–2.23 stock vs 2.14–2.31 this PR), so ITL is the cleaner signal. **GSM8K** (full 1319, 5-shot chat, greedy, flexible extract): stock **89.99%** (1187), this PR **89.92%** (1186), stderr ±0.83%. Per question, 19 flip to correct and 20 flip to wrong, consistent with split-K reduction order changing near-tie greedy tokens. ### Operator benchmark (1× H20) 108 configurations (tokens 1–16/24/32 × heads 8/16 × top-k 0/64/512), CUDA graphs, cold-L2 input rotation, median of 3 alternating rounds, CUDA-event timing. title: [ROCm][Bugfix] Pass per-sequence context lengths to the AITER paged MQA-logits kernels
body:
## Error

MTP with native DSA-indexer decode above `next_n=2` crashes during warm-up on MI355X (seen at `next_n=3` and `next_n=6`). GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP4, `num_speculative_tokens=5` (`next_n=6`), Gluon paged MQA logits:

```
Memory access fault by GPU node-4 (Agent handle: 0x20465ea0) on address 0x792dc0bf1000. Reason: Unknown.
```

Where it does not crash, the indexer silently uses wrong causal bounds: in a direct call at `next_n=3`, the 8192-token sequence loses its last 2 valid positions in every row (9/12 rows correct).

## Cause

With native decode (`next_n > 1`), `rocm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` receives a `(B, next_n)` table of per-row context lengths, `[b, j] = L_b - next_n + j + 1`, built in [`indexer.py#L1136-L1152`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2df122e65e87dc12870ce5f0180b49f012e7a53b/vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py#L1136-L1152). The AITER Gluon `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` and `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_stage1` kernels read the table as a flat `[B]` array and some sequences get another row's length.

Example: 4 requests, `next_n=3`, context lengths 8192 / 1500 / 3000 / 700:

| `b` | `j=0` | `j=1` | `j=2` | `L_b` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 8190 | 8191 | **8192** | 8192 |
| 1 | 1498 | 1499 | **1500** | 1500 |
| 2 | 2998 | 2999 | **3000** | 3000 |
| 3 | 698 | 699 | **700** | 700 |

The kernel expects `[8192, 1500, 3000, 700]` and computes each row's bound itself. Reading the `(4, 3)` table as `[4]`, it gets the first four values in memory, `[8190, 8191, 8192, 1498]`: request 0 loses its last 2 positions in every row, and requests 1 to 3 get lengths past their own KV pages, the likely source of the fault. Column `j = next_n - 1` equals `L_b`, which is what the kernel needs.

## Fix

Pass the kernels the last column, which is the per-sequence length. `[B]` and `(B, 1)` inputs, the C4A Triton path and the torch fallback are unchanged.

On ROCm native decode is used for `next_n` 1 and 2 today, so MTP with one speculative token goes through this path. #59421 raises that cap, which needs this fix.

## Test Plan

- `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_rocm_paged_mqa_context_lens.py` (new): the helper returns the per-sequence lengths for a `(B, next_n)` table and passes `[B]` / `(B, 1)` through unchanged.
- Direct call of `rocm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` on one MI355X against a torch reference: `B=4`, `next_n=3`, contexts 8192/1500/3000/700, block size 64.

## Test Result

| Gluon | Rows correct | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| This PR | 12/12 | max rel diff 2.4e-7 |
| Before | 9/12 | the 8192-token sequence loses its last 2 valid positions in every row |

With this fix, GLM-5.3 MTP at `next_n=3` and `next_n=5` completes the full throughput sweep, GPQA (0.889 / 0.904) and RULER niah_single_2 (1.0 / 1.0).


| next_n (spec tokens) | GPQA | NIAH | Geomean tok/s/GPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| no MTP | 0.879 | 1.00 | 2435.5 |
| 3 (2) | 0.889 | 1.00 | 3309.1 |
| 5 (4) | 0.904 | 1.00 | 3607.8 |

Throughput per GPU:

| Conc | 8k/1k no MTP | 8k/1k n=3 | 8k/1k n=5 | 60k/600 no MTP | 60k/600 n=3 | 60k/600 n=5 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 544.4 | 1105.3 | 1337.0 | 2925.1 | 4067.3 | 4422.3 |
| 8 | 897.5 | 1650.6 | 2015.3 | 3889.2 | 4658.8 | 4408.6 |
| 16 | 1415.4 | 2177.6 | 2648.5 | 4550.6 | 4948.6 | 5050.4 |
| 32 | 2058.7 | 3061.8 | 3638.4 | 4938.2 | 5175.0 | 5303.4 |
| 64 | 2853.3 | 4013.9 | 4447.8 | | | |
| 128 | 3741.3 | 4715.5 | 4291.3 | | | |
| 256 | 4603.2 | 4663.6 | 5208.6 | | | |

The no-MTP run is the same setup without speculative decoding (decode paged MQA logits on the FlyDSL kernel instead of Gluon).

title: [ROCm][Perf] Allow DSA indexer native decode above next_n=2
body:
## Purpose

On ROCm, `_supports_native_decode` is `next_n in (1, 2)`, so MTP with 2+ speculative tokens is flattened to one row per draft token and each row re-reads its sequence's KV. The AITER paged kernels have no such limit. This adds `VLLM_ROCM_INDEXER_NATIVE_DECODE_MAX_NEXT_N` (default 2, today's behaviour) to raise the cap.

**Needs #59420** above `next_n = 2` (otherwise `Memory access fault` in warm-up).

title: [ROCm][Perf] gfx950: use FlyDSL paged MQA logits kernel for the sparse indexer decode
body:
## Purpose

Uses the AITER FlyDSL paged (decode) MQA-logits kernel for the sparse indexer on gfx950 when AITER provides it, instead of the Gluon kernel. No new env var, same as #59280 for prefill and #49544 for gfx942.

## Dependency

Needs ROCm/aiter#4221 (merged after AITER v0.1.23, so not yet in the version vLLM main pins). Without it, or on anything but gfx950, the existing Gluon kernel is used, so this is a no-op until the next AITER bump.

## Details

- The kernel takes one context length per sequence, so it gets the last column of the `(B, next_n)` per-row table.
- `SplitKV` is passed explicitly. The kernel's default reads `context_lens.max()` on the host, which fails under CUDA graph capture (`hipErrorStreamCaptureUnsupported`); it is bounded by `max_model_len` instead.
- FlyDSL is only used for the shapes it supports (KV block size 64, 32 indexer heads, `next_n <= 8`); anything else stays on Gluon.

## Test Plan

- `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_rocm_flydsl_paged_mqa_logits_dispatch.py` (new): FlyDSL on gfx950 when the kernel is available; Gluon when AITER lacks it, with 64 heads, or on gfx942; per-sequence context lengths and `SplitKV` passed to FlyDSL. 4/4 pass on MI355X.
- End to end A/B on GLM-5.3 (MXFP4 experts, FP8 attention), TP4, MI355X, CUDA graphs on. The difference between the two runs is the decode paged MQA-logits kernel (Gluon before, FlyDSL with this change).
  - Standard decode, no speculative decoding (`next_n = 1`). Same build for both runs, an earlier one (Sep 20) with ROCm/aiter#4221 applied.
  - `deepseek_mtp` with 2 speculative tokens (`next_n = 3`, native decode via #59421 with #59420).

title: [KV Offload] Pre-fault the CPU offload region with multiple threads
body:
## Purpose

Cut the startup cost of `OffloadingConnector`'s CPU tier, whether it runs alone or behind `MultiConnector` with `NixlConnector`.

With a 100 GB CPU offload region, startup takes **+59s** over a no-connector baseline at TP1 (NIXL + Offload) and **+45s** at TP2 (Offload). Almost all of it is spent preparing the shared `/dev/shm` region, not in NIXL. This PR parallelizes the biggest piece, the page pre-fault, which roughly halves the overhead at TP1 and TP2.

## Where startup time goes

I timed the path with debug logs plus temporary timers around NIXL registration. The timers are not part of this PR. Setup: Qwen3-0.6B, 1× H100, `cpu_bytes_to_use=100GB`, TP1.

| Step | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NIXL `register_memory` (GPU KV, 28 regions) | 0.002s | UCX over `cuda_ipc,cuda_copy,tcp` (RDMA not measured, see Limitations) |
| NIXL local xfer dlist (1,154,440 descs) | 0.030s | `_build_fa_local` + `prep_xfer_dlist` |
| **Offload: `MADV_POPULATE_WRITE` loop** | **48.4s** | 54,495 `madvise` calls on one thread, ~2 GB/s |
| Offload: `cudaHostRegister` (whole region) | ~9s | 2 × ≤64 GB registrations |

At TP4 (100 GB total), each rank's populate loop takes **17.4s**. The ranks already run in parallel, and together they reach ~5.7 GB/s, which is the kernel ceiling described below. Then **every rank `cudaHostRegister`s the entire 100 GB region**, which takes **~17s** while all ranks run at once.

Why the populate is slow:
- `/dev/shm` is a user-mounted tmpfs without a `huge=` option, so the region is backed by 4 KiB pages. Pre-faulting means allocating and zeroing about 26M pages for 100 GB. The kernel does this at ~1–2 GB/s per thread.
- The loop calls `mmap.madvise`, which does not release the GIL. That rules out Python threads as written.

## The change

- **`_populate_ranges()`**
  - Takes the rank's `(offset, length)` ranges, one per chunk row, and splits them into contiguous shards across a `ThreadPoolExecutor`.
  - Each thread calls libc `madvise(MADV_POPULATE_WRITE)` through ctypes, which releases the GIL for the duration of the syscall.
- **Error handling**
  - A failing `madvise` raises `OSError(errno)` in its worker thread.
  - `ex.map` re-raises that error in the caller, so the existing failure and cleanup behavior in `__init__` is kept.
- **Unchanged paths**
  - With `num_threads <= 1`, or when the kernel lacks `MADV_POPULATE_WRITE` (EINVAL → `_fallback_populate_write`), the code runs the original serial loop.
  - The fallback read-modify-write path stays single-threaded.
- **Thread count**
  - `CPUOffloadingSpec` passes `populate_threads = max(1, 16 // world_size)`, so about 16 threads run node-wide across all ranks.
  - `SharedOffloadRegion` defaults to `populate_threads=1`, so other callers (tiering, the scheduler-side region, EC shared region) are unaffected.
- **Safety**
  - Shards cover disjoint page ranges within a rank.
  - Ranks already populate disjoint cells. When a cell is not page-aligned, two ranks may pre-fault the same boundary page. That page is written with `MADV_POPULATE_WRITE`, which does not modify data, the same as today.
  - The unit test checks that bytes written beforehand are preserved.

### Microbenchmark: populate a 20 GB `/dev/shm` mapping (one process)

| Threads | Populate | Throughput |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10.7–21.5s | 1.0–2.0 GB/s |
| 4 | 5.2s | 4.1 GB/s |
| 16 | 3.5–3.8s | 5.6–6.1 GB/s |
| 32 | 3.4s | 6.3 GB/s |
| 64 | 6.3s | 3.4 GB/s (contention) |

Throughput stops improving at 16–32 threads and drops at 64. That is why the thread count is capped at ~16 node-wide rather than scaled to the CPU count. The machine is a 384-core node with ~1.2 TB of page cache, so part of each fault is reclaim. The absolute rates will vary by machine, but the shape of the curve should hold.

### Why not skip the populate and let `cudaHostRegister` fault the pages?

`cudaHostRegister` faults pages in itself, so skipping the populate step is possible. On 20 GB it is slower:

| Strategy | Time |
|---|---|
| `cudaHostRegister` only (it faults the pages) | 9.4s |
| 1-thread populate + register | ~13s (10.7–11.0s + 2.1s) |
| 16-thread populate + register | ~5.6s (3.5s + 2.1s) |

The populate step is also still needed when pinning fails or is unavailable (the pageable fallback).

## Relationship to other PRs (not a duplicate)

- **#51414 / #54578** (connector "ready" state and async CPU offload init) move this work off the critical path, so the engine serves from GPU-only KV cache until offload is ready. This PR reduces the work itself.
  - It shortens blocking startup today.
  - It would shorten time-to-connector-ready once async init lands. #54578 reports `connector_ready_s` ≈ 102s at 128 GB.
  - The two changes compose. Async init also needs `madvise` to release the GIL, which ctypes gives here.
- **#58852** adds hugetlbfs backing for the HiSparse host pool, a different buffer. The huge-pages follow-up below would do the same for offload.

## Test Plan

Unit tests:

```bash
pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py \
       tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_gpu_worker.py \
       tests/v1/kv_offload/test_factory.py
```

The new test `test_threaded_populate_touches_exactly_the_given_ranges` splits every other page across 3 threads. It then checks with `mincore` that exactly those pages are resident and that a byte written beforehand is preserved.

End-to-end: I timed from launch until `/health` responded.

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --enforce-eager [-tp N] --kv-transfer-config \
  '{"kv_connector":"MultiConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"connectors":[
     {"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both"},
     {"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
      "kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use":100000000000}}]}}'
```

Environment:
- 8× H100 80GB, 384 CPUs, 1.5 TB RAM
- RHEL 9.6, kernel 5.14.0-570
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, nixl 1.4.1
- `shmem_enabled=never`, `/dev/shm` mounted without `huge=`
- NIXL runs used `UCX_TLS=cuda_ipc,cuda_copy,tcp,sm`

## Test Results

Unit tests: 138 passed and 1 skipped on the three files above before the new test was added. All 52 tests in `test_shared_offload_region.py`, including the new one, pass with no skips. pre-commit is clean.

End-to-end startup:

| Config | Baseline (no connector) | Before | After | Populate before → after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NIXL + Offload (MultiConnector), TP1 | 37.3s | 96.0s | **63.4s** | 48.4s → 19.6s (16 threads) |
| Offload, TP2 | 58.2s | 103.6s | **80.7s** | 33.2s → 15.4s (8 threads/rank) |
| Offload, TP4 | 60.3s | 88.9s | not measured | 17.4s → (expected ~same) |

`init engine` time went from 60.3s to 28.9s at TP1 (MultiConnector) and from 47.3s to 30.4s at TP2 (Offload). Each configuration was measured once, so treat the numbers as indicative.

This change affects only startup, not model outputs, so no accuracy evals were run.

## Limitations

- **TP≥4:** the ranks already fault in parallel and reach the ~6 GB/s node-wide ceiling, so I expect little gain there. TP4 was not re-measured with this change.
- **`world_size`:** the thread split uses `parallel.world_size` as a stand-in for the number of ranks per node. Multi-node deployments get fewer threads than they could use. That is safe, but not optimal.
- **RDMA:** NIXL's RDMA memory registration was not measured, because the test host limits locked memory (`ulimit -l`) to 8 MB.
  - A related trap: with default UCX transports and that limit, UCX's UD transport logged tens of millions of `ibv_reg_mr ... ulimit -l` errors.
  - The engine never became ready within 10 minutes.
  - If anyone reports NIXL startup "hangs", check `ulimit -l` first.

## Possible follow-ups (not in this PR)

1. **Huge pages for the region.**
   - With anonymous THP as a proxy, 20 GB populated in **1.5s instead of ~11s** and `cudaHostRegister` took **1.1s instead of ~2s**.
   - `/dev/shm` ignores `MADV_HUGEPAGE` unless it is mounted with a `huge=` option. The sysfs `shmem_enabled` setting covers only the kernel's internal shm mount.
   - Doing this needs a configurable mmap path (hugetlbfs or a `huge=within_size` tmpfs, similar to #58852) or deployment docs, plus a harmless `MADV_HUGEPAGE` hint.
2. **Redundant pinning.**
   - Every rank registers the whole region, so the pinning work is TP× redundant (~17s concurrent at TP4 for 100 GB).
   - Registering only each rank's own cells, one call per chunk row, barely helped: 1.31s vs 1.39s on 20 GB with 4 ranks. Per-call overhead dominates.
   - Huge pages (fewer, larger pages to pin) are the more promising fix.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to profile the startup path, write this change, and run the tests and benchmarks above. The submitter has reviewed every changed line.

title: [Bugfix][Attention] Sync vllm-flash-attn pin to include the SM90 SplitKV fix
body:
## Purpose

Fix #59362.

On SM90, the FA4 CuTe-DSL forward kernel ignores `num_splits`: `flash_fwd_sm90.py` builds
`BlockInfo` without passing `num_splits`, so `BlockInfo.get_n_block_min_max()` falls back to
the constructor default `Int32(1)` and every split processes the **full** KV range. The
SplitKV work partitioning is effectively a no-op — decode gets slower, not faster, as
`num_splits` grows past 1.

The fix already landed upstream as vllm-project/flash-attention#198
("Fix SM90 SplitKV block range partitioning", `6d11b3c1`). This PR only moves the CMake
`GIT_TAG` pin forward by one commit to pick it up:

```diff
 cmake/external_projects/vllm_flash_attn.cmake
-          GIT_TAG 9cd61de38763d712bb6ce56e2a02cc2bf718c89f
+          GIT_TAG 6d11b3c1b6ca7dac0b111bb0db63ca16eeb19a46
```

`compare 9cd61de...6d11b3c1` on `vllm-project/flash-attention`: `ahead_by: 1`, `behind_by: 0`,
one file changed (`flash_attn/cute/flash_fwd_sm90.py`), `+1/-0`:

```python
             qhead_per_kvhead_packgqa=self.qhead_per_kvhead if const_expr(self.pack_gqa) else 1,
+            num_splits=num_splits,
         )
```

This affects both default decode (`num_splits=0` → library heuristics) and full-CUDA-graph
decode (`num_splits=32` via `flash_attn_max_num_splits_for_cuda_graph`), so it is not
limited to one execution mode (vllm/v1/attention/backends/flash_attn.py, the
`max_num_splits` computation).

## Duplicate-work check

- `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "59362 in:body"` → no results.
- No PR is cross-referenced from #59362; the issue had no assignee and no comments.
- `cmake/external_projects/vllm_flash_attn.cmake` on `main` still pins `9cd61de`; the last
  change to that file was #54819 (the FA sync that introduced this regression).
- This is not a busywork PR: it fixes a 2.7x long-context decode regression on H20/SM90.

## Test Plan

Environment: 8x H20 (SM90), driver 535.247.01 / CUDA 13.0, `vllm==0.30.0` wheel
(`torch 2.13.0+cu130`, `nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.1`), single GPU
(`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=4`).

The wheel ships a vendored copy of `flash_fwd_sm90.py` whose imports are rewritten to
`vllm.vllm_flash_attn.cute.*`; it is otherwise **byte-identical in logic** to the file at
pin `9cd61de` (verified by diff: only 2 import hunks, same 2182 lines). Therefore
"wheel file + the one upstream line" is an exact stand-in for rebuilding with the new pin.
Both arms were measured from a cold JIT (the CuTe DSL disk cache is disabled by default —
`FLASH_ATTENTION_CUTE_DSL_CACHE_ENABLED` defaults to `"0"`), so no stale-kernel
contamination is possible.

Three levels of evidence, all scripts attached below:

1. **Kernel repro** (issue geometry: `SEQK=7040, PAGE=32, HD=512, NQ=16, NKV=2, BS=1`,
   CUDA-graph replay timing, sweeping `num_splits` in (0, 1, 4, 16, 64)).
2. **End-to-end decode** — Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B, `attention_backend="FLASH_ATTN"` +
   `attention_config={"flash_attn_version": 4}` (FA4 is not the SM90 default; this overrides
   it explicitly), TP=1, greedy, `ignore_eos`, 64 decode steps at ctx≈5900 and ctx≈600.
3. **Numerical cross-check vs a dense fp32 torch reference** to confirm the fix changes only
   performance, not accuracy.

A/B order was run both ways (shipped→fixed and fixed→shipped) to rule out machine-load drift.

## Test Result

### 1. Kernel level — issue geometry (hd512, SEQK=7040)

| `num_splits` | before (µs) | after (µs) | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 (auto) | 883.1 | **36.2** | **24.4x** |
| 1 | 876.6 | 876.5 | 1.00x |
| 4 | 874.4 | 230.0 | 3.80x |
| 16 | 878.8 | 64.7 | 13.6x |
| 64 | 882.9 | **48.4** | **18.2x** |

Before the fix the timing is flat (±1%) across all `num_splits` and
`max|o(ns=1) - o(ns=64)| == 0.0` — the kernel never reads `num_splits`. `num_splits=1` is
unchanged as expected (one split already covers the whole KV, and the fix is a no-op there).

### 2. Kernel level — Qwen3-1.7B geometry (hd128, SEQK=5900)

| `num_splits` | before (µs) | after (µs) | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 (auto) | 223.0 | **36.4** | **6.13x** |
| 1 | 220.4 | 220.4 | 1.00x |
| 4 | 222.7 | 63.0 | 3.53x |
| 16 | 222.9 | **41.3** | **5.40x** |
| 64 | 223.2 | 65.5 | 3.41x |

### 3. End-to-end (Qwen3-1.7B, FA4, H20)

64-token greedy decode, median of 3, raw wall time:

| ctx | before (s) | after (s) | speedup |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 5900 | 0.525 / 0.525 / 0.525 | 0.192 / 0.192 / 0.193 | **2.73x** |
| 600 | 0.183 / 0.184 / 0.184 | 0.148 / 0.149 / 0.149 | 1.23x |

Reverse-order re-run reproduces the same numbers (0.524 / 0.192 at ctx=5900), so this is not
load drift. Within-arm spread is ±0.5%.

### 4. Numerical correctness

Against a dense fp32 reference (`softmax_scale = 1/sqrt(head_dim)`), hd128/SEQK=5900:

- All `num_splits` values match the fp32 reference with the same relative error as before the
  fix (2.951e-3, i.e. ~1 bf16 ulp) — for both arms.
- After the fix, outputs across `num_splits` differ by at most 2.44e-4 (`3.2e-3` relative),
  i.e. the expected bf16 reassociation across different reduction orders — not an accuracy
  change.

This change does not touch model code, weights, or numerics; it only restores the intended
SplitKV partitioning. No eval regression is expected or observed.

> Note for anyone re-running the issue's kernel script: it uses `softmax_scale=1.0` with
> `head_dim=512`, where logits have stddev ≈ 22.6 and softmax is nearly one-hot, so output
> diffs there are not a correctness metric. Use `1/sqrt(head_dim)` when cross-checking
> numerics.

## AI usage

AI assistance (CodeBuddy, model DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) was used for the investigation,
benchmark harnesses, and drafting this PR. I ran all the tests above myself on the target
hardware and reviewed every changed line end-to-end.

---

<details>
<summary>Reproduction scripts (attached for review)</summary>

- `kernel_repro.py` — kernel-level A/B with CUDA-graph replay timing and output-consistency
  checks; `kernel_repro_hd128.py` — same, with Qwen3-1.7B geometry.
- `e2e_decode.py` — vLLM end-to-end decode benchmark.
- `ref_check.py` + `ref_diag.py` + `hd512_perm.py` — fp32 reference cross-checks.
- `swap_fa.sh` + `run_*.sh` — the A/B file switcher and runners (pin the FA file under test
  by md5).

</details>

title: [ROCm][Perf] AITER FlyDSL kernels for the QSA indexer and sparse GQA
body:
## Purpose

vLLM hook for [ROCm/AITER#5996](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5996) (draft, head `d8713662d1` or later): the FlyDSL QSA K1 indexer and K2 sparse GQA. Both kernels read vLLM's strided per-layer cache views in place (K2 since `d10d02a`, K1 since `8deab1a`), and `qsa_k1_selection_serves` (from `663bd6f`) rejects token budgets outside K1's baked contract. Keep this PR as a draft until #5996 is in an AITER release that vLLM's ROCm image pins.

On ROCm, Qwen4Exp QSA runs three Triton/HIP stages: paged MQA scoring over the compressed indexer cache, HIP top-k, and Triton sparse paged GQA. ROCm/aiter#5996 implements the scoring+top-k half (K1) and the sparse GQA (K2) in FlyDSL.

With `VLLM_ROCM_QSA_FLYDSL=1`:

- `QSAIndexer._select` calls `flydsl_select_paged_tokens`. K1 writes the compressed block ids, then the existing Triton `expand_qsa_block_indices_cuda` builds the token indices. The output is the same `[tokens, 2051]` buffer as before, so MTP's `skip_topk` reuse is unaffected. Rows are chunked by the same fp32 score-workspace cap as the Triton path.
- `Qwen4ExpQSAFlashAttentionImpl.forward_qsa` calls `flydsl_sparse_paged_attention`, which runs K2 directly on the K|V cache views into the existing output.
- Anything a kernel cannot serve (the kernel's own `*_serves` checks, K1's token budget, a strided output) logs once and stays on Triton. If the flag is set but AITER has no FlyDSL QSA module, startup fails rather than silently falling back.
- The kernels are called directly rather than through `aiter.ops.flydsl.qsa_layer`, because the indexer and attention run at different points in the layer (top-k reuse across MTP steps, cache update in between). #5996 now admits the TP2/TP4/TP8 shards to `auto`, so the shape no longer forces this.

The flag stays opt-in and off by default: at TP2 the FlyDSL path is currently slower than the Triton path in every measured cell (below).

---

## Test Plan

- Unit: `pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_flydsl.py` (CPU; AITER stubbed). Covers:
  - off by default
  - K1 plus Triton expand
  - chunking by the score workspace
  - K1 reading a strided indexer view in place
  - K1 fallbacks: token budget outside K1's contract, unserved shape
  - K2 writing in place on the interleaved K|V views
  - K2 fallbacks: unserved shape, strided output
  - the flag without AITER raises
- Serving A/B, `VLLM_ROCM_QSA_FLYDSL=0` vs `1` on one image, TP2, `amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4`: 8k/1k c4, c16, c64 and 60k/600 c4; four repeats in two batches, with the arms swapped across GPU pairs.
- GSM8K 5-shot on the checkpoint card's recipe, both arms, same servers as the A/B.
- [ ] TODO: GPU numerics, K1 and K2 against the Triton path on real paged caches from a serving run (decode, prefill, MTP)
- [ ] TODO: trace split of K1 / K2 / expand / glue at 8k c64, to find where the time goes
- [ ] TODO: GPQA (thinking, medium) with the flag on; TP1 and TP8

---

## Test Result

- Unit: 10 passed.

**Serving**, MI355X TP2, one-factor A/B: both arms run the same image (vLLM nightly `ac68c308` with this PR @ `644184dcc8`, ROCm/aiter#5996 @ `d8713662d1`, and the rest of the Flash-Next ROCm stack) and differ only in `VLLM_ROCM_QSA_FLYDSL`. K1 and K2 both run on the flag-on arm. `flag off → flag on`, mean of the four repeats:

TODO

The one positive repeat at 8k c4 is a slow flag-off cell (385 tok/s against 462–470 in the other three), not a FlyDSL win. The loss grows with concurrency and context, and its TPOT is the same in every repeat, so it is the kernels, not the node.

```bash
# plus the checkpoint card's ROCm environment and flags, identical in both arms
VLLM_ROCM_QSA_FLYDSL=1 \
vllm serve amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-seqs 256 --no-enable-prefix-caching --trust-remote-code
vllm bench serve --model amd/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Quark-MXFP4 --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
  --max-concurrency 64 --num-prompts 128
```

**Accuracy**, GSM8K 5-shot (flexible-extract), same servers:

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| flag off | 0.9606 | 0.9598 | 0.9598 | 0.9651 | 0.9613 |
| flag on | 0.9613 | 0.9629 | 0.9598 | 0.9659 | 0.9625 |

No accuracy change.

---
<details>
<summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary>

- [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)".
- [x] The test plan, such as providing test command.
- [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results
- [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model.
</details>

---

title: [Bug][HiSparse] Engine crash: "Cannot get N free blocks" allocating the hot region at admission under GPU-pool pressure
body:
### Your current environment

vLLM main @ `93dd80f636`, 1× B200, Model Runner V2 (`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`). Also reproduces on #55398 before and after merging main.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Under HiSparse GPU-pool pressure, admitting a new request can crash the engine in `HiSparseHotManager.allocate_new_blocks`: admission does not count the request's hot region (4 blocks here), then allocation fails.

```
  File "vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 1209, in schedule          # waiting-queue admission
```

2. Submit a 4k-token prompt that shares a prefix with an aborted one; it is never admitted either. Abort it after 20 s.

title: [Bugfix][HiSparse] Size the KV cache from the groups HiSparse allocates
body:
## Purpose

With HiSparse, a GPU pool too small for one `max_model_len` request passes the startup check, and requests then wait forever with no error ([report](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55398#issuecomment-5903470382): `--num-gpu-blocks-override 160`, two 6k prompts never run).

The startup check sized HiSparse from the model's grouped specs rather than the groups HiSparse actually allocates. So it counted only indexer pages, missing the resident and hot groups, and used the wrong block size for the override.

## Changes

- HiSparse's grouping hook now returns the groups it allocates, and workers report its derived resident/hot caches. The standard startup check, override conversion and cross-rank sync then work for HiSparse unchanged.
- KV cache layout resolution skips specs without per-layer views, such as these caches, which lay out their own raw backing.
- Resident groups are sized by their admission window (`max_admission_blocks_per_request`), which #59494 now enforces at runtime.
- Auto-fit uses the startup check's criterion, so it can't pick a length that check rejects.
- Removed the HiSparse-specific memory estimate and the cross-worker `min(available_memory)` workaround.
- Projection returns a group unchanged when all its layers are on the worker, so HiSparse's group flags survive.

A pool that can't hold one request now fails the standard "max seq len" check at startup, before KV cache allocation.

## Test Plan

- Unit test: a 160-block pool is rejected at `max_model_len=8192`, and the boundary is exact at 32768 with 2048 tokens in flight (656 blocks rejected, 657 accepted). Auto-fit with 657 blocks starts. Layout resolution is unaffected by the derived caches.
- B200 (shrunk GLM-5.3, dummy weights), on this branch merged with #59494: TP=1 and TP=2 including ranks with unequal memory, 131k context, auto-fit, the reported setup, and `test_hisparse.py`.

## Test Result

- Unit tests pass.
- B200, this branch (includes #59494):
  - Too-small pools fail at startup: 160 blocks at 8192, 2400 blocks at 131072.
  - Pools that fit serve: 1000 blocks at 8192, auto-fit, and 3200 or 4000 blocks at 131072 with a 120k-token prompt. Without #59494, the 4000-block case livelocks.
  - TP=2 serves, including with unequal ranks.
  - The reported setup at 700 blocks: both 6k prompts complete.
  - `test_hisparse.py`: 4 passed.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for this PR.

title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Use a zero default for masked scales in the MXFP8 GEMM
body:
## Purpose

This fix changes masked scale data from 127 (value 1.0 for e8m0) to 0 (value 2^(-127). This change is benign in terms of accuracy as the main value side already loads corresponding lanes for mfma as 0. So, scales get multiplied by 0 and has no accuracy effect.

When other=127, triton 3.8.0+gitc0a142ff leads to reading stale LDS data for the lanes corresponding to the masked scales due to a compiler bug. This bug is fixed on upstream triton but this fix resolves stale data reading issue for both compiler versions.

With other=127 and triton 3.8.0+gitc0a142ff, if LDS addresses corresponding to the masked lanes have "NaN", this leads to the result and produce inaccurate results. This is a rare case but it can still happen in practice. Reproduction relies on what LDS contains from previous runs.

This is a cleaner solution as hardware can already handle writing 0s to the masked lanes almost for free compared to writing any other value.

title: [Bugfix][V1] Prevent scheduler stall stranding completed async KV loads
body:
## Purpose

Fix a scheduler stall in the V1 engine when asynchronous KV loads (`WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`) complete while the KV cache is saturated. Under this condition the engine can drop to zero running requests and stop making progress indefinitely, even though it has runnable requests whose KV is already resident on device.

This affects any deployment using an async-loading KV connector (`OffloadingConnector` / tiered CPU+disk offloading, disaggregated prefill, etc.), and is most easily reproduced with a small GPU KV cache under concurrent multi-turn load.

### Root cause

The waiting loop in `Scheduler.schedule()` drains the waiting queue from the front and **`break`s** (not `continue`s) as soon as `allocate_slots()` returns `None` for the request at the front — i.e. the moment the KV cache cannot fit the front request.

A request in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` whose async load has already finished is:
- in `finished_recving_kv_req_ids` (so `_try_promote_blocked_waiting_request` would return `True`),
- already holding its KV blocks **resident** (allocated when it was admitted),
- **non-preemptible**.

When the cache is saturated, the front of `skipped_waiting` can be a block-starved request while these promotable, load-complete requests sit further back in the queue. The loop exits on the block-starved front before it ever reaches them — even though running one would free the very blocks the front request needs. With nothing else runnable, `running` falls to 0 and the
engine deadlocks: the requests that could break the logjam are never reached.

### Fix

Before entering the waiting loop, move requests whose async load has completed (`WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` **and** in `finished_recving_kv_req_ids`) to the front of `skipped_waiting`, so they are reached and promoted before any block-starved request can `break` the loop. A promoted request reuses its resident blocks (no new allocation), so it schedules even at zero free blocks, runs, and frees memory — draining the backlog.

The change is order-preserving among the promoted requests and is a no-op unless a load has actually completed, so it does not affect scheduling when the cache is not under pressure.

## Test Plan

Reproduce the stall with a tiny GPU KV cache under concurrent multi-turn load through an async-loading connector, and confirm the engine keeps scheduling and the workload runs to completion.

Config used to reproduce (tiered CPU-primary + FS-secondary offloading,
`OffloadingConnector` / `TieringOffloadingSpec`):
- `NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B`, TP=1
- GPU KV cache pinned to 3 GiB, `max_num_seqs=64`
- 450 conversations × 12 turns, 1 output token/turn (so a scheduled request finishes immediately and frees its blocks)
- CPU primary tier 16 GiB, FS secondary tier

A scheduler probe recorded, per `schedule()` call, the number of running requests and the number of `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` requests that are already in `finished_recving_kv_req_ids` but still sitting in `skipped_waiting`
("promotable-but-stuck").

## Test Result

**Before the fix** — the engine wedged and never recovered:

running=0/64  skipped_waiting=454  finished_recving_set=6
wfr_total=6   wfr_promotable_stuck=6

6 requests had completed their async load and held resident blocks, but were never reached; `running` stayed at 0 and the run never completed.

**After the fix** — same preconditions present, no stall:

running peaked 18/64   wfr_total=11 (in skipped_waiting)   wfr_promotable_stuck=0 GPU KV cache saturated; primary tier fully saturated (primary_free=0) tier_promotions_to_gpu=64032  promotion_ok=16337

[run] done. wall=12.9s  generations=5400  rounds=12   (exit 0)

All 12 rounds / 5400 generations completed cleanly; `wfr_promotable_stuck` stayed at 0 throughout and `running` never fell to 0. The post-fix run had *higher* KV pressure than the wedged baseline (12 turns/conversation vs 8, DRAM primary tier fully saturated), so the difference is attributable to the fix and not to reduced load.

title: [HiSparse] Standardize terminology and add a nomenclature to the design doc
body:
## Purpose

Standardize HiSparse terminology and document it. Several concepts had two or three names each (e.g. "spill", "materialize" and "write back" for the same copy; "valid" and "clean" for the same page state; "reuse" meaning both a prefix hit and the pool reallocating a block), which made reviews harder than they needed to be.

Draft: this touches the same coordinator code as in-flight HiSparse PRs, so it should land after them.

## Changes

- **Design doc:** a new nomenclature section in `docs/design/hisparse.md`, one line per term, noting where code names differ. The doc's prose is aligned with it, and the write-back transaction and ownership table now describe scheduler-owned residency updates (#60647) instead of block-table edits.
- **Renames (no behavior change):**
  - `spill` → **write-back** for the GPU-to-host page copy, which runs eagerly every step, not only under memory pressure. The tracked object, which also covers restores, is a **page transfer**: `_PendingSpill` → `_PendingTransfer`, `pending_spills` → `pending_transfers`, `spills_to_send` → `transfers_to_send`, `update_spills` → `update_transfers`, `_complete_host_writes` → `_complete_transfers`, `max_spill_pages` → `max_transfers_per_step`.
  - `plan_prefix_materialization` → `plan_write_backs` (it covers every sealed page, not only a prefix).
  - `valid_pages` / "clean" → **durable** (`durable_pages`, `pinned_durable_pages`, `_page_became_durable`); `ready_prefix_pages` → `num_durable_prefix_pages`.
  - HiSparse's "unpin" → **release** (`released_pages`, `_release_page`, `_release_durable_pages`); core's `BlockPool.unpin_blocks` is unchanged. "Release" now means only that: dropping a transfer or publication lease is **free** (`release_completed_host_cow_copies` → `free_completed_host_cow_copies`).
  - `swap_in` → **`resolve_residency`**: it resolves every top-k position to a physical row, and copies from host only on a miss. The private kernel launch is now `_launch_residency_kernel`.
  - HiSparse's pool "reuse" → **evict**, matching core's `_maybe_evict_cached_block` (`_on_block_reused` → `_on_block_evicted`). `BlockPool.unpin_blocks(on_reuse=...)` is unchanged.
  - "Copy" now means only a **GPU copy** (was also "shadow page"). The host copy-on-write path is named `cow` (`_retained_cow_copies`, `take_host_cow_copies`, `host_cow_copies`, `completed_host_cow_dst_ids`).
  - GPU-copy bookkeeping is prefixed `gpu_copy`: `copies` → `gpu_copies`, `_copy_by_block` → `_gpu_copy_by_block`, `_record_copy`/`_drop_copy` → `_record_gpu_copy`/`_drop_gpu_copy`, `copies_recorded_blocks` → `gpu_copies_recorded_up_to`, `_owners` → `_gpu_copy_readers`, `_lose_page` → `_unmap_evicted_page`.
  - "Resident" → **device** for HiSparse's GPU-held pages and groups, since core's `KVCacheGroup.host_resident` uses "resident" for host-held: `HiSparseResidentSpec`/`HiSparseResidentManager` → `HiSparseDeviceSpec`/`HiSparseDeviceManager`, `resident_managers` → `device_managers`, `get/drop/revive_resident_page` → `get/drop/revive_device_page`, `all_context_pages_resident` → `all_context_pages_on_device`, and the other `resident_*` names. "Residency" and `host_resident` are unchanged. `HiSparseLayout.device_groups` (every group in the shared GPU pool) → `device_pool_groups`, so "device group" names only the page group, and `source_group` → `host_group`.
  - "Hot region" → **hot buffer** in prose. **Hot cache** is the GPU group and tensor that holds every request's hot buffer.
  - Hot-buffer requests: `require_hot`/`has_hot`/`hot_required` → `request_hot_buffer`/`has_hot_buffer`/`hot_buffer_requests`.
  - `pending_pages` → `in_flight_transfers`; `restore` flag → `is_restore`; `transition_watermark` → `read_from_host_watermark`; `has_pending_reclamation` → `has_pending_block_frees` (matching the connector method that wraps it).
  - `_PendingPublication.detached_blocks` → `leased_host_blocks`, `_publish_detached_blocks` → `_publish_finished_prefix`.
  - "Source" no longer means the host group in prose; `resident_source_index` → `resident_group_index`.
  - In the coordinator, "block" names an allocation and "page" an index or count (`page_idx`, `num_host_pages`).
  - Test names and docstrings follow the renames, including HiSparse code and tests that landed after this PR was opened.
  - "Adopt" → **revive**: a host-prefix hit takes back a released GPU copy before the pool evicts it (`_revive_gpu_copies`, `revive_resident_page`, `pages_to_adopt` → `pages_to_revive`). Not "reclaim", which elsewhere in vLLM means the pool taking memory back.
  - Host group: `HiSparseSourceManager` → `HiSparseHostManager`, `KVCacheGroupRole.HISPARSE_SOURCE` → `HISPARSE_HOST`.
  - Scheduler-to-worker types: `SparseKVOffloadCommand` → `HiSparseTransferCommand` (`build_offload_command` → `build_transfer_command`), `SparseKVPageTransfer` → `HiSparsePageTransfer`, `SparseKVRowMirror` → `HiSparseRowMirror`, `SparseKVResidencyUpdate` → `HiSparseResidencyUpdate`; `after_forward` → `runs_after_forward`.
  - Publication: `publish_when_ready` → `publish_when_durable`, `_publish_host_blocks_if_ready` → `_publish_if_durable`, `publication` → `pending_publication`.
  - Host prefix hits and imports: coordinator `commit_computed_blocks` → `record_host_prefix_hit`, `complete_host_import` folded into `finish_host_import`, its only caller, `_pending_imports` → `_pending_import_tokens`.

No config or public API renames. Outside HiSparse, the changes are HiSparse call sites in `index_group.py`, the sparse-MLA backends (`flashmla_sparse.py`, `flashinfer_mla_sparse_sm120.py`) and `sparse_mla_attention.py`; the HiSparse manager classes, docstrings and call sites in `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py`; and in `kv_cache_interface.py`, `KVCacheGroupRole.HISPARSE_SOURCE` → `HISPARSE_HOST` and `HiSparseResidentSpec` → `HiSparseDeviceSpec`.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_planning.py tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_connector.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_stats.py tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py tests/v1/test_kv_cache_spec_registry.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_config.py -k "hisparse or resolve or transfer or host or residency or registry or role or revive or write_back or device"
```

## Test Result

215 passed, 3 skipped, 2 failed on macOS (CPU/MPS; GPU-only kernels skipped). The 2 failures, `test_draft_layer_rows_mirrored_after_drafter[FULL|NONE]`, fail identically on `main` on this platform (MPS tensor → numpy). Pre-commit (ruff, mypy) passes.

Note that normal builds still use cutedsl 4.7.1, and only cu134 builds will overwrite with 4.8.0, hence the need to support both versions.

title: [HiSparse] Report host-pool block residency as HiSparse metrics
body:
## Purpose

With HiSparse and `--kv-cache-metrics`, host-pool block residency (how long evicted prefixes stay recoverable from host) is not observable: since #58725 the host pool has no metrics collector, because sharing the device collector mixed host and device samples through colliding block IDs. Sizing `host_pool_gib` needs this signal.

This gives the host pool its own `KVCacheMetricsCollector` (same sample rate, only with `--kv-cache-metrics`) and reports its eviction samples through the scheduler-side HiSparse connector stats as:

- `vllm:hisparse_host_block_lifetime_seconds`
- `vllm:hisparse_host_block_idle_before_evict_seconds`
- `vllm:hisparse_host_block_reuse_gap_seconds`

Like the device `vllm:kv_block_*_seconds` histograms (which keep covering only the GPU pool), they are registered only with `--kv-cache-metrics` and use the same buckets and `custom_histogram_buckets` overrides.

## Test Plan

```
pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_stats.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_connector.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_metrics.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_multi_connector.py \
  -k "hisparse or host or stats or metrics"
```

`test_hisparse_host_residency_reported_as_hisparse_metrics` fails on main (the host pool records nothing) and passes here; it also checks that host evictions don't reach the device collector. `test_prom_metrics_observe_host_metrics[False]` checks the histograms aren't registered without `--kv-cache-metrics`.

E2E on 1×H100: shrunk DeepSeek-V3.2 (4 layers, dummy weights), FP8 KV, `--max-model-len 8192 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 2000000000`, `HiSparseConnector` with `host_pool_gib: 0.05` (319 host blocks, so it evicts), `--kv-cache-metrics --kv-cache-metrics-sample 1.0`. Load: `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 16 --max-concurrency 4`, seeds 1 ×12, 2 ×4 twice (identical prompts, for host prefix hits), 3 ×16, 4 ×16.

## Test Result

Unit at `47edcd2dbd`: 93 passed (macOS, CPU; `test_draft_layer_rows_mirrored_after_drafter` needs CUDA, not run).

E2E at `a3d71bfdc3` (before histogram gating), 52/52 requests succeeded, no errors:

```
vllm:hisparse_host_block_lifetime_seconds_count          1222.0   _sum 18154.99
vllm:hisparse_host_block_idle_before_evict_seconds_count 1222.0   _sum 16770.81
vllm:hisparse_host_block_reuse_gap_seconds_count          124.0   _sum  1383.02
vllm:kv_block_lifetime_seconds_count                     1264.0   _sum 12034.04
vllm:kv_block_reuse_gap_seconds_count                       0.0
```

Host and device histograms stay separate: all prefix reuse was on host (124 reuse gaps = 7936 prefix-hit tokens / 64), and the device reuse-gap count stays 0. Without `--kv-cache-metrics` (same load, 40/40 succeeded) the host collector records nothing.

Metrics only; no change to caching or scheduling behavior.

title: [Perf][DeepSeek V4.1] Humming indexed MoE GEMM with EP on Hopper, and a named MoE activation format
body:
## Purpose

With `--moe-backend humming` and expert parallelism, Humming runs DeepSeek-V4.1's MXFP4 experts on its grouped GEMM. On Hopper the indexed GEMM is much faster for this model. This PR makes `get_humming_moe_gemm_type()` return `indexed` when all of these hold:

- the experts are MXFP4 with DeepSeek V4 routing;
- `model_type` is `deepseek_v41` or `deepseek_v41_text`;
- the device is CUDA SM90;
- there are no all2all kernels, or the backend is `allgather_reducescatter`.

Without EP, Humming already picks indexed, so nothing changes there. `VLLM_HUMMING_MOE_GEMM_TYPE` still overrides the choice. Since #56997, Humming is the default MXFP4 MoE backend on SM90, so V4.1 with EP on Hopper otherwise runs the grouped GEMM by default; this PR moves that default path to indexed too. The rule applies with BF16 activations and with per-token FP8 activations (`--quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token`).

The MXFP4 MoE method (DeepSeek V4/V4.1, Kimi-K3, plain mxfp4) now runs `quantization_config.moe.activation`:

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash -tp 8 --enable-expert-parallel \
    --moe-backend humming --quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token
```

- Humming takes the named format as a fixed input schema, with its input-schema fallback off.
- Other explicit backends must run the named format, and `auto` keeps only the backends that do. Before, these models ignored the name on every backend. Now a backend that does not run it stops vLLM, on every platform (CUDA, ROCm, XPU, CPU). The DeepSeek V4 MegaMoE backends (`deep_gemm_mega_moe`, `aiter_mega_moe`) build their own experts and do not read the name. On ROCm, the Kimi-K3 AITER path, which skips the backend selector, now refuses a named activation instead of ignoring it. For example, `fp8_per_token` with `flashinfer_trtllm` now stops vLLM instead of running MXFP8. A draft model with its own `speculative_config.moe_backend` inherits the target's `quantization_config`, so the same rule applies to it.
- The startup log prints the format Humming runs: `Humming MoE activations: fp8_per_token (group size 0, scale dtype float32)`. The line appears for every Humming MoE model, gpt-oss included.
- On SM90 Humming, `mxfp8` and `fp8_per_block_dynamic` stop vLLM at startup, before the weights load. Humming has no e8m0 input scales on WGMMA, and humming 0.1.16 rejects fp32 group scales with MXFP4 weights (#60600). Group-wise scales are also 1.2x to 24x slower than per-token in the SM90 Humming GEMM at M >= 256 (numbers in the review reply).
- `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` still works as on main, with no early check: a format Humming cannot run fails while the weights convert, as before. With `--moe-backend humming`, setting it together with `moe.activation` is an error.
- gpt-oss is unchanged. With no name, nothing changes.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_moe.py -k "named_activation or activation_on_sm90 or humming or indexed"
pytest tests/quantization/test_quantization_config_args.py \
    tests/quantization/test_humming_mxfp4_block_fp8.py tests/kernels/moe/test_b12x.py \
    tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py tests/quantization/test_gfx950_moe.py
pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_gfx942_int4.py
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_ocp_mx_moe.py -k unsupported_reasons
```

`test_humming_deepseek_v41_hopper_uses_indexed_gemm_with_ep` calls `get_humming_moe_gemm_type` and checks that V4.1 with EP gets indexed, with and without `allgather_reducescatter`, and that DeepEP, SM100 and DeepSeek V4 keep the grouped GEMM. It does not need the humming package.

`test_deepseek_v4_mxfp4_backend_must_run_named_activation` checks on any GPU that `auto` and `flashinfer_trtllm` refuse `fp8_per_token`, and that `humming` refuses the env JSON plus a name ("not both"). `test_humming_deepseek_v4_activation_on_sm90` checks that SM90 Humming accepts `fp8_per_token` and refuses `mxfp8`. It skips on other GPUs, so in CI it runs only in the optional H100 FP8 MoE kernels job; `kernels-moe-test` runs on L4. The Kimi-K3 AITER refusal has no unit test: it is a short guard, and a test would have to mock the whole K3 path.

`user_moe_activation_override()` (was `_user_moe_activation_override()`) is now public because `quantization/mxfp4.py` imports it; the existing monkeypatches in `test_b12x.py`, `test_ocp_mx_moe.py` and `test_gfx950_moe.py` use the new name.

Startup check: `vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash -tp 8 --enable-expert-parallel --moe-backend humming` on 8x H200, with these additions:

- A: `--quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token` and DSpark speculative decoding (`--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":1}'`; V4.1 has no classic MTP draft), then one completion request.
- B: `--quantization-config.moe.activation mxfp8`.
- C: `--quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_block_dynamic`.
- D: `--quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token` with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"dtype":"float8e4m3"}'`.
- E: only `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"dtype":"float8e4m3"}'`, then one completion request.
- `auto`: no `--moe-backend` and no activation name, then one completion request.

Throughput: offline `LLM` runs of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 8x H200, TP8+EP, `--moe-backend humming`, 2 repeats. Prefill is 16 random 8192-token prompts with 1 output token. Decode is 64 random 512-token prompts with 256 output tokens. The GEMM type was set with `VLLM_HUMMING_MOE_GEMM_TYPE`.

## Test Result

Unit tests on one H200: the `test_moe.py` selection above, 41 passed (the SM90 test runs there, not skipped). The other selector and config tests: 1741 passed, 17 skipped. `test_gfx942_int4.py`: 7 passed. The `test_ocp_mx_moe.py` test that patches the renamed function: 1 passed. pre-commit is clean.

Startup check on 8x H200. B, A and the `auto` run are on this PR's head (one commit on e2414ec1db). C, D and E ran on an earlier head (194da61de1), before the error messages were shortened:

- B (`mxfp8`): stops in model init, before any weights load:
  `ValueError: Humming MoE cannot run activation=mxfp8: SM90 WGMMA needs float32 input scales`
- A (`fp8_per_token`, DSpark): ready after 341 s, completion `" Paris. The Eiffel Tower is in Paris."`. The log shows:
  ```
  [fused_humming_moe.py:146] Using indexed gemm for humming moe
  [mxfp4.py:529] Using 'HUMMING' Mxfp4 MoE backend.
  [moe.py:633] Humming MoE activations: fp8_per_token (group size 0, scale dtype float32)
  [mxfp4.py:2142] Using HummingIndexedExperts
  ```
  The DSpark draft builds its own MoE (16/128 experts per rank) through the same method and prints no different backend or format line.
- `auto` (no `--moe-backend`, no activation name): ready after 221 s, completion `" Paris."`. The log shows:
  ```
  [fused_humming_moe.py:146] Using indexed gemm for humming moe
  [mxfp4.py:808] Using 'HUMMING' Mxfp4 MoE backend.
  [moe.py:633] Humming MoE activations: bf16 (group size 0, scale dtype None)
  [mxfp4.py:2142] Using HummingIndexedExperts
  ```
- C (`fp8_per_block_dynamic`): stops at model init. On this head the check is the same; the message is now:
  `ValueError: Humming MoE cannot run activation=fp8_per_block_dynamic: No compatible Humming input schema for HummingInputSchema(... input_scale_group_size=128, input_scale_dtype=float32 ...) with weight schema HummingWeightSchema(b_dtype=float4e2m1, bs_dtype=float8e8m0, weight_scale_group_size=32 ...) on SM90 (allow_fallback=False)`
- D (env JSON plus name): stops at model init. On this head the message is now:
  `ValueError: Set quantization_config.moe.activation or VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG, not both.`
- E (env JSON only): ready after 430 s, completion `" Paris."`, and the log shows `Humming MoE activations: fp8_per_token (group size 0, scale dtype float32)`. On this head the env JSON gets no startup check, as on main.

Indexed vs grouped throughput:

| Activations | Prefill | Decode |
|---|---|---|
| BF16 | +47% | +63% |
| per-token FP8 (reference) | +24% | +36% |

For reference, with FP8 at decode, grouped is 16% slower than Marlin (2,222 vs 2,648 output tok/s) and indexed is 14% faster.

An end-to-end run on TP4+EP logged `Using indexed gemm for humming moe` and `HummingIndexedExperts`.

## AI assistance

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used to implement the change and tests, run the benchmarks, and draft this description. The submitter reviewed every changed line and the results.

title: [Bugfix][MRV2] Clear stale draft probabilities on request slot reuse
body:
## Purpose

Fix incorrect token acceptance when Model Runner V2 reuses a worker slot for a new request.

When a prefix-cache hit leaves one input token to process, vLLM can pad the step with placeholder draft IDs set to zero. The worker resets those IDs when assigning the slot, but previously retained the old request’s draft probabilities. Verification could then accept the new placeholders using probabilities from an unrelated request.

This was observed as bogus `!!!` prefixes with Kimi-K3/DSpark, where token ID zero is `!`. The regression reproduces the underlying error: verification emits `[0, 0, 0, 17]` when the controlled target output should be `[17]`. Greedy verification hides this particular defect.

This change:

- Resets cached draft probabilities when a request is assigned a worker slot.
- Initializes them to match the zero placeholder IDs until real drafting produces new probabilities.
- Resets DFlash2’s cached candidate IDs so the next sparse draft also removes the temporary token-zero entry.

Token zero remains a valid output; the fix does not filter or prohibit it.

Related work was checked:
- #46533 rejects invalid negative draft IDs. This fixes a different case: valid zero IDs paired with stale probabilities.
- #47926 addresses missing draft-context KV after prefix-cache restoration. It does not reset the cached proposal probabilities used for verification.

AI assistance was used for the investigation, implementation, and regression tests.

## Test Plan

The regression uses the real scheduler, request-slot lifecycle, GPU input-assembly kernels, and rejection sampler. Model outputs are controlled, so no model weights are required.

The primary test:
1. Schedules a cold 33-token request and supplies its final draft scores and output.
2. Completes that request, then submits an identical request.
3. Verifies the 32-token prefix-cache hit, padded speculative positions, and reuse of the same worker slot.
4. Builds the second request’s inputs through the production GPU kernels and checks the emitted tokens.

Four DSpark cases at K=3 cover:
- Stochastic sampling with block verification—the K3 serving configuration.
- Stochastic sampling with standard verification.
- Greedy sampling as a control.
- Legitimate token-zero output as a control.

A separate DFlash2 test checks that the next sparse draft removes the temporary zero entry. Its new candidates deliberately exclude zero; otherwise the next write could overwrite the stale entry and hide a broken reset.

Run the focused regression:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash2.py \
```

title: [Bugfix][HiSparse] Fix a chunked-prefill preemption livelock
body:
## Purpose

Fix a HiSparse prefill livelock: a long chunked prefill can be preempted and recomputed from token 0 forever, with no progress and no error.

Two things combine:

1. **The prefill outgrows the pool it was admitted into.** Admission caps each request's resident pages at the in-flight window (`HiSparseResidentSpec.max_admission_blocks_per_request`), assuming older pages move to host. At runtime, a request keeps its resident pages pinned until free GPU blocks fall below a fixed watermark (a tenth of the pool). A chunk that needs more than that is never switched to host reads, so the request is preempted.
2. **The preempted request resumes from nothing.** Host pages were only published once the **whole** computed prefix was durable. Host writes trail a chunked prefill by about a chunk, so nothing was published until the prefill ended. The request found no prefix hit, recomputed from 0, and was preempted at the same point again.

## Changes

`vllm/v1/hisparse/coordinator.py`:
- Publish the durable prefix of a pending publication as it becomes durable (`min(computed tokens, ready pages)`), instead of all-or-nothing. A preempted prefill resumes from it. When the whole prefix is durable this publishes exactly what it did before.
- `update_residency` also switches a request to host reads (asks for a hot region, then releases its written-back pages) once its resident pages fill the window admission reserved for it. Runtime then enforces the assumption admission makes, so these preemptions no longer happen.

`vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py`: `max_admission_blocks_per_request` becomes public so the coordinator can read it; `HiSparseResidentManager` declares it as `int` (always set for resident specs). No behavior change.

## Test Plan

- New `test_hisparse_preempted_prefill_resumes_from_durable_prefix`: chunk 1's writes are acked after chunk 2 is allocated, then the request is preempted; the resumed request must hit chunk 1's pages.
- New `test_hisparse_prefill_reads_host_once_it_fills_admission_window[4-True, 3-False]`: a prefill that fills its admission window requests a hot region while free blocks are still above the watermark; one below it does not.
- `test_hisparse_terminal_prefix_waits_for_all_workers_and_preserves_identity` now expects the page every worker finished writing to be published (it previously pinned all-or-nothing publication).
- Engine repro on H100: shrunk DeepSeek-V3.2 (8 layers: indexer + 8 resident groups share the GPU pool), 8192-token chunks, eager.
- `tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py`; HiSparse unit tests across `tests/v1` (`-k hisparse`).

## Test Result

| Repro | main | publication fix only | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1×120k prompt, 4000 blocks | livelock (250 preemptions, stuck at 24576 tokens) | 35 steps, 1 preemption | 32 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 1×120k prompt, 12000 blocks | livelock (125 preemptions, stuck at 81920) | 26 steps, 1 preemption | 23 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 2×60k prompts, 4000 blocks | livelock (333 preemptions) | 40 steps, 2 preemptions | 34 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 3×40k prompts, 6000 blocks | 35 steps, 2 preemptions | 29 steps, 2 preemptions | 24 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 1×120k, 1024-token chunks | 126 steps | 126 steps | 126 steps |

- Each new test fails without its fix. `test_prefix_caching.py` passes on CPU.
- H100: `test_hisparse.py` 4 passed; HiSparse unit tests 169 passed.

title: [HiSparse] Switch to host reads once a request fills its admission window
body:
> **Stacked on #59494.** Optional: #59494 alone fixes the livelock; this avoids the preemptions behind it.

## Purpose

Admission caps each request's resident pages at the in-flight window (`HiSparseResidentSpec.max_admission_blocks_per_request`, derived from `max_in_flight_tokens`), on the assumption that older pages move to host. At runtime, though, a request keeps its resident pages pinned until free GPU blocks fall below a fixed watermark (a tenth of the pool). A chunked prefill whose next chunk needs more than that outgrows the pool it was admitted into and is preempted, even though its written-back pages could have been released. With #59494 it resumes from host, but the preemption is still wasted work.

## Changes

`HiSparseCoordinator.update_residency` also switches a request to host reads (asks for a hot region, then releases its written-back pages) once its resident pages fill the window admission reserved for it. Runtime then enforces the same assumption admission makes, with no second estimate. `HiSparseResidentManager` exposes that window as a read-only `max_admission_blocks_per_request` property; nothing else in `vllm/v1/core` changes.

Released pages stay readable until the pool reuses them, so a long request that switches early only pays for its hot region.

## Test Plan

- New `test_hisparse_prefill_reads_host_once_it_fills_admission_window[4-True, 3-False]`: a prefill that fills its admission window requests a hot region while free blocks are still above the watermark; one below it does not.
- Same H100 engine repro as #59494 (shrunk DeepSeek-V3.2, indexer + 8 resident groups sharing the GPU pool), `tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py`, and HiSparse unit tests (`-k hisparse`).

## Test Result

| Repro | main | #59494 | this PR (on #59494) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1×120k prompt, 4000 blocks, 8192-token chunks | livelock | 35 steps, 1 preemption | 32 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 1×120k prompt, 12000 blocks | livelock | 26 steps, 1 preemption | 23 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 2×60k prompts, 4000 blocks | livelock | 40 steps, 2 preemptions | 34 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 3×40k prompts, 6000 blocks | 35 steps, 2 preemptions | 29 steps, 2 preemptions | 24 steps, 0 preemptions |
| 1×120k, 1024-token chunks | 126 steps | 126 steps | 126 steps |

- The `4-True` case fails on #59494 alone. `test_prefix_caching.py`: 168 passed (CPU).
- H100: `test_hisparse.py` 4 passed; HiSparse unit tests 165 passed (plus #59494's updated assertion).

title: [Bugfix][V1] Prevent scheduler stall stranding completed async KV loads
body:
## Purpose

Fix a scheduler stall in the V1 engine when asynchronous KV loads (`WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`) complete while the KV cache is saturated. Under this condition the engine can drop to zero running requests and stop making progress indefinitely, even though it has runnable requests whose KV is already resident on device.

This affects any deployment using an async-loading KV connector (`OffloadingConnector` / tiered CPU+disk offloading, disaggregated prefill, etc.), and is most easily reproduced with a small GPU KV cache under concurrent multi-turn load.

### Root cause

The waiting loop in `Scheduler.schedule()` drains the waiting queue and **`break`s** (not `continue`s) as soon as `allocate_slots()` returns `None` for a request — i.e. the moment the KV cache cannot fit that request's next chunk.

A request in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` whose async load has already finished is:
- in `finished_recving_kv_req_ids` (so `_try_promote_blocked_waiting_request` returns `True` and it is scheduled this pass),
- already holding its KV blocks **resident** (allocated when it was admitted), so it reuses those blocks and needs no new allocation,
- **non-preemptible**.

When the cache is saturated, a block-starved request can be reached before these ready-to-run requests. The loop then `break`s on the block-starved request while the requests that could free the cache are still queued — even though running one would free the very blocks the others need. With nothing else runnable, `running` falls to 0 and the engine deadlocks: the requests that could break the logjam are never reached.

### Fix

At the `allocate_slots() is None` exit, if any completed async load is still queued (`finished_recving_kv_req_ids` is non-empty), skip the block-starved request — move it to the step-local skipped queue and `continue` — instead of ending the loop. This lets the loop reach the ready request, which schedules against its resident blocks, runs, and frees memory.

Properties:
- **Policy-independent.** It acts at the allocation-failure site, wherever queue selection (`FCFS` or `PRIORITY`) placed the block-starved request; it does not rely on reordering a queue, so it holds under both scheduling policies.
- **No-op off the deadlock path.** When no async load has completed, `finished_recving_kv_req_ids` is empty and the loop `break`s exactly as before, so normal back-pressure on a full cache is unchanged.
- **Terminates.** The skipped request leaves the active queue for `step_skipped_waiting`, which is not reconsulted until the loop ends, so the active queue strictly shrinks.

## Test Plan

Reproduce the stall with a tiny GPU KV cache under concurrent multi-turn load through an async-loading connector, and confirm the engine keeps scheduling and the workload runs to completion.

Config used to reproduce (tiered CPU-primary + FS-secondary offloading, `OffloadingConnector` / `TieringOffloadingSpec`):
- `NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B`, TP=1
- GPU KV cache pinned to 3 GiB, `max_num_seqs=64`
- 450 conversations × 12 turns, 1 output token/turn (so a scheduled request finishes immediately and frees its blocks)
- CPU primary tier 16 GiB, FS secondary tier

A scheduler probe recorded, per `schedule()` call, the number of running requests and the number of `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` requests that are already in `finished_recving_kv_req_ids` but still sitting in the waiting queue ("promotable-but-stuck").

## Test Result

**Before the fix** — the engine wedged and never recovered:

```
running=0/64  skipped_waiting=454  finished_recving_set=6
wfr_total=6   wfr_promotable_stuck=6
```

6 requests had completed their async load and held resident blocks, but were never reached; `running` stayed at 0 and the run never completed.

**After the fix** — same tiered config under genuine saturation (`primary_free=0`, `tier_promotions_to_gpu=60498`, 55.6% of promotions blocked on a full DRAM tier), the promotable-but-stuck condition arose repeatedly and cleared every time instead of wedging:

```
wfr_total=62  wfr_in_skip=62  wfr_promotable_stuck=62   (peak)
wfr_total=37  wfr_in_skip=37  wfr_promotable_stuck=34
wfr_total=49  wfr_in_skip=49  wfr_promotable_stuck=24
...  (6 distinct promotable-stuck spikes: 62, 34, 24, 17, 13, 4)
```

Each spike was followed by `wfr_promotable_stuck=0` with `running` advancing again — i.e. the skip-not-break branch reached the completed-load WFR requests, promoted them onto their resident blocks, and they finished and freed. That branch fired **655 times** over the run. Where the stock scheduler wedged permanently at `wfr_promotable_stuck=6`, the fixed build clears spikes an order of magnitude larger.

```
[run] done. wall=29.6s  generations=5400 rounds=12    EXIT=0
```

No crashes, no stall; all 450 conversations completed 12 turns each.

title: [Feature]: Route FlashInfer sparse-MLA decode autotune through the PP-aware tuning group and cache
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Follow-up from #57197, as requested in review.

After #57197, `flashinfer_autotune` (`vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py`) chooses its tuning group and cache file based on pipeline parallelism:
- **PP = 1:** it tunes over the world group and uses the shared cache file.
- **PP > 1:** each stage's TP group tunes on its own and uses a per-stage cache file (`<cache>_tp_<ranks>`).

`_run_flashinfer_sparse_mla_decode_autotune` (`vllm/model_executor/warmup/flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup.py`) is a second consumer of the same FlashInfer autotune cache, and it does not follow that selection yet:
- It tunes on world rank 0 and broadcasts and barriers over the world group.
- It reads and writes the unsuffixed cache file from `resolve_flashinfer_autotune_file`.
- Its `AutoTuner.load_configs` runs before `flashinfer_autotune`, so under PP > 1 its world-level results feed into the per-stage tuning that follows.

This only matters on SM12x with the FlashInfer sparse-MLA decode backends (DSv3.2 / DSv4 / DSv4.1) and PP > 1. It is consistent today when all stages run the same attention shapes, but the two consumers disagree on which group and file they use.

**Proposal:** factor the group and cache-path choice from `flashinfer_autotune` into a small helper, e.g. `_autotune_group_and_cache(runner) -> (group, cache_path)`, and use it in both places. With PP > 1, each stage's TP leader would then tune sparse-MLA decode for its own stage and write the per-stage file. PP = 1 behaviour is unchanged.

### Alternatives

Keep the sparse-MLA decode autotune on the world group, and document that its tactics come from stage 0 under PP > 1.

### Additional context

The warmup order (sparse-MLA decode autotune before `flashinfer_autotune`) is intended and stays as it is.
