- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill.
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.
- [x] **Design Fit:** Reuse existing configuration/allocation logic and connector placement state.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Regression, counterexample and real NPU serving/accuracy evaluation recorded above; GPU device validation not claimed.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Local formatting checks passed.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Root cause, exact runtime dependencies, evidence and limitations included.

title: [Distributed] Lazily initialize unused NCCL2 process groups
body:
Co-authored-by: OpenAI Codex <codex@openai.com>
Signed-off-by: Tushar Jain <tushar00jain@users.noreply.github.com>

### Summary

#### Pipeline-parallel groups

Fix pipeline-parallel group creation when `split_group` is enabled. NCCL pipeline-parallel groups consistently use `new_group` instead of `split_group`.

On the NCCL2 path, pipeline-parallel groups use `nccl-lazy` for independently initialized per-peer communicators, allowing communication with different pipeline peers to overlap.

#### Lazy NCCL2 process groups

Create NCCL2 groups with `lazy_init` when their normal communication path uses a vLLM device communicator such as PyNCCL, DeepEP, or another custom backend. NCCL2 remains available as a fallback and initializes automatically if it is used.

Singleton groups and vLLM’s optional world subgroup are also initialized lazily. This avoids registering GPU memory for NCCL2 communicators that may never be used, while preserving correctness for groups that are used later. Legacy NCCL behavior is unchanged.

The default group is also created with `lazy_init`.

#### Attention Test Initialization

Remove unnecessary distributed initialization from V1 attention tests that do not perform distributed communication.

MLA, sparse MLA, DSpark, and Mamba selector tests now use single-rank TP metadata without creating NCCL process groups. This avoids repeated NCCL initialization and teardown across parameterized cases and addresses the B200 attention-test timeout regression.

### Test plan

- Verified pipeline-parallel groups use `ProcessGroupNCCLLazy`.
- Verified disjoint pipeline-parallel P2P transfers overlap.
- Verified a device-communicator-backed group leaves its NCCL2 communicator uninitialized until a direct PyTorch collective uses it.
- Ran representative CI failure tests and measured 1,168–2,334 MiB/GPU savings from lazy singleton initialization, versus the 133–164 MiB CI shortfall.
- Ran the exact DBO + DeepEP high-throughput test; NCCL2 completed without OOM and peaked only 230 MiB/GPU above legacy NCCL.
- Verified affected V1 attention tests run without distributed initialization; Mamba selectors and representative MLA/HiSparse cases passed, while the DSpark matrix had 10 passes and 20 architecture-gated skips on H100.

title: [Bugfix][DSv4.1] Declare 64-token kernel blocks for SM120 sparse backends
body:
### Summary
On SM120, the DSV41 sparse-MLA backends declare only `[128]`-token kernel blocks (`get_supported_kernel_block_sizes` returns `[64 if family(90) else 128]` / `[128]`), so serving with `--block-size 64` dies in block-size negotiation:

```
ValueError: No common block size for 64 (FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41: [128]; DEEPSEEK_V41_INDEXER: [128])
```

This declares `[64]` on SM12x for the two sites (indexer backend, sparse MLA backend, FlashInfer sparse backend), mirroring the existing SM90 branch. The SWA/backend selection is untouched.

The approach is @aagallo's (described in #59203); this PR adds the validated matrix below.

### Matrix validation (8x RTX PRO 6000, SM120, TP8)
Stack: vLLM `0.31.1rc1.dev158+gab905a885` + FlashInfer `0.7.1rc5`, `--block-size 64 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}'`, DeepGEMM switched between PR14 head (`40592bd`) and the current pin (`1e1842a`):

| vLLM tree | DeepGEMM | result |
|---|---|---|
| stock | `1e1842a` | fails negotiation (error above) |
| this PR (uniform `[64]`) | `40592bd` | serves, 17x19=323 |
| this PR (uniform `[64]`) | `1e1842a` | serves, 17x19=323 |
| per-layer variant (`[64,128]` + `64*max(1,cr)` specs) | `40592bd` | serves, 17x19=323 |
| per-layer variant | `1e1842a` | serves, 17x19=323 |

All four patched cells boot in ~90-160 s and answer correctly; zero failures. An earlier `attention.hpp:484` observed with uniform-64 on an older stack (0.30.1rc1.dev738 + FlashInfer main @c11f8ba + DeepGEMM 6901431) does not reproduce on current main with either DeepGEMM build — details in #59203.

Pairs naturally with #57292 (fail-fast when FlashInfer lacks runtime page sizes).

Addresses the SM120 serving failure in #59203.

### Test Plan
- [x] 5-cell matrix above (serve + correctness per cell)
- [ ] pre-commit / CI

---

## Requirements & validation (added after review)

**FlashInfer requirement: `flashinfer-python >= 0.7.1rc5` (runtime page sizes).** Measured end to end on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120):
- pinned `0.7.0.post1` + this PR: does **not** serve — fails in ~110 s with `page_block_size=32 is unsupported; decode kernels are instantiated only for page_block_size=64` (64-token kernel blocks give ratio-2 layers 32-token compressed pages; the pin has no runtime page sizes). Stock fails on the pin as well.
- `0.7.1rc5` + this PR: serves at default and `--block-size 64`; `--block-size 128` does not serve on this stack in either declaration form (see matrix below), so the PR buys default-64 — the only geometry that serves on the default BLHNC layout.

Landing order per review discussion: after the FlashInfer bump (#60948), or together with the #57292 guard.

**Matrix (stock / A=[64] / C=[64,128] x default / 64 / 128, GSM8K n=100):** stock fails both ways (assertions upthread); A and C serve at default and 64 (GSM8K 89-91%, no variant-dependent degradation); 128 fails under both declarations (A: BLHNC layout guard; C: FlashInfer `block_kv == 32 or block_kv == 64`). Decode throughput of the four servable configs is within <1% at c1/c4.

**Unit test:** `tests/v1/attention/test_dsv41_indexer_block_sizes.py` pins the SM12x declarations (indexer, FlashInfer sparse), the deliberately-unchanged sparse_mla base declaration, the SWA/compressor geometry, and resolved sizes for default / 64 / 128.

Coordinated with #56509 (same failure, overlapping declarations).

title: [WIP][DSv4.1] Opt in to mHC coefficient overlap on SM90
body:
## Overview

Draft: add an experimental, explicit opt-in for DeepSeek-V4.1 mHC coefficient overlap on Hopper (SM90), reusing the stream path introduced by #57603. Hopper remains disabled by default; GPU validation is pending.

## Claims

- `KernelConfig.enable_mhc_overlap=None` preserves SM100 automatic selection; `True` additionally permits SM90, and `False` disables overlap.
- Existing DeepGEMM, shape, ubatching, FULL CUDA graph and small-batch restrictions remain. SM90 uses the ordinary TP collective and cannot select the SM100-only fused all-reduce.
- No speedup, numerical equivalence, model quality or production-readiness claim is made in this draft.

## Validation

CPU only, using this branch's Python source on Linux, Python 3.12.3 and pytest 9.1.1, in an isolated container with no GPU devices (2 CPU cores / 4 GiB). Installed dependencies were inherited from a vLLM v0.28.0 image; this was not a fresh main wheel build.

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES= NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu \
  PYTHONPATH=$PWD PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/kernels/mhc -o addopts= \
  -q tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_dispatch.py
```

**14 passed**, covering opt-in/default/off selection, unsupported architectures, missing DeepGEMM, shape/ubatching fallback and exclusion of the SM100 collective. These mock capability checks validate dispatch only. Source-only version metadata and torch deprecation warnings were emitted.

```bash
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files vllm/config/kernel.py \
  vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/ops/mhc.py \
  tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_dispatch.py tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_kernels.py
git diff --check
```

All applicable hooks pass, including mypy, config validation and Buildkite test tethering. The new dispatch tests are in the existing mHC suite. The replay test now permits SM90 but **has not been run on GPU**; the existing dedicated NVIDIA mHC CI job uses B200.

Before marking ready:

- [ ] Verify that the tested DeepGEMM dependency contains the SM90 register-lifetime repair tracked by deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#448 / #59129; this draft does not implement that fix.
- [ ] Run the mHC replay test and independent numerical references on Hopper, including stream ordering and repeated graph replay.
- [ ] Verify eager/piecewise/large-batch fallback, TP modes and an SM100 regression run.
- [ ] Run DeepSeek-V4.1 end-to-end model evaluation and matched baseline/opt-in serving measurements, including `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`.
- [ ] Reassess the existing 16-token threshold on Hopper and complete human line-by-line review. Human review is not asserted.

## Details

The existing eligibility gate excludes SM90. This change makes Hopper experimental and opt-in via `--kernel-config '{"enable_mhc_overlap": true}'`; omitting it preserves defaults. This is a proposed serving configuration, not a GPU-validated launch recipe. The existing configuration hash includes the new field.

This reuses vLLM's TF32 prenorm coefficient path. It does **not** port the compensated-BF16 projection from sgl-project/sglang#41251. Kernel arithmetic, the existing stream schedule and the GB200-derived 16-token threshold are unchanged. The all-reduce architecture guard is needed because its caller can now also create an mHC stream on SM90.

Duplicate-work checks on 2026-10-09 covered issue #57448 and open/closed PRs matching mHC, overlap, SM90 and Hopper. No equivalent Hopper coefficient-overlap PR was found: #57603 targets SM100; #59802 targets ROCm; #59129 packages the separate DeepGEMM correctness repair. This draft depends on confirming that repair rather than duplicating it.

AI assistance (OpenAI Codex) was used for investigation, implementation, tests and this description. This is WIP awaiting GPU resources; model evaluations and performance results are not yet available.

title: [WIP][Kernel][DSv4.1] Add compensated BF16 mHC prenorm for SM90
body:
## Purpose

Draft a compensated BF16 mHC prenorm primitive for Hopper, adapted from SGLang's `hc_mix_stats_bf16x3` in sgl-project/sglang#39664 and sgl-project/sglang#41251. It splits the FP32 mixing weight into three BF16 components, accumulates their projections separately in FP32, and computes the input squared norm in the same pass.

This initial draft contains a kernel, correctness tests and a comparison benchmark. **Serving dispatch is intentionally not wired yet. No kernel or end-to-end speedup, numerical equivalence, or production-readiness claim is made.** Integration and default selection depend on real SM90 measurements against the current fused mHC path, not only against a standalone GEMM.

## Implementation

- Accept caller-owned prepared weights and output buffers; no allocation or CPU/GPU synchronization in the projection wrapper.
- Write `[splits, tokens, mix]` projection and `[splits, tokens]` squared-norm partials, compatible with the existing prenorm epilogue layout.
- Support split counts 1/4/16, token tiles 32/64/128, empty batches, masked tails, and contiguous offset views. These are tuning candidates, not validated performance defaults.
- Reuse the existing mHC correctness suite. Add FP64 reference, cancellation/weight-reconstruction, output-boundary and changed-input/weight CUDA graph tests.
- Add a CUPTI benchmark that checks correctness before timing and sweeps both DeepGEMM and candidate configurations with CUDA graphs and cold L2. Weight preparation, allocations and the common epilogue are excluded from the reported prenorm timing.

The prepared weights occupy 6 bytes per original FP32 element, in addition to any retained original weight. The caller must rebuild them after weight updates. Different accumulation orders can change outputs; batch invariance is not promised. SGLang's bundled serving gains are not an estimate for this isolated kernel or for vLLM.

## Duplicate check and provenance

Checked #57448 and public open/closed PR searches for `mHC`, `compensated`, `bf16x3`, `SM90`, and Hopper on 2026-10-09. No open PR implementing this compensated mHC projection was found.

- #60768 only opts SM90 into the existing TF32 coefficient-overlap path; this is an independent kernel draft, not a duplicate or dependency.
- #57603 implements small-batch overlap; #56633 fuses post/pre; #56962 integrates Mega-mHC. They are relevant baselines, not this BF16x3 projection.
- #60376 is a router-GEMM optimization on SM100, not mHC prenorm on SM90.
- #59129 concerns the separate DeepGEMM SM90 correctness fix and must be accounted for when benchmarking the baseline.

The SGLang kernel's Apache-2.0 attribution is retained. Reviewed source: `python/sglang/kernels/ops/layernorm/mhc.py` on SGLang main around `5d8e98b7fdd83907616b1ff8ca68229f2ae95b34`. This adapts its numerical approach to vLLM's output layout and caller-owned workspace; it does not copy SGLang's runtime dispatch or Sinkhorn implementation.

## Validation completed

CPU-only Linux container, Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1. Source under test was overlaid into an isolated source checkout; dependencies came from the existing vLLM v0.28.0 image, not a newly built wheel. Container used `runc`, no GPU device nodes, empty `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void`, no network, 2 CPU cores and 4 GiB RAM. `torch.cuda.is_available()` was false.

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH=$PWD PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/kernels/mhc -o addopts= \
  -q tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_kernels.py -k bf16x3
```

**3 passed, 9 GPU cases skipped, 320 deselected.** CPU checks cover random, cancellation and scaled FP32 weight decomposition, including preserving the original weight. Source-only version/extension warnings and torch deprecation warnings were emitted.

**18 SM90 offline compilations passed:** explicit `GPUTarget("cuda", 90, 32)`, K=5120/20480, splits=1/4/16, BLOCK_M=32/64/128, N=24, BLOCK_N=32, BLOCK_K=64, four warps and three stages. PTX/cubin were generated without loading or launching a CUDA kernel. This proves compilation only, not GPU numerical correctness or speed.

All applicable pre-commit hooks passed, including Ruff, mypy, SPDX and Buildkite test tethering; `git diff --check` passed. The existing mHC CI job exercises the suite on B200; actual SM90 execution remains a validation gap.

## Before ready for review

- [ ] Run the 9 CUDA correctness/replay cases on SM90, including bounds checking.
- [ ] Run `benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mhc_bf16x3.py` on H20/H200 and retain all configurations, not only winners.
- [ ] Integrate opt-in dispatch with weight-update handling and startup warmup only if the kernel is competitive against the actual fused post/pre baseline.
- [ ] Compare the complete mHC boundary and full serving performance; evaluate model quality after integration.

title: [Performance]: Reduce load_weights synchronization overhead for DeepSeek V4 Flash weight updates on H200
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

Profiling repeated weight updates for **DeepSeek V4 Flash on NVIDIA H200** revealed substantial CPU waiting and accounting overhead inside `load_weights`.

The transfer method involves sorting all weights by layer into buckets of ≤8 GB, with each bucket triggering a `load_weights` operation.

For the second `load_weights` invocation in each trace, the combined experimental optimizations reduced profiled CPU duration from **1,923.691 ms to 276.823 ms**, an **85.61% reduction / 6.95× speedup**.

**Original loading flow**

The baseline follows the existing layerwise reload path:

1. `load_weights` routes incoming weight names to parameters, shards, and experts.
2. `online_process_loader` buffers weights and calls `get_numel_loaded` to track layer completion. Accounting executes the original loader against meta parameters under `CopyCounter`.
3. Once a layer is ready, `_layerwise_process` materializes its parameters and replays the buffered loaders for actual loading.
4. Quantization post-processing prepares MXFP4 MoE weights for Marlin: repack `w13` and `w2`, then permute and encode their scales per expert.
5. Processed values are copied into the existing kernel tensor storage.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as Caller
    participant Model as DeepSeek V4 load_weights
    participant Loader as Reload / weight_loader
    participant Map as Expert ID map
    participant Marlin as Marlin preparation
    participant GPU as CUDA runtime / GPU
    rect rgb(255, 242, 238)
    Note over Caller,GPU: main - second call - relative offsets in ms
    Caller->>Model: load_weights() [t=0.000 ms]
    activate Model
    Note over Model,Loader: Loading / dispatch before Marlin: t=0.000 to 1297.992 ms
    loop Interleaved accounting and actual loading (aggregated, not expanded)
        Model->>Loader: get_numel_loaded x1552
        Note over Model,Loader: Exclusive totals: accounting 94.848 ms
        Loader->>Map: map_global_to_local x3048
        Note over Loader,Map: Mapping cumulative CPU duration: 959.661 ms
        Map->>GPU: GPU expert_map scalar read / item() x3048
        Note over Map,GPU: D2H x3048
        GPU-->>Map: Scalar result after synchronization
        Map-->>Loader: Local expert ID
    end
    Model->>Marlin: prepare_moe_mxfp4_layer_for_marlin [t=1297.992 ms]
    activate Marlin
    Marlin->>GPU: repack_weight #1 [t=1298.015 to 1301.462 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU invocation duration 3.447 ms
    Marlin->>GPU: repack_weight #2 [t=1301.492 to 1304.639 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU invocation duration 3.146 ms
    Marlin->>Marlin: scales preparation #1 [t=1304.668 to 1612.284 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU duration 307.616 ms
    Marlin->>Marlin: scales preparation #2 [t=1612.320 to 1919.894 ms]
    Note over Marlin,GPU: CPU duration 307.574 ms
    Note over Marlin,GPU: Across both scales entries: permutation x128 / 304.153 ms
    Note over Marlin,GPU: H2D x256
    Marlin-->>Model: Preparation returns [t=1919.963 ms]
    deactivate Marlin
    Model-->>Caller: load_weights returns [t=1923.691 ms]
    deactivate Model
    end
```

Accounting and actual loading are interleaved as layers become ready. Expert ID mapping occurs in both paths.

**Bottlenecks and implemented optimizations**

1. **GPU scalar reads during expert ID mapping**

   The baseline reads `expert_map[global_id].item()` from a GPU tensor for host-side decisions. Across **3,048 lookups**, the trace records **3,048 D2H transfers and 3,048 stream synchronizations**.

   Mapping consumes **959.661 ms**, including **870.633 ms** in CPU stream synchronization, while the corresponding D2H transfers total only **7.177 ms** of GPU time. This identifies frequent host waiting as the main cost.

   **Optimization:** cache a Python list whenever the expert map is created or recalculated, and use it for host-side ID and locality queries. #60779 

   **Observed result:** mapping duration falls to **0.287 ms**. Lookup count remains **3,048**, while D2H transfers and stream synchronizations inside these lookups fall to **zero**.

2. **Replaying expert loaders for loaded-element accounting**

   The baseline invokes `RoutedExperts.weight_loader` both for accounting and for actual loading: **3,048 calls**, including **1,524 accounting calls**.

   **Optimization:** use a counting fast path that determines the loaded-element count without re-entering the expert loader.

   **Observed result:** total expert-loader calls fall to **1,524**, all on the actual loading path. `CopyCounter.__torch_dispatch__` invocations fall from **4,936 to 96**.

   The fast path still checks expert placement, so expert-map lookup count remains unchanged.

3. **Synchronization in Marlin scales preparation**

   The baseline PyTorch scales path performs permutation and MXFP4 encoding per expert. These operations account for **256 H2D transfers and 256 stream synchronizations**, with **594.433 ms** spent in CPU stream synchronization.

   **Optimization:** implement scale permutation and encoding with CUDA operators. #60780

   **Observed result:** the two scales-preparation entries fall from **615.190 ms to 7.704 ms**, and their H2D transfers and stream synchronizations fall to **zero**.

   Permutation and encoding still each execute **128 times** in this experiment. Scales-related GPU kernel time improves from **1.983 ms to 1.230 ms (1.61×)**; the much larger CPU-duration improvement reflects reduced host waiting and dispatch overhead.

### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

**Performance comparison**

The following breakdown assigns non-overlapping intervals within the selected `load_weights` invocation. Nested mapping time is removed from accounting and loader rows, and scale substeps are separated from their parent entries.

| Step | Baseline CPU duration (ms) | Optimized CPU duration (ms) | Baseline share | Optimized share |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Expert ID mapping | 959.661 | 0.287 | 49.89% | 0.10% |
| Loaded-element accounting, excluding mapping | 94.848 | 24.382 | 4.93% | 8.81% |
| Actual loader work, excluding mapping/accounting | 18.955 | 17.966 | 0.99% | 6.49% |
| Scales permutation | 304.153 | 2.591 | 15.81% | 0.94% |
| MXFP4 scales encoding | 308.717 | 3.183 | 16.05% | 1.15% |
| Other scales-entry work | 2.320 | 1.931 | 0.12% | 0.70% |
| Weight repack | 6.593 | 6.613 | 0.34% | 2.39% |
| Other work / gaps | 228.444 | 219.871 | 11.88% | 79.43% |
| **Total** | **1,923.691** | **276.823** | **100%** | **100%** |

Rounded rows may differ slightly from the total.

Expert mapping and scales preparation account for approximately **81.87%** of the baseline window. Actual loader work excluding mapping and accounting changes only modestly, from **18.955 ms to 17.966 ms**.

**Measurement scope**

- The window includes accounting, actual loaders, Marlin preparation, and CPU waiting. It excludes outer broadcast, bucket reconstruction, final synchronization/finalization, GC, and `empty_cache`.
- These are **profiled inclusive CPU durations**. GPU work can remain outstanding when the function returns.
- Matching operation counts do not establish identical tensor inputs or numerical correctness. The optimized full-update trace broadcasts approximately **0.0400% more bytes**.
- Repeated measurements with identical inputs and profiling disabled, plus CUDA numerical parity and model-output validation, are needed to establish the end-to-end benefit.

Related discussion: [#54477 — Direct Weight Reload for RL Training](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54477). This report contributes measurements and targeted optimizations within the existing layerwise reload path.

AI assistance was used to review the code and draft this issue.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

```text

GPU: NVIDIA H200
Profiled rank: 0
World size: 4
Profiled MoE preparation: MXFP4 → Marlin
CUDA runtime: 13.0
NCCL: 2.28.9
Profiler setting: with_stack=True
TP / EP configuration: 4 / 4
```

title: [Perf][MoE] Avoid GPU synchronization in expert ID lookups
body:
## Overview

Part of #60778 (bottleneck 1: GPU scalar reads during expert ID mapping).

During layerwise weight reloading (`load_weights`, e.g. RL weight updates for DeepSeek V4 Flash), the host-side expert ID queries in `ExpertMapManager` (`map_global_to_local`, `is_local_expert`, `get_local_expert_ids`, `get_compressed_map_string`) read scalars from the GPU-resident `_expert_map` tensor via `expert_map[global_id].item()`. Each lookup issues a D2H copy and a CUDA stream synchronization. In the profiled `load_weights` invocation this amounts to 3,048 D2H transfers and 3,048 stream synchronizations, costing 959.661 ms of CPU time (~50% of the window), of which 870.633 ms is host waiting in stream synchronization — while the corresponding D2H transfers take only 7.177 ms of GPU time.

This PR caches a host-side copy of the expert map (`_expert_map_cpu`, a Python list) and serves all host-side lookups from it:

- `_expert_map_cpu` is rebuilt alongside `_expert_map` in `_calculate_expert_maps()`, the single place where the map is created or recalculated (including EPLB-driven `update()`), so the two always stay in sync.
- GPU-side consumers of `_expert_map` are untouched.
- The cost is one extra `.cpu().tolist()` per map (re)computation, amortized across all subsequent lookups.

## Claims

Measured on the profiled second `load_weights` call reported in #60778 (DeepSeek V4 Flash, NVIDIA H200, world size 4, TP/EP = 4/4, MXFP4 → Marlin):

- Expert ID mapping CPU duration: **959.661 ms → 0.287 ms**
- D2H transfers inside expert ID lookups: **3,048 → 0**
- CUDA stream synchronizations inside expert ID lookups: **3,048 → 0**
- Lookup count is unchanged (3,048) and returned IDs are unchanged (same underlying map) — no functional change.

## Validation

- Added `tests/distributed/test_expert_placement.py::test_expert_map_manager_lookups_follow_ep_updates`, which verifies that `map_global_to_local`, `is_local_expert`, `get_local_expert_ids`, and `get_compressed_map_string` return the expected IDs/locality/map-string on the initial EP configuration, and remain in sync after `ExpertMapManager.update()` reconfigures placement (EP rank change, then EP disabled): `pytest tests/distributed/test_expert_placement.py::test_expert_map_manager_lookups_follow_ep_updates`.
- The performance numbers above come from the profiling experiment in #60778 (repeated weight updates for DeepSeek V4 Flash on H200). Lookup behavior is otherwise unchanged, so existing MoE/EPLB test coverage continues to apply.

## Details

- `_expert_map_cpu` is `None` iff `_expert_map` is `None`, preserving the existing identity-mapping behavior when EP is disabled.
- `map_global_to_local` still returns a plain Python `int` (previously via `.item()`); `is_local_expert` now returns a Python `bool` instead of a 0-dim tensor, which is equivalent in boolean contexts.
- Combined with the other optimizations tracked in #60778, the profiled `load_weights` window drops from 1,923.691 ms to 276.823 ms; this PR contributes the expert-ID-mapping portion.

title: [Rust Frontend] Compose answer constraints into parser-owned output grammars
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->
## Overview

Step 4 of the parser-owned output grammar rollout, stacked on #59190 (Kimi K3 full-output grammar). The request's own structured-output constraint (`response_format` or `structured_outputs`, the "answer constraint" below) now composes into the parser-built output grammar instead of competing with it. Composition follows the Python frontend's `Parser._apply_structural_tag` (#56086).

Most of the diff is regenerated grammar replay snapshots: about 3,300 of the roughly 4,100 added lines are under `rust/src/chat/tests/grammar_replay/`. The code and test changes are about 800 lines.

## Claims

- `tool_choice=auto` with tools and an answer constraint keeps both: split parsers build `Or[tool calls built as required, answer]` inside the reasoning wrapper. Today a tool grammar replaces the answer constraint, so the answer is unconstrained; without a tool grammar the native constraint applies after reasoning and leaves no room for tool calls.
- With no callable tool (no tools, or `tool_choice=none`), a parser with a reasoning grammar wraps the answer and constrains the output from token zero (`reasoning_ended = Some(true)`) instead of through the engine's reasoning gate.
- Kimi K3 places the answer inside its `response` channel for every tool choice. `auto` and `required` keep the paths with both an answer and calls, and allow the empty `response` channel the chat template writes before tool calls.
- `required` and named tool choices on split parsers keep today's behavior: the answer constraint is ignored with a one-time warning, as in Python.

## Validation

```bash
cd rust
cargo test -p vllm-parser -p vllm-chat -p vllm-server
cargo test -p vllm-chat --test roundtrip --test grammar_replay
cargo clippy -p vllm-parser -p vllm-chat -p vllm-server --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

- Tests: `vllm-parser` 560, `vllm-chat` 354 (plus integration tests), `vllm-server` 453, all passing on every commit; Clippy and rustfmt pass.
- Grammar replay (#59143): the tool-call roundtrip gains three variants with a JSON schema: `none_schema` and `auto_schema_content` are answered with schema-valid content, `auto_schema_calls` with tool calls only. All 74 generations (36 existing, 38 new) pass with XGrammar 0.2.7 (the harness pin) and 0.2.8 (`requirements/common.txt`): 70 are replayed from token zero, and the 4 final-output-only grammars (MiniMax M3, Seed-OSS) are compiled.
- GPU smoke on GB200 with the Rust frontend (temperature 0, JSON schema `{answer: string, confidence: number}`), checking that every response is either schema-valid content or valid tool calls:
  - Qwen3-8B, `qwen3` reasoning + `hermes` tools (reasoning wrapper, from token zero): 10/10. `none` and `auto` with an arithmetic prompt return schema-valid content after the reasoning; `auto` with a weather prompt returns a valid call, streaming and not; thinking off returns content without reasoning; `required` returns a call and logs the ignored constraint once; a request without tools returns schema-valid content; 16 concurrent mixed requests return 8 calls and 8 schema-valid answers.
  - DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (FP8, TP4, eager), `deepseek_v41` reasoning + DSML tools (reasoning wrapper, from token zero): the same 10 cases pass, including 16 concurrent mixed requests returning 8 calls and 8 schema-valid answers.
  - Each server first receives a composed request, because the engine instantiates its structured-output backend from the first request: the Rust frontend sends native constraints as guidance and parser-built grammars as xgrammar, and guidance cannot compile the latter. This first-request issue predates this PR; see Details.
- Not run: model evaluation, and Kimi K3 serving (its weights need several nodes; the grammar replay covers its token-zero grammar).

## Details

- Answer normalization (`answer_format`) mirrors Python's `structured_outputs_to_format`: JSON schema, JSON object, regex, choice, EBNF grammar, and structural tags in both the current `format` and legacy `structures`/`triggers` shapes. Like Python, it ignores the request's whitespace and `additionalProperties` options, which no backend reads per request. Lark grammars (Rust has no Lark-to-EBNF converter) and structural tags that do not parse keep their native constraint.
- The output processor normalizes the answer at construction, next to the tools and tool choice it already captures, so `ChatOutputProcessor::build_output_grammar` keeps its signature.
- Tool parsers compose the answer: they implement `build_call_format` for a given tool choice (the default uses the structural-tag builder), and the provided `ToolParser::build_visible_format` adds the answer on top. `CombinedParser` takes that visible language, or the answer alone without a tool grammar, and lets the reasoning parser wrap it.
- A grammar is built whenever a reasoning or tool parser is active; a request with neither keeps its own constraint. When the reasoning parser cannot wrap an answer-only grammar (`kimi`, `minimax_m3`, `cohere_cmd`, `seed_oss`), the grammar covers the final output, behind the engine's reasoning gate as before; such a request now compiles on xgrammar, where engine-level `disable_any_whitespace` and `disable_additional_properties` do not apply, as for every parser-built grammar.
- Known limits, shared with Python: a tool parser without a structural-tag builder (GLM-4.5, MiniMax M3, Seed-OSS) leaves the answer alone, which excludes tool calls. Required tool grammars built from `triggered_tags` admit text after the calls, so under `auto` a generation can call a tool and then write unconstrained text.
- Structured-output backend: the engine instantiates one backend from the first structured-output request, and the Rust frontend sends native constraints as guidance and parser-built grammars as xgrammar. This predates this PR (strict and required tool grammars already mix with native constraints), but composition moves more requests to xgrammar. On a server with a tool parser and no reasoning parser, a schema request with tools now gets an xgrammar grammar while one without tools stays native on guidance; if the latter arrives first, later composed grammars fail to compile (`KeyError: 'triggers'`, since guidance reads only legacy structural tags). With a reasoning parser, every schema request now gets an xgrammar grammar. Selecting the backend in the Rust frontend is a separate change.
- Replay files now hold each distinct grammar once with the generations of every variant that builds it, since `auto_schema_content` and `auto_schema_calls` build the same grammar.
- Duplicate check: open PRs on Rust structured outputs, response formats, and output grammars include #47176 (request validation in the server) and #50543 (Python K3 rendering); neither composes answer constraints into output grammars.

title: [Refactor][KV Offload] Split shared offload regions into concrete classes
body:
## Overview

Refactor shared CPU offload storage into explicit region implementations while preserving main's layout, population, pinning, barrier, and cleanup behavior.

This provides a stable foundation for future offloading optimizations, including the work in [#59544](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59544), [#59545](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59545), [#59546](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59546), and [#59547](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59547).

## Claims

- **Decoupled responsibilities:** common mmap lifetime management stays in the base class; layout-specific view, populate, and pin behavior stays in concrete classes.
- **Explicit implementation selection:** each caller constructs the intended implementation directly (`DirectRankRegion`, `ReplicatedRegion`, `GlobalRegion`, `CanonicalRegion`, or `HiSparseRegion`).
- **Independent optimization surface:** each layout can later optimize its own populate, pin, or address strategy without adding branching to shared code.
- **Clear ownership:** the region owns tensors backed by its mmap, including CUDA registration, rollback, and release.
- **No performance behavior change in this PR:** current byte ranges, barrier ordering, view layout, and registration behavior remain unchanged.

## Validation

- `tests/v1/kv_offload`: **666 passed, 2 skipped**.
- Ruff, mypy, and all pre-commit hooks passed.
- No model evaluation is required because this is a structural refactor with no model or serving behavior change.

## Details

`SharedOffloadRegion` now owns mmap creation, mapping synchronization, low-level page population, pinned-address tracking, cleanup, and failure rollback. Typed view interfaces separate tensor views from complete memoryviews:

```python
region.populate()
region.pin()
view = region.get_view(...)
region.cleanup()
```

Region implementations:

- `DirectRankRegion`: rank-local strided worker slots.
- `ReplicatedRegion`: replicated data in slot 0.
- `GlobalRegion`: complete row-major memoryview for the Tiering scheduler; no CUDA pin.
- `CanonicalRegion`: canonical tensor views with existing population and pin behavior.
- `HiSparseRegion`: creator-only population, HiSparse registration ranges, and segmented pinning.

This is separate from the mmap ownership and startup-cleanup fix in [#53073](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53073), which changes pathname ownership semantics. It is also not a duplicate implementation of Etelis's recent optimization PRs [#59544](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59544), [#59545](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59545), [#59546](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59546), or [#59547](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59547). Those PRs change offloading behavior and performance; this PR only establishes the concrete region boundaries needed to integrate similar optimizations cleanly in follow-up changes.

title: [Kernel] LiteTopK prefill for GLM-5.2 FP8 TP8 on SM100
body:
## Overview

This is a focused split and kernel refinement of the LiteTopK prefill work in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48726, targeting **GLM-5.2 FP8 with TP8 on SM100/B200**.

As suggested by **@tkoniy from the Hunyuan team**, this version replaces **hotsample with fixed random page sampling** and improves the paged-cache scoring and h2048 selection path.

cc @LopezCastroRoberto @ibrahimnd2000 — please take a look at this focused LiteTopK prefill kernel update and its integration scope.

## Validation

Prepared against vLLM main `e31b823bf59bdd96d09fdcf310c5fb02e934d3bf`. The patch applies cleanly to that commit: **14 files changed, 3740 insertions, 18 deletions**.

Validated on a single B200 using PyTorch 2.13/CUDA 13, the updated main Python sources, and pre-existing vLLM core binaries. Both the LiteTopK CUDA extension and main's pinned DeepGEMM (`1e1842a833699298f7afc02eefb2ed168fff6938`, version 2.8) were compiled from source. DeepGEMM tests use the real patched `out=` implementation, with no allocation-and-copy adapter.

Coverage includes deterministic sampling, partial pages and causal bounds at TP rank offsets 0 and 7, selector boundary/tie/overflow cases, unsupported model and parallel-layout rejection, caller-owned DeepGEMM output, and the existing CP metadata regression. Ruff check/format and `git diff --check` passed. The nested DeepGEMM patch also applies cleanly to its pinned source.

**Full eight-GPU GLM-5.2 inference, model accuracy/quality evaluation, and end-to-end performance measurements have not been run for this main-based revision.** The available validation used one GPU; this description makes no model-quality or speedup claim and does not reuse the earlier hotsample results from #48726.

## Details

The supported target is GLM-5.2. Runtime qualification uses `model_type="glm_moe_dsa"` and `(index_n_heads, index_head_dim, index_topk)=(32, 128, 2048)` because the configuration does not provide a reliable GLM-5.2-only version tag. Other checkpoints with the same configuration are not separately qualified by these tests.

Enable with `VLLM_LITETOPK=1`, TP8, and prefix caching disabled. The optimized path handles single-request prefill chunks of 8192 or 8128 query tokens, split into 1024 or 1016 rows per TP rank, with 64-token KV pages. The default context range is 196608–1048576 tokens. Rank-local results are all-gathered, and ranks agree on whether the fused path succeeded before consuming the result.

The scoped LiteTopK path excludes DeepSeek models, TP4, PCP/DCP, FP4/compressed indexer cache, and prefix-cache reuse. Existing main behavior for these configurations and for decode is retained. The patch contains no hotsample or carry implementation. References to DeepSeek in the shared indexer classes and kernel license identify upstream infrastructure and provenance.

Selection uses high24 score keys, dropping the low eight FP32 bits; it is not a bitwise-equivalent FP32 TopK promise. Invalid or overflowing candidate output fails closed. Planned unsplit chunks cannot safely fall back to allocating full dense logits.

DeepGEMM receives a caller-owned output slab through a separately registered `out` operator with mutation/alias annotations. Its existing allocating operator retains its schema. LiteTopK requires the patched bundled backend or an external backend exposing the same `out=` API.

This extracts and refines the GLM prefill component of #48726; it does not reproduce that PR's LiteDSA or DeepSeek V4 features. The related open decode work (#59921, #59922, #57109) and the single-launch prefill WIP (#60618) were checked. This patch retains separate sample, scan, selection, and mapping stages, so it is not a single-launch implementation. Maybe @ LopezCastroRoberto can help to improve this PR like #60618. 
---

title: [Bug]: MiniMax-M3: PP startup, NIXL+PP prefill, NIXL/offload+HMA+DSpark, offload+PP, Mooncake recompute loop, MSA prefill OOM
body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```text
vLLM:    main @ ab5266769e (2026-10-01), built from source, VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
GPU:     1 node, 4x NVIDIA GB200 (SM100), aarch64, driver 580.126.09
Python:  torch 2.13.0+cu130, flashinfer-python 0.7.0.post1, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.1, transformers 5.17.0
KV:      nixl 1.4.1, mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13 0.3.13.post1, vllm-router for PD
```

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

I ran a functional sweep of MiniMax-M3 feature combinations on main at ab5266769e (2026-10-01): 101 server configurations covering TP/EP/DP/PP, PD (NIXL pull and push), KV offload, MooncakeStore, DSpark spec decode, multimodal input, structured output and cudagraph modes. It checks function, not performance. Five failures remain; I re-checked each one by reading the code at f0a5f111f2 (2026-10-09), not by re-running. 1 and 4 are already tracked; I can split 2, 3 and 5 into separate issues if that is easier to triage.

**Update (2026-10-12):** 6 and 7 were found later on main at 83773ecdf3 (2026-10-12), while writing a CI test for these combinations and running BFCL on the full model. The CI test is #61370: it guards the combinations that work against regressions. Its description also has a pairwise compatibility matrix.

| # | Combination | Failure | Existing issue / PR | Workaround |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | PP on SM100 | startup: `Workers disagree on supported KV cache layouts` | #54710; fix #54795 (open) | a dense layer on every stage (PP2 only) |
| 2 | NIXL + hybrid KV cache manager (HMA) + DSpark | startup: `KV cache view cannot be partitioned into NIXL regions` | none | `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` |
| 3 | NIXL (pull or push) + PP on the prefill instance | startup: `num_regions % num_local_layers == 0` | #52913; #53360, #43366 (open) | none |
| 4 | OffloadingConnector + PP with unequal stages | startup: shared mmap `TimeoutError` | #50821; #50653 (partial, open) | none |
| 5 | MooncakeStoreConnector + `kv_load_failure_policy=recompute` | a failing load is retried forever; requests never finish | #55297 (open, needs rebase) | `kv_load_failure_policy=fail` |
| 6 | CPU KV offload (OffloadingConnector or SimpleCPUOffloadConnector) + hybrid KV cache manager (HMA) + DSpark | OffloadingConnector: startup assertion; both: KV offloaded to CPU is never reloaded | none | `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` |
| 7 | Full MiniMax-M3 under concurrent prefill (seen with DSpark, TP4) | `CUDA out of memory` in the MSA sparse prefill; the engine dies | none | lower `--gpu-memory-utilization` (0.85 worked) |

**Setup**

- Model: `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` cut to its first 10 decoder layers, so each config fits on 1–4 GPUs. The cut copies the tensors of layers 0–9 plus the vision tower into a new checkpoint with `num_hidden_layers: 10`: layers 0–2 are full attention + dense MLP, 3–9 are MSA sparse attention + MoE. It does not produce meaningful text, so the checks below test numerical consistency, not output quality. Unless noted, runs use `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}'` and `--block-size 128`.
- Draft: `nvidia/MiniMax-M3-DSpark`, with `dflash_config.target_layer_ids` remapped to `[1,2,4,6,8,9]` for the 10-layer target.
- Per config: start `vllm serve` (PD behind `vllm-router`), then send greedy completions with top-5 logprobs compared against a single-instance baseline, chat with reasoning, streaming, 24 concurrent requests, a prefix-cache cold/warm pair, a tool call, a JSON-schema request, an image request and a 768-token decode. PD runs also check `vllm:prompt_tokens_by_source{source="external_kv_transfer"}` on the decode instance. Offload and Mooncake runs call `/reset_prefix_cache` and require the next request to load from external KV.

<details>
<summary>What works (62 of 101 configurations pass)</summary>

All 62 greedy comparisons matched the baseline token for token. In all 15 PD configurations that passed, the decode instance got every prompt token over NIXL, with no failed transfers.

| Area | Passing combinations |
|---|---|
| Parallelism | TP1/2/4, TP4+EP, DP2×TP2+EP, DEP4 (`flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`). PP2, PP2×TP2, PP2+MM and PP2+MooncakeStore pass only with the workaround in (1). |
| DSpark | k=3/7/8 with FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, FULL_DECODE_ONLY, PIECEWISE, eager, async scheduling off, chunked prefill, a 100k-token prompt and KV-pressure preemption |
| PD (NixlConnector, NixlPushConnector) | TP1→TP1, TP2→TP2, TP2→DEP2, TP2+EP→DEP2, DP2+EP2→DEP2, UCX RDMA without cuda_ipc, a 64k-token prompt, client abort mid-stream, an image request through the router. Prefill = MultiConnector(NIXL + MooncakeStore) or MultiConnector(NIXL + OffloadingConnector). |
| KV offload | OffloadingConnector (TP1, TP2, DEP4), SimpleCPUOffloadConnector, all with DSpark and `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` (with the hybrid manager on, see 6) |
| MooncakeStore | embedded and standalone store, TCP and RDMA, TP4+EP+MM, two instances sharing one store over RDMA |
| Other | V1 model runner, image input, xgrammar structured output with the reasoning parser, hybrid KV cache manager on (no connector), KV events, encoder CUDA graph with the `FLASH_ATTN` ViT backend, fp8 KV on FlashInfer TRT-LLM attention |

Rejected at startup with a clear error (expected): `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` with M3 sparse attention (supported since #59300, merged after the tested commit; not tested), `indexer_kv_dtype=nvfp4`, `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe` and EPLB with this MXFP8 MoE, `fp8_e5m2` KV with this checkpoint, DBO + spec decode, DCP with TP ≤ the number of KV heads, PCP.

</details>

The repros below use `$M3` for the 10-layer cut and `$DSPARK` for the remapped draft. On the full 60-layer checkpoint they need enough TP to fit, and `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=2,58` instead of `2,8`. The full model was not run.

#### 1. PP on SM100 fails with `Workers disagree on supported KV cache layouts` (#54710)

Every PP config with the default layer split fails at startup:

```
File "vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py", line 285, in resolve_kv_cache_layout
AssertionError: Workers disagree on supported KV cache layouts: [['LBHNC', 'BLHNC'], ['LBNHC', 'LBHNC', 'BLNHC', 'BLHNC', 'BHLNC', 'LHBNC']].
```

MiniMax-M3 has full-attention layers only at 0–2. On SM100 FlashInfer declares `(LBHNC, BLHNC)` and `MiniMaxM3SparseBackend` declares nothing, so stage 0 reports FlashInfer's set and every MSA-only stage reports the default six. The open fix #54795, which intersects the per-worker lists, would pick `LBHNC`, the layout the workaround below ends up using.

- `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=2,8` puts a dense layer on each stage, and PP2 then starts and serves correctly. On the full 60-layer model that means a 1/59 or 2/58 split. For PP≥4 no layer partition works, because there are only 3 dense layers.
- A DSpark draft configured with `"attention_backend":"FLASH_ATTN"` (which declares no layouts) does not help: PP2 + DSpark fails the same way.

<details><summary>Repro</summary>

```bash
vllm serve $M3 --trust-remote-code --block-size 128 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}' \
  --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager --enable-prefix-caching \
  --pipeline-parallel-size 2
# starts with VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=2,8
```

</details>

#### 2. NIXL + hybrid KV cache manager + DSpark: `KV cache view cannot be partitioned into NIXL regions`

With the hybrid KV cache manager on (no `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`), the DSpark draft and NixlConnector, KV registration fails. A single instance is enough to reproduce it:

```
[base_worker.py:975] User-specified logical block size (2048) does not match physical kernel block size (128). Using the latter.
AssertionError: KV cache view cannot be partitioned into NIXL regions: layer=language_model.model.layers.0.self_attn.attn, cache_nbytes=13839106048, num_blocks=844672, block_stride=131072, physical_page_size=16384, cache_shape=(105584, 4, 128, 256), cache_stride=(131072, 32768, 256, 1)
```

The draft's sliding-window layers make the manager unify page sizes, so the KV groups end up with different block sizes (`kv cache group sizes [256, 256, 2048, 2048, 128]`, lcm 2048). NixlConnector derives one block size and one physical-per-logical ratio for all groups ([`_sync_block_size_with_kernel`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f0a5f111f2/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_worker.py#L989)), so the full-attention view cannot be split into regions. Two controls pass: hybrid manager + DSpark without a connector, and PD + DSpark with the hybrid manager off. #59586 fixes the same assertion for MLA rows only.

<details><summary>Repro</summary>

```bash
vllm serve $M3 --trust-remote-code --block-size 128 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}' \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"'"$DSPARK"'","num_speculative_tokens":3,"attention_backend":"FLASH_ATTN","kv_cache_dtype":"fp8"}' \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_buffer_device":"cuda"}'
```

</details>

#### 3. NIXL with PP on the prefill instance: `num_regions % num_local_layers == 0`

With `--pipeline-parallel-size 2` on the prefill instance (plus the workaround from 1), both NixlConnector and NixlPushConnector fail in `register_kv_caches`:

```
File "vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_worker.py", line 1794, in register_kv_caches
    assert num_local_layers > 0 and self.num_regions % num_local_layers == 0
```

Under PP the worker computes the remote region offset as `regions_per_layer * start_layer` ([L1816](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f0a5f111f2/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_worker.py#L1816)), which assumes every layer registers the same number of regions. MiniMax-M3 registers 1 region per dense layer and 2 per MSA layer (KV plus indexer K), so a stage that holds both kinds cannot satisfy the assertion. These counts come from the code and fit every observed case; region counts are not logged. Name-based routing (#50494, #50499) is only enabled with the hybrid KV cache manager or packed layouts. Separately, PP producers on the pull path are not supported yet (#52913; open PRs #53360, #43366).

<details><summary>Repro (the prefill instance fails at startup; no decode instance or request needed)</summary>

```bash
VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=2,8 vllm serve $M3 --trust-remote-code \
  --block-size 128 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}' \
  --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager --enforce-eager --pipeline-parallel-size 2 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlPushConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_buffer_device":"cuda"}'
# same failure with "kv_connector":"NixlConnector"
```

</details>

#### 4. OffloadingConnector + PP: shared mmap size mismatch (#50821)

When PP stages have different KV bytes per block (here because of `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=2,8`; a spec-decode draft on the last stage has the same effect), startup fails:

```
TimeoutError: Timed out waiting for mmap file to reach 34359738368 bytes
```

The log also shows `FileExistsError: ... /dev/shm/vllm_offload_<engine_id>.mmap`; that is the chained context of the normal joiner path, and the failure is the `TimeoutError`.

Each stage computes `worker_kv_bytes_per_block` from its own layers ([offloading/config.py#L137-L151](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f0a5f111f2/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/config.py#L137-L151)), multiplies it by the world size and sizes the region from that ([kv_offload/cpu/spec.py#L109-L120](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f0a5f111f2/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/spec.py#L109-L120)), and every stage maps the same `/dev/shm` region. The creator truncates the file to its own size while each joiner waits for its own. On a single node this is how #50821 surfaces. #50653 only unifies `num_chunks`, so the row stride and the region size still differ per stage. Which stage creates the file is a race; both runs here failed with PP1 as the creator. If the stage with the larger region total creates it, startup should succeed with overlapping layouts. That last part is inferred from the code and was not observed.

<details><summary>Repro</summary>

```bash
VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=2,8 vllm serve $M3 --trust-remote-code \
  --block-size 128 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}' \
  --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager --enable-prefix-caching --pipeline-parallel-size 2 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"block_size":128,"cpu_bytes_to_use":34359738368,"offload_prompt_only":true}}'
```

</details>

#### 5. MooncakeStoreConnector + `kv_load_failure_policy=recompute` retries a failing load forever

When store loads keep failing from block 0 (here Mooncake TCP transfers return `-800` under 8 concurrent loads), the requests never finish:

```
# instance B, repeated ~106k times in 10 min
WARNING [scheduler.py:3348] Recovered from KV load failure: 1 request(s) rescheduled (9984 tokens affected).
```

The failure rewinds `num_computed_tokens` to 0 and the request returns to WAITING. The connector lookup then reports the same hit, so the same load is retried with no cap and no backoff. #55297 fixes this for the `invalid_block_ids` path. When the model has more than one KV cache group (for example with the hybrid manager on and a sliding-window draft), load failures arrive through `failed_recving` ([`_handle_failed_recving`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/f0a5f111f2/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L3351)), which #55297 does not cover. That last point is from reading the code and was not run.

<details><summary>Repro</summary>

The `-800` failures depend on the Mooncake 0.3.13.post1 TCP limits (see below). Any load that keeps failing from block 0 triggers the same loop under `recompute`.

```bash
mooncake_master --rpc_port=50051 --rpc_address=127.0.0.1 --default_kv_lease_ttl=10000
# store.json: {"local_hostname":"127.0.0.1","metadata_server":"P2PHANDSHAKE","master_server_address":"127.0.0.1:50051","global_segment_size":"64GB","local_buffer_size":"4GB","protocol":"tcp","device_name":""}
MC_FORCE_TCP=1 python -m mooncake.mooncake_store_service --config=store.json
# client.json: {"mode":"standalone-store","metadata_server":"P2PHANDSHAKE","master_server_address":"127.0.0.1:50051","global_segment_size":0,"local_buffer_size":"2GB","protocol":"tcp","device_name":""}

# instance A (GPU 0, port 8001, lookup_rpc_port 1) and B (GPU 1, port 8002, lookup_rpc_port 2)
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 MC_FORCE_TCP=1 MOONCAKE_CONFIG_PATH=client.json vllm serve $M3 --port 8001 \
  --trust-remote-code --block-size 128 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}' \
  --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager --enable-prefix-caching \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeStoreConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_load_failure_policy":"recompute","kv_connector_extra_config":{"load_async":true,"lookup_rpc_port":1}}'
```

Send a ~10k-token greedy prompt to A, then, 0.5 s later, 8 concurrent identical requests with the same prompt to B. B's store loads fail with `-800` (`TCP lane queue-full rejection`) and the 8 requests never complete. The observed run also loaded the DSpark draft, which is not expected to matter.

</details>

#### 6. CPU KV offload + hybrid KV cache manager + DSpark: offloaded KV is never reloaded

Found with MiniMax-M3 cut to 6 layers (3 dense + 3 MSA/MoE) with `--load-format dummy` and the `nvidia/MiniMax-M3-DSpark` config, at 83773ecdf3. The check: send a 421-token prompt, call `/reset_prefix_cache?reset_external=false`, resend it and look at `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`.

| Connector | HMA on, no DSpark | HMA off + DSpark | HMA on + DSpark |
|---|---|---|---|
| OffloadingConnector (`block_size: 128` in `kv_connector_extra_config`) | reloads | reloads | startup: `AssertionError: If 'block_size' is specified in kv_connector_extra_config, there must be at least one KV cache group, and all groups must have the same block size.` |
| OffloadingConnector (no `block_size`) | not run | not run | starts; resend has `cached_tokens: 0` |
| SimpleCPUOffloadConnector (`lazy_offload: false`) | reloads | reloads | starts; resend has `cached_tokens: 0` |

The DSpark draft's sliding-window layers make the hybrid manager use KV cache groups with different block sizes (the same trigger as 2). With that layout, both CPU offload connectors fall back to recomputing the prompt. They do not fail, so the only symptom is that CPU hits are lost. I have not traced where the lookup misses.

<details><summary>Repro</summary>

```bash
# $M3_DUMMY: MiniMax-M3 config with num_hidden_layers=6 and the per-layer lists cut to [0,0,0,1,1,1]
# $DSPARK_DUMMY: nvidia/MiniMax-M3-DSpark config.json with target_layer_ids=[0..5], num_target_layers=6
VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1 vllm serve $M3_DUMMY --load-format dummy --block-size 128 \
  --language-model-only --enable-prefix-caching --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"'"$DSPARK_DUMMY"'","num_speculative_tokens":3}' \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"SimpleCPUOffloadConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use_per_rank":8589934592,"lazy_offload":false}}'
# send a ~400-token prompt, POST /reset_prefix_cache?reset_external=false, resend: cached_tokens == 0
# with --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager, or without --speculative-config, the resend is a CPU hit
```

</details>

#### 7. MSA sparse prefill workspace is not reserved by memory profiling (OOM)

`MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8`, TP4, DSpark (`num_speculative_tokens: 8`), default `--gpu-memory-utilization` (0.92), `--max-model-len 65536 --max-num-seqs 64`. With 32 concurrent BFCL chat requests the engine died within seconds of the first batch:

```
File "vllm/third_party/fmha_sm100/cute/interface.py", line 679, in _try_blackwell_sparse_prefill
    partial = torch.empty((topK, *q.shape), dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=q.device)
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1010.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 184.31 GiB of which 1001.44 MiB is free.
```

The sparse prefill allocates `partial` (`topK × q`, bf16) and `stats` per call ([MSA `interface.py#L679-L680`](https://github.com/vllm-project/MSA/blob/968061ab16cb14991a5c7d4c0e8eabf531be0dcf/python/fmha_sm100/cute/interface.py#L679-L680)). During the memory profiling run, `MiniMaxM3SparseBackend.forward` returns before any attention runs ([`sparse_attention_msa.py#L255`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/83773ecdf3/vllm/models/minimax_m3/nvidia/sparse_attention_msa.py#L255)), so this workspace is never counted, and the KV cache takes the memory it needs. The MSA warmup that does run sparse prefill comes after the KV cache is allocated. The same load without DSpark (62.6 GiB KV per GPU vs 55.0 GiB with the draft) did not OOM, and the DSpark run passed at `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85`. So DSpark only removes the headroom; it does not cause the OOM.

#### Other observations

- P/D KV dtype mismatch (fp8 prefill, bf16 decode): both instances start and `/health` is OK, but every request fails. The decode instance reports `SPLIT region 0: remote P KV block_len 131072 must equal local 262144 ...`, or `NIXL compatibility hash mismatch` with `enforce_handshake_compat=true`. Expected: fail at startup or handshake with a message that names the dtype mismatch. #60124 reports the same opaque hash error for a different mismatched field.
- Mooncake TCP transport (0.3.13.post1): 8 concurrent ~10k-token store loads overflowed the per-peer TCP queue (`TCP lane queue-full rejection`, `-800`). RDMA worked. kvcache-ai/Mooncake#3710 raises these limits; it merged after 0.3.13.post1, first ships in v0.3.14-rc1, and was not tested here.

The test harness and this report were prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code). Every failure above was reproduced on the hardware listed, except the points marked as code reading.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [ROCm][Kimi-K3] Mono MoE as a vLLM kernel (vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/mono)
body:
**Draft.** One kernel launch for a Kimi-K3 MoE layer at decode, routed experts and shared expert together, for steps
of up to 32 tokens on MI355X (gfx950). Opt-in with `VLLM_ROCM_MONO_DECODE=1`. The layout under
`vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/mono/` follows [#60397](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60397) (DeepSeek-V4.1).

**Related:** [#60683](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60683) runs Kimi-K3's decoder layers as two
persistent launches, K1 (the KDA attention block) and K2 (o_proj through the latent MoE and its all-reduces), on
speculative-verify steps of at most 8 rows, and is faster there. At its current head it needs speculative decoding:
plain decode, and any step above 8 rows, takes the stock path. This PR is one launch for the MoE's experts, for plain
and speculative steps of up to 32 rows. The two are meant to stack: #60683 for speculative steps up to 8 rows, this
launch for everything else up to 32.

## Results

`moonshotai/Kimi-K3`, TP8, one MI355X node per study, stock (vLLM nightly `81198e97`) against
the same image plus this PR. MI355X OOB serving settings, 8k input / 1k output, median TPOT in ms, one run per cell. Every request
succeeded and no server logged a memory access fault.

| Decode mode | Concurrency (rows per step) | Stock | This PR | Δ TPOT |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Plain | 1 (1) | 14.31 | 13.48 | −5.8% |
| Plain | 4 (4) | 19.22 | 16.76 | −12.8% |
| Plain | 16 (16) | 27.46 | 26.78 | −2.5% |
| Plain | 32 (32) | 36.90 | 37.06 | +0.4% |
| DSpark k = 3 | 1 (4) | 4.94 | 4.28 | −13.4% |
| DSpark k = 5 | 2 (12) | 4.35 | 4.10 | −5.7% |
| DSpark k = 7 | 2 (16) | 3.63 | 3.48 | −4.1% |
| DSpark k = 5 | 4 (24) | 5.31 | 5.29 | −0.4% |
| Plain, DCP8 | 4 (4) | 20.51 | 18.09 | −11.8% |

- Gains through 16 tokens a step, neutral at 17–32. Above 32 the launch is off, and this PR matches stock within ±1% (no
  fallback cost).
- 60k / 600 and 128k / 1k at concurrency 3–4: −6% to −8%. Both DSpark draft backends (TRITON_MLA, ROCM_AITER_MLA)
  show the same gains.
- GPQA Diamond (thinking, 16 threads so every step is on the launch): stock 0.9091, this PR 0.9091.

Measured at this PR's head (0734ac29ff). Full tables, MoE layer timings and a like-for-like comparison with #60683
above 8 tokens will follow in a companion issue.

## Rows per step: stock vs #60683 vs this PR

Median TPOT in ms, 8k input / 1k output, TP8, all three builds on one MI355X node. A step carries `concurrency` rows in
plain decode and `concurrency × (k + 1)` rows with DSpark (TRITON_MLA drafter). Bold marks the fastest build when it
beats stock by more than 1%.

| Rows per step | Decode | Stock | #60683 mono decode (at 9c6c96d8ef) | Mono MoE (this PR) |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | plain, c1 | 14.27 | **11.00 (−23%)** | 13.61 (−5%) |
| 2 | plain, c2 | 14.91 | **12.01 (−19%)** | 14.49 (−3%) |
| 4 | plain, c4 | 19.09 | **14.01 (−27%)** | 16.69 (−13%) |
| 4 | DSpark k=3, c1 | 5.16 | **3.58 (−31%)** | 4.47 (−13%) |
| 8 | plain, c8 | 20.84 | **17.59 (−16%)** | 20.19 (−3%) |
| 8 | DSpark k=3, c2 | 5.67 | **4.49 (−21%)** | 5.43 (−4%) |
| 8 | DSpark k=7, c1 | 2.87 | **2.22 (−23%)** | 2.79 (−3%) |
| 12 | plain, c12 | 25.73 | 26.04 (+1%) | **25.16 (−2%)** |
| 16 | plain, c16 | 27.05 | 27.29 (+1%) | **26.36 (−3%)** |
| 16 | DSpark k=3, c4 | 6.91 | 6.95 (+1%) | **6.64 (−4%)** |
| 16 | DSpark k=7, c2 | 3.66 | 3.68 (+1%) | **3.58 (−2%)** |
| 32 | DSpark k=3, c8 | 9.36 | 9.25 (−1%) | **9.17 (−2%)** |
| 32 | DSpark k=7, c4 | 4.61 | 4.62 (+0%) | 4.60 (−0%) |

- #60683 was measured at 9c6c96d8ef (Oct 10). That head also served plain decode, through a standalone MoE launch;
  its current head (0917105) refuses configs without speculative decoding, so its plain-decode rows would be stock.
- Up to 8 rows, #60683 is fastest (−16% to −31%). From 9 rows its launch is off, and this PR is the
  only one ahead of stock (−2% to −4% at 12–16 rows).
- These rows used this PR's 16-token build. At 32 rows its launch only took the smaller steps (requests finishing,
  fewer accepted drafts). With the cap at 32 it takes the full steps too, and is neutral against stock there
  (Results above).
- The plain-decode rows come from the same inference-testing settings as the Results. The DSpark rows are an earlier
  run on the same node with this PR's previous serving setup (fp8 KV cache, custom all-reduce), so compare builds
  within a row, not against the Results.
- A single-node rerun with this PR's head is queued: plain decode at 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 and 32 rows, and
  DSpark k = 3 at 4–32 rows.

## What it does

- **The kernel:** one persistent launch per MoE layer: top-k, expert sort, a4w4 gemm1 and gemm2 for the routed
  experts, and the bf16 shared expert, which runs in CUs that routing leaves idle. It replaces seven kernels on
  two streams. The shared expert loops over 16-row blocks (`M_MAX = 32`, one compile per 16-token bucket).
  `mono/README.md` describes the stages, tickets, hand-offs and numerics.
- **vLLM side:** `mono_decode.py` (`MonoLatentMoE`) decides which layers and steps take the launch;
  `ROCmLatentMoERunner` only dispatches to it. A step takes it on gfx950, at M ≤ 32, with AITER's a4w4 SiTUv2 MoE
  (the default) and vLLM's bf16 KimiMLP shared expert. Anything else runs the stock path unchanged.
- **AITER:** nothing vendored. gemm1 is AITER's a4w4 stage-1 body, traced with device-scope output stores; gemm2 comes
  from AITER's `compile_gemm2_a4w4_port` hook. The JIT cache key includes a digest of the package and of the AITER
  sources it traces.
- **Tests:** `tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_mono_gate.py` (CPU, which calls take the launch) and
  `test_amd_mono_moe.py` (gfx950, against `biased_grouped_topk` + `fused_moe` + KimiMLP at TP8 shapes, eager and graph
  replay, M 1–32, M 33 refused). They run in the existing MI355 Kimi-K3 step and pass on MI355X at this
  head (27 passed).

Debug tooling (layer recording, replay benchmark, fault probe) is on a separate branch,
[amd-mghanimi/vllm#13](https://github.com/amd-mghanimi/vllm/pull/13). This PR carries no debug code.

title: [Perf] Prefer DeepSelect over persistent_topk for large indexer top-k batches on SM100/SM103
body:
## Description

The sparse indexer decode top-k auto chain is `cooperative -> persistent -> per_row`. `cooperative_topk` applies only within `AUTO_COOPERATIVE_MAX_ROWS`, so anything larger goes to `persistent_topk`. For GLM-5.3-Flash with MTP k=7 at 32 seqs that is every verify batch: 256 rows, all on `persistent_topk`, which bins logits into a coarse histogram and can silently drop true top-k candidates when a trained indexer clusters its scores in one bin (#51782). The vendored DeepSelect extension handles exactly these shapes on the SM100/SM103 family and measured 191 us vs 616 us at 256 rows / 1M KV when it landed (#56464), but it stayed opt-in only.

This adds a `deep_select` branch in `_resolve_auto` between cooperative and persistent. The existing support checks (`_has_deep_select`, `_HAS_DEEP_SELECT_C`, `is_deep_select_supported`) stay, so other devices and unsupported strides/dtypes fall through to `persistent_topk` unchanged.

Measured on GLM-5.3-Flash (NVFP4), 8x B300 (SM103), TP8, FP8 KV cache, MTP k=7, 1M context, `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, seed 42, medians of 3 warm runs:

| workload (1024-in / 1024-out) | TPOT mean | TPOT p99 | TTFT median |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 concurrent | 5.40 -> 5.05 ms (-6.5%) | 8.26 -> 7.05 ms (-14.6%) | 288 -> 341 ms |
| 32 concurrent | 7.85 -> 6.89 ms (-12.2%) | 12.24 -> 12.84 ms | 1113 -> 1073 ms |
| 128K prompt, 64 out | 8.24 -> 6.82 ms (-17.2%) | 8.24 -> 6.82 ms | 502 -> 477 ms |

These are medians of 3 warm passes within one boot per arm; across reboots of the unpatched build, c8 and c32 TPOT varied by roughly 25% and 12% on this setup, so the smaller deltas are directional and the workload-level trend is the signal. Measured on GLM-5.3-Flash only; the auto choice also covers the DSA indexer path on this device family, which I have not benchmarked here.

title: [Perf] Reuse the trtllm-gen sparse MLA decode runner and preallocate its output
body:
## Description

Every sparse-MLA layer calls the FlashInfer `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla` wrapper per step with no `out=`. The wrapper re-validates inputs, constructs a fresh `TrtllmGenMlaDecodeRunner` plus `TuningConfig`, runs `AutoTuner.choose_one`, and `torch.empty`s the output (up to 33.5 MB at 4096-row batches), per layer, per step. Under `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` attention is an eager break in the piecewise sections, so prefill-mixed steps re-execute that whole Python chain once per sparse layer, about 12 times per engine step.

The runner bakes no query-shape state, so one runner per layer keyed by the KV cache (data_ptr/shape/dtype/top-k capacity) serves every batch. This launches it directly with `tactic=-1` into a per-layer bf16 output buffer sliced per call, with module-scope imports. The DCP path (`return_lse`) keeps the public wrapper because it needs per-call LSE; the HiSparse mixed-step second call gets an `out_offset` so decode and prefill slices stay disjoint before the concat. Runner construction asserts the same two hard constraints the wrapper enforces (head count, block size). Complements #60070 (the counter buffer kwarg) without overlapping it.

Measured on GLM-5.3-Flash (NVFP4), 8x B300 (SM103), TP8, FP8 KV cache, MTP k=7, 1M context, `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, seed 42, medians of 3 warm runs, patch applied alone:

| workload (1024-in / 1024-out) | TPOT mean | TPOT p99 |
|---|---|---|
| 8 concurrent | 5.40 -> 4.82 ms (-10.7%) | 8.26 -> 7.07 ms (-14.4%) |
| 32 concurrent | 7.85 -> 6.74 ms (-14.1%) | 12.24 -> 12.14 ms (-0.8%) |
| 32K prompt, 64 out | 7.96 -> 7.59 ms (-4.6%) | 8.13 -> 8.10 ms |
| 512K prompt, 64 out | 4.32 -> 4.10 ms (-5.1%) | 4.32 -> 4.10 ms |

Medians of 3 warm passes within one boot per arm; across reboots of the unpatched build, c8 and c32 TPOT varied by roughly 25% and 12% on this setup, so the smaller deltas are directional and the workload-level trend is the signal. Spec-dec acceptance rates were not separately instrumented; the win is attributed to the removed launch-path work, not to acceptance changes.

title: [Perf] Shard the GLM kpool decode indexer across the attention TP group
body:
## Description

`wq_b` is `ReplicatedLinear` and `wk` runs with TP disabled, so the GLM kpool decode scorer's inputs are bit-identical on every attention-TP rank: the paged MQA logits GEMM, the top-k, and the pool expand all run `tp_size` times per sparse layer per step, about 12 times per engine step with k=7 drafting.

This adds an opt-in row sharding behind `VLLM_GLM_KPOOL_DECODE_INDEXER_ROW_SHARD`. Rank `r` scores only requests `r::tp_size` via an `index_select` gather, builds the per-rank DeepGEMM schedule in-op, and the expanded pool ids (int32, about 2051 per row) are all-gathered and reordered locally. K-cache and tail-cache writes stay replicated, so outputs are unchanged. Every gate is host-side metadata identical on every rank, so CUDA-graph capture/replay and rank consistency hold. Verify batches at 32 or fewer requests keep the replicated path: the all-gather costs more than the GEMM it saves at that size.

Measured on GLM-5.3-Flash (NVFP4), 8x B300 (SM103), TP8, FP8 KV cache, MTP k=7, 1M context, `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, seed 42, medians of 3 warm runs, patch applied alone:

| workload (1024-in / 1024-out) | TPOT mean | TPOT p99 | TTFT median |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 concurrent | 5.40 -> 4.74 ms (-12.2%) | 8.26 -> 7.10 ms (-14.0%) | 288 -> 286 ms |
| 32 concurrent | 7.85 -> 7.44 ms (-5.2%) | 12.24 -> 13.30 ms (+8.7%) | 1113 -> 1150 ms |
| 8x 128K prompts, 64 out | 159.8 -> 170.0 ms | 162.2 -> 170.0 ms | 6.14 -> 5.27 s (-14.3%) |

Draft until the comparison at `num_requests >= tp_size` with 512K-1M context is run: that is the shape the sharding is built for, and the c32 TPOT delta above sits within run-to-run variance for that workload. The p99 cost at 32 concurrent is real.

title: [Bugfix] Gate the FA4 masked-MHA sparse prefill on prefill-query quantization, not KV cache dtype
body:
## Description

`_is_masked_mha_available` rejects the FA4 masked-MHA sparse prefill whenever the KV cache is quantized: `fa_version == 4 and not is_quantized_kv_cache(kv_cache_dtype)`. That conflates the KV cache dtype with the prefill query dtype. The masked path never reads FP8 KV as FP8: context rows go through the same `gather_and_maybe_dequant_cache` the dense path already uses, and the suffix K/V are the current step's bf16 projections. An FP8 prefill query is what the kernel cannot consume, and for NoPE-dims models like GLM-5.3-Flash it is unreachable anyway: no prefill backend supports the `(256, 0, 256)` dims for prefill query quantization, so the query is always bf16. As the gate stood, every prefill token past 2048 context rode per-token sparse MQA with topk random KV gathers, inside the regime where the measured threshold table already routes masked MHA ahead of MQA.

This gates on the actual prefill-query quantization state instead. `fp8_ds_mla` / `nvfp4_ds_mla` and the other packed byte formats stay excluded via an explicit dtype allow-list, the HiSparse routing is untouched, and with no config present the gate stays conservative-off for quantized dtypes, preserving current behavior.

| config | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.3-Flash: fp8 KV, FA4, prefill q bf16 | masked-MHA vetoed, per-token sparse MQA for all prefill past 2048 ctx | masked-MHA eligible |
| fp8 KV, prefill query quantization on + backend supports it | vetoed | vetoed (unchanged) |
| fp8_ds_mla / nvfp4_ds_mla / e5m2 / per-token-head / nvfp4 KV | vetoed | vetoed (dtype allow-list) |
| auto / f16 / bf16 KV | unchanged | unchanged |
| fa3 / non-SM100 | unavailable | unavailable |

Draft until the unlocked path is run end-to-end with an FP8 KV cache; the table above is code-verified but not yet executed.

title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Use absolute maxima for vision FP8 scaling
body:
## Overview

Use the absolute maximum when recording Q/K/V history for vision FP8 dynamic scaling. A negative outlier currently produces an undersized scale and clips during quantization: `[-8, 1]` dequantizes to `[-1, 1]` instead of `[-8, 1]`.

## Claims

- Negative values contribute their magnitude to the dynamic FP8 scale, including all-negative tensors.
- Extend the existing scale-update regression with a negative outlier in Q, all-negative K, and positive V. No new test cases or backend-selection changes.

## Validation

Tested the actual `MMEncoderAttention._quantize_qkv_fp8` path on one H20-3e (SM90), torch 2.13.0+cu130 / vLLM 0.31.0, with the affected Python module matching upstream main. The probe initializes the scale buffers directly, without constructing an unsupported cuDNN FP8 attention backend, and compares the original method with the one-line fix.

Both the aligned-head CUDA quantizer (head dimension 64) and padded-head Triton quantizer (72) produced:

| Q input | Before: dequantized Q | After: dequantized Q |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[-8, 1]` | `[-1, 1]` | `[-8, 1]` |
| `[-8, -1]` | both approximately `-1.18e-38` | `[-8, -1]` |
| `[8, 1]` | `[8, 1]` | `[8, 1]` |

K/V use the same inputs scaled by 2/4. All six fixed configurations recovered these exactly representable inputs with zero error; the positive controls also passed before the fix. The CPU reproduction independently produced the same results.

Commands run:

```bash
.venv/bin/python probe_cpu.py
/runtime-venv/bin/python /work/probe_gpu.py
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mm_encoder_attention.py \
  tests/kernels/core/test_vit_fp8_scaling.py
```

All probes and pre-commit checks passed. The probe scripts are local validation harnesses; the existing regression remains in `tests/kernels/core/test_vit_fp8_scaling.py`.

The existing pytest module is gated on supported FP8 attention hardware and was not run on H20. Validation here targets the deterministic scale calculation and real GPU quantization; no full-model quality or performance claim is made.

## Details

`Tensor.amax()` returns the largest signed value. FP8 scaling needs the largest magnitude; use `tensor.abs().amax()` before updating the existing circular history. This applies to models using the shared vision FP8 dynamic-scaling path, including DeepSeek V4.1. Static-scale loading and BF16 attention are unchanged. The added absolute-value operation stays on device and introduces no host synchronization.

Targeted searches for open PRs covering `MMEncoderAttention`/`amax`, vision FP8 scaling, and absolute-maximum fixes found no duplicate.

AI assistance was used to identify, implement, and validate this change with Codex.
