title: [ROCm][DSv4] EPLB for the AITER MegaMoE backend
body:
## Overview

DeepSeek-V4's AITER MegaMoE backend (`--moe-backend aiter_mega_moe`) rejected `--enable-eplb`. This PR hooks it into vLLM's EPLB, the same way the DeepGEMM MegaMoE path does. On DeepSeek-V4-Pro, ATOM's EPLB for the same kernels cuts the long-context prefill step by 14.6%. The last three commits are generic EPLB changes that MegaMoE EPLB needs on ROCm; each can be split out.

## Claims

- `--enable-eplb` works with `--moe-backend aiter_mega_moe`. It rebalances by permutation only (`num_redundant_experts=0`), as ATOM does.
- `EPLBConfig.max_rebalances` (new; default 0 = no limit, unchanged behaviour): stop after N rebalance points and keep the placement.
- ROCm: `torch_nccl` expert-weight transfers no longer hang RCCL.
- ROCm: the "skip rearrange" check no longer vetoes every MegaMoE rebalance.

Usage (sync EPLB; `torch_nccl` requires `use_async: false`):

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro --data-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --moe-backend aiter_mega_moe --all2all-backend mori_high_throughput \
  --enable-eplb --eplb-config '{"use_async": false, "communicator": "torch_nccl", "max_rebalances": 2}'
```

## Validation

The numbers below come from a lab branch: vLLM 77154ca6 plus this change, alongside unrelated local patches. Setup: DeepSeek-V4-Pro on 8x MI355X, TP1 x DP8 attention, EP8 AITER MegaMoE, DSpark draft. EPLB ran with window 100 / interval 200 and at most 2 rebalances. The lab counted only engine steps that contain a prefill; that counting is not part of this PR, and a larger window and interval in engine steps give a similar cadence.

Prefill probe: each of the 8 ranks prefills 8,107 new tokens at ~108K context next to 16 decoding requests:

| | EPLB off | EPLB on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| prefill step (ms, median of 6 rounds) | 1102 | 944 (-14.3%) |
| MegaMoE combine wait per step (ms, mean over ranks; worst rank) | 167 (180) | 36 (55) |
| MegaMoE stage1 / stage2 per step (ms) | 165 / 231 | 164 / 225 |
| decode step at 16 req/rank (ms) | 55.6 | 55.5 - 56.3 |

ATOM gets -14.6% on the same probe. The gain is the combine wait: the expert GEMM time per rank stays the same, but the busiest rank no longer holds every rank back.

- gsm8k (lm-eval, real speculative decoding) with EPLB on: 0.9719 / 0.9727 (two runs).
- A rebalance moves ~2.5k of each rank's 2.9k expert slots across 61 layers. The first one took 5.2-5.7 s in the probe and load runs, ~2.3 s of it RCCL connection setup, and up to ~12 s under heavier live traffic. Later ones take ~2.5 s. ATOM's migration takes 5.4 s.
- Stress test under load: 34 forced full-permutation rebalances while serving 32 concurrent requests, 0 request errors, correct greedy answers before and after.
- Unit tests (CPU): `tests/distributed/test_eplb_utils.py` (ring pairing, cap, per-layer imbalance) and `tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_aiter_mega_moe.py -m cpu_test` (weight views, remap before the runtime choice, MixtureOfExperts registration; importing it needs a ROCm build).

E2e and validation on this upstream branch are still to be added.

## Details

**MegaMoE EPLB (commit 1).**
- The AMD `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM` implements `MixtureOfExperts` over the MegaMoE layers only; other AMD MoE paths keep `num_moe_layers == 0`.
- `DeepseekV4AiterMegaMoEExperts.get_expert_weights()` returns per-expert row views of the finalized w13 / w2 weights and scales. The a16w4 shuffles are within-expert, so EPLB rewrites rows in place. MegaMoEV2 reads the weights by pointer at every launch, so CUDA graphs stay valid.
- `forward()` maps logical to physical ids with `eplb_map_to_physical_and_record` (load recording included) before the runtime choice. The fixed-slot decode runtime (#61262) and the prefill runtime therefore both dispatch physical ids. Per-expert slot capacity does not depend on placement.
- Redundant experts are rejected.
- The DSpark draft is not registered: its MoE only sees decode-sized batches, and it keeps its own static placement.

**`max_rebalances` (commit 2).** Every rebalance point blocks all EP ranks. A skipped point still pays an all-reduce, a host sync and the policy, and an applied one moves weights for seconds. When the placement only needs to adapt once (ATOM uses `ATOM_EPLB_MAX_REBALANCES=2` here), the cap stops further points; the remap stays and load recording stops.

**ROCm ring P2P order (commit 3), root cause.**
- `rearrange_expert_weights_inplace` posts a layer's sends and receives as one `batch_isend_irecv`: about 340 ops per rank here.
- With RCCL 2.27.7 on MI355X this deadlocks on some transfer plans. The trigger is a rank that sends to many peers while it also exchanges with one peer in both directions.
- It is deterministic for a given plan. A torch-only 8-GPU reproducer hangs on the same seeded plans every time, with one batch per layer and also with ATOM-style 32-expert chunks. In serving it killed the engine at the execute timeout during the first rebalance.
- The fix: on ROCm, `TorchDistNcclEplbCommunicator` runs the layer as ring batches. Batch d holds the sends to rank + d and the receives from rank - d, in the same d order on every rank, so a send and its receive meet in the same batch with one peer per direction.
- Results: 4k seeded plans in the reproducer and 4k plans through `rearrange_expert_weights_inplace` (random and default-policy plans), no hang, 0 misplaced rows, ~47 ms per layer.
- A no-op `EplbCommunicator.prepare_transfer()` hook lets the communicator create its group's communicator with a collective first, because a ring batch need not involve every rank. Other platforms keep one batch per layer.

**Per-layer skip check (commit 4).** The ROCm-only check skips a placement unless the rank-load imbalance improves by 5%. It summed each rank's load over all layers before taking max/mean, so per-layer skews on different ranks cancelled out. MegaMoE's per-layer max/mean of ~1.77 (to ~1.12 after rebalancing) read as 1.063 -> 1.118, and every rebalance was skipped. Each MoE layer waits for its busiest rank, so the check now uses the sum over layers of max over the sum over layers of mean, the same quantity `log_balancedness` reports.

**Not included / follow-ups.**
- This PR keeps the profile-time dummy rearrangement. With `torch_nccl` it all-gathers one layer of expert weights, and its load all-reduce creates the EP group's RCCL communicator, which MoRI otherwise never uses. Together that costs ~12 GiB of KV cache per rank here: 95.7 -> 83.3 GiB with EPLB on, vs 93.8 GiB in the lab with that step skipped. This can follow separately.
- `pynccl` transfers are not ring-ordered.
- No redundant experts.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to write this change, its tests and this description; the measurements come from the author's runs.

---

title: [KVOffload][P2P][CI] Add e2e PD test matrix for the P2P KV-offload tier
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Adds an end-to-end PD test matrix for the P2P KV-offload tier (`OffloadingConnector` + `TieringOffloadingSpec` + `p2p` secondary tier) and wires it into Buildkite, mirroring `nixl_integration/config_sweep_accuracy_test.sh`. Today the tier has only unit tests. The existing `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/run_accuracy_test.sh` isn't run by any CI step, and as written it can pass while proving nothing.

## Claims

- **Asserts KV actually moves.** New `test_p2p_transfer.py` sends fully unique prompts through the proxy and requires the decoders' `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits` to grow by at least half the prompts' full-block tokens. gsm8k alone passes when the decoder silently recomputes.
- **Fixes multi-prefiller routing in `p2p_connector_proxy.py`.** Every decode was pointed at the first prefiller's P2P port, so `NUM_PREFILL_INSTANCES>1` fetched from the wrong peer. `--p2p-connector-host/--p2p-connector-port` now take one value per prefiller, and the proxy uses the coordinates of the instance that ran the prefill.
- **Makes the driver usable for a matrix.** New knobs: prefiller DP (`PREFILLER_DP_SIZE`), handshake mode (`P2P_MODE=pd|p2p`), `CANONICAL_LAYOUT`, `EXPECT_TRANSFER`, `ENFORCE_EAGER`, `--attention-backend`. Robustness fixes:
  - P2P control ports are strided per instance, so the per-DP-rank ports (base + dp index) can't collide.
  - Each instance pins `VLLM_PORT` / `VLLM_DP_MASTER_PORT`.
  - Cleanup escalates TERM→KILL, also reaps orphaned `VLLM::` DP processes and stale `/dev/shm/vllm_offload_*.mmap`, and waits for ports to free.
  - Every DP rank is warmed before the accuracy run.
  - `MAX_MODEL_LEN` 512 → 2048, because gsm8k 5-shot prompts are longer.
  - `CPU_BYTES` 200 MB → 2 GiB, so the source tier doesn't evict KV before the decoder pulls it at 100 concurrent requests.
- **Adds a 16-config sweep in 4 slices with 4 Buildkite steps.**
  - Attention: dense, MoE and MLA models.
  - Cache types beyond plain attention: hybrid GDN/SSM state, sliding window, fp8 KV.
  - Deployments: both handshake modes, mixed TP, 2×2 instances, decoder-first, DP prefiller, DP-EP decoder.
- **Accuracy check for the new models.** Adds gsm8k expected values for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and gemma-3-1b-it. Without them the accuracy check was skipped.

## Validation

The full sweep ran unmodified (`config_sweep_accuracy_test.sh`, plus `DP_EP=1` and `MLA=1`) on one 4× H200 host, vLLM nightly `0.32.0rc1.dev100+g77154ca61`. **13/13 pass, and every slice exits 0.** The Llama baseline on a single plain vLLM instance (eager, block 128, max-len 2048) is 0.332 strict-match.

| Slice | Config | Model | Tokens over P2P | gsm8k (expected) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| default | TP1 → TP1, pd | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.337 (0.33) |
| default | TP1 → TP1, p2p | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.338 (0.33) |
| default | TP1 → TP2, pd, canonical | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.343 (0.33) |
| default | TP2 → TP1, p2p, canonical | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.337 (0.33) |
| default | TP1 → TP2, pd, direct layout, `EXPECT_TRANSFER=0` | Llama-3.2-1B | 0 (expected 0) | 0.331 (0.33) |
| default | 2 prefillers × 2 decoders, pd | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.339 (0.33) |
| default | TP1 → TP1, decoder-first | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.337 (0.33) |
| DP_EP | TP1 → DP-EP=2, pd | deepseek-vl2-tiny | 5120/5120 | 0.202 (0.19) |
| DP_EP | TP2 → DP-EP=2, p2p, canonical | deepseek-vl2-tiny | 5120/5120 | 0.197 (0.19) |
| DP_EP | DP=2 prefiller → TP1, pd | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.335 (0.33) |
| MLA | TP1 → TP1, pd | DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat | 5120/5120 | 0.660 (0.65) |
| MLA | TP1 → TP2, p2p, canonical | DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat | 5120/5120 | 0.656 (0.65) |
| MLA | TP2 → TP1, pd, canonical | DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat | 5120/5120 | 0.661 (0.65) |

The `FEATURES=1` slice ran later on the same hardware with a newer nightly, `0.32.0rc1.dev281+g49cb2bbf7`. **3/3 pass.**
Single-instance baselines: Qwen3.5-0.8B 0.329, Llama-3.2-1B with fp8 KV 0.337, gemma-3-1b-it 0.257.

| Slice | Config | Model | Tokens over P2P | gsm8k (expected) | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FEATURES | TP1 → TP1, p2p (hybrid GDN + attention) | Qwen3.5-0.8B | 5120/5120 | 0.334 (0.33) | 161 s |
| FEATURES | TP1 → TP1, pd (sliding window 512) | gemma-3-1b-it ¹ | 5120/5120 | 0.251 (0.25) | 153 s |
| FEATURES | TP1 → TP2, pd, canonical, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` | Llama-3.2-1B | 5120/5120 | 0.335 (0.33) | 100 s |

¹ The validation pod's HF token couldn't read the gated `google/gemma-3-1b-it` repo, so these runs used
the ungated `unsloth/gemma-3-1b-it` copy (same config: 512-token window, every 6th layer global). The
sweep keeps `google/gemma-3-1b-it`, which other CI-run tests already use.

The transfer assertion catches real recomputes. Mixed TP on the direct layout fails it (0 of 5120 tokens) while gsm8k still passes. Before this change that case went green.

```bash
bash tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/config_sweep_accuracy_test.sh
DP_EP=1 bash tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/config_sweep_accuracy_test.sh
MLA=1 bash tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/config_sweep_accuracy_test.sh
FEATURES=1 bash tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/config_sweep_accuracy_test.sh
```

`pre-commit` passes on all changed files (shellcheck, ruff, test-tethering and Buildkite key checks). The proxy routing was also checked with mocked transports (per-instance ports, DP rank offset, single-value broadcast, wrong-count rejection).

## Details

**Mixed TP needs `canonical_layout: true`.** While building the matrix we found that the default ("direct") host layout isn't byte-identical across TP sizes. A CPU chunk stores each worker's page back to back (`|W0|W1|`, `vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/spec.py`), so a TP1 chunk and a TP2 chunk hold the same KV in a different byte order.

- **Default model runner (MRV2):** the parallelism-agnostic exemption is disabled (`offloading/config.py`, `not use_v2_model_runner`). TP-mismatched peers fail the config-fingerprint check and the decoder recomputes, which is safe.
- **`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`:** the exemption applies, TP1 and TP2 share a namespace, every block transfers, and the decoder decodes garbage (gsm8k 0.0 to 0.005). The FS tier reproduces it too: a TP1 engine writes on MRV1 and a TP2 engine reads back gibberish. So it's the shared layout claim, not the P2P data plane.
- **This PR doesn't change that code.** The mixed-TP configs run with `CANONICAL_LAYOUT=1`, which is correct on both runners. One direct-layout config pins the current safe fallback (`EXPECT_TRANSFER=0`); it should flip to a transfer check once the direct layout is portable. The direct-layout claim will be reported separately. Related: #61822 documents `canonical_layout`.
- **MLA:** `deepseek-vl2-tiny` (used by the NIXL DP_EP configs) has `use_mla: false`, so it covers MoE/EP only. The MLA slice uses DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat. Without canonical layout, MLA mixed TP is refused on both runners: `replicated_layout` is only set for TP > 1, so TP1 and TP2 hash differently.

**Which cache types are covered, and why.** The `FEATURES` step covers the cache types whose offload path differs from plain attention:
- Hybrid: several KV groups, Mamba state pages, align-mode hit rounding.
- Sliding window: window-limited lookup and dropping out-of-window blocks; the 512-token window is shorter than the prompts.
- fp8 KV: different page bytes and dtype in the fingerprint.

Two cache types are deliberately left out:
- **MLA + DSA indexer:** the indexer is a plain `MLAAttentionSpec`, so it follows the MLA path already covered. There's no small checkpoint, and the sparse-MLA kernels need SM90+.
- **DeepSeek-V4 compressed attention:** it needs ≥4 large GPUs and is already covered by `kv-offload-large` and the optional DSv4 PD step.

The new step runs in parallel with the others, so wall-clock CI time doesn't grow: three configs, about 7 minutes in total on H200.

**CI resources.**
- The default, DP_EP and FEATURES steps target `l4` × 4 and the MLA step `h100` × 4. MLA is marked `optional` because V2-Lite (16B, ~31 GB bf16) doesn't fit an L4 at TP1.
- Validation ran on H200 only. L4 runtime is unmeasured. The default, DP_EP and MLA steps use the NIXL steps' 55-minute timeout with up to 7 configs; the FEATURES step uses 40 minutes for 3 configs.
- No AMD mirror in this PR.

**Not duplicating existing work.** Searching open PRs for the P2P accuracy driver, `p2p_connector_proxy`, tiering P2P CI and canonical-layout mixed TP finds nothing overlapping. Open P2P PRs (#61667, #60374, #60257) touch the tier's runtime, not its e2e tests.

title: [Bug][HiSparse] Shutdown stalls ~90s: every TP rank unpins the full shared host pool and EngineCore blocks on dying workers
body:
### Summary

Shutting down a HiSparse server (TP8, `--shutdown-timeout 90`) stalls for about 90s. The API server eventually force-kills EngineCore. The cause is the HiSparse pinned host pool: every worker has to unpin it, and EngineCore can't exit until all workers have done so.

```
21:39:42 [core.py:1666] EngineCore: request processing complete; starting resource teardown
21:39:42 [multiproc_executor.py:479] Executor: waiting for worker exit count=8
21:39:47 [multiproc_executor.py:491] Executor: workers still running after grace period; sending SIGTERM count=8
21:39:51 [multiproc_executor.py:501] Executor: workers still running after SIGTERM; sending SIGKILL count=8
            <-- 80s with no logs -->
21:41:12 [utils.py:648] Process manager: force killing remaining processes count=1
21:41:12 [system_utils.py:225] force killing sub process VLLM::Worker_DP pid 159   (x8, still alive)
```

Requests drain immediately. All of the time is spent waiting for the worker processes to die.

### Root cause

1. **Every TP rank pins the entire shared host region.** `allocate_hisparse_host_pools` (`vllm/v1/hisparse/runtime.py`) calls `cudaHostRegister` on the whole shared `/dev/shm` mmap in every rank. Each rank must therefore unpin all of it on exit, and the ranks contend with each other while doing so.
2. **The 5s worker grace period is far too short.** `VLLM_WORKER_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=5` expires long before `release_pinned_state()` finishes, so shutdown always falls through to SIGTERM and then SIGKILL. The `HiSparse: unpinned X GiB ...` log line never appears.
3. **SIGKILL doesn't help.** The kernel still has to unpin every page during process exit, and this is *slower* than a graceful `cudaHostUnregister`.
4. **EngineCore blocks on the dying workers with no timeout.** `_ensure_worker_termination` returns right after `p.kill()`. The workers are `daemon=True`, so Python's multiprocessing atexit handler (`_exit_function`) joins them with no timeout. EngineCore can't exit until the kernel finishes tearing them down, which ends in the API server's force-kill. The stall is invisible because the EngineCore teardown logs are debug-level.

### Isolated reproduction (no vLLM server)

The script below copies HiSparse's shared-pool setup: N spawned daemon processes each `mmap` one `/dev/shm` file and `cudaHostRegister` all of it. It then times either graceful unregister or SIGKILL. I ran it on H100s with 7 processes on 7 GPUs:

| Pool | register (per proc) | graceful unregister (per proc) | all procs gone after SIGKILL |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 GiB | 3.6–4.3s | 0.4–1.1s | 3.6s |
| 64 GiB | 17s | – | ~20s |
| 128 GiB | ~30.5s | 2.9 → 13.5s (one after another) | 21.7s (vs 16.6s graceful) |

In a variant where the parent sends SIGKILL and then returns from `main` **without** calling `join()`, the parent process still took another **20s** to exit at 64 GiB. That is the multiprocessing atexit join on daemon children.

At 128 GiB, the slowest graceful unregister already takes 13.5s, well past the 5s grace period. Extrapolating these timings, the ~80s stall in the log above corresponds to a pool of a few hundred GiB per DP rank. The `host_pool_gib` in the original run hasn't been confirmed yet.

<details><summary>pin_teardown.py</summary>

```python
"""Mimic HiSparse shared host pool: N procs mmap one /dev/shm file and
cudaHostRegister it. Then time graceful unregister vs SIGKILL exit."""
import mmap
import multiprocessing as mp
import os
import signal
import sys
import time

PATH = "/dev/shm/claude_pin_teardown.mmap"


def worker(rank, gpu, size, mode, ready, go):
    import torch

    torch.cuda.set_device(gpu)
    fd = os.open(PATH, os.O_RDWR)
    m = mmap.mmap(fd, size, mmap.MAP_SHARED, mmap.PROT_READ | mmap.PROT_WRITE)
    t = torch.frombuffer(m, dtype=torch.int8)
    cudart = torch.cuda.cudart()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    err = cudart.cudaHostRegister(t.data_ptr(), t.nbytes, 0)
    assert err.value == 0, err
    reg = time.perf_counter() - t0
    ready.put((rank, reg))
    go.wait()
    if mode == "graceful":
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        err = cudart.cudaHostUnregister(t.data_ptr())
        ready.put((rank, time.perf_counter() - t0))
    else:
        time.sleep(10_000)


def main():
    gib, nproc, mode = float(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]
    gpus = [int(g) for g in sys.argv[4].split(",")]
    size = int(gib * 2**30) // mmap.PAGESIZE * mmap.PAGESIZE
    fd = os.open(PATH, os.O_CREAT | os.O_RDWR, 0o600)
    os.ftruncate(fd, size)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    m = mmap.mmap(fd, size)
    for off in range(0, size, 1 << 30):  # populate pages
        m[off : off + (1 << 30)] = b"\0" * min(1 << 30, size - off)
    print(f"populate {gib} GiB: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s", flush=True)

    ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")
    ready, go = ctx.Queue(), ctx.Event()
    procs = [
        ctx.Process(target=worker, args=(r, gpus[r % len(gpus)], size, mode, ready, go),
                    daemon=True)
        for r in range(nproc)
    ]
    for p in procs:
        p.start()
    regs = [ready.get() for _ in procs]
    print("register s:", sorted(round(r, 1) for _, r in regs), flush=True)

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    if mode == "graceful":
        go.set()
        unregs = [ready.get() for _ in procs]
        print("unregister s:", sorted(round(r, 1) for _, r in unregs), flush=True)
        for p in procs:
            p.kill()
    else:
        for p in procs:
            os.kill(p.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
        for p in procs:
            print(f"  pid {p.pid} state={open(f'/proc/{p.pid}/stat').read().split()[2]}",
                  flush=True)
    if mode == "killexit":
        print(f"killexit: parent returning from main at {time.time():.1f}", flush=True)
        os.unlink(PATH)
        return
    for p in procs:
        p.join()
    print(f"{mode}: all procs gone after {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s", flush=True)
    m.close()
    os.close(fd)
    os.unlink(PATH)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Usage: `python pin_teardown.py <GiB> <nproc> {graceful|kill|killexit} <gpu,list>`
</details>

### Possible fixes

- **Short term:** when HiSparse is enabled, scale the worker grace period with the pinned pool size (measured at roughly 0.1–0.15 s/GiB with 7 ranks). Workers then take the faster graceful path and log the unpin time. Also bound and log the post-SIGKILL wait in the executor, so the stall is visible instead of a silent hang that ends in a force-kill.
- **Real fix:** pin the shared region once and share it across local TP ranks (for example, cuMem host allocation plus IPC handles), instead of having every rank run `cudaHostRegister` on the whole region. This cuts both teardown and startup registration (~30s at 128 GiB) by roughly the TP size.

### Related

- #61668: reuses the pinned host pool after graph profiling (startup side, different issue)
- #54553: bounds EngineCore shutdown on fatal error (different trigger, same "waiting on wedged workers" symptom)

---
This issue was investigated with AI assistance (Claude Code). The code-path analysis and the reproduction numbers above come from that investigation, run on the reporter's machine.

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash specialized decode on GB300
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

This PR adds an NVIDIA specialized decode for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300, for the small decode batches that agentic serving runs. It supports:
- one GB300 tray at TP4;
- DSpark speculative decoding with 5 draft tokens;
- FULL-graph decode steps of up to 384 rows (64 requests × 6 tokens). Prefill, mixed batches and larger batches fall back to the stock forward.

It is opt-in via `--additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}'`, the same switch as #61867. With the default (`auto`), the model runs exactly as on upstream `main`. The model changes are all under `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/`; outside it, the PR only adds tests and a CI step.

The integration follows #61867: the model owns a decode executor that takes over FULL-graph decode steps. The stacked follow-up #61869 puts the DSpark draft model on the same executor. Both follow the RFC #59665 fast-track process. Related: #57448 (DeepSeek-V4.1 tracking), #59725 (Cake kernels).

## Claims

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray with DSpark, the same build with the switch on and off:
- Decode step (one speculative step, including the draft): **18.3% faster at batch 1** (5,355 → 4,375 µs), 13.7% at batch 8 and 11.3% at batch 32.
- InferenceX AgentX traces: **P90 interactivity up 16–24%** at every concurrency from 1 to 64, with throughput per GPU up 1–6% and TTFT unchanged.
- GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond, AIME25 and RULER NIAH stay within one point of the switch-off model, and the DSpark acceptance length does not change.

## Validation

### Correctness

The reference is the same build with the switch off. GPQA-Diamond and AIME25 use reasoning effort high and temperature 0.6.

| Task | Samples | Switch off | Switch on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GSM8K, strict match (c1 / c8 / c32) | 1,319 per cell | 0.973 / 0.972 / 0.973 | 0.974 / 0.970 / 0.975 |
| GPQA-Diamond | 198 × 16 | 0.796 | 0.788 |
| AIME25 | 30 × 16 | 0.994 | 0.990 |
| RULER NIAH single / multikey-2 / multikey-3, 32K / 128K / 256K (c1 and c8) | | 1.0 in every cell | 1.0 in every cell |
| DSpark acceptance length on GSM8K (c1 / c8 / c32) | | 3.93 / 3.95 / 3.93 | 3.93 / 3.96 / 3.97 |

- **GPQA-Diamond.** Paired by question over the 16 repeats, on − off is −0.79 ± 0.56 points (bootstrap 95% interval −2.2 to +0.6). The first eight repeats gave −1.6 points, mostly answers that ran past the 16,384-token limit without a final answer; the second eight gave +0.06.
- **Later revisions.** GSM8K at c8 was rerun after each later change, with its mean acceptance length: 0.972 and 3.92 on `main` `429a3da` (FlashInfer 0.7.1), 0.975 and 3.95 on `011fa68c`, 0.971 and 3.97 after the move into the executor, 0.976 and 3.96 with the CuTe DSL kernels, 0.972 and 3.99 after the rebase onto `main` `03ee2e13` (FlashInfer 0.7.2), and 0.975 and 3.92 after the rebase onto `main` `aa3564ce`. That rebase also changed compiled code in `main` (DeepGEMM's build, the top-k kernels), so the decode step was timed across it on one GB300 tray (old `main` wheel and branch against new, blocks old-new-new-old, two repeats each): B1 +0.1%, B8 +0.8%, B32 +0.4%, all within noise (|t| < 2), so the performance numbers in this description still stand. After each rebase the kernel, numerics and layers tests pass again (run at the tip of #61869, which contains this PR).

The tests check each kernel against the stock op it replaces, the TP4 collectives bitwise against the unfused path, and a five-layer model served with the switch on and off:

<details><summary>Tests, sanitizers and CI</summary>

```bash
# One SM100-family GPU: each kernel against the stock op it replaces
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_kernels.py -v
# Four GPUs: TP4 collectives bitwise against the unfused reference, and graph replays
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_numerics.py -v
.venv/bin/python -m tests.models.deepseek_v41.nvidia.specialized_decode.test_numerics --replays 100000  # race stress
# Four GB300: five-layer model on random weights at TP4 with DSpark, switch on vs off
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_layers.py -v
```

| Check | What it covers | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kernel tests | Each kernel against the stock op it replaces, at every supported row count, eagerly and replayed from a CUDA graph | 90 passed |
| Numerics (TP4) | The fused collectives bitwise against the unfused reference over 1,000 graph replays; the indexer top-k equal up to boundary ties | Passed |
| Race stress | 100,000 graph replays: collectives bitwise, top-k sets equal throughout | Passed before the restructure, which changed no kernel |
| Layers test (4× GB300) | A five-layer model at TP4 with DSpark, served with the switch on and off; the activations of every layer are compared within tolerance. The test checks which paths each layer took, that the executor ran on the switch-on steps and that it never ran with the switch off | Passed |
| compute-sanitizer (CUDA 13.0.2) over the kernel tests | memcheck, synccheck, racecheck | memcheck: no errors. synccheck: no report in this PR's kernels. Kernels that are not this PR's are left uninstrumented, because synccheck aborts every kernel it reports: FlashInfer's TRT-LLM-gen kernels and CuTe DSL dense GEMMs, and vLLM's `LLBf16SplitK`, which this PR calls ("Divergent thread(s) in block"). racecheck: FlashInfer's CuTe DSL split-K `mm_bf16`, which the LM head calls, reports shared-memory hazards; upstream calls the same kernel from its BF16 linear backend. No other test reports a hazard: cooperative top-k, the sparse-MLA KV counters, the MXFP8 projections, the index key store, Engram, the side-stream table builds and the metadata graphs are racecheck-clean. Those were run over the DSpark PR's kernel tests, which include all of this PR's, before the restructure, which changed none of them. The CuTe DSL routed-expert kernels were checked with all three tools at this revision: no memcheck error, no synccheck report and no race hazard. |
| pre-commit | All hooks | Passes on every changed file |

**CI.** A new 4×B200 step runs the kernel, numerics and layers tests. Like the other 4×B200 steps, it is optional, so it runs nightly rather than on every PR. No CI agent has four GB300, so the layers test skips there; it and the end-to-end results were run on GB300 outside CI.

</details>

### Performance

All runs use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray (TP4) with DSpark (5 draft tokens), Model Runner V2 and FULL CUDA graphs for decode. The switch-off arm is upstream `main` at the same base. These numbers were measured before the code moved into the executor and before the routed-expert kernels were ported to CuTe DSL; both changes were then compared with the revision before them and moved the decode step by at most 1.3% (see "Since these measurements" below).

AgentX throughput per GPU against P90 interactivity, upstream (switch off) and this PR (switch on), with the InferenceX DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash GB300 vLLM curve for reference:

![AgentX throughput against interactivity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yaoyaoding/vllm/75c4f9b4c668f368921bf802ff83875b83d7f337/agentx_frontier_main.svg)

**Decode step.** The speculative step with its draft, timed from the client over long-context decodes, in ABBA blocks on one tray (one server per block), on `main` `429a3da` (FlashInfer 0.7.1). Every switch-on block beats every switch-off block.

| Batch | Switch off (µs) | Switch on (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 5,355 | 4,375 | −18.3% |
| 8 | 10,598 | 9,151 | −13.7% |
| 32 | 17,483 | 15,516 | −11.3% |

On the older base `2c74fd1`, the same ABBA gave −20.5%, −17.4% and −13.1%. The switch-on step is the same there (4,371 µs at batch 1); `main` has since made the switch-off step faster.

**AgentX.** The InferenceX AgentX trace corpus for 3,600 s per concurrency, upstream `main` `2c74fd1` against this PR on that base. Each cell reads switch off → switch on.

| Conc | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) | Change | Total tok/s/GPU | TPOT p50 (ms) | TTFT p50 (s) | E2E p50 (s) | Requests |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 655.2 → 811.3 | +23.8% | 7,402 → 7,861 (+6.2%) | 1.46 → 1.14 | 0.81 → 0.93 | 2.1 → 2.0 | 326 → 341 |
| 4 | 557.7 → 681.7 | +22.2% | 9,590 → 10,055 (+4.9%) | 1.50 → 1.17 | 0.36 → 0.43 | 1.2 → 1.1 | 735 → 759 |
| 8 | 478.3 → 560.9 | +17.3% | 16,443 → 16,985 (+3.3%) | 1.52 → 1.27 | 0.37 → 0.39 | 1.2 → 1.2 | 1,431 → 1,449 |
| 16 | 365.5 → 452.6 | +23.8% | 29,444 → 29,727 (+1.0%) | 1.95 → 1.54 | 0.37 → 0.37 | 1.3 → 1.1 | 2,720 → 2,737 |
| 32 | 256.8 → 297.0 | +15.7% | 61,732 → 62,969 (+2.0%) | 2.68 → 2.03 | 0.72 → 0.84 | 2.3 → 2.2 | 4,867 → 4,951 |
| 64 | 175.8 → 211.5 | +20.3% | 100,638 → 101,811 (+1.2%) | 4.30 → 3.53 | 4.90 → 5.55 | 8.3 → 8.6 | 10,410 → 10,463 |

The TTFT column compares two trays, and the difference is the trays', not this PR's; a same-tray run shows TTFT unchanged:

<details><summary>TTFT on one tray</summary>

Each arm in the table above ran on its own tray. AgentX TTFT is mostly the API server's single-threaded work before the engine sees the request: chat-template rendering and tokenization of the whole conversation. Its speed differs between trays and over time by up to 15% (2.3–3.3 s of API-server CPU per million prompt tokens). aiperf's per-request `request_ack_ns` separates that work from the engine, and the cross-tray TTFT differences above are all in it; the engine part is equal. This PR changes only worker-side code.

To take the tray out of the comparison, three AgentX blocks ran on one tray, one server each, in the order upstream → this PR → upstream, at c4 for 1,200 s each:

| Block | TTFT p50 / p90 (s) | API-server CPU per M prompt tokens (s) | TPOT p50 (ms) | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Upstream | 0.229 / 1.179 | 2.72 | 1.46 | 545.2 |
| This PR | 0.233 / 1.157 | 2.69 | 1.13 | 702.6 |
| Upstream | 0.224 / 1.177 | 2.73 | 1.46 | 553.8 |

Paired over the same 272 requests, this PR's TTFT is 2.5 and 3.2 ms below the two upstream blocks. The two upstream blocks differ from each other by 0.6 ms.

</details>

<details><summary>Since these measurements: the executor restructure, the CuTe DSL port, and the switch-off check</summary>

**Restructure.** Following #61867, the paths moved from the stock layers into the executor, with no kernel change. Both revisions were measured with the switch on, on `main` `d6f0b7a4`, on one tray with one server each (each value the mean of two blocks):

| Batch | Before (µs) | Executor (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,344 | 4,347 | +0.1% |
| 8 | 9,061 | 9,096 | +0.4% |
| 32 | 15,545 | 15,464 | −0.5% |

On AgentX at c16 (two 1,200 s runs per revision, same tray), P90 interactivity is 405.9 before and 399.4 tok/s/user with the executor, and total throughput 20,924 and 20,957 tok/s/GPU. Runs of the same revision differ by up to 3% in P90 interactivity, so neither metric moves beyond run-to-run noise.

**CuTe DSL kernels.** The routed-expert front, route and GEMM kernels were first written in CUDA and compiled with NVRTC at run time. They are now CuTe DSL kernels with the same schedule and arithmetic, and their outputs are bitwise those of the CUDA versions. Kernel time (CUPTI, cold L2, median, µs), CUDA → CuTe DSL:

| Kernel | 1 row | 6 rows | 8 rows |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Front | 3.46 → 3.04 | 4.51 → 4.06 | 5.06 → 4.64 |
| Route | 2.32 → 2.18 | 2.18 → 1.95 | 2.37 → 2.30 |
| GEMM1 | 10.06 → 9.76 | 18.62 → 17.60 | 18.91 → 17.76 |
| GEMM2 | 7.30 → 6.24 | 11.23 → 10.37 | 11.49 → 10.62 |

The decode step with the CUDA and the CuTe DSL kernels, in the same-tray ABBA (switch on in both, each value the mean of two blocks):

| Batch | CUDA (µs) | CuTe DSL (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,356 | 4,298 | −1.3% |
| 8 | 9,113 | 9,178 | +0.7% |
| 32 | 15,483 | 15,430 | −0.3% |

Both CuTe DSL blocks are faster at batch 1. These kernels take up to 8 rows, so at batch 8 and 32 (48 and 192 rows per step with DSpark) both arms run the same code, and the differences are block-to-block spread: the two CUDA blocks differ by 0.8% at batch 8.

**Switch off.** With the switch off, this branch matches upstream at the base (measured against `2c74fd1`): the decode step stays within ±0.5% at batch 1 and 32 and is 1.3–1.8% faster at batch 8 (two same-tray ABBA halves); GSM8K at c8 is 0.971 (upstream 0.972); AgentX c1 gives P90 interactivity 657.2 against upstream's 655.2, with TPOT p50 1.46 ms in both.

</details>

## Details

### Where the time goes

Agentic workloads such as AgentX send long multi-turn conversations (median 350K tokens of context, almost all prefix-cached) and wait for each reply before sending the next turn. Each server therefore decodes only 1 to 64 requests at a time, and users see the time per output token.

At batch 1, stock vLLM's speculative step takes about 5.4 ms: one target forward that verifies six tokens, plus the DSpark draft. There is no single hotspot.

- **GPU.** A step runs about 1,600 kernels, most of them a few microseconds long. One target layer without an indexer is a serial chain of about 105 µs: about 50 µs of attention (quantize, `wq_a`/`wkv`, norm-quant, `wq_b`, KV insert, index build, `q_lens` and counter fixes, FMHA, `wo`, publish, all-reduce) and about 53 µs of MoE (front 14, GEMM1 19, GEMM2 12, finalize and all-reduce 6). The GEMMs see 1 to 48 rows but run kernels tuned for larger batches; the all-reduce + mHC at each of the 80 sublayer boundaries is fused only up to 16 rows; and layers with the sparse-attention indexer add their own chain of small kernels (logits, top-k and index tables).
- **Host.** The host loop is busy about 4.95 ms of the 5.37 ms step, and about 2.2 ms of that builds attention metadata for the target's and the draft's KV-cache groups. A GPU-only speed-up beyond about 0.4 ms would just expose the host.

So the executor removes kernels and launch gaps, uses kernels sized for 1 to 8 rows, moves independent work onto side streams, and takes host work out of the step loop.

### What changed

Each row is one optimization and the saving we measured when it was added, as a batch-1 decode-step ABBA on one tray unless a batch is named. They were measured one at a time on a development branch, so they do not add up exactly to the end-to-end figure. The full list of paths and their gates is in `nvidia/specialized_decode/AGENTS.md`.

| Optimization | Why | Saving when added |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fused all-reduce + mHC** | | |
| One fused Lamport all-reduce + mHC kernel at every sublayer boundary up to 384 rows (stock: 16). The next layer's mHC coefficients are computed on a side stream up to 48 rows. | Above 16 rows, the stock path runs a separate all-reduce, mHC and copies at each boundary. | −11.4% at batch 8 (48-row cap); −4.5% at batch 32 (384-row cap) |
| The fused kernel also writes the next attention input as MXFP8. | That removes a separate quantize kernel per layer. | −54 µs |
| `wo_b`'s GEMM epilogue stores straight into the fused kernel's mailbox. | That removes a copy kernel; the fused kernel then only collects. | −41 µs |
| The MoE finalize is deferred into the fused kernel at the Engram and final boundaries too, in a residual-only variant. | These boundaries previously ran the finalize and all-reduce separately. | −36 µs |
| The aux hidden-state means for DSpark are computed on the mHC side stream. | They were on the critical path. | −23 µs |
| **GEMMs for 1–8 rows** | | |
| Routed experts: one fused front kernel (routing, MXFP8 quantization, permutation) and two `tcgen05` GEMM kernels, all in CuTe DSL. The top-k reduction is left to the next boundary's fused kernel. | FlashInfer's TRT-LLM-gen MoE path is tuned for larger M and launches more kernels. | −192 µs (GEMMs), −114 µs (front and finalize) |
| `fused_wqa_wkv`, `wq_b` and `wo_b` on FlashInfer's low-latency CuTe DSL MXFP8 GEMM, with tactics pinned per shape. | The stock MXFP8 GEMM is a persistent kernel sized for larger batches. Pinning keeps the fastest measured tactic per shape instead of the autotuner's pick. | −53 µs, then −62 µs from pinning |
| Compressor, indexer-weight and indexer `wk` projections on vLLM's low-batch BF16 split-K GEMM. The index key store reads `wk`'s FP32 output. | At 1–8 rows these skinny GEMMs give cuBLAS few output tiles; split-K spreads the long K over the SMs. | −60 µs |
| LM head on FlashInfer's CuTe DSL BF16 GEMM, and logits gathered with the custom all-gather. | The stock path uses cuBLAS plus an NCCL all-gather. | −15 µs, −27 µs |
| **Sparse-attention indexer and attention** | | |
| Compressed layers that share an index source reuse one sparse-index table. Sparse-MLA decode launches on a KV-counter buffer that is zeroed once. | Each layer rebuilt the same table and zeroed counters before every launch. | −207 µs (1,578 → 1,486 kernels per step) |
| The tables of every KV-cache group are built once per key, on a side stream. | Each group rebuilt its tables serially. | −103 µs |
| Candidate blocks are selected with `cooperative_topk` over the valid columns. | The stock top-k scans the padded width. | −86 µs |
| Indexer query, compressor and index-key work, and candidate expansion with its MQA-logits schedule, run on side streams. Each joins at its first reader. | They are independent of the attention chain until then. | −50 µs, −33 µs |
| Dense indexer rows are sharded over the TP ranks and all-gathered, on pure-decode steps of at least 8 requests. | The indexer is replicated on every rank, and its cost grows with batch and context. | −1.9% at batch 8, −7.6% at batch 32 |
| **Host and launch overhead** | | |
| Attention-metadata builds are recorded into CUDA graphs at capture, one per decode batch shape and KV-cache group, and replayed. | These Python and Triton builds were about 2 ms of the host loop. | −86 µs, then −27 µs |
| Each Engram layer's KV projection chain (table-row lookup, all-gather, MXFP8 quantize, `wkv` GEMM) runs ahead of the layer on the Engram prefetch stream. | It reads only table rows looked up from the token IDs, so it need not wait for the layer's input. Each Engram layer's main-stream span drops from 70 to 6 µs. | −90 µs |
| Decode steps skip the per-request replay-start upload when the device already holds zeros. | Decode steps only ever upload zeros. | −24 µs |

### vLLM integration

As in #61867, the model owns a decode executor (`specialized_decode/runtime/decode.py`). With the switch on, the model returns a model state subclass (`specialized_decode/runtime/model_state.py`) that builds the executor once the weights are loaded, then tunes and compiles its kernels before memory profiling. For each forward, the model asks the executor for a step (`plan()`). Only FULL-graph captures of pure decode steps of up to 384 rows get one. The backbone runs its embedding and Engram hashing as usual, then hands its decoder layers to the step (`run()`). Every other forward runs the stock layers, which the executor does not modify.

| Package (`nvidia/specialized_decode/`) | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `__init__.py` | The opt-in, and `unsupported()`, which lists every requirement the deployment misses |
| `runtime/` | The executor and its per-step gates, the model state, warm-up, attention-metadata CUDA graphs |
| `boundary/` | The mHC between sublayers on the fused all-reduce + mHC kernel, and the publishing `wo_b` GEMM |
| `attention/` | Low-batch MXFP8 and BF16 projections, the row-sharded indexer, candidate overlap, shared sparse-index tables and the sparse-MLA decode |
| `moe/` | The MoE step with a deferred finalize, and the low-batch routed-expert kernels in CuTe DSL |
| `engram/` | The Engram KV projection ahead of the decoder layers |
| `logits/` | The low-batch LM head and the logits gather |

**Scope.** The switch is validated on one deployment:
- GB300 (SM103), MRV2, TP=4, with no PP, DP, EP or CP and no micro-batching;
- DSpark without adaptive verification;
- `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41` with an fp8 KV cache and the MXFP4 indexer with sparse logits;
- FULL graphs for decode only;
- no `torch.compile` of the model (the executor runs inside the forward), and no sleep mode (the routed-expert GEMMs and the publishing `wo_b` bind weight addresses);
- DeepGEMM and NVLink multicast;
- no LoRA, KV transfer or batch invariance.

Any other deployment raises at start-up on every TP rank, listing every missing requirement. Eligibility is combined across ranks with a MIN all-reduce, so ranks always agree. We made it an opt-in because the set is validated end to end on this one deployment; within it, each path still dispatches at run time on host state that every rank shares, as #59665 asks. It can become the default on that deployment in a follow-up.

**Rank lockstep.** The paths contain cross-rank collectives, so a rank that diverged would hang rather than fall back. Every per-step gate therefore reads only host state that all TP ranks share: row and request counts, and the graph mode. Nothing is read back from the GPU in steady state. For example, the row-sharded indexer runs only on even row slices, because DeepGEMM's paged MQA logits need 8-byte-aligned indices on every rank.

**With the switch off.** Inside `nvidia/`, the shared files take small seams with the same behavior:
- `model.py`: the backbone hands its decoder layers to the executor's step when it gets one, and the model picks the model state class;
- `model_state.py`: the replay-start upload and the attention-metadata build become methods, which the executor's model state overrides;
- `vl_model.py`: takes the model state class from the language model;
- `ops/o_proj.py`: a `wo_b_proj` keyword for the publishing `wo_b`;
- `ops/cute_dsl/all_reduce_mhc.py`: the fused all-reduce + mHC source is parameterized by its row count and variants, and built at 16 rows as before when the switch is off.

**FlashInfer version.** Three paths use FlashInfer internals: the publishing `wo_b` GEMM, the fused kernel's MXFP8 layer input, and the pinned MXFP8 GEMM tactics. They run only on `flashinfer-python==0.7.2`, the version `main` pins; the internals they use are unchanged from 0.7.1, where they were first checked. On any other version, each warns once and takes the stock path, so a FlashInfer bump should recheck them.

---

title: [Perf][Spec Decode][DSv4.1] DSpark draft on the specialized decode, with a fused Markov loop and a post-forward CUDA graph
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

This is the DSpark half of the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash specialized decode on GB300 (#61868). With `decode_backend` set to `latency_specialized`, it:
- gives the DSpark draft model a decode executor of its own, on the target executor's kernels and streams;
- fuses the Markov sampling loop, and shards it by vocabulary over the TP ranks at small batches;
- captures the work between the target forward and the draft forward (sampling, the request-state update and the draft input preparation) in a CUDA graph.

With the switch off, the only shared change is that DFlash-family drafters prepare all their KV-cache groups in one launch, with the same outputs.

**Depends on #61868** and is stacked on it. Until that lands, this branch also contains its commits; only the last commit, the DSpark changes, is under review here.

## Claims

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray with DSpark, the switch on in both arms, this PR against #61868:
- Decode step: **another 6.4% faster at batch 1** (4,354 → 4,075 µs), 4.3% at batch 8 and 1.9% at batch 32. Together with #61868, the batch-1 step is about 24% faster than with the switch off.
- InferenceX AgentX traces: P90 interactivity up another 5–10% at concurrency 1 to 32. At concurrency 64, turns finish sooner, so the closed loop admits more requests: throughput per GPU rises 15% and TTFT p50 falls from 5.55 to 1.46 s, while P90 interactivity drops 12% at the larger batch.
- Accuracy and the DSpark acceptance length are unchanged.

## Validation

### Correctness

GPQA-Diamond uses reasoning effort high and temperature 0.6.

| Task | Samples | Switch off (upstream base) | #61868 | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GSM8K, strict match (c1 / c8 / c32) | 1,319 per cell | 0.973 / 0.972 / 0.973 | 0.974 / 0.970 / 0.975 | 0.973 / 0.972 / 0.976 |
| GPQA-Diamond | 198 × 16 (this PR: × 8) | 0.796 | 0.788 | 0.791 |
| RULER NIAH single / multikey-2 / multikey-3, 32K / 128K / 256K (c1 and c8) | | 1.0 in every cell | 1.0 in every cell | 1.0 in every cell |
| DSpark acceptance length on GSM8K (c1 / c8 / c32) | | 3.93 / 3.95 / 3.93 | 3.93 / 3.96 / 3.97 | 3.95 / 3.96 / 3.95 |

GSM8K at c8 was rerun after each later change, with its mean acceptance length:

| Revision | #61868 | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` `429a3da` (FlashInfer 0.7.1) | 0.972, 3.92 | 0.973, 3.95 |
| `main` `011fa68c` | 0.975, 3.95 | 0.972, 3.90; repeated: 0.974, 3.96 |
| Executor restructure, `main` `d6f0b7a4` | 0.971, 3.97 | 0.973, 3.95 |
| CuTe DSL kernels | 0.976, 3.96 | 0.973, 3.94 |
| Rebased onto `main` `03ee2e13` (FlashInfer 0.7.2) | 0.972, 3.99 | 0.975, 3.97 |
| Rebased onto `main` `aa3564ce` | 0.975, 3.92 | 0.975, 3.96 |

The acceptance length moves by about ±0.03 between identical runs, because the batches, and with them the generated text, differ from run to run.

The new samplers are tested bitwise against the eager loop, and the five-layer model test checks that both executors and the post-forward graphs run only with the switch on:

<details><summary>Tests, sanitizers and CI</summary>

```bash
# One SM100-family GPU: the fused Markov loop and the sharded chain (one rank)
# bitwise against the eager loop, eagerly and replayed from a CUDA graph
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_kernels.py -v
# One GPU: three draft groups prepared in one launch vs single-group runs
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py -v
# Four GPUs: the main PR's TP4 numerics
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_numerics.py -v
# Four GB300: five-layer model at TP4 with DSpark, switch on vs off
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/specialized_decode/test_layers.py -v
```

| Check | What it covers | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kernel tests | The fused Markov loop and the sharded chain (one rank) bitwise against the eager loop: temperatures 0, 1 and 0.6, a padding row, BF16 and FP32 logits, eagerly and replayed from a CUDA graph. The Markov weights are integer-valued, so the bias is exact in any reduction order. | 94 passed |
| Multi-group DFlash prepare | Three draft groups with their own block tables and block sizes, prepared in one launch, against single-group runs | 6 passed |
| Numerics (TP4) | #61868's collectives | Passed |
| Layers test (4× GB300) | With the switch on, the target's and the draft's executors both run, and the draft's layers take the executor's attention and routed-expert GEMMs; with it off, neither executor runs. The draft samples probabilistically, so the fused and the sharded samplers run at TP4. The switch-on run must replay its post-forward graphs; the switch-off run must build none. | Passed |
| compute-sanitizer (CUDA 13.0.2) over the kernel tests | memcheck, synccheck, racecheck | memcheck: no errors. synccheck: no report in this PR's kernels. Kernels that are not this PR's are left uninstrumented, because synccheck aborts every kernel it reports: FlashInfer's TRT-LLM-gen kernels and CuTe DSL dense GEMMs, and vLLM's `LLBf16SplitK`, which both PRs call ("Divergent thread(s) in block"). racecheck: FlashInfer's CuTe DSL split-K `mm_bf16`, which the LM head calls, reports shared-memory hazards; upstream calls the same kernel from its BF16 linear backend. No other test reports a hazard: cooperative top-k, the sparse-MLA KV counters, the MXFP8 projections, the index key store, Engram, the side-stream table builds, the metadata graphs and the fused Markov sampler are racecheck-clean. Those were run before the restructure, which changed none of them. The CuTe DSL kernels (the routed-expert kernels with the draft finalize, and the sharded Markov chain) were checked with all three tools at this revision: no memcheck error, no synccheck report and no race hazard. |
| pre-commit | All hooks | Passes on every file both PRs change |

After each rebase, onto `main` `03ee2e13` (FlashInfer 0.7.2) and then onto `aa3564ce`, the kernel (94), prepare (6), numerics and layers tests pass again at this PR's tip. Since the first of these, the Markov samplers mix the draft step into the seed, as `gumbel_sample` does since #61161, so they still draw the eager loop's tokens.

**CI.** The prepare test runs in V1 Spec Decode. The kernel tests run in the nightly 4×B200 step that #61868 adds. This PR adds `spec_decode/dspark/`, the code its Markov-sampler tests cover, to that step's source dependencies. No CI agent has four GB300, so the layers test skips there; the post-forward graph and the sharded chain's cross-rank exchange were validated on GB300 outside CI.

</details>

### Performance

All runs use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray (TP4) with DSpark (5 draft tokens), Model Runner V2, FULL CUDA graphs for decode, and the switch on in both arms. Like #61868's, these numbers predate the move into the executors and the CuTe DSL port; see "Since these measurements" below for both.

AgentX throughput per GPU against P90 interactivity for upstream (switch off), #61868 and this PR, with the InferenceX DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash GB300 vLLM curve for reference:

![AgentX throughput against interactivity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yaoyaoding/vllm/75c4f9b4c668f368921bf802ff83875b83d7f337/agentx_frontier_dspark.svg)

**Decode step.** The speculative step with its draft, timed from the client over long-context decodes, in ABBA blocks on one tray (one server per block), both PRs on `main` `429a3da` (FlashInfer 0.7.1). Every block of this PR beats every block of #61868.

| Batch | #61868 (µs) | This PR (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,354 | 4,075 | −6.4% |
| 8 | 9,016 | 8,628 | −4.3% |
| 32 | 15,677 | 15,376 | −1.9% |

Before that merge, an earlier revision measured −5.6%, −4.3% and −1.7%.

**AgentX.** The InferenceX AgentX trace corpus for 3,600 s per concurrency, on base `2c74fd1`. Each cell reads #61868 → this PR; "vs switch off" compares this PR with upstream `main` at the base.

| Conc | P90 interactivity (tok/s/user) | Change | vs switch off | Total tok/s/GPU | TPOT p50 (ms) | TTFT p50 (s) | E2E p50 (s) | Requests |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 811.3 → 889.5 | +9.6% | +35.8% | 7,861 → 8,034 (+2.2%) | 1.14 → 1.05 | 0.93 → 0.74 | 2.0 → 1.5 | 341 → 398 |
| 4 | 681.7 → 723.4 | +6.1% | +29.7% | 10,055 → 10,791 (+7.3%) | 1.17 → 1.06 | 0.43 → 0.42 | 1.1 → 1.1 | 759 → 792 |
| 8 | 560.9 → 598.8 | +6.8% | +25.2% | 16,985 → 17,188 (+1.2%) | 1.27 → 1.13 | 0.39 → 0.32 | 1.2 → 1.0 | 1,449 → 1,457 |
| 16 | 452.6 → 474.3 | +4.8% | +29.7% | 29,727 → 29,805 (+0.3%) | 1.54 → 1.42 | 0.37 → 0.38 | 1.1 → 1.0 | 2,737 → 2,739 |
| 32 | 297.0 → 311.9 | +5.0% | +21.5% | 62,969 → 63,374 (+0.6%) | 2.03 → 1.92 | 0.84 → 0.72 | 2.2 → 2.0 | 4,951 → 4,985 |
| 64 | 211.5 → 185.7 | −12.2% | +5.7% | 101,811 → 117,256 (+15.2%) | 3.53 → 3.83 | 5.55 → 1.46 | 8.6 → 4.0 | 10,463 → 11,522 |

At c64, AgentX's closed loop admits more requests when turns finish sooner: 11,522 against 10,463. The batch is larger, so P90 interactivity is lower, but this PR serves 15.2% more tokens per GPU, and TTFT p50 falls from 5.55 to 1.46 s.

<details><summary>Since these measurements: the executor restructure and the CuTe DSL port</summary>

**Restructure.** Following #61867, the draft layers moved from the stock layers into a draft executor, with no kernel change. The decode step before and after, in the same-tray ABBA as #61868's (switch on in both, each value the mean of two blocks):

| Batch | Before (µs) | After (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,077 | 4,060 | −0.4% |
| 8 | 8,830 | 9,173 | +3.9% |
| 32 | 15,308 | 15,239 | −0.5% |

Part of the batch-8 difference came from the post-forward graphs. Their key held input addresses, and the host-backed temperature, seed and prefill-length buffers rotate through a pool, so a batch shape could take up to four of the 32 graphs; which shapes were left to run eagerly depended on the order in which they first appeared. This revision copies those buffers in the region's existing copy launch, so each batch shape takes one graph (see Design notes). The same ABBA at this revision, against the revision before the restructure:

| Batch | Before (µs) | This revision (µs) | Change |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4,072 | 4,016 | −1.4% |
| 8 | 8,850 | 9,068 | +2.5% |
| 32 | 15,312 | 15,204 | −0.7% |

The rest of the batch-8 difference is in a GEMM this PR does not change. It stays on fresh servers serving only batch 8 (two servers per arm, 3,000-token decodes): 8,887 → 9,108 µs. Profiles late in those decodes differ in one kernel, the stock `wo_b` projection at 48 rows. It runs FlashInfer's `cute-dsl` MXFP8 GEMM with the tactic the autotuner picks when the server starts. Both profiled servers of this revision picked an unclustered tactic (grid 1×1×80), 15.3 µs per call; both profiled servers before the restructure picked clustered ones (grids 1×4×20 and 2×2×20), 7.8 and 8.0 µs. Over 40 layers that is about 310 µs per step, the whole difference. Pinning these tactics above 8 rows, as #61868 does up to 8, would remove the dependence on the server start.

**CuTe DSL kernels.** The draft finalize and the sharded Markov chain were first written in CUDA and compiled with NVRTC at run time. They are now CuTe DSL kernels with the same schedule and arithmetic, and their outputs are bitwise those of the CUDA versions. Kernel time (CUPTI, cold L2, median of ABBA blocks, µs), CUDA → CuTe DSL:

| Kernel | 1 row | 2 rows | 4 rows | 8 rows |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Draft finalize | 2.74 → 2.27 | 2.82 → 2.26 | 3.04 → 2.42 | 3.20 → 2.54 |

| Sharded Markov chain, one TP4 rank's 32,320-token shard | 1 row | 4 rows | 8 rows |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 base logits | 38.0 → 35.7 | 44.4 → 42.8 | 44.2 → 43.1 |
| FP32 base logits | 37.8 → 33.1 | 42.2 → 39.0 | 42.5 → 39.6 |

With the whole 129,280-token head on one rank, which no supported deployment runs, the CuTe DSL chain is 1.7–11.8% faster, except with BF16 base logits at 4 and 8 rows (+2.4% and +3.9%).

</details>

## Details

### Where the time goes

DSpark proposes 5 tokens a step with three draft layers and a Markov head that samples the tokens one position at a time. In stock vLLM at batch 1, the draft side takes about 770 µs of the 5.4 ms step, and #61868 leaves it on the stock paths:
- **Draft layers (about 310 µs).** They run the stock all-reduce, attention and MoE kernels, which #61868 already replaced in the target.
- **Draft head and Markov loop (about 280 µs).** The loop is sequential over the 5 positions, with several small kernels per position, and the logits are all-gathered before sampling.
- **Drafter preparation (about 180 µs).** It does a separate launch per draft KV-cache group.
- **Host.** Sampling, the request-state update and the draft input preparation run eagerly between the target and draft graphs. DSpark `propose` was about 1.5 ms of the host loop.

So this PR moves the draft layers onto the target's paths, fuses the Markov loop, and graphs the region between the target forward and the draft forward.

### What changed

Each row is one optimization and the saving we measured when it was added, as a batch-1 decode-step ABBA on one tray. They were measured one at a time, so they do not add up exactly to the end-to-end figure.

| Optimization | Why | Saving when added |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A draft executor (`specialized_decode/runtime/draft.py`) runs the draft layers on the target's fused all-reduce + mHC kernel and mailbox. | They ran the stock all-reduce and mHC at every sublayer boundary. | −61 µs |
| The draft layers use the executor's attention, the routed-expert GEMMs and the MXFP8 GEMMs. The draft finalizes its own MoE with a new CuTe DSL kernel (`moe/routed_expert_finalize_cute.py`). | The target's fused finalize is built for the target's top-k. | −56 µs (routed-expert GEMMs) |
| **Fused Markov loop:** one sampling kernel per draft position after the unchanged bias GEMM (`spec_decode/dspark/fused_sample.py`). | The eager loop launches several kernels per position. | −93 µs |
| **Sharded Markov chain:** the whole chain runs in one cooperative kernel per rank, with the Markov head sharded by vocabulary over the TP ranks. Ranks agree on each position's winner through a symmetric-memory mailbox (`sharded_markov.py`, with the kernel in CuTe DSL in `sharded_markov_cute.py`). With a plain vocabulary shard, it reads the draft LM head's local shard and skips the logits all-gather. | That removes the remaining per-position launches and the all-gather. | −8 to −20 µs for the chain, −19 µs for the local shard |
| **Post-forward CUDA graph:** sampling, `postprocess_sampled` and the draft input preparation are captured as one graph per shape (`v1/worker/gpu/post_forward_cudagraph.py`). | This region ran eagerly from the host between the target and draft graphs. | −37 µs |
| The draft context work that reads only the target hidden states (the hidden-state combine and each draft layer's context-KV projection) runs on a side stream beside sampling. | It does not depend on the sampled tokens. | −28 µs |
| All draft KV-cache groups are prepared in one launch: `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` gains a group grid dimension and reads `BlockTables`' per-group pointer tables. | It launched once per group. | −19 µs |

Every change except the last takes effect only with the switch on. The multi-group launch applies to every DFlash, DFlash2, LiLiCorr and DSpark user and writes the same outputs.

### Design notes

**Structure.** The DSpark draft model registers itself when it is built with the switch on. The target's model state from #61868 then builds the draft's executor right after the target's, on the same fused kernel, mailbox and mHC side stream, and the draft model's forward asks it for a step the same way (`plan()`, then `run()`). The model state also offers Model Runner V2 the post-forward CUDA graphs, through a `post_forward_cudagraphs` attribute that `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/post_forward_cudagraph.py` reads. The speculator takes the fused and sharded samplers only when the draft model hands it the Markov weights, which it does only with the switch on.

**With the switch off.** The only shared change is the multi-group prepare:
- Group 0 writes the shared outputs, and each group writes its own query and context slot mappings.
- `prepare_context_anchor` now runs after the input preparation. LiLiCorr's anchor reads only target hidden states and `query_start_loc`, which that kernel does not write.
- The padding loops use a fixed 1,024-wide block.

With the switch off, no model state offers post-forward graphs, so `PostForwardCudaGraphs.create` returns None, and the DSpark model shares no Markov weights, so the eager loop is unchanged.

**Post-forward graphs: correctness and limits.**
- *Eligibility.* Uniform decode steps without logprobs, prompt logprobs, grammar or logits processing. It is decided per step on the host, from state every TP rank holds identically.
- *Sampling draws.* They come from per-request seeds and positions, so a replay draws what the eager kernels draw.
- *Step tensors.* The per-step tensors that `prepare_inputs` allocates are copied into buffers the graphs own, in one launch. So are the host-backed temperature, seed and prefill-length buffers, which rotate through a small pool of pinned host buffers; the region reads the copies.
- *Graph key.* It holds the addresses of the other inputs, so a moved buffer captures a new graph instead of replaying a stale one. A batch shape therefore has one key.
- *Replay.* A replay waits for the previous step's output copy stream.
- *Capture and memory.* The first step of a shape runs eagerly, and the second captures. Graphs are captured while serving, into one memory pool of their own that the start-up memory profile does not see. That pool holds about one region's temporaries at the largest batch, mostly its logits.
- *Limit.* Past 32 graphs, further shapes run eagerly, which costs performance only.
- *Trade-off.* On graph steps, the async copy of the sampled tokens starts after the draft input preparation instead of before `postprocess_sampled`.

**Sharded chain: rank lockstep.**
- The exchange is a cross-rank spin inside the draft step and its FULL graph, so every rank must launch it the same number of times.
- Installation depends only on configuration, and CPU MIN all-reduces at load make the ranks agree on it.
- The per-call choice depends only on the padded batch shape. It applies up to 8 request rows (4 at 8 ranks).
- Steady state reads nothing back from the GPU.
- The draws reproduce the fused path, except for the bias reduction order before its BF16 rounding, so a bias element can differ from cuBLAS's in its last bit.

**Relation to #59511 (in this PR's base).** #59511 captures the DFlash context combine and anchor in the draft FULL graph, staging the aux hidden states. With the switch on, this PR runs the combine, plus the DSpark context-KV projection, earlier: on a side stream inside the post-forward graph. `prepare_draft_inputs` then stores the hidden states and publishes the anchor before the side stream forks. Without the side stream, #59511's path applies unchanged.

title: [Perf][DeepSeek V4] Default to block FP8 MoE activations on Hopper with EP
body:
## Overview

Proof of concept: on Hopper with expert parallel, run DeepSeek V4 / V4.1 MXFP4 experts on Humming with block FP8 (group 128) activations by default instead of BF16. Related to #59488 (opt-in `--quantization-config.moe.activation` for the same method), which this would rebase onto.

## Claims

- DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4 + EP on H200: +25% decode output throughput (TPOT 25.2 -> 20.0 ms) and +6% prefill-heavy throughput, with GSM8K unchanged.
- Scope: `Mxfp4MoEMethod` with the HUMMING backend, DeepSeek V4 routing (V4 and V4.1), expert parallel, SM90. Everything else keeps the current BF16 default, and `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` still overrides.

## Validation

DeepSeek-V4-Flash on 4x H200, Humming MoE backend (the SM90 default). Baseline is `main` (BF16 activations). The FP8 column was measured with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"a_dtype": "float8e4m3", "input_scale_group_size": 128}'`. That override resolves to the same Humming layer config as this PR's `kFp8Dynamic128Sym` (group 128, `DynamicGroup`, float32 scales on SM90).

| Config | Workload | BF16 (main) | FP8 GS128 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP4 + EP | GSM8K 5-shot (1319 q) | 0.951 | 0.948 | within noise |
| TP4 + EP | decode: 512 in / 1024 out, conc 128 (3 runs) | 4757 / 4911 / 4906 tok/s | 6131 / 6135 / 6128 tok/s | **+25%** |
| TP4 + EP | prefill: 8192 in / 64 out, conc 32 | 28939 tok/s total | 30780 tok/s total | +6.4% |
| TP4 + EP | low concurrency: 2048 in / 512 out, conc 4 | 422.6 tok/s | 421.0 tok/s | -0.4% |
| TP4 (no EP) | GSM8K 5-shot | 0.948 | 0.951 | within noise |
| TP4 (no EP) | decode (1 run) | 5249 tok/s | 4473 tok/s | -15% |
| TP4 (no EP) | prefill | 29873 tok/s total | 30309 tok/s total | +1.5% |
| TP4 (no EP) | low concurrency | 485.9 tok/s | 455.9 tok/s | -6% |

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash --tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel --max-model-len 16384
python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000 --max-concurrency 256
vllm bench serve --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 512 --random-output-len 1024 --num-prompts 512 --max-concurrency 128 --ignore-eos
```

Tests: `pytest tests/quantization/test_humming_mxfp4_block_fp8.py` passes (11). The new test fails without the source change.

## Details

DeepSeek V4 MXFP4 experts go through `Mxfp4MoEMethod`, which passes no activation key. On SM90 the Humming backend then builds its input schema from `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` and defaults to BF16. This PR sets `activation_key = kFp8Dynamic128Sym` in that case. #59815 already plumbs the key into Humming's input schema with fallback disabled. The DeepSeek V4 checkpoint declares block FP8 GS128 with UE8M0 scales for its FP8 layers, so block FP8 matches what the model was built for.

Why only with EP: under EP each rank runs full-size experts (hidden 4096, intermediate 2048), where Humming's FP8 x MXFP4 kernels are faster. Under TP4 the intermediate is split to 512 per rank, and dynamic activation quantization costs more than it saves. Gating on DeepSeek V4 routing keeps other MXFP4 models (Kimi K3, plain mxfp4) unchanged.

Limitations:
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash was not run; it shares the routing and method, so it gets the same default. #59488 reports the indexed GEMM is faster for V4.1 with EP on Hopper, and the FP8 gain should be re-measured on that path.
- Measured on H200 with the default all2all backend. DeepEP v2 and H100/H20 were not measured.
- The FP8 column was measured with the equivalent env override. I could not rerun end to end on this exact build because the shared machine's GPUs were taken.
- Not a duplicate: #59488 adds an opt-in activation format for the same method, and this PR changes the default for one configuration. #53184 fuses SwiGLU with per-token FP8 quantization for W2. #53709 dequantizes experts to block FP8 instead.

title: [Refactor]: Split MRV2 CUDA graph capture planning by batch type
body:
### Motivation

In MRV2, `CudaGraphManager._init_candidates()` interleaves decode-only and prefill/mixed descriptor generation with candidate indexing. Decode-specific rules—speculative query lengths, rounding and variable-length batches—are mixed with the general capture rules.

### Proposed change

- Extract `_get_decode_capture_descs()` and `_get_mixed_capture_descs()`.
- Keep `_init_candidates()` responsible for combining, sorting and indexing their results.
- Add regression coverage for mode/LoRA selection and capture order after rounding and deduplication.

Both builders use the existing shared capture sizes. Capture order, dispatch priorities and public configuration stay unchanged.

### Validation

Compare capture plans and dispatch decisions against main, and run Qwen3 with fixed/dynamic speculative decoding, adaptive verification and TP=2.

Related: #61024.

title: [Refactor][MRV2] Split decode and mixed CUDA graph capture planning
body:
## Overview

Split MRV2 CUDA graph descriptor generation into decode-only and prefill/mixed builders. `_init_candidates()` retains the shared sorting and candidate indexing. Fixes #61881.

## Claims

Preserves the shared capture sizes, descriptor order and dispatch priorities. Adds regression tests for mode/LoRA selection and rounded-size deduplication.

## Validation

Baseline: `957d512e96`. H100, BF16, MRV2; both checkouts use the same native build.

- 87 tests passed on the updated branch, including 16 added cases; pre-commit passed.
- 960 configurations / 76,800 dispatch comparisons: identical capture plans, candidate lists and decisions.
- Composition with #56136 (`6ab4d6a43f`): reproduced the missing-import failure before the follow-up; both merge orders now produce the same conflict-free file, and all 46 combined planner/dynamic-SD tests pass.
- Follow-up Qwen3-4B/DFlash MRV2 smoke: 41 requests, dynamic K=5/3/1, FULL target/drafter replay, and nonzero acceptance.
- Qwen3 engine A/B: matching capture plans and actual FULL graph replay in every configuration below; nonzero speculative acceptance.

| Target / drafter | TP | Speculation |
|---|---:|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 1 | Disabled |
| Qwen3-8B / Qwen3-0.6B | 1 | K=3 |
| Qwen3-4B / DFlash | 1, 2 | Dynamic K=5/3/1 |
| Qwen3-4B / DSpark | 1 | Adaptive verification |

The full TP=1 workloads cover 128/4096 input tokens, 1/256 output tokens, concurrency 1/8/64 and staggered arrivals. Adaptive and TP=2 runs include varied chat/code prompts.

<details>
<summary>Commands and output comparison</summary>

```bash
uv run --no-project .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dynamic_sd_cug.py \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_mode.py \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_dispatch.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2_cudagraph_profiling.py -q

uv run --no-project .venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run --files \
  vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_cudagraph_manager.py
```

Initial validation had three GPU memory-profiling failures across baseline/candidate; all passed after isolation. The follow-up rerun passed all 87 tests without retries.

Greedy tokens matched for 1,022 requests / 123,382 output tokens against baseline runs/repeats. Initial asynchronous differences on 1 adaptive and 4 TP=2 requests also occurred in unmodified-upstream A/A runs; those repeats matched the candidate. This is not a claim of bitwise reproducibility or a speedup.

</details>

## Details

Decode planning retains speculative-length expansion, variable-length handling, rounding and deduplication; mixed planning retains its request-shape constraints. `FULL` keeps its mixed-routine semantics. Runtime dispatch and graph capture are unchanged.
Retains `defaultdict(list)` for descriptor aggregation, preserving the import needed when composed with #56136.

No duplicate refactor found in issue/PR searches. Related #56136 changes candidate ladders, #60265 changes the default capture ceiling, and #60989 adds standalone-draft graph support; this PR changes none of those policies.

title: [Spec Decode] Keep the trailing prefix-cache block for hybrid models
body:
## Description

Regarding: EAGLE/MTP prefix caching on hybrid (attention + Mamba) models

When serving GLM-5.3-Flash with MTP in P/D on B300s, I noticed every warm turn missed one more cached block than the same deployment with speculation off. With a fixed 77K-token shared prefix, MTP hits exactly 73,728 tokens (32 blocks) every time while spec off hits 76,032 (33 blocks), so each turn recomputes ~2.3K extra prompt tokens, about 60% more prefill work, which is what saturates prefill and drives TTFT up under load

I find that the main cause is the EAGLE trailing-block drop. It exists so a request never reuses the draft-layer KV slot at a producer's chunk end, since that slot was written with the producer's lookahead token. With one MTP head (or EAGLE) that is a single slot, and a stale one can only lower acceptance, since target verification keeps outputs exact. For regular attention the drop costs one ordinary block, but in Mamba `align` mode the attention block is sized to hold a Mamba state page (2304 tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash), so the drop recomputes a whole block on every prefix hit

This makes `disable_eagle_block_drop` default to auto (`bool | None = None`) and resolves it in `VllmConfig` right after the hybrid config hooks, so the scheduler, workers and KV connectors all read the same value:
```text
disable = method in {eagle, eagle3, mtp}
          and is_hybrid and enable_prefix_caching and mamba_cache_mode == "align"
          and num_prefill_lookahead_tokens == 1
```
an explicit setting still wins, and multi-module MTP (several lookahead slots per chunk boundary), DFlash/DSpark and non-hybrid models keep the drop

I tested this on GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 with MTP7 in 1P/1D NIXL (prefill DEP TP4×DP2/EP8, decode 2× TP4, NVFP4 KV, 1M context, 16 B300s) using native AgentX (`semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126`, 900 s per point, one run each), comparing the current drop against `disable_eagle_block_drop=true` on our internal fork, which carries the same drop logic:

| C | TTFT p50 drop → keep | out tok/s drop → keep | prefill prefix hit drop → keep | draft acceptance drop → keep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 500 → 517 ms | 1,293 → 1,303 | 0.876 → 0.892 | 0.409 → 0.417 |
| 128 | 723 → 639 ms | 3,402 → 3,398 | 0.842 → 0.859 | 0.385 → 0.379 |
| 256 | 1,097 → 946 ms | 5,366 → 5,427 | 0.841 → 0.858 | 0.398 → 0.398 |
| 384 | 6,576 → 2,544 ms | 6,487 → 6,896 | 0.803 → 0.826 | 0.395 → 0.391 |

acceptance doesn't move, and the gain shows up once prefill becomes the bottleneck (C64/C128 are within single-run noise). Correctness gates, including ~990K-token retrieval, tool calls and streaming, passed with the block kept. I also tried `--prefix-match-unit` below the block size, which shrinks the drop to one hash unit, but mid-block hits copy a whole block per KV group on this model and were slower overall, so it isn't a substitute today
