title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Read GPU Engram tables from peers' HBM instead of DP collectives
body:
## Purpose

With `cpu_offload: false`, DeepSeek-V4.1's Engram tables live in HBM, but every lookup still goes through DP collectives: a pynccl `all_gather` of the hash ids and an `all_to_all_single` of the rows on the node-local `edp` group. Decode runs in FULL CUDA graphs, which do not honor `eager_break_during_capture`, so these collectives are captured next to MegaMoE's cross-rank kernels. In DEP decode on GB200, every rank then blocks in `graph.replay()` of the same decode graph at the first real step (seen with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`); host-offloaded tables, with no NCCL in the graph, never hang. I did not pin down the exact NCCL/MegaMoE interaction. This PR removes the collectives instead: GPU tables are row-sharded over the Engram DP group in symmetric memory, and each rank looks up only its own tokens, reading every row from the owning peer's HBM. Lookups need no collective, barrier or graph break.

* **Kernel.** `_engram_lookup_kernel` gains `PEER_ROWS`. With it, `weight` is a per-rank pointer table: a row's owner is `id // PEER_ROWS`, and its scales follow the rows in the same symmetric buffer. Tables are read-only after loading, so reads need no synchronization.
* **When.** `cpu_offload: false`, TP=1 and an Engram DP group (co-located DP replicas). The table sets `dp_size = 1`, as `dp_shared_memory` does, and `DeepseekV4Model` reads that to skip the hash gather and dummy hashes. Host tables keep `dp_shared_memory` / `EngramPeerExchange`, since symmetric memory cannot map another process's host memory.
* **Across nodes.** By default the group stays node-local. With `embedding_across_dp: true` (off by default), GPU tables are split over every DP rank, e.g. 1/32 of the table per GPU at DEP32; all DP ranks must then share one NVLink domain, as on GB200 NVL72. A group with the DP group's ranks reuses `_DP` instead of building a second communicator: a separate 32-rank group cost ~1.1 GiB/GPU and failed `gpu_memory_utilization=0.95`.
* **Not covered.** GPU tables with TP > 1 keep head sharding and its collectives. Peer mode stages BF16 rows per layer rather than `EngramBatch`'s packed MXFP8 rows, so `wkv` quantizes its own input; feeding packed peer rows to `EngramBatch` is a possible follow-up.

## Where it matters

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode-only on GB200, DEP16 / DEP32 (DP x TP1 + EP), 16 requests/rank, MegaMoE, MegaAttention, DSpark (5 tokens, synthetic acceptance 3.51), EPLB, full decode CUDA graphs, `DecodeBenchConnector` replaying an agentic coding trace. Unprofiled steady state (+60 to +240 s), one run each, on a development tree based on `fe4df3df` with #61767; its Engram code is identical to main. Without this PR, `cpu_offload: false` hangs in this setup, so the baseline is the default host offload. GPU tables use `embedding_across_dp: true`.

| | host offload | GPU tables, peer read |
| -- | --: | --: |
| DEP16 step (ms) | 14.13 | 13.71 |
| DEP16 output (tok/s/GPU) | 3,777 | 3,827 |
| DEP32 step (ms) | 13.15 | 12.90 |
| DEP32 output (tok/s/GPU) | 3,877 | 3,939 |
| Model memory, DEP16 / DEP32 (GiB/GPU) | | 28.9 / 20.3 |

## Microbenchmark

Both Engram layers' lookups for one decode step, 96 tokens/rank, 16 ranks on 4 GB200 nodes, CUDA graph replay with fresh ids, median over ranks.

| Table layout | us/step |
| -- | --: |
| Host UVA (offload) | 233-324 |
| HBM, heads over 4 GPUs + `all_gather` + `all_to_all` (main; hangs in FULL graphs) | 46.7 |
| HBM, rows over 16 GPUs + `all_gather` + `reduce_scatter` | 180.6 |
| HBM, rows over 16 GPUs, peer read (this PR) | 19.8 |

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/distributed/test_engram_dp_shard.py -q
pre-commit run --files vllm/distributed/parallel_state.py vllm/models/deepseek_v41/common/engram.py vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/model.py tests/distributed/test_engram_dp_shard.py
```

* `test_engram_table_shared_across_dp_replicas` (4 GPUs): the TP1 x DP4 GPU-table case now takes the peer path, asserts that no DP `all_gather` runs, and replays a FULL CUDA graph with fresh ids.
* `test_engram_group_creation_honors_model_and_options`: TP1 x DP4 cases for the node-local group vs `embedding_across_dp`, and `_DP` reuse.

## Test Result

On 4 x GB200: 29 passed. Pre-commit (ruff, format, typos, mypy) passes.

## Accuracy

GSM8K with lm-eval 0.4.13: 1319 problems, 5-shot completions, temperature 0, 1024-token cap, concurrency 32. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, MegaAttention, MXFP4 indexer cache with sparse logits, DeepGEMM mega MoE, DSpark (5 tokens), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--max-model-len 8192`.

| | Engram tables | strict match | flexible extract |
| -- | -- | --: | --: |
| this PR, DEP8 over two GB200 nodes | GPU, rows over all 8 DP ranks (peer read) | 92.57% (±0.72) | 92.72% |
| #61371, DEP4 | host offload | 92.87% (±0.71) | |

The first revision of this PR gave 92.87% / 92.95% on the same setup.

<details>
<summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
# head node
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --port 8123 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHMLA_MEGA_ATTN_DSV41","indexer_kv_dtype":"mxfp4","indexer_sparse_logits":true}' \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 128 \
  --data-parallel-size 8 --data-parallel-size-local 4 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --data-parallel-address <head> --data-parallel-rpc-port 13345 \
  --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":false,"embedding_across_dp":true}' \
  --kernel-config '{"moe_backend":"deep_gemm_mega_moe","enable_flashinfer_autotune":false}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"enable_adaptive_verification":true}' \
  --numa-bind
# second node: the same command plus --headless --data-parallel-start-rank 4

lm_eval --model local-completions \
  --model_args model=deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash,base_url=http://localhost:8123/v1/completions,num_concurrent=32,max_retries=3,tokenized_requests=False,tokenizer_backend=None \
  --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --gen_kwargs temperature=0,max_gen_toks=1024
```

</details>

## Not a duplicate

I searched open PRs for `engram symmetric memory`, `engram peer`, `engram cpu_offload`, `engram hang` and `engram DP`. #59923 and #56512 cover the exchange for host-offloaded tables; #60625 changes head sharding for TP16/TP32 and keeps the collectives.

title: [Bug]: Adaptive verification fails at startup with the default attention backend on FA2 GPUs
body:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py (trimmed) ```text ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 11.4.0-1ubuntu1~22.04.3) 11.4.0 Clang version : Could not collect CMake version : version 3.22.1 Libc version : glibc-2.35 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.14.0+cu130 Is debug build : False CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ROCM used to build PyTorch : N/A XPU used to build PyTorch : N/A ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.11 (main, Oct 7 2025, 15:34:39) [Clang 20.1.4 ] (64-bit runtime) Python platform : Linux-6.8.0-138-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True CUDA runtime version : 13.0.88 CUDA_MODULE_LOADING set to : GPU models and configuration : GPU 0: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition Nvidia driver version : 580.178.04 cuDNN version : Could not collect HIP runtime version : N/A MIOpen runtime version : N/A Is XNNPACK available : False ============================== Versions of relevant libraries ============================== [pip3] flashinfer-python==0.7.1 [pip3] nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.8.0 [pip3] torch==2.14.0+cu130 [pip3] triton==3.8.0 ============================== vLLM Info ============================== ROCM Version : Could not collect vLLM Version : 0.32.0rc1.dev199+g8f111b22e (git sha: 8f111b22e) vLLM Build Flags: CUDA Archs: Not Set; ROCm: Disabled; XPU: Disabled GPU Topology: GPU0 CPU Affinity NUMA Affinity GPU NUMA ID GPU0 X 0-23 0 N/A ```
The relevant code is unchanged on today's main (`153a17166e`). ### Describe the bug With `enable_adaptive_verification: true` and no `--attention-backend`, startup fails on an RTX PRO 6000 (SM120): ``` vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B --max-model-len 4096 --speculative-config '{"method": "eagle3", "model": "AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3", "num_speculative_tokens": 4, "enable_adaptive_verification": true}' ``` ``` ValueError: Adaptive verification replays decode cudagraphs whose per-request query lengths vary up to 5, but FlashAttentionBackend allows none. Pass enable_adaptive_verification=false in the speculative config, or use a backend that does. ``` The selector picks FLASH_ATTN (FA2 on this GPU) because the only adaptive check in `validate_configuration` is `supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch`, which FA2 passes. The varlen graph check that rejects it runs later, in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/adaptive_verification.py`, and FA2's metadata builder declares `AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_BATCH` (`flash_attn.py`; FA3 and FA4 declare `ALWAYS`). With `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN` the same config starts and serves. With `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, FA2 is excluded for the KV dtype and the selector lands on TRITON_ATTN by itself, so the failure only shows up with BF16 KV. From the source I'd expect every FA2 GPU (SM8x, SM12x) to behave the same; I've only run it on SM120. Would it be right to have the selector skip backends whose decode graphs can't replay varlen batches when adaptive verification is on, so these GPUs fall through to TRITON_ATTN? I can put up a PR if that's the preferred direction.

title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Apply stop strings only after reasoning ends
body:
## Overview

Client stop strings are matched against the model's reasoning as well as its answer. If the reasoning contains a stop string, generation ends inside `<think>` and the response has no content. This PR keeps stop strings dormant until the request's reasoning parser sees reasoning end.

Fixes #62085. Also fixes #53066, and item 3 of #58647.

## Claims

- On a server with `--reasoning-parser`, chat requests (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/messages`) whose prompt leaves the model mid-reasoning no longer stop inside the reasoning. Stop strings still apply to the response that follows.
- A stop string has to start in the response. A match that spans the end of the reasoning is ignored, which matters when the end marker decodes to no text.
- No change for requests without stop strings, prompts that are not mid-reasoning (thinking disabled), servers without a reasoning parser, or endpoints that do not resolve reasoning state (`/v1/completions`, `/v1/responses`, offline `LLM`).

## Validation

**End to end:** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP=8 on H100, `--reasoning-parser deepseek_v41`. The repro from #62085 is a classifier prompt with `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]`; it is the same request Claude Code's auto-mode safety check sends.

| Request | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/messages`, `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]` | 100/100 empty (stopped inside reasoning) | **50/50 `<block>no`** |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, `stop: ["</block>"]` | `content: null` | **20/20 `<block>no`**, reasoning kept |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, thinking disabled (control) | `<block>no` | 20/20 `<block>no` (stop still applies) |

<details><summary>Repro command</summary>

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/messages -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash", "max_tokens": 2048,
  "stop_sequences": ["</block>"],
  "system": "You are a security classifier. Decide whether the shell command should be blocked.\nIf it should be blocked, output <block>yes</block>. Otherwise output <block>no</block>.",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Command: ls -la\nYour response MUST begin with <block>."}]
}' | jq -c '{stop_reason, text: [.content[]|select(.type=="text")|.text]}'
```
</details>

**Unit tests:** in `tests/detokenizer/test_stop_string_while_stop_model_terminates.py`. All 8 new cases fail with the new behavior disabled.
- A stop string in the reasoning is ignored and the one in the response is honored, with tokens fed 1, 3 or all at a time (as with speculative decoding).
- A stop string spanning a reasoning end that decodes to no text does not match.
- With the real `qwen3` parser and Qwen3 tokenizer, `reasoning_ended=False` defers stops and `reasoning_ended=None` keeps the old behavior.

**Existing suites:** `pytest tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py tests/v1/engine/test_fast_incdec_prefix_err.py tests/tokenizers_/test_detokenize.py tests/detokenizer/{test_check_stop_strings,test_min_tokens,test_stop_string_while_stop_model_terminates}.py` gives 692 passed and 1 failed. The failure, `test_logprobs_processor[7-5-FINAL_ONLY]`, was intermittent: it passes 8/8 when rerun on both this branch and `main`. CI runs `tests/detokenizer` in "Detokenizer" (`.buildkite/test_areas/misc.yaml`).

**Model evals:** the GSM8K eval sends stop strings only in `/v1/completions` mode, which this change does not touch. The end-to-end table above is the evidence for the affected path.

## Details

**Root cause.** `BaseIncrementalDetokenizer.update()` runs `check_stop_strings` over all detokenized text. With think-in-prompt templates (DeepSeek-V4/V4.1, Qwen3, GLM, ...), that text starts inside the reasoning. A stop string there ends the request before `</think>`, so the parser returns no content.

**Design.** This reuses the reasoning-state plumbing that structured outputs already has, rather than matching marker strings:
- The chat serving layer already resolves `reasoning_ended` per request from the request's own parser and template kwargs (`resolve_reasoning_ended`), and sends it on `EngineCoreRequest` together with `reasoning_parser_kwargs`. Stop strings are deferred only when it is `False`, so thinking-off requests and endpoints that do not resolve it keep today's behavior.
- A new `ReasoningEndFinder` in `detokenizer.py` finds the end of reasoning in the output token ids. It uses the same parser class structured outputs uses (`--reasoning-parser`, built with the request's `reasoning_parser_kwargs`).
  - Engine-based parsers: `find_reasoning_end`, which also handles implicit ends such as a tool-call start token, where content starts at that token.
  - Legacy parsers: `is_reasoning_end_streaming`.
- Once reasoning ends, `check_stop_strings` gets `search_start` at the first content character, so a match cannot start in the reasoning text. `min_tokens` and dropping overflow tokens after a stop are unchanged.
- `OutputProcessor` resolves the parser class by name the first time it is needed. Only API-server chat paths set `reasoning_ended=False`, and they have registered the parser by then, so a plugin parser cannot fail offline `LLM` startup.

**Cost.** Only requests that have stop strings and are mid-reasoning pay anything. On DeepSeek-V4.1 and Qwen3 parsers that is about 90–150 µs per request to build the parser, and about 0.7 µs per decode step until reasoning ends. There is no change to the model runner or scheduler, and no GPU work.

**Behavior change.** A chat client that relied on a stop string to cut reasoning short now gets it applied only to the response. This matches the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, where stop sequences apply to the output text.

**Limitations.**
- `resolve_reasoning_ended` returns `True` for `include_reasoning=False` and for grammar-from-parser (Mistral) requests. That is a structured-outputs choice, and those requests keep today's behavior.
- `/v1/responses` does not resolve reasoning state yet.

**Related PRs.** #52486 and #38533 also target this.
- #52486 searches the output text for a hardcoded `</think>` and arms itself when the prompt's last token is `<think>`. It never reads the deployment's parser markers (its config lookup raises on the frontend and is swallowed) and does not handle special-token markers that are stripped from the text. It also conflicts with the current `update()`.
- #38533 uses the parser on token ids, as this PR does, but it is built on the old parser classes, has merge conflicts, and does not use the per-request `reasoning_ended` resolution.

title: [RFC][Experimental]: Model- and platform-customized KV cache planning
body:
**Status:** draft · **PRs:** #53558 (builder, model hook, checks), wangxiyuan/vllm#2 (Qwen3.8 and Kimi-K3 hooks, golden plans) · **Related:** #58638 (grouping with drafters), #42449 / #61452 (KV cache spec refactor) This RFC updates the design of #44276 ("Model customized KVCache Planning"). The design changed substantially during review of #53558, so we track it here as a separate RFC; #44276 keeps the earlier discussion. Design doc with comments: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZnTISAsNuP9qNsbpF4FIPGPsYd_5TbdaBTrVhpW0N4A/edit?tab=t.v32av17qd6tq ## TL;DR We currently heavily rely on a heuristic-based KV cache grouping method in core, `get_kv_cache_groups()`, for every model. The heuristic still works so far, but new hybrid models, drafters, cache precisions and platforms will likely add further complexities to this method. Some examples: quite a few new models changed it (DSV4, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DSV4.1-Flash); a drafter can re-cut a whole model (Kimi-K3 + DSpark: 4 → 20 groups); and vllm-ascend monkey-patches about 680 lines of vLLM to use its own DSV4 plan. This RFC proposes an **experimental** pluggable `KVCacheConfigBuilder` API, which lets models and platforms own their KV cache plan, while core keeps the planning flow and checks every plan: | part | who | what | where | | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | | builder | platform | overrides grouping and placement | #53558 | | grouping hook | model | returns the model's KV cache groups | #53558 | | checks | core | rejects a malformed plan at startup, from any source | #53558 | | golden plans | tests | one readable plan file per model | wangxiyuan/vllm#2 | The APIs are experimental: their signatures can change, in particular when #61452 changes the KV cache group data structure. Non-goals: for models where the existing heuristic already works well, we don't change anything. The API is mainly for (1) new model and speculator support and (2) platform customization for now. --- ## 1. The problem Currently, we heavily rely on the heuristic-based `get_kv_cache_groups()` in vLLM core for all models, especially recent hybrid models. We see these issues. ### 1.1 Models Recent models, such as DSV4, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DSV4.1-Flash, have complex architectures: 1. More than three types of `KVCacheSpec`: full attention / MLA, SWA, linear attention / Mamba state, circular buffer, etc. 2. Different precisions for layers. DSV4 has an fp8 main KV cache, but the indexer cache can be fp4 or fp8. This is not only a memory question: precision changes the page size, and the page size decides the grouping. On DSV4.1-Flash, an mxfp4 indexer changes the plan from 7 groups to 9, although the SWA layers did not change: ``` packed layout: block size = widest group (main MLA + indexer pages) fp8 indexer: block 135,168 B → 8 SWA pages fit → 40 SWA layers / 8 = 5 groups mxfp4 indexer: block 114,688 B → 6 SWA pages fit → 40 SWA layers / 6 = 7 groups ``` 3. Different speculators. A drafter can use MLA or GQA, with or without SWA. In many cases its layers cannot merge with the target layers, so they form a new bucket. The heuristic sizes all groups by the smallest bucket, so a small draft bucket re-cuts every target group: ``` Kimi-K3: buckets [69 KDA, 24 MLA] group size 24 → 4 groups Kimi-K3 + DSpark: buckets [69 KDA, 24 MLA, 5 SWA] group size 5 → 20 groups ``` For many models, like Kimi-K3, Qwen3.5/3.6 and MiMo-V2.5, adding a DSpark/DFlash drafter blows up the groups from a few to 20 or more (Qwen3.5-27B + DFlash: 70). Each group prepares its own attention metadata every step, so this eats much of the drafter's speedup. #58638 has the measurements and improves the heuristic for these cases. ### 1.2 Features Additionally, there are new features that make KV cache grouping and planning more complex: 1. Different KV cache layouts: block-major or layer-major, for example. The layout is chosen before grouping and selects the grouping algorithm (block-major packs pages of different sizes into one block; layer-major first makes all page sizes equal). So a grouping decision depends on a placement decision. 2. HiSparse, which optionally keeps the indexer KV in GPU HBM but offloads the main attention KV. It adds layers that the model does not have and a second (host) memory pool, and today it is a separate branch inside the heuristic. 3. Speculators that add a hidden-state cache. This exists: the hidden-state extraction method adds one hidden-state cache layer, and the heuristic has a special case to keep it in its own group. ### 1.3 Parallelism and P/D In addition, we need to handle different parallelism, and P/D with heterogeneous TP: * TP can partition some specs but not others (like MLA). Each spec must declare this correctly; a missing declaration once changed a drafter's grouping (#59733). * P/D disaggregation with heterogeneous TP requires the same KV cache grouping on P and D: NIXL sends block IDs as one list per group and pairs the lists by position. This is implicitly assumed today, but not enforced: the NIXL compatibility hash does not include the grouping. With custom plans, P and D can more easily end up with different plans, for example when one side runs a platform builder and the other does not. ### 1.4 Why one heuristic does not scale All of these create uncertainties for the heuristic. They also make day-0 model support harder: a new model must modify the heuristic to match the grouping plan it has in mind, while being careful not to break other models. In practice, DSV4, Kimi-K3, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DSV4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash each changed core planning, and most of them needed follow-up fixes. The heuristic now has checks by model name, and it finds draft layers by guessing from layer positions. This also makes adding speculators tricky: a speculator can silently change the KV cache grouping plan and add a high metadata preparation cost. In other words, the KV cache grouping plan is implicit and error-prone. It is also hard for other (non-NVIDIA) platforms to use their own KV cache grouping and allocation plans. For example, vllm-ascend uses a different plan for DSV4-Pro (it groups layers into tuples and pads SWA pages to the MLA page size), and it has to monkey-patch vLLM to make that plan work. ## 2. Goals vLLM core: 1. Hooks that allow platforms and each model to customize KV cache planning. Platform overrides come at a higher priority. The APIs are general enough to cover all the cases above. 2. vLLM core stays stable and robust. 1. Stable: a day-0 model does not need to modify the core heuristic to get a new grouping plan, and all its changes stay in the model's directory. 2. Robust: vLLM core detects a malformed custom plan and rejects it at startup. Platforms and models: 1. The grouping logic is simple and intuitive. A model can directly define its groups and their roles (e.g., "full", "SWA1", "SWA2", "compressor state"). 2. The logic stays in Python to be generic. A static, structured form of each plan (YAML) is generated for humans and agents to read: the "golden" KV cache plan. 3. Tests check whether a commit, for example a new speculator, changes a grouping plan. The change becomes explicit in review instead of a silent regression. Non-goals: worker-driven allocation (#42449); several memory pools in the builder interface (HiSparse stays in core); custom schedulers, prefix-cache coordinators or admission rules. ## 3. Design ### 3.1 Overview Core keeps one planning flow, and no plugin can change it. Plugins make only two decisions: how to group the layers, and how to place a list of groups in memory for a given number of blocks.

*Figure 1: Core runs the planning flow and calls the builder for grouping and placement. The gold box is future work.* The flow, once at startup: merge the specs of all workers → group → check → project the groups onto each PP stage → find the number of blocks (block-count override, automatic max model length, admission check) → place each worker's KV cache → reduce all ranks to the same number of blocks. Memory profiling at startup uses the same builder. Keeping the flow in core matters, because the steps after grouping (PP projection, memory accounting, the block-count override, cross-rank agreement) must behave the same for every model and platform. vllm-ascend's patches today copy and change parts of this flow; with the builder, they only make the two decisions. PP also needs nothing new: core projects any plan onto the stages, whatever its source. ### 3.2 Platforms: the builder A platform selects a builder class (`Platform.get_kv_cache_config_builder_cls`). The builder has two methods: ```python class KVCacheConfigBuilder: def get_kv_cache_groups(self, vllm_config, kv_cache_spec) -> list[KVCacheGroupSpec]: ... def get_kv_cache_config_from_groups(self, vllm_config, kv_cache_groups, num_blocks) -> KVCacheConfig: ... ``` The default builder calls the model hook if the model has one, else the core heuristic. A platform builder that overrides grouping has priority; it reaches the model hook only through `super()`. Core finds the bytes per block by asking the builder to place one block, so a platform with a different placement does not need to compute memory separately. A plan that depends on the hardware belongs here. vllm-ascend's DSV4 plan is one: its grouping (layer tuples, padded SWA pages) and its placement depend on each other, so both decisions should come from one shared function in the builder. vllm-ascend#18359 moves the Ascend plans into a builder and removes most of the patches. ### 3.3 Models: the grouping hook A model class can implement `SupportsKVCacheGrouping` and return its groups directly: ```python class SupportsKVCacheGrouping(Protocol): @classmethod def get_kv_cache_groups(cls, vllm_config, kv_cache_spec) -> list[KVCacheGroupSpec]: ... ``` The model author knows the architecture, so the hook states the intended grouping instead of hoping the heuristic finds it. Two examples: **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.** Its 48 layers repeat a period of 4: three GDN (linear attention) layers and one QSA layer. A QSA layer has three caches: the main cache, a compressed key cache and a raw key ring. One replicated PLE state also exists. The hook returns 6 groups: | group | layers | why apart | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | GDN, position 0 | layers 0, 4, …, 44 | one group per position in the period | | GDN, position 1 | layers 1, 5, …, 45 | | | GDN, position 2 | layers 2, 6, …, 46 | | | PLE state | layer 1 | replicated across TP, the GDN state is sharded | | QSA raw key ring | layers 3, 7, …, 47 | scratch ring, not prefix-cached | | QSA main + compressed keys | layers 3, 7, …, 47 | share one block table | This is the same plan the heuristic gives today; the hook makes it explicit, so a change in the heuristic cannot change it. **Kimi-K3 + DSpark.** The hook groups the target layers as if there were no drafter, and puts the 5 draft layers in a group of their own: 4 + 1 groups instead of 20. This is only an example. The better fix is in the core heuristic, which RFC #58638 and its PRs (#58207, #58380) improve for drafters. The point is that a hook can unblock a model first, without waiting for a core change, and the hook can go away when core catches up. Three rules for hook authors, learned from these two hooks: 1. **Group in the layout's terms.** On a layer-major layout, all groups must have one page size. The first Kimi-K3 hook made the page sizes equal for target and draft layers separately, so the plan had two page sizes, and core rejected it at startup. The hook can reuse core's helpers: make page sizes equal over all layers first, then split. 2. **Work on any subset of layers.** During startup profiling, a worker calls the hook with only its own PP stage's layers. 3. **Keep the hook a function of the config and the specs.** Then the golden plan (§3.5) captures its behavior. ### 3.4 Checks Core checks every plan right after grouping, from any source (heuristic, model hook, platform builder), and stops startup with an error that names the problem: 1. Every layer is in exactly one group. 2. For a group whose layers have different specs, the group's spec describes exactly the group's layers. Placement problems also stop startup: core places one block with the builder before it computes the number of blocks, so a plan that the layout cannot hold fails there (this is how the first Kimi-K3 hook failed). Core cannot check more than the structure. It cannot compare a group's spec with the merge of its layers' specs, because core itself changes specs during grouping (it pads pages and changes block sizes). And it cannot judge whether a valid plan is a good plan, for example whether 20 groups are too many. That is the job of the golden plans. ### 3.5 Golden plans Each model has one plan file that shows its KV cache grouping in a readable form. A GPU script starts the real engine for each case (real model config, dummy weights), records the plan through the platform builder and the model hook, and checks that every worker received its part. The script writes the file; nobody edits it by hand. A PR that changes a grouping includes the new plan, so reviewers see the change as a diff. Part of the Kimi-K3 plan: ``` cases: tp1: {structure: tp1, groups: 4} tp4: {structure: tp1, groups: 4} tp1-dspark: {structure: tp1-dspark, groups: 5} structures: tp1-dspark: - kind: MambaSpec layers: ['language_model.model.layers.{0-88:4}.self_attn'] # ... two more MambaSpec (KDA) groups and one MLA group, as in tp1 - kind: SlidingWindowSpec sliding_window: 2048 layers: ['model.layers.{93-97}.self_attn.attn'] ``` A plan records only the grouping decision: which layers share a block table, the spec type of each group, and flags that are not default (for example, eagle group or host memory). Every grouping source produces exactly this, so one format covers all of them. The file has no bytes, block sizes, page sizes or block counts. A file lists each distinct plan once and maps cases to it (above, `tp1` and `tp4` share one plan), and it writes layer ranges compactly (`{0-88:4}` is layers 0, 4, …, 88). CPU tests read only the plan files and check two rules across cases: tensor parallelism does not change the grouping, and a speculator keeps the target grouping. These rules are policies, not laws. A precision change, for example, changes the grouping on purpose (§1.1). So each known exception is listed with its reason, for example DSV4.1 + DSpark. For now, a plan is a reviewed snapshot, not a formal spec, for three reasons: 1. **The plan depends on inputs the file does not record.** The grouping depends on page sizes, and page sizes depend on the GPU, the attention backend and the KV cache layout. The current plans come from GB200; Hopper can give different plans. A formal spec would have to name these inputs, and the file would no longer be simple. 2. **The format follows an experimental API.** #61452 will change the group data structure, and a versioned schema now would freeze choices that will change. 3. **Nothing regenerates the plans yet.** No CI job runs the GPU script, so a plan can drift from the code. As a first step, each case should record the layout it was made with, because the layout selects the grouping algorithm. A versioned schema and a CI job that regenerates the plans on GPUs (first optional, then gating) are future work. ## 4. Future work - **Core knows the draft layers.** The worker knows which layers belong to the drafter, but sends core only the specs. If it also sent the draft layer names, core could group target and draft layers apart by default (as the Kimi-K3 hook does today) and mark eagle groups exactly, instead of guessing from layer positions. - **Explicit P/D grouping match.** When a model or platform customizes the grouping, P and D can compare their plans when they connect, and reject a mismatch. This would also be the first reader of plans outside the tests, which is the point where a versioned plan format becomes necessary. - **Golden plans in CI.** Regenerate the plans on GPUs in CI, first as an optional step, then as a gate once its runtime and stability are known. ## 5. Alternatives considered | alternative | why not | | :---- | :---- | | Only improve the heuristic (#58207, #58380) | Helps every model and should land, but platforms still cannot use their own placement, and each new model still has to fit one shared heuristic. | | A role per layer instead of full groups (core builds the groups from the roles) | It hides layout details from the hook, but it is less direct and less general than stating the groups, and core would still decide the final grouping. | | A YAML file as the model's input | YAML cannot see spec properties (TP replication, precision) or draft layers, which exist only at runtime. YAML is the right output, not input. |

title: [Bugfix][Model Loader] Evict loaded shards when checkpoint exceeds RAM
body:
## Overview

When a safetensors checkpoint is larger than 90% of available RAM, `safetensors_weights_iterator` now evicts each shard from the page cache (`posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`) once the caller has released its tensors, so a load keeps about one shard cached instead of the whole checkpoint. For DeepSeek-V4.1 this builds on #58857: on main the VL wrapper sorts the full weight stream, which keeps every shard mapped until loading ends, and mapped pages cannot be evicted. Refs #57469, #58625.

## Claims

- Default mmap path only (`--safetensors-load-strategy` unset or `lazy`), Linux only, and only when the checkpoint exceeds 90% of available RAM, the same rule that already turns off auto-prefetch. Checkpoints that fit, and eager, torchao and prefetch loads, behave as before. One info line when it is on.
- A shard is evicted only after the last tensor handed out from it is gone. A caller that holds tensors gets no eviction for those shards.
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at TP4 in a 702 GiB container: page cache stayed at 6.2 to 12.9 GiB (median 9.6) for the first 13 minutes of a 475 GiB load and peaked at the largest shard, 92.1 GiB, instead of growing with the checkpoint. That run also had the same streaming change as #58857 and other fixes applied; details below.

## Validation

**Unit test.** `pytest tests/model_executor/test_weight_utils.py -k "evicts_released_shards or drop_checkpoint_cache"`: 5 passed. The new test writes a 3-shard checkpoint and mocks `os.posix_fadvise` to record which shard it was called on and to assert that every tensor from that shard is already gone.

| Case | Shards evicted |
|---|---|
| caller streams, holding only the current tensor | 1 and 2 (3 is still referenced when the iterator ends) |
| caller holds every tensor, like `sorted()` | none |
| checkpoint fits in RAM | none |

Each case fails when its part of the change is removed (the whole change, the weakref check, the RAM gate). The test is skipped off Linux; I ran it on macOS with `sys.platform` patched to `linux` and a stub `posix_fadvise`, so CI on Linux is its first run as committed. The rest of `test_weight_utils.py` and `model_loader/test_ep_weight_filter.py` pass locally (95 passed, 1 skipped; one test errors at setup because the local run did not load `tests/conftest.py`). `ruff check` and `ruff format` are clean, and mypy reports no new errors in `weight_utils.py`.

**GPU.** 4x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (sm_120, PCIe), RunPod container with a 702.2 GiB memory limit, `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (48 shards, 475.25 GiB), `--tensor-parallel-size 4 --engram-config.cpu_offload true`, DSpark with 5 speculative tokens, CUDA graphs. Both runs on nightly `49cb2bbf` plus #60762 (needed to boot DSv4.1 on sm_120). cgroup memory sampled every 5 s.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Extra code | none | the same wrapper change as #58857 (my own overlay of it, without a `clone()`), this PR's eviction, and a `drop_checkpoint_cache` call after the VL wrapper's load (not in this PR) |
| Env | | `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=pinned_max_round_threshold_mb:64`, so torch pins the Engram tables at exact size (the problem #59849 addresses in vLLM) |
| Checkpoint on | network FUSE volume | local overlay disk |
| Load | progress bar finished in 7m35s, then memory climbed about 9 GiB/min with workers in D state | 814 s main weights, 302 s DSpark draft pass, ready in 1339 s |
| Peak container memory | 695.1 GiB, then RunPod stopped the container at 98% of its limit | 290.6 GiB: anon 8.2, shmem 189.2 (pinned Engram tables), other page cache 92.1 |
| Served | never | 10.7K and 106K-token prompts |

The after run is not an isolated test of this PR, since it also changed the wrapper, the pinned allocation size and the disk. What it shows for this change is the cache during the load. The container sat at 204.6 to 211.4 GiB of 702.2 GiB for the whole stream, so the cgroup was never near its limit, yet page cache outside the Engram shmem stayed at 6.2 to 12.9 GiB until the last 25 s. There page cache reached 80.9 and then 92.1 GiB as the two Engram table shards came through. The iterator evicted the first (80.9 to 15.9 GiB by the next sample); the last one is the shard this PR leaves to the kernel, and the post-load `drop_checkpoint_cache` released it (92.1 to 6.2 GiB within 10 s). vLLM logged `Checkpoint size: 475.25 GiB. Available RAM: 499.62 GiB.`, so the 90% gate here would have been on; the code in that run evicted unconditionally.

## Details

**Why.** The default loader reads every shard through an mmap. Once a shard's tensors are on the GPU its pages are clean page cache, and that cache is charged to the container's cgroup. The kernel does not reclaim it until the cgroup reaches its limit or the host runs short, but some runtimes act earlier: RunPod stops a container at 98% of its memory limit, which is how the before run ended. With a checkpoint this size next to large pinned host allocations (189 GiB of Engram tables at TP4 here), the cache alone can carry a container to that line.

**Gate.** It reuses the existing 90%-of-available-RAM rule, so a checkpoint that fits stays cached for the next load, which was the objection to the unconditional release in #59527. Available RAM is read once when the iterator starts, honoring cgroup limits through `_get_available_ram_bytes`.

**Why the last tensor.** Every tensor from a shard keeps the shard mapped, and `DONTNEED` skips mapped pages, so evicting earlier does nothing. Loaders release tensors in order, and only once the next one reaches them, so the iterator keeps a weakref to the last tensor it handed out from each shard and checks them after every yield. If a caller holds tensors, as the DSv4.1 VL wrapper's `sorted()` does on main, those shards are never evicted; that is why DSv4.1 needs #58857 to benefit.

**Not changed here.**

- The last shard is still referenced when the iterator returns, so it stays cached until the kernel needs the memory. For the DSv4.1 VL wrapper a `drop_checkpoint_cache` after its load releases it; that sits on top of #58857's change to the same function, so I left it out of this PR.
- With several TP ranks on one host, a rank that finishes a shard first can evict pages a slower rank has not read yet, and that rank reads them from disk again. This only happens when the checkpoint does not fit. I did not measure load time with and without eviction, so I make no claim about load time.
- `multi_thread_safetensors_weights_iterator`, fastsafetensors, RunAI and instanttensor loading are unchanged. #58625 (opt-in release after loading) is complementary: it frees the cache after the load, this keeps it bounded during the load.
- `_drop_page_cache` returns early off Linux, which also clears the two macOS mypy errors in `drop_checkpoint_cache` that #61836 fixes.
- Not a fix for #57469: that report's remaining failure is pinned host memory (shmem-rss), which is #59849's area.

**AI assistance.** The code, test and this description were drafted with Claude (the commit carries `Assisted-by: Claude`). I reviewed the full diff, and the GPU runs above are mine.

---

<details>
<summary> Pull Request Checklist </summary>

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill. (Mandatory for agents, optional for humans).
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.

- [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.
</details>

title: [Benchmark][Attention] Support int8_per_token_head KV cache in attention_benchmarks
body:
**TL;DR**
- `benchmarks/attention_benchmarks` could not time an `int8_per_token_head` KV cache, and it timed every backend over an all-zero cache because the runner never wrote the cache.
- This PR allocates the cache the way the attention layer does, writes random K/V before timing, gives each layer its own impl, rejects the dtype on backends that cannot read it, and adds `configs/int8_per_token_head.yaml`; `auto` and `fp8` allocations are unchanged.
- With it, `int8_per_token_head` on main measures 1.48-2.29x slower than bf16 in the 12 cells we ran (RTX 3080), and the kernel numbers in #62113 come from this tool.

## Overview

`benchmarks/attention_benchmarks` cannot currently time attention on an `int8_per_token_head` KV cache. `--kv-cache-dtype` accepts only `auto` and `fp8`. Also, `_create_kv_cache` builds the spec without `kv_quant_mode`, so `TritonAttentionBackend.customize_spec` adds no inline scales. Also, the runner never writes the KV cache, so every kernel is timed over an all-zero cache. This PR allocates the cache the way the attention layer does, writes it before timing, gives each layer its own impl, rejects the dtype on backends that cannot read it, and adds a config.

AI assistance was used: an AI coding agent wrote the code and tests under my direction, drafted this description, and automated the test and benchmark runs; I chose the approach and reviewed every changed line and the results.

The kernel numbers in #62113 (16-byte-aligned per-token-head KV slots) were measured with this tool change and can be reproduced with it.

## Claims

- `--kv-cache-dtype int8_per_token_head` allocates the packed `[K | k_scale | V | v_scale]` cache through the backend's `customize_spec`, so `TRITON_ATTN` runs on the layout it serves.
- Each layer gets its own impl, as in a model. `TritonAttentionImpl` binds its scale views to the first cache it sees, so with a shared impl every layer read layer 0's scales.
- Before timing, the runner writes random K/V for every cached token through `impl.do_kv_cache_update`, the path the attention layer uses. Until now it called only `forward`, which for `TRITON_ATTN`, `FLASH_ATTN` and `FLASHINFER` does not write the cache (`forward_includes_kv_cache_update = False`), so all of them were timed over zeros. Backends whose `forward` writes the cache are left as they were.
- New `configs/int8_per_token_head.yaml` (decode, 4-token verify, prefill; head_dim 128 and 256).
- `--kv-cache-dtype int8_per_token_head` on a backend whose `supports_kv_cache_dtype` rejects it (only `TRITON_ATTN` lists it) or on any MLA backend raises an error instead of timing a different cache.
- `auto` and `fp8` allocations are unchanged.

## Validation

**Why it is needed.** On main, `int8_per_token_head` is slower than the bf16 cache in all 12 cells we measured, at 1.48–2.29× the bf16 time, although it reads about half the bytes. This tool change is what made that measurable. Per layer, median (IQR) of 5 processes, cache populated by this PR:

| Hq/Hkv/D | cell | bf16 (`auto`) | int8_per_token_head | int8 / bf16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12/2/256 | q1s8k | 48.8 (0.0) µs | 103.9 (0.1) µs | 2.13 |
| | q1s128k | 667.5 (1.0) µs | 1424.4 (0.6) µs | 2.13 |
| | q8s128k | 1155.0 (3.4) µs | 1772.7 (2.3) µs | 1.53 |
| | q8ks128k | 855.7 (0.9) ms | 1265.5 (0.7) ms | 1.48 |
| 32/8/128 | q1s8k | 58.4 (0.2) µs | 87.2 (1.1) µs | 1.49 |
| | q1s128k | 814.4 (1.2) µs | 1364.4 (1.0) µs | 1.68 |
| | q8s128k | 1240.8 (3.6) µs | 2023.9 (3.8) µs | 1.63 |
| | q8ks128k | 903.2 (1.7) ms | 1346.0 (1.6) ms | 1.49 |

*RTX 3080 (sm_86), 220 W cap, image `8c1434bf…5035e`, vLLM `g49cb2bbf7` (attention files = `fa75d3456d`), Triton 3.8.0, this branch's `benchmarks/` mounted read-only.*

Equivalent command (5 processes per arm; each ran both head configs and both dtypes through the tool's `run_benchmark`):

```bash
cd benchmarks/attention_benchmarks
python benchmark.py --backends TRITON_ATTN --kv-cache-dtype {auto,int8_per_token_head} \
  --num-layers 8 --block-size 16 --head-dim {256,128} --num-q-heads {12,32} --num-kv-heads {2,8} \
  --batch-specs q1s8k q1s32k q1s128k q8s128k q8ks32k q8ks128k
```

**Cache fill on GPU.** After the fill, 99.0 % (12/2/256) and 99.1 % (32/8/128) of the int8 K/V bytes are non-zero (the rest are quantized zeros), the scales are real (0.013–0.046, none equal to the zero-cache value 1.0), the bf16 cache is 100 % non-zero, and the attention output is finite and non-zero in every probed case. Without the fill, the same probe gave an all-zero output.

The fill changes the numbers. Compared with earlier runs over a zero cache (same image, tool without the last commit), prefill/extend kernels take 8–24 % longer for int8 and 17–37 % longer for bf16. For the per-token-head slot alignment change we measured with this tool, the int8 speedup on those cells dropped by 0.10–0.21× (e.g. 2.09× → 1.88×); on decode cells it moved by at most 0.10×.

**Checks.**
- `pre-commit run --from-ref f8112704d5 --to-ref HEAD` passes on all 6 changed files. In the nightly image with no GPU visible, `python benchmark.py --help` works, `runner` and `mla_runner` import, and the guard rejects `int8_per_token_head` for `FLASH_ATTN`, `FLASHINFER`, `TRITON_MLA`, `FLASHMLA` and `FLASHINFER_MLA` while `TRITON_ATTN` passes it.
**GPU checks** (RTX 3080 20GB, sm_86, nightly image `sha256:8c1434bf…`, branch head):
- `benchmark.py --config configs/int8_per_token_head.yaml`: all 18 cells ran in one process with finite times, for int8 and with `kv_cache_dtype: auto`. Without a wait after the cache fill, cell 13 (`2q4s128k`) hit an illegal memory access, because `do_bench_cudagraph` times on a side stream; the fill now ends with a device sync.
- Cache fill on FLASH_ATTN, FLASHINFER and TRITON_ATTN (bf16 and int8), 12/2/256 and 32/8/128, q1s8k/q1s32k/q8ks32k: cache non-zero (bf16 100 %, int8 99 %), output finite and non-zero.
- `--kv-cache-dtype int8_per_token_head` on FLASH_ATTN / FLASHINFER, and `fp8` on TRITON_ATTN (sm_86), print a per-cell error instead of timing a different cache.
- All 10 runs completed without errors.
- The kernel received the packed cache: 520-byte slots at D=256 and 264-byte slots at D=128, with the V pointer at `% 16 = 4`.
- A `torch.profiler` run confirmed that q8s128k takes the 3D split-K path (`reduce_segments` launched) and q8ks128k the 2D path.

## Details

- `runner.py` maps the dtype with `STR_DTYPE_TO_TORCH_DTYPE` and passes `kv_quant_mode=get_kv_quant_mode(kv_cache_dtype)`, as `Attention.get_kv_cache_spec` does. For `fp8` the spec now carries `FP8_PER_TENSOR`, which no backend's `customize_spec` acts on.
- Only `int8_per_token_head` is added to the CLI choices, because it is the mode validated here.
- Cache fill: request `i` owns blocks `[i * max_blocks_per_request, ...)` of the benchmark's block table, so its `kv_len` tokens map to slots `i * max_blocks_per_request * block_size + arange(kv_len)`. One random K/V pair per request is written into every layer's cache; the transient tensors are one request's K/V. The fill ends with a device sync, because `do_bench_cudagraph` times on a side stream that does not wait for the default stream.
- Known tool limits, not changed by this PR:
  - The tool hard-codes the `meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B` config, which is a gated repo; our runs used a local stand-in config. The `auto` cache and q/k/v take that config's dtype (bf16 here); `BenchmarkConfig.dtype` is not used for them.
  - The metadata builder is built without a speculative config, so split-K scratch is sized for one query token.
  - The tool exports only mean and std, so the medians above are taken across processes.
- No unit test: `attention_benchmarks` has no test suite.
- Measured only on RTX 3080 (sm_86); other GPUs were not run.

**Duplicate search** (2026-10-16):

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "attention_benchmarks kv-cache-dtype"    # #59774
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "attention_benchmarks do_kv_cache_update" # none
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "attention_benchmarks per_token_head"    # none
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "int8_per_token_head"                    # none touch benchmarks/
gh pr diff 59774 --repo vllm-project/vllm   # runner.py: same spec change inside a ROCm backend PR
```

Draft #59774 (ROCm Octave KV backend, 27 files) includes an equivalent spec change in `runner.py`: it passes `kv_quant_mode` and opens `--kv-cache-dtype` to every cache dtype. It does not write the cache, give each layer its own impl, or add the config. This PR is the small, standalone version. If #59774 lands first, this PR reduces to the cache fill, the per-layer impl and the config.

title: [Bug]: Model Runner V2 hangs during speculative decoding warmup with pipeline parallelism
body:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug **Description** Code version: based on `main` commit [`[de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995)`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995). With pipeline parallelism and speculative decoding enabled, Model Runner V2 runs the additional greedy warmup pass only on the last PP stage. Upstream stages skip this pass, leaving the last stage waiting for intermediate tensors that will never arrive. This can be reproduced during GLM-4.7-Flash initialization, before serving any requests. **Reproduction** Use four GPUs for TP2 × PP2. Save the following as `repro.py`: ```python from vllm import LLM if __name__ == "__main__": LLM( model="zai-org/GLM-4.7-Flash", dtype="bfloat16", tensor_parallel_size=2, pipeline_parallel_size=2, distributed_executor_backend="mp", max_num_seqs=1024, max_num_batched_tokens=8192, gpu_memory_utilization=0.65, speculative_config={ "method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 1, }, kernel_config={"enable_jit_warmup": True}, cpu_distributed_timeout_seconds=120, ) ``` Run: ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 \ VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 \ VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \ .venv/bin/python repro.py ``` The CPU communication timeout is shortened to 120 seconds to obtain the failure sooner. **Actual behavior** The first PP stage finishes warmup and CUDA Graph capture. The last PP stage blocks during the additional greedy warmup pass and eventually fails: ```text warmup_kernels # additional greedy=True pass → _warmup_kernels → worker_execute_model(prefill_output) → irecv_tensor_dict → recv_object → torch.distributed.recv RuntimeError: ... Timed out waiting 120000ms for recv operation to complete ``` **Relevant code** In [`[vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py#L232)`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py#L232), the additional pass is gated on the rank-local sampler: ```python rejection_sampler = model_runner.rejection_sampler # ... temporarily disable adaptive verification ... try: _warmup_kernels(model_runner, worker_execute_model, worker_sample_tokens) if rejection_sampler is not None: # Greedy batches skip logits processing, so rejection kernels # also see model-dtype logits instead of FP32. _warmup_kernels( model_runner, worker_execute_model, worker_sample_tokens, greedy=True ) ``` However, [`[vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py#L465)`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/de7eeaa87bc19ecf088472d5f4471cdc9a5ab995/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py#L465) initializes samplers only on the last PP stage: ```python if self.is_last_pp_rank and not self.is_pooling_model: # ... initialize self.sampler ... custom = self.model_state.custom_sampler(self.sampler) if custom: self.vllm_config._check_supports_watermarking(custom_sampler=True) self.sampler, self.rejection_sampler = custom elif self.speculative_config is not None: self.rejection_sampler = RejectionSampler( self.sampler, self.speculative_config, self.device, watermark_key=speculative_target_watermark_key( self.vllm_config.watermark_config ), ) ``` Consequently, non-last stages have `rejection_sampler=None` and skip the second pass, while the last stage executes it and waits for their inputs. **Expected behavior** All PP stages should execute matching warmup forward sequences. The additional speculative warmup pass should use a condition shared across PP stages, rather than the existence of a rank-local rejection sampler. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

With prefix caching on (the default), the model config switches `mamba_cache_mode` to `"align"`. For this model that gives `chunk_size=256` and `block_size=512`. Once a prefill crosses a block boundary inside the prompt, the checkpoint path added in #57329 kicks in, and it doesn't work on CPU: - `mamba_chunk_scan_combined_varlen` calls `_mamba_chunk_scan_combined_fwd_cpu` on CPU. That function accepts `return_intermediate_states` and `last_chunk_indices`, but ignores them and always returns one final state per sequence. `conv_ssm_forward` then indexes that tensor with per-chunk indices. For 513 tokens the chunks are [0, 256), [256, 512), [512, 513), so the index is 2 and the tensor has 1 row. - Even past that, `store_prefill_checkpoint` in `ops/ssd_checkpoint.py` only has a Triton kernel. I tried #54505 (which makes the CPU chunk scan return per-chunk states), and it gets past line 878 but then fails at `_store_prefill_checkpoint_kernel[grid]` with `TypeError: 'function' object is not subscriptable`. What I checked (single prompt, greedy, fp32): | Code | Prompt tokens | Result | |---|---|---| | main 5be4266f5c | 512 / 513 | ok / `IndexError` (index 2) | | ce49c47cbb + #61151 | 64, 256, 512 | ok | | ce49c47cbb + #61151 | 513, 768, 1024, 1025, 1300 | `IndexError`: index 2, 2, 3, 4, 5 | | ce49c47cbb + #61151, `MambaPrefillCheckpointBuilder.build()` returns `None` | 1300 | ok | | `e11962fc1c^` (parent of #57329) | 1300 | ok, same tokens as the row above | | `e11962fc1c` (#57329) | 1300 | same `IndexError` | For the two historical commits I reused the C++ extension built from current main, since the failing code is all Python. Workaround: `enable_prefix_caching=False`. With that, greedy output matches HF transformers (fp32) token for token on prompts up to 1356 tokens. I've only run granite-4.0-h, on macOS. From the code I'd expect the other `MambaMixer2` models (nemotron_h, falcon_h1, zamba2, mamba2) and Linux CPU to hit the same path, since the CPU chunk-scan override applies to any CPU platform, but I haven't checked. There are two ways to fix this, and I've pushed both as separate commits on https://github.com/vietnamesekid/vllm/tree/fix/cpu-mamba2-prefill-checkpoints: 1. Quick fix, vietnamesekid/vllm@dc2f4b975796a92cc70b8cfe54f8c0bb833903c4: skip internal prefill checkpoints on CPU. `MambaMixer2.get_kv_cache_spec` leaves `num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks` at 0 on CPU, the same way GDN does with `_exports_checkpoints`, so the scheduler goes back to splitting a long prefill at the last block boundary, as before #57329. 2. Root-cause fix, vietnamesekid/vllm@38db093842c3a7420d86e4150f22b3ed337c0854: the CPU chunk scan returns per-chunk states when they are requested (it runs the existing C++ kernel one chunk at a time), and `store_prefill_checkpoint` gets a CPU version. This also removes the gate from 1. Both fix the crash at 513 and 1300 tokens. On requests that reuse 1024 cached tokens, both give the same tokens as a run with prefix caching off, and the number of cache hits is the same with either one. The difference is the prefill split: with 1, a 1300-token prompt runs as 1024 + 276 tokens in two steps; with 2, it runs in one step, as #57329 intended. With 2 `tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba2_checkpoint_state.py` also passes on CPU (8/8). On main, 7 of its 8 tests fail when run on CPU, because `store_prefill_checkpoint` is Triton-only, the file isn't part of the CPU CI. Let me know which one you'd like, and I'll open a PR for it. cc @roikoren755 @ZJY0516

title: [Spec Decode] Fix adaptive verification startup on FA2 GPUs
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Fixes #62094. With `enable_adaptive_verification` and no `--attention-backend`, the selector picks FLASH_ATTN on GPUs where it runs FA2 (SM8x, SM12x), and the worker then rejects it after the weights load, because FA2's decode cudagraphs cannot replay variable per-request query lengths. Automatic selection now skips such backends for the target model's layers, as it already skips backends that plan from CPU query lengths. No other open PR addresses #62094 (searches under Details).

## Claims

- The issue's command starts and serves: the target model's attention layers run TRITON_ATTN, the EAGLE-3 drafter stays on FLASH_ATTN, and selection logs one INFO line, `Adaptive verification precluded higher-priority attention backend(s) FLASH_ATTN, FLASHINFER. Using TRITON_ATTN instead.`
- An explicit `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN` on FA2 is rejected at backend selection, before the weights load, instead of after.
- Nothing changes with adaptive verification off, or where FLASH_ATTN runs FA3 or FA4 (FA3 builders declare `ALWAYS`, and FA4 builders do since #60908).

## Validation

RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (SM120), torch 2.14.0+cu130. The GPU runs used this branch's two commits applied to main `153a17166e`, so the compiled extensions match a main build. The touched files are identical there and at the branch base. Qwen/Qwen3-4B with AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3, 4 speculative tokens, BF16 KV, `--max-model-len 4096 --seed 0`, both model revisions pinned:

```
python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_attention_selector.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py
python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_attention_selector.py -k adaptive_verification
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B --max-model-len 4096 --seed 0 --speculative-config '{"method": "eagle3", "model": "AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3", "num_speculative_tokens": 4, "enable_adaptive_verification": true}'
vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B --dataset-name custom --dataset-path mtbench_prompts.jsonl --custom-output-len 256 --temperature 0 --ignore-eos --seed 0 --max-concurrency 1 --num-prompts 16
```

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| main, the issue's command | selects FLASH_ATTN, logs `Loading weights took 6.05 seconds`, then dies with `ValueError: Adaptive verification replays decode cudagraphs whose per-request query lengths vary up to 5, but FlashAttentionBackend allows none.` |
| this PR, the issue's command | serves; target layers on TRITON_ATTN, drafter on FLASH_ATTN, the INFO line above logged once |
| this PR, `--attention-backend FLASH_ATTN` | rejected before any weights load: `Selected backend AttentionBackendEnum.FLASH_ATTN is not valid for this configuration. Reason: ['variable-length decode cudagraphs not supported, this is needed for adaptive verification']` |
| this PR, `"enable_adaptive_verification": false` | FLASH_ATTN, no INFO line |

Serving on this PR (MT-Bench prompts, greedy, 256 output tokens; every request succeeded with the expected input and output token counts): with adaptive verification, mean TPOT 3.72 ms at c=2 over 4 prompts (warm-up) and 3.94 ms at c=1 over 16 prompts; with it off, 3.75 ms at c=2 over 4 prompts.

Against main with `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, the configuration that works there today, measured earlier on a tree whose code equals this branch (only a comment differs), applied to the same main, two runs per latency cell, main against this PR: mean TPOT 4.041 against 4.005 ms at c=1 (16 prompts) and 5.83 against 5.90 ms at c=32 (80 prompts), with overlapping run ranges; mean acceptance length 2.00 against 2.01 at c=1; chat GSM8K (one run per arm, 250 questions, flexible match) 0.936 against 0.940.

Tests on SM120:

- `test_attention_selector.py` and `test_adaptive_verification.py`: 113 passed with this PR, 107 on main (22 skipped each).
- The six new selector cases alone, with this branch's test file on main's code: 5 failed, 1 passed. Four fail with `TypeError` because `AttentionSelectorConfig` has no `use_varlen_decode_cudagraphs` field on main, and the target-layer case selects FLASH_ATTN where it expects TRITON_ATTN. The one that passes checks that `eagle_head` drafters keep FLASH_ATTN, which main also does. All six pass with this PR.

CI runs these cases in the L4 Attention Kernels shards; they mock the SM120 backend order and FA2's declaration, so they do not need SM12x hardware.

## Details

- Root cause: FA2's metadata builder declares `UNIFORM_BATCH`, which the worker's `get_varlen_cudagraph_unsupported_backend` rejects for target layers, but the selector's only adaptive-verification check was `supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch()`, which FA2 passes. A backend hook `supports_varlen_decode_cudagraphs()` (default True) is now checked in `validate_configuration()`.
- FlashAttention's hook reads the builder's declared `_cudagraph_support` instead of calling `get_cudagraph_support()`. That method takes the layer's KV cache spec, and `Attention.get_kv_cache_spec()` builds the spec from the backend being selected, so the selector has none to pass. `FlashAttentionMetadataBuilder.get_cudagraph_support()` returns the declaration unchanged, so the selector and the worker read the same value. Open #58591 adds a branch there that returns `ALWAYS` for FA4 with adaptive verification, which FA4 already declares since #60908, so the two would still agree.
- Scope: the requirement applies to target layers only, through `AttentionSelectorConfig.use_varlen_decode_cudagraphs`, set like `use_adaptive_verification` but off under the `eagle_head` tag, following the tag check from #47808's review: drafters built under that tag replay FULL graphs only for untrimmed batches of uniform length, so they can keep FA2. It is a field because selections are cached per config.
- Placement: @he-yufeng suggested in #62094 failing in `_validate_adaptive_verification`, or reusing the worker's `get_varlen_cudagraph_unsupported_backend`, rather than falling back. Neither has the backends at config time: they are resolved per layer during model construction, and the worker predicate walks attention groups and their KV cache specs, which exist only after that. So automatic selection skips FA2 and logs what it skipped at INFO, not WARNING: adaptive verification is opt-in and this fallback is how it runs on these GPUs, so there is nothing for the user to fix. An explicit FLASH_ATTN still fails, now at selection. The worker check stays as the per-layer backstop.
- Not a duplicate. Open PRs on 2026-10-17: `gh pr list -R vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "62094 in:body"` returns only this PR; `--search "adaptive verification FlashAttention"` adds #58591 (FA4 cudagraphs for adaptive verification, no FA2 selection change) and unrelated work; `--search "adaptive verification FA2"` adds only unrelated work.
- Limits:
  - Drafters built under other tags (for example `draft_model`, `dflash_head`, `extract_hidden_states`) keep the requirement, while the worker checks target layers only. For them the selector is stricter than the worker: with a target that does not use FLASH_ATTN (an MLA model, say) and a `draft_model` drafter on SM12x, the drafter moves from FA2 to TRITON_ATTN. I have not measured that case.
  - Other backends that declare `UNIFORM_BATCH` without a varlen bound (TRITON_MLA, FLASHMLA, ROCM_AITER_FA) still fail at the worker as on main; they can follow the same pattern if wanted.
  - Only SM120 was run. FA3 (SM90) keeps FLASH_ATTN through its `ALWAYS` declaration, which this PR does not change.

This change was prepared with AI assistance.

title: [Feature][KV Offload] Enable canonical offload for chunked-local attention

<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Enable certified canonical KV offloading for `ChunkedLocalAttentionSpec` using the existing mapping and scheduler paths. Implements my [claimed cache-type slice](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61886#issuecomment-6217606040) of #61886.

**Depends on #62160.** This branch includes that prerequisite; merge the storage fix first. [Feature-only diff](https://github.com/xiaoba17/vllm/compare/a99a46153a3b13034339b32942773b44d0cb651d...3172b52d123acf1bea4f78313089d58354e9ac3a).

## Claims

- Compatible chunked-local and mixed chunked-local/full-attention caches pass the static canonical portability gate.
- Unsupported head configurations, quantization and parallel layouts remain rejected.
- Targeted tests cover cross-TP byte reconstruction, tensor strides/offsets and chunk-boundary store/load behavior.

## Validation

Final tested commit: `3172b52d12`.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_config.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_canonical_mapping.py \
  tests/v1/kv_offload/test_file_mapper.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_worker.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/kv_offload/test_factory.py
```

**702 passed, 2 skipped** on Linux. These totals include existing regressions, not only new cases. Pre-commit passed. Mapping tests exercise TP1/TP2/TP4; real GPU tests use TP1/TP2.

**2× RTX 5090**, deterministic tiny Llama4 (3 chunked-local layers + 1 full-attention layer), FP16/eager/Triton, chunk size 128 and block size 16: **10 inference processes passed**, covering independent filesystem producer/read pairs, six pressure cycles and a fresh TP1 read after pressure.

| KV heads | Direction | Cold/reload cache-hit contexts | Max absolute logprob delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (replicated at TP2) | TP1 → TP2 | 240/240 in each phase | 0.001486 |
| 1 | TP2 → TP1 | 240/240 in each phase | 0.003836 |
| 2 (sharded at TP2) | TP1 → TP2 | 240/240 in each phase | 0.001499 |
| 2 | TP2 → TP1 | 240/240 in each phase | 0.001481 |

Compare all 512 vocabulary logprobs at 240 fixed teacher-forced contexts with offload-disabled TP1 references; tolerance 0.005. Prompt lengths straddle 64/128/256/384/512 boundaries. Nonzero filesystem reads and increasing CPU→GPU counters confirm reuse rather than recomputation. Pressure validation constrains the CPU cache to 512 KiB; misses/skipped stores are expected there. The subsequent fresh TP1 reader hits 240/240 contexts in both phases.

[Commands, CPU logs, numerical/transfer results, environment and source hashes](https://github.com/xiaoba17/vllm/tree/10218a6806b5fff79919eb02fff11c265d2c41de). The custom dual-GPU harness was run outside CI and is archived with its original host paths; no new GPU CI job is claimed. Unit tests extend suites already covered by Buildkite.

## Details

Only the static certification gate needs production changes beyond #62160: runtime canonical mapping already operates on attention tensors and the scheduler already handles chunked-local windows. Tests verify these paths rather than introducing another mapping or scheduler implementation.

Usage: set `canonical_layout: true` in `OffloadingConnector`'s `kv_connector_extra_config` on every sharing instance. For filesystem reuse use `spec_name: "TieringOffloadingSpec"`, a CPU budget and a shared FS secondary tier as in the archived harness. This extends the supported cache types for that existing option; the canonical-layout usage documentation is being added in #61822, so this PR does not duplicate its guide.

Duplicate-work check: no open PR implements this chunked-local gate extension. #61822 is documentation, #51691 is quantization, and #60782 is a shared-region refactor. Recurrent/Mamba and general filesystem/object-store test infrastructure claimed by others in #61886 remain outside this change.

Limits: random tiny weights establish execution/cache correctness, not trained-model quality or throughput. The sharded model has one near-tied argmax change among 240 contexts in each direction; tolerance passes, but tokenwise/bitwise equality is not claimed. No TP4 GPU, CUDA Graph or multi-node validation. GPU/native extensions use baseline `8e25bbca19`; latest-main mergeability was checked separately.

title: [Bugfix][KV Connector] MoRIIO READ: trim to prompt blocks before clipping SWA groups
body:
## Overview

MoRIIO READ pairs prefill and decode sliding-window blocks by clipping each block list from its end. A lookahead tail that only one leg allocated shifts the decoder's window by one block, so the decoder reads the wrong KV for the end of the prompt. This PR trims both lists to the prompt's blocks before clipping.

## Claims

- Fixes wrong outputs in MoRIIO READ P/D for sliding-window hybrid models when the two legs have different lookahead tails. On DeepSeek-V4-Pro, ~14% of prompt lengths were affected.
- Also fixes the full-attention pairing when only the prefiller has a lookahead tail.
- No change when both legs hold the same number of blocks.

## Validation

| Check | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| New unit test, 4 tail combinations | 3/4 fail | 4/4 pass |
| `test_moriio_hma_scheduler.py` + `test_moriio_routing.py` (macOS, CPU) | – | 111 passed |
| + `test_moriio_connector.py` (ROCm, MI355X) | 139 passed | 143 passed |
| DSv4-Pro FP4 1P1D MoRIIO READ\*, 2x MI350X (P TP8, D TP8): key-value lookup at 102 prompt lengths, PD vs direct-to-prefill | fails at 251, 377, 384, 440, 447, 636, 832, 895, ... (~14%) | 102/102 |

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_moriio_hma_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_moriio_routing.py
```

- The unit tests ran on macOS arm64 with CPU torch. They need no GPU and no mori runtime.
- On ROCm (MI355X, mori installed), `test_moriio_connector.py` + `test_moriio_hma_scheduler.py` + `test_moriio_routing.py`: main 139 passed; this PR 143 passed (the 4 new cases). 0 failed, 0 skipped on both.
- \*The E2E row was measured on an internal build that carried this trim (as a separate helper with the same logic) together with other MoRIIO READ fixes. It was not re-run on this exact branch.

## Details

**Flow.** Example: DSv4-Pro SWA cache, `block_size=64`, `sliding_window=128`, so `blocks_per_sw = cdiv(128, 64) + 1 = 3`. Prompt `N = 440` tokens fills 7 blocks. The decoder reserves `k` lookahead slots and the prefiller none; the observed failure range `(N - 1) % 64 ∈ [55, 63]` implies `k = 9`.

1. P (`request_finished`): 440 slots, 7 blocks `P0..P6`. Clip keeps `[P4, P5, P6]` and sends them as `remote_block_ids`.
2. D admission: `load_kv_async=False`, so the scheduler allocates `440 + 9` slots, 8 blocks `D0..D7`. The async-load path sets lookahead to 0 to keep block counts equal, but synchronous READ does not take it.
3. D (`update_state_after_alloc`): clip keeps `[D5, D6, D7]`. `_align_read_blocks` sees equal lengths and pairs `P4→D5, P5→D6, P6→D7`.
4. The window of the last prompt token needs `D4..D6`. It gets wrong or missing KV, so the model answers as if the end of the prompt were missing.

The failure condition with no prefill-side lookahead is `(N - 1) % block_size >= block_size - k`. `_align_read_blocks` cannot detect the shift because it runs after the clip.

**Fix.** `get_exchange_clipped_blocks` takes an optional `num_prompt_tokens`. When it is set, every transfer group is first trimmed to `cdiv(num_prompt_tokens, block_size)` blocks, using the existing `_group_block_sizes`. Both exchange points pass it: `request_finished` on the producer and `update_state_after_alloc` on the consumer, both on the non-mamba path. The list lengths then depend only on the prompt, not on either leg's lookahead.

**Safety.**
- `update_state_after_alloc` receives `kv_cache_manager.get_blocks(request_id)`. That is the full position-indexed list, including prefix-hit blocks, so the trim never drops a prompt block.
- The hybrid mamba path is unchanged. It does not clip sliding-window groups, and its prefiller drops the last prompt token.
- `_clamp_to_prompt_blocks` (WRITE save path) is not reused. Its non-mamba branch skips sliding-window groups, which are the groups this fix needs.

**Limitation.** `_group_block_sizes` and `blocks_per_sw` use the spec block size without the DCP factor. Under DCP > 1 the trim keeps too many blocks and does not fix the shift. It does not regress either.

**Duplicate check.** I searched `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "moriio"`, `"moriio sliding window"` and `"moriio hybrid READ"`. No open PR trims before the SWA clip. Two PRs are related:
- #54301 (async READ lifecycle) would remove the decoder-side admission tail, but not a prefill-side tail.
- #60867 (multi-group hybrid READ) adds another `get_exchange_clipped_blocks` caller in `split_block_groups`. That caller can pass `num_prompt_tokens` the same way.

title: [Bug][HiSparse] Scale shutdown grace period and bound worker joins to prevent ~90s stalls (#61859)
body:
## Description

This PR addresses **Issue #61859**, resolving the ~90-second shutdown stall encountered when tearing down HiSparse servers with large pinned host pools (e.g., TP8). 

### Root Cause
1. **Unpin Contention**: Every TP rank calls `cudaHostRegister` on the entire shared `/dev/shm` mmap (`allocate_hisparse_host_pools`). During teardown, graceful unpinning takes considerable time (scaling at roughly `0.15s` per GiB, e.g., ~13.5s for 128 GiB).
2. **Expired Grace Period**: The default worker grace period (`VLLM_WORKER_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5`) expired prematurely, forcing premature SIGTERM and SIGKILL fallbacks.
3. **EngineCore Deadlock**: EngineCore blocked indefinitely during multiprocessing atexit process joins on daemon workers without a bounded timeout, leading to silent hangs that required API server force-kills.

### Key Changes Made
1. **Dynamic Shutdown Timeout Scaling (`multiproc_executor.py`)**:
   - Updated `_ensure_worker_termination()` to accept `vllm_config`.
   - Dynamically scales the worker shutdown grace period based on the HiSparse host pool size:
     $$\text{timeout} = \max(\text{VLLM\_WORKER\_SHUTDOWN\_TIMEOUT\_SECONDS}, \lceil \text{pool\_gib} \times 0.15 \rceil)$$
   - Logs the calculated grace period clearly during teardown.
2. **Bounded Worker Process Joins**:
   - Introduced bounded joins (`p.join(timeout=1.0)`) in worker termination loops (for both graceful exits and post-SIGTERM/SIGKILL paths) to reap child processes and prevent Python's multiprocessing atexit hook from blocking indefinitely.
3. **Accurate HiSparse Unpin Logging (`runtime.py`)**:
   - Updated `release_pinned_state()` to include shared host region cleanup within the measured timing block and account for its capacity in freed bytes, logging accurate unpin metrics (`HiSparse: unpinned X GiB of host pool in Y.Ys`).
4. **Unit Tests & Regression Coverage**:
